rationale: Work control often depends on organizational roles (contractors, subcontractors) for execution.
conditions: when assigning responsible parties or contractors

subject: IfcWorkControl
rationale: Work control may depend on cost schedules to track budget against work performed.
conditions: when work control is linked to cost tracking and budgeting

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: IfcWorkPlan typically references an IfcWorkCalendar to define working days, holidays, and shifts for scheduling construction tasks.
conditions: When scheduling tasks and resources

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: An IfcWorkPlan is always assigned to an IfcProject which defines the overall project context and units.
conditions: As the root context for the work plan

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: IfcWorkPlan can contain one or more IfcWorkSchedule entities that define the detailed scheduling of tasks.
conditions: When work breakdown structure is defined

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: IfcWorkPlan aggregates tasks (IfcTask) that represent construction or project activities to be performed.
conditions: When tasks are defined within the work plan
exceptions: IfcWorkPlan does not directly contain IfcTask. In the IFC schema, IfcWorkPlan contains IfcWorkSchedule entities, and IfcWorkSchedule contains IfcTask entities. IfcTask is not directly contained within IfcWorkPlan; the containment is indirect via IfcWorkSchedule. For IFC2x3 and IFC4, IfcWorkPlan has an inverse relationship to IfcWorkSchedule through IsDecomposedBy, while IfcWorkSchedule decomposes into IfcTask.

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: Tasks within an IfcWorkPlan require resources (labor, material, equipment) defined via IfcConstructionResource or its subtypes.
conditions: For resource allocation to tasks

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: IfcWorkPlan is a subtype of IfcProcess and thus supports the overall process modeling by grouping work schedules and tasks.
conditions: When modeling construction or project processes

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: IfcWorkPlan inherits from IfcWorkControl, which provides attributes for identification, creation date, start/finish times, and total float.
conditions: When formal work control is needed

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: By linking tasks to IfcConstructionProductResource (materials), the work plan improves material logistics and reduces waste.
conditions: When planning material procurement and usage
exceptions: If material resources are not tracked in the BIM model

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: The work plan can reference equipment resources, improving equipment utilization and avoiding conflicts.
conditions: When planning equipment usage and scheduling

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: IfcWorkPlan uses IfcRelAssignsToProcess relationships to associate tasks, resources, products, and controls.
conditions: For relating products, resources, or controls to the work plan

subject: IfcWorkPlan
rationale: Tasks within a work plan can have predecessor/successor relationships defined via IfcRelSequence.
conditions: When task sequencing and dependencies are modeled

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: A work schedule depends on a work calendar to define working days, holidays, and shifts for scheduling tasks.
conditions: when scheduling work tasks

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: IfcWorkSchedule contains and organizes IfcTask entities; it depends on tasks to define the actual work items to be scheduled.
conditions: for defining scheduled work items

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: An IfcWorkSchedule is a container that groups IfcTask entities into a logical schedule.

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: Work schedules rely on work time definitions (e.g., weekly working hours) to properly allocate tasks.
conditions: when defining recurring time periods

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: The schedule supports resource management by providing a timeline for when construction products are needed.
conditions: when resources are assigned to scheduled tasks

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: Equipment resource planning depends on the schedule to know when equipment is required on site.
conditions: when equipment allocation is time-dependent

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: Work schedules depend on predecessor/successor relationships between tasks to define the correct sequence of work.
conditions: when tasks have precedence relationships
exceptions: for simple schedules without task dependencies

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: The work schedule is part of a project context and depends on the IfcProject for units, time settings, and overall context.
applicability: IfcWorkSchedule is related to IfcProject via IfcRelDeclares or IfcRelAggregates depending on IFC schema version, not a direct 'depends_on' relationship. The relationship exists but the nature is contextual.
conditions: for context and unit settings

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: An IfcWorkSchedule can be nested within an IfcWorkPlan and depends on it for higher-level planning context.
conditions: when the schedule is part of a larger work plan
exceptions: standalone schedules without a parent work plan

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: Work schedules often connect to cost schedules for earned value management and budget tracking.
conditions: when cost and schedule are integrated

subject: IfcWorkSchedule
rationale: Key dates and milestones (IfcEvent) are essential reference points for work schedule progress.
conditions: when milestones or time events are defined

subject: IfcWorkTime
rationale: IfcWorkTime defines time-related work patterns and is typically associated with an IfcWorkCalendar that organizes working and non-working days and shifts.
applicability: All project types using IFC scheduling

IfcWorkTime requires IfcWorkCalendar only holds in the context of actively using the work time within a calendar assignment. IfcWorkTime can be instantiated standalone without being linked to any calendar.
conditions: When work times need to be scheduled and managed within a project calendar

subject: IfcWorkTime
rationale: IfcWorkTime can reference an IfcRecurrencePattern to define regular repeating work times (e.g., every Monday to Friday).
conditions: When work times are recurring on a regular schedule (daily, weekly, monthly, etc.)
exceptions: IfcWorkTime may exist without recurrence if it defines an exception date

subject: IfcWorkTime
rationale: IfcWorkTime defines when work can be performed, directly supporting the scheduling of IfcTask entities in a work plan.
conditions: When tasks are scheduled in a construction or facility management context

subject: IfcWorkTime
rationale: IfcWorkTime entries (regular working times, exceptions, holidays) are aggregated within IfcWorkSchedule via IfcWorkCalendar to define overall project timelines.
conditions: When creating a complete work schedule for a project

subject: IfcWorkTime
rationale: IfcWorkTime can contain an IfcTimePeriod to specify the start and end time of a work interval within a day.
conditions: When a specific time range is defined (start time and end time within a day)

subject: IfcWorkTime
rationale: IfcWorkTime defines structured recurring or exceptional work periods, while IfcTimeSeries may define arbitrary time-dependent data; overlapping use could create inconsistencies.
applicability: Scheduling where both regular patterns and irregular time series coexist
conditions: When time series data attempts to define irregular schedules that conflict with recurring work patterns
exceptions: They can complement each other if used for different scheduling aspects

subject: IfcZone
rationale: An IfcZone is a grouping of IfcSpaces (rooms or areas) for analysis or organizational purposes, so it logically contains IfcSpaces.
applicability: IfcZone does not directly 'contain' IfcSpace in the IFC schema sense of containment (IfcRelContainedInSpatialStructure). IfcZone groups spaces via IfcRelAssignsToGroup, not via spatial containment. This assertion is at best a loose semantic statement and could mislead users about the IFC relationship type.

subject: IfcZone
rationale: IfcZone can also group IfcSystems (like HVAC zones or electrical zones) in addition to spaces.

subject: IfcZone
rationale: A Zone typically requires IfcSpaces to define its spatial extent and membership for analysis purposes.
conditions: IfcZone is defined as a collection of spaces
exceptions: IfcZone can also be defined solely by systems without spaces

The assertion 'IfcZone depends_on IfcSpace' already has an existing exception stating 'IfcZone can also be defined solely by systems without spaces', which contradicts the depends_on claim. A zone can exist without spaces if defined by systems, so the dependency is not strict.

subject: IfcZone
rationale: IfcZone is assigned to groups via IfcRelAssignsToGroup relationship, enabling zone-based analysis.

subject: IfcZone
rationale: Zones used for MEP analysis connect to service distribution relationships.
conditions: when zone represents a service-distribution area

subject: IfcZone
rationale: IfcZone requires the IfcRelAssignsToGroup relationship object to link zone to its members (spaces/systems).
conditions: to formally define zone membership
exceptions: zone can exist as an empty container

subject: Roof
rationale: A roof depends on the structural frame (beams, columns, trusses) to support its dead load and live loads like snow, rain, or maintenance access.
applicability: The assertion 'Roof depends_on Structural Frame for load transfer' with applicability 'all building types' is too broad. Some building types (e.g., tensile membrane structures, air-supported structures, some geodesic domes) have roofs that are self-supporting or rely on non-frame structural systems (e.g., shell structures, cable nets) rather than a distinct structural frame. In these cases, the roof itself acts as the structural system or depends on a different structural concept.
conditions: for load transfer

subject: Roof
rationale: A roof requires a deck / sheathing (e.g., plywood, metal decking, concrete) to span between supports and provide a substrate for roofing materials.
conditions: as base layer
exceptions: The assertion 'Roof requires Roof Deck' with applicability 'all building types' has exceptions. Some roofing systems, such as standing seam metal roofs on purlins (with no continuous deck), some thatch roofs, or tile roofs on battens without a full deck, do not require a roof deck as a base layer. The deck is not universally required across all building types.

subject: Roof
rationale: A roof requires a waterproof or water-resistant membrane (e.g., built-up roofing, single-ply membrane, metal roofing) to shed water and protect the building interior.
applicability: The assertion 'Roof requires Waterproof Membrane' with applicability 'all building types' is overly broad. Some buildings use self-waterproofing roofing systems (e.g., standing seam metal roofs with continuous seam integrity, some slate or tile systems on appropriate underlayment) where the primary roofing material itself provides waterproofing without a separate membrane layer. Additionally, some vernacular or temporary buildings may not incorporate a distinct waterproof membrane.
conditions: to prevent water ingress

subject: Roof
rationale: Roofs typically require thermal insulation to meet energy codes and prevent heat loss/gain between interior and exterior.
conditions: for thermal performance
exceptions: unconditioned buildings

subject: Roof
rationale: Flashing is required at roof edges, valleys, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations to direct water away and prevent leaks.
conditions: at penetrations and edges

subject: Roof
rationale: Underlayment (e.g., felt paper, synthetic underlayment) provides a secondary water barrier beneath shingles or tiles.
conditions: between deck and roofing material
exceptions: some metal roof systems

subject: Roof
rationale: By shedding water, the roof protects the underlying structural frame from moisture-induced deterioration (rot, corrosion).
conditions: from water damage

subject: Roof
rationale: The roof connects to exterior walls at the top plate or parapet, where load transfer and weather sealing occur.
applicability: The assertion 'Roof connects_to Exterior Walls at roof-to-wall intersections' with applicability 'all building types' has limitations. In buildings without exterior walls (e.g., some canopy structures, pavilions, roofs supported directly on columns without enclosing walls, some stadium roofs, or air-supported structures), there are no exterior walls to connect to at roof-to-wall intersections. The roof terminates at columns or other supports instead.
conditions: at roof-to-wall intersections

subject: Roof
rationale: In many buildings, the roof assembly connects to or is finished on the underside by a ceiling system.
conditions: in finished buildings
exceptions: open-structure buildings

subject: Wall
rationale: Load-bearing walls require a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: wall must be load-bearing
exceptions: non-load-bearing partition walls

subject: Wall
rationale: Studs, plates, and headers form the structural skeleton of framed walls.
conditions: for framed construction
exceptions: masonry or concrete walls

subject: Wall
rationale: Exterior walls require cladding (e.g., siding, brick veneer, stucco) for weather protection.
conditions: exterior walls
exceptions: interior walls

The assertion 'Wall requires Wall Cladding' for exterior walls has an unlisted exception: structural walls that are part of a rainscreen system or back-ventilated facade may have an air gap and secondary drainage plane that is not 'cladding' in the conventional sense, but rather a curtain wall or panel system that may not be classified as typical wall cladding. Also, exposed cast-in-place concrete tilt-up walls or log walls may serve as both structure and finish without separate cladding.

subject: Wall
rationale: Walls forming the thermal envelope require insulation for energy efficiency and code compliance.
applicability: all building types with thermal envelope requirements
conditions: exterior walls
conditioned spaces
exceptions: unconditioned spaces
some interior partition walls

subject: Wall
rationale: Vapor retarders prevent moisture migration into wall cavities, reducing mold risk.
applicability: The assertion 'Wall requires Vapor barrier' with condition 'exterior walls in cold or mixed climates' does not account for varying building code editions. Modern IRC/NBC requirements have shifted Class I/II vapor retarder placement and requirements depending on the climate zone, wall assembly moisture profile, and whether the assembly is vented. A blanket 'requires Vapor barrier' may conflict with contemporary code provisions that restrict vapor barriers in certain assemblies (e.g., Class III allowed in zone 4 marine with insulated sheathing).
conditions: exterior walls in cold or mixed climates
exceptions: hot-humid climates
some interior walls

subject: Wall
rationale: Interior walls require finish materials such as drywall, plaster, or paneling.
conditions: interior walls
exceptions: exposed structural or utility walls

subject: Wall
rationale: Load-bearing walls support roof trusses, rafters, or roof deck above.
conditions: wall is load-bearing
perimeter or shear wall
exceptions: non-load-bearing interior partitions

subject: Wall
rationale: Walls enclose insulation material within their cavities or as continuous layers.
applicability: all building types with thermal envelope
conditions: insulated walls
exceptions: uninsulated walls

subject: Foundation
rationale: Concrete is the primary material used to form foundation footings and slabs.
conditions: For shallow foundations
exceptions: Some shallow foundations (e.g., light-weight structures like patios, sheds, or temporary structures) may use crushed stone, gravel, or compacted earth pads instead of concrete. Additionally,在某些 jurisdictions, masonry (brick/stone) foundations were historically used without concrete.

subject: Foundation
rationale: Foundation walls and footings support the edges and interior of floor slabs.
conditions: All building types
exceptions: Foundation does NOT directly support floor slab in buildings with crawlspaces or basements where the floor slab is supported by independent footings, compacted ground, or a separate slab-on-grade within the foundation perimeter. In such cases, the foundation wall supports the structure above, but the slab is independently supported.

subject: Foundation
rationale: Footings support foundation walls, which in turn support the structure above.
conditions: For buildings with basements or crawlspaces

subject: Foundation
rationale: Foundation walls are vertical structural elements that form part of the foundation system.
conditions: For basement and crawlspace foundations

subject: Foundation
rationale: Grade beams connect pile caps or piers and distribute loads between deep foundation elements.
conditions: For deep or pile foundations

subject: Beam
rationale: A beam requires a foundation or supporting structure to transfer its loads safely to the ground.
applicability: The assertion 'Beam requires Foundation' with condition 'beam must transfer loads to ground' is too broad. Beams in upper stories of multi-story buildings transfer loads through columns or walls to lower floors, not directly to the foundation. The condition conflates 'ultimate load path to ground' with 'direct physical connection to foundation'.
conditions: beam must transfer loads to ground
exceptions: continuous foundation systems may integrate beams differently

subject: Beam
rationale: Beams typically depend on columns or walls as vertical supports to carry loads.
applicability: The assertion 'Beam depends_on Column' with condition 'beam spans between vertical supports' contradicts the existing exception which acknowledges cantilevered beams. But further, beams can also span between walls (two walls), between a wall and a column, or be supported by other beams (transfer beams). The 'depends_on Column' relationship is too restrictive.
conditions: beam spans between vertical supports
exceptions: cantilevered beams do not always require columns at both ends

subject: Beam
rationale: A beam may require a load-bearing wall as a support element.
conditions: beam transfers loads to a wall below
exceptions: beams in moment frames do not require load-bearing walls

subject: Beam
rationale: Beams support floor and roof slabs by carrying their dead and live loads.
conditions: beam is placed under a floor or roof slab to carry its weight
exceptions: flat slabs may not require beams

The assertion 'Beam supports Slab' has an exception for flat slabs, but also fails to account for one-way slabs spanning between beams vs. two-way flat plates, waffle slabs, or ribbed slabs where beams may be implicitly integrated as joists or ribs. Additionally, precast hollow-core slabs spanning between walls may not require beams.

subject: Beam
rationale: Beams can support walls above openings (lintels) or at intermediate floors.
applicability: buildings with masonry or partition walls
conditions: beam acts as a lintel or spandrel above openings or at floor levels
exceptions: non-load-bearing walls do not require beam support

subject: Beam
rationale: Roof beams support the roof covering and any imposed loads such as snow.
conditions: beam is part of roof framing to carry roof loads
exceptions: roofs with trusses or rigid frames may not use simple beams

The assertion 'Beam supports Roof' with exception for trusses or rigid frames is generally sound, but it omits important exceptions: stressed skin panels, space frames, shell structures, tensile membrane roofs, and folded plate roofs are all roof systems that do not employ beams for support.

subject: Beam
rationale: The beam itself is made of concrete as the base material.
conditions: beam is a reinforced concrete element
exceptions: steel or timber beams do not contain concrete

subject: Beam
rationale: Beams are typically connected to columns at their ends to form a frame.
conditions: beam end connects to a column via a joint or connection
exceptions: beams may also connect to walls or other beams

subject: Slab
rationale: Concrete slabs require concrete as the primary material.
conditions: When slab is concrete slab

subject: Slab
rationale: One-way and two-way slabs often depend on beams to transfer loads to columns.
conditions: When slab is supported by beams
exceptions: Flat slab systems
Waffle slabs

subject: Slab
rationale: Slabs transfer their loads to columns (directly or through beams) which carry the load to the foundation.
exceptions: The assertion 'Slab depends_on Column' with applicability 'all buildings' does not hold for flat slab systems where slabs transfer loads directly to columns without beams but can also be false for ground-floor slabs on grade (slab-on-grade) which bear directly on soil and do not depend on columns.

subject: Slab
rationale: The slab's load path ultimately depends on the foundation system for soil support.
exceptions: The assertion 'Slab depends_on Foundation' with applicability 'all buildings' does not hold for slabs-on-grade where the slab IS the foundation (monolithic slab foundations). Also, in some structural systems, intermediate suspended slabs depend on beams and columns rather than directly on the foundation.

subject: Slab
rationale: In load-bearing wall construction, slabs depend on masonry or concrete walls for support.
conditions: When slab bears on walls

subject: Slab
rationale: Slabs provide the structural substrate for floor finishes such as tiles, wood, carpet, or toppings.
exceptions: The assertion 'Slab supports Floor Finish' with applicability 'all buildings' does not hold for exposed architectural concrete slabs where the slab surface itself serves as the finished floor (e.g., polished concrete floors, exposed aggregate finishes). Also not applicable for unfinished slabs in utility spaces, parking garages, or industrial/warehouse areas where no floor finish is applied.

subject: Slab
rationale: The underside of a slab serves as the ceiling for the floor below, or supports a suspended ceiling.
conditions: When slab is an upper floor or roof

subject: Slab
rationale: Slabs provide support for interior partition walls that do not bear directly on beams.
conditions: When non-load-bearing partitions sit on the slab
exceptions: The assertion 'Slab supports Partition Wall' with condition 'When non-load-bearing partitions sit on the slab' does not hold for curtain wall systems or demountable partition systems that are supported from overhead tracks (suspended from the ceiling/upper slab) rather than bearing on the slab below. Also not applicable for partitions that bear on a screed/underlayment that is not structurally part of the slab.

subject: Slab
rationale: Concrete slabs contain concrete as the bulk material.
exceptions: Steel deck slabs
Timber slabs
Hollow core slabs

subject: Slab
rationale: Slabs connect to stairs, which provide vertical circulation between slab levels.
exceptions: The assertion 'Slab connects_to Stair' with applicability 'multi-story buildings' does not always hold. In buildings where stairs are isolated from floor slabs via expansion joints or seismic joints, the stair structure may be independently supported by its own foundation or walls without connecting to intermediate slabs. Also, in some designs, stairs land on beams rather than directly on slabs.

subject: Slab
rationale: Slabs connect to shear walls to transfer diaphragm forces and provide lateral stability.
conditions: When lateral load resistance is required
exceptions: The assertion 'Slab connects_to Shear Wall' with condition 'When lateral load resistance is required' is not universally true. In dual structural systems, slabs may connect to moment-resisting frames for lateral resistance while shear walls are present but not connected to every slab. Also, in buildings where shear walls are isolated (e.g., elevator/stair cores with slip joints), the slab may not connect structurally to the shear wall.

subject: Column
rationale: A column requires a foundation to transfer its loads safely into the ground.
conditions: must transfer vertical loads to ground

subject: Column
rationale: Columns often depend on beams to collect and transfer floor/roof loads to them.
conditions: when column supports beam ends or transfers loads from beams
exceptions: columns in flat slab systems where slabs bear directly on columns

The assertion 'Column depends_on Beam' does not account for columns in moment-resisting frames where beams are rigidly connected and the dependency is mutual or reversed; also, columns in load-bearing wall construction may not depend on beams at all. The existing exception covers flat slabs but not other systems like two-way slabs with drop panels where columns directly support slabs.

subject: Column
rationale: Column capitals increase the bearing area and reduce punching shear stress.
conditions: in flat slab or flat plate concrete systems to resist punching shear
exceptions: columns without capitals in conventional beam-column frames

Column depends on Column Capital does not hold for flat plate systems (as opposed to flat slabs) where no column capitals exist and the slab bears directly on the column. The existing exception mentions 'columns without capitals in conventional beam-column frames' but does not cover flat plate (no capitals) systems within the stated applicability of 'concrete flat slab structures'.

subject: Column
rationale: Columns support floor and roof slabs by transferring their loads downward.
conditions: when columns are positioned below slabs to carry floor loads

subject: Column
rationale: Columns provide vertical support to beams at intermediate and end points.
conditions: when beam ends rest on column tops or corbels
exceptions: continuous beams that span past columns

The assertion 'Column supports Beam' does not account for columns in moment-resisting frames where beams frame into column sides (not resting on top) and the connection is moment-resisting rather than simple support. Also, columns supporting steel beams via shear tabs or fin plates where the beam is attached to the column web or flange, not resting on top or corbels.

subject: Column
rationale: Columns carry roof dead and live loads down to the foundation.
conditions: columns are part of the gravity load path for roofing

subject: Column
rationale: A concrete column contains concrete as its primary structural material.
applicability: The assertion 'Column contains Concrete' restricts applicability to 'concrete structures', but composite steel-concrete columns (e.g., concrete-filled steel tube, encased steel sections) also contain concrete yet may not be classified strictly as concrete structures. The existing exceptions list steel, timber, and masonry columns but does not mention composite columns that do contain concrete.
conditions: when column is cast-in-place or precast concrete
exceptions: steel columns
timber columns
masonry columns

subject: Column
rationale: The column base connects to the foundation through base plates or direct embedment.
conditions: at column base

subject: Column
rationale: Columns connect to beams at intersections forming moment or shear connections.
conditions: at beam-column joints
exceptions: The assertion 'Column connects_to Beam' applies to 'frame structures', but in precast concrete construction, columns may have corbels with beams sitting on top (bearing connection) which is more of a support relationship than a moment-resisting connection; also, in timber post-and-beam, connections are often via brackets or joinery, and the nature of the connection differs from a rigid beam-column joint.

subject: Column
rationale: The column top connects to the underside of slabs.
conditions: at slab-column interface

subject: Door
rationale: A door requires a frame to be mounted and to function as a proper barrier.
conditions: for structural support and alignment
exceptions: Pocket doors, sliding barn doors, and some automatic doors do not use a traditional door frame. They use a pocket frame, track system, or minimal jamb instead.

subject: Door
rationale: Standard hinged doors require hinges to attach to the frame and allow opening/closing.
conditions: for swinging doors
exceptions: sliding doors or pivot doors use different hardware

subject: Door
rationale: Exterior doors depend on a threshold to seal the bottom gap and prevent water ingress.
conditions: at exterior doors or doors between different floor levels
exceptions: interior doors on same level flooring

subject: Door
rationale: Doors with integrated access control support the overall building security system.
conditions: when equipped with electronic locks or sensors
exceptions: non-secured interior doors

subject: Door
rationale: Many commercial and fire-rated doors contain a door closer mechanism for automatic closure.
conditions: for self-closing doors, typically commercial or fire-rated
exceptions: residential doors without automatic closing requirement

Some fire-rated doors in stairwells of residential buildings use electromagnetic hold-open devices linked to fire alarms rather than traditional door closers, or use concealed closers that are not 'Door Closer' as commonly understood (surface-mounted).

subject: Door
rationale: The door panel connects to the door frame through hinges or pivots.
conditions: via hinges or pivot hardware

subject: Door
rationale: The door frame connects to the surrounding wall structure for support.
conditions: through the door frame assembly
exceptions: Sliding patio doors, pocket doors, and some specialized glass doors connect to wall through a track or header system, not necessarily 'through the door frame assembly' — the door frame itself may be minimal or integrated differently.

subject: Window
rationale: A window requires a frame to hold the glass in place and provide structural integrity
conditions: for structural support and mounting
exceptions: Structural windows (e.g., curtain wall systems, storefront framing) may not require a separate 'window frame' as the frame is integrated into the wall assembly or the glass is structurally glazed directly into the framing system.

subject: Window
rationale: Sealants are needed to weatherproof the window assembly
conditions: to prevent air and water infiltration around the glass

subject: Window
rationale: Weatherstripping seals gaps between operable sashes and the frame
conditions: for energy efficiency and preventing drafts

subject: Window
rationale: Operable windows need a sash to hold the glass and allow opening/closing
conditions: for operable windows with moving parts
exceptions: fixed windows do not require a sash

subject: Window
rationale: Handles, hinges, locks, and cranks are needed for window operation
conditions: for operation of operable windows
exceptions: fixed windows do not require hardware

subject: Window
rationale: Window flashing systems are critical for directing water away from the window opening to prevent leaks
conditions: for water management and drainage

subject: Window
rationale: The window assembly includes a frame that surrounds and supports the glazing

subject: Window
rationale: Modern windows often contain sealed insulated glass units with multiple panes and gas fills
conditions: for multi-pane windows
exceptions: single-pane windows do not contain IGU

subject: Window
rationale: The bottom of the window connects to a sill that helps shed water away from the wall
exceptions: Some window installations, especially in certain commercial curtain wall systems or flush-glazed assemblies, may not have a traditional window sill; the window connects directly to the framing mullion or a condensation gutter instead.

subject: Window
rationale: Even the best windows have lower R-values than insulated wall assemblies, creating thermal weak points
applicability: The assertion frames the relationship as a conflict, but in passive house and net-zero energy design, triple-glazed or high-performance windows are intentionally used as part of the thermal envelope strategy, not as a conflict with thermal insulation. The description acknowledges triple glazing as an exception, which suggests the base assertion may be too broad.
conditions: windows are generally weaker thermal barriers than insulated walls
exceptions: high-performance windows with triple glazing minimize this conflict

subject: Stair
rationale: Stairs require treads as the horizontal walking surface.
conditions: for safe foot placement
exceptions: Stair Tread is not always a separate required element; monolithic concrete stairs, prefabricated metal stairs, or stairs with integral treads (e.g., cast-in-place concrete with no separate tread piece) do not have a distinct Stair Tread component.

subject: Stair
rationale: Risers define the vertical height between treads, though open-riser stairs are an exception.
applicability: The existing exception correctly notes open-riser stairs may omit risers but does not note that building codes typically limit open-riser stair usage based on riser opening dimensions (e.g., IBC 1011.7.2 allows open risers but restricts opening to 4-3/8 inches) and may restrict their use in certain occupancy types or egress paths.
conditions: for vertical step separation
exceptions: open-riser stairs may omit risers

subject: Stair
rationale: Handrails provide essential support and are required by most building codes (e.g., IBC, ADA).
applicability: all stair types subject to building codes
conditions: for user safety and fall prevention
building codes typically require handrails on at least one side
exceptions: very short stairs with few steps may be exempt per code

subject: Stair
rationale: Guardrails prevent falls at open sides of stair runs and landings.
conditions: where stairs are open on one or both sides
exceptions: stairs enclosed by walls on both sides
Guardrails may not be required on stair sides if the drop height is below a certain threshold (e.g., less than 30 inches per IBC/IRC), even if the stairs are open on one side.

subject: Stair
rationale: Stringers are the inclined structural members that support stair steps, common in framed construction.
conditions: as primary structural element supporting treads and risers
exceptions: monolithic concrete or prefabricated stairs may not use separate stringers

subject: Stair
rationale: Landings provide resting points and safe transition areas required by code.
conditions: at top and bottom of stairs
every 12 feet of vertical rise maximum
exceptions: some private stairs may have different requirements

subject: Stair
rationale: The fundamental purpose of stairs is to enable vertical movement between building levels.
conditions: as primary means of moving between floor levels
exceptions: elevators, ramps, or escalators may supplement or replace stairs

subject: Stair
rationale: Nosings provide visual contrast and extra slip resistance at tread edges.
conditions: at the leading edge of each tread
exceptions: some modern designs may omit nosings for flush appearance

Stair nosing may be omitted not only in modern flush designs but also in code-compliant scenarios where treads are designed with a sloped or rounded front edge that is not a distinct 'nosing,' or where nosing is integral to the tread material (e.g., certain prefabricated metal stairs).

subject: Stair
rationale: Stairs connect structurally to floor slabs at each level for load transfer and continuity.
conditions: at top and bottom landings
exceptions: Stairs do not always connect to a Floor Slab at top and bottom landings. Examples include stairs that terminate at a wood-framed floor deck (not a slab), outdoor stairs terminating at grade, or stairs connecting to a metal grate platform.

subject: Stair
rationale: Stairs typically connect to corridors or hallways to provide building-wide circulation.
conditions: as access path to and from stairs

subject: Curtain Wall
rationale: Glass or other infill panels form the visible skin of the curtain wall and provide daylight, views, and enclosure.
applicability: All building types with curtain walls
conditions: Must comply with thermal and safety glazing codes
exceptions: Curtain walls in structural glass systems (e.g., glass fins, point-supported glass) may use glass panels that function as both structure and infill, but formally they do not always require a separate 'glazing panel' as the glass itself may be the structural member. Additionally, spandrel areas may use metal panel infill or opaque insulated panels rather than glazing panels.

subject: Curtain Wall
rationale: Thermal breaks (typically polyamide or PVC strips) in aluminum frames reduce thermal bridging and condensation risk.
applicability: The assertion states 'Required in cold climates or energy-code compliant buildings' but the existing exception already covers interior-conditioned mullion systems. However, there are additional exceptions such as curtain walls with thermally broken frames that integrate the thermal break directly into the frame extrusion, meaning a separate 'thermal break' component (e.g., polyamide strip) may not be required as an additional element.
conditions: Required in cold climates or energy-code compliant buildings
exceptions: May not be required in fully interior-conditioned mullion systems

subject: Curtain Wall
rationale: Thermal expansion joints are needed within the curtain wall system to accommodate differential movement between the wall and the building structure due to temperature changes.
applicability: Large buildings, long runs of curtain wall
conditions: Required at regular intervals and at building expansion joints
exceptions: Some curtain wall systems, particularly unitized systems with built-in stack joints and interlocking gaskets, may incorporate thermal movement accommodation through the joint design itself rather than requiring a separate expansion joint component. Small or single-bay curtain wall installations may also not require expansion joints if thermal movement is negligible.

subject: Ceiling
rationale: Ceilings depend on the structural floor or roof slab above them for attachment and load transfer.
conditions: For load-bearing support above

subject: Ceiling
rationale: Ceilings support lighting fixtures such as recessed lights, surface-mounted lights, or chandeliers.
applicability: Ceilings support lighting fixtures only in the context of surface-mounted or suspended ceiling systems. In exposed structure designs (e.g., open ceilings, industrial ceilings with exposed deck), lighting fixtures may be supported directly by the structural slab or by hanging rods from the structure, not by the ceiling itself. The assertion lacks this contextual limitation.

subject: Ceiling
rationale: A suspended ceiling grid supports acoustic ceiling tiles or panels for sound absorption.
conditions: If suspended ceiling system is used

subject: Ceiling
rationale: Ceilings often contain insulation materials for thermal regulation and sound attenuation between floors.
conditions: For thermal or acoustic purposes

subject: Ceiling
rationale: Ceilings connect to walls at their perimeter, forming the boundary of interior spaces.

subject: Ceiling
rationale: Ceilings typically connect around structural columns that penetrate through the floor/ceiling assembly.

subject: Ceiling
rationale: Ceilings with insulation improve the thermal performance of a building by reducing heat transfer.

subject: Ramp
rationale: Building codes universally require handrails on ramps exceeding a 1:20 slope for safety and accessibility.
conditions: when slope exceeds 1:20 (5%)
exceptions: private residential ramps with very low usage

The assertion requires handrails when slope exceeds 1:20 (5%), but many accessibility codes (e.g., ADA, ICC A117.1) actually require handrails when the slope exceeds 1:12 (8.33%) for non-residential ramps, and the 1:20 threshold is the point at which a walkway becomes a ramp (i.e., requires handrails at 1:20 is actually correct for commercial/public buildings — however, the stated exception for 'private residential ramps with very low usage' is underspecified: what constitutes 'very low usage'? No threshold is provided, making the exception ambiguous and unenforceable.

subject: Ramp
rationale: Landings are required by accessibility standards (ADA, IBC) for safe stopping, turning, and resting.
conditions: at top and bottom of ramp
at changes in direction
every 30 feet (9m) of continuous run
exceptions: The assertion requires landings at top and bottom, at changes in direction, and every 30 feet. However, in certain code jurisdictions (e.g., some Canadian building codes), the maximum distance between landings is 9m (30 ft) only for ramps with slope up to 1:10; steeper ramps may require more frequent landings (e.g., every 6m for slopes between 1:10 and 1:8). The assertion does not account for slope-dependent landing spacing.

subject: Ramp
rationale: Elevated ramps require footings or foundation walls to transfer loads to the ground.
applicability: The existing exception says 'ground-level ramps on compacted fill' do not require a foundation, but this is incomplete. Many code-compliant ramp designs use frost-protected shallow foundations, helical piles, or precast concrete blocks — these are still foundation systems but different from traditional poured concrete footings. The distinction between 'foundation' and 'non-foundation' support is not well-handled by this simple dependency.
conditions: for exterior or elevated ramps
exceptions: ground-level ramps on compacted fill

subject: Ramp
rationale: Separate ramp and stair paths can create awkward circulation or redundant routes.
conditions: when both occupy the same circulation path without integration
exceptions: when ramp and stair are designed as an integrated assembly

subject: Partition
rationale: Gypsum board is the most common facing material applied to partition framing to create finished wall surfaces.
conditions: for interior finish applications
exceptions: alternate finishes like plaster, plywood, or glass may be used

subject: Partition
rationale: Partitions are anchored at their base to the floor slab or subfloor structure.
conditions: at the base of all partitions
exceptions: suspended or demountable partitions may not connect directly

Partitions may connect to a structural slab (floor structure) but with an intervening furring channel, sleepers, or raised access floor system, meaning the partition does not directly connect to the floor structure itself. This indirect connection is common in sound-rated assemblies and raised floor environments.

subject: HVAC System
rationale: HVAC systems require ductwork to distribute conditioned air throughout the building.
applicability: all buildings with forced air HVAC
conditions: for air distribution
exceptions: Ductless HVAC systems (e.g., mini-split heat pumps, VRF/VRV systems, through-wall units, PTACs) distribute conditioned air without ductwork, directly releasing air into zones. The assertion 'HVAC System requires Ductwork' does not hold for these widely used system types even in buildings with forced air HVAC.

subject: HVAC System
rationale: Condensers reject heat absorbed from the building interior to the outdoors.
conditions: for heat rejection in cooling mode
exceptions: air-source vs water-source configurations vary

subject: HVAC System
rationale: The thermal performance and airtightness of the building envelope directly affect HVAC sizing and efficiency.
conditions: for thermal insulation and airtightness to reduce load

subject: HVAC System
rationale: HVAC systems connect to plumbing for condensate removal and for hydronic heating/cooling loops.
applicability: buildings with hydronic HVAC or condensate management
conditions: for condensate drainage and hydronic heating/cooling
exceptions: air-cooled systems without hydronic loops

Even in buildings with condensate management, condensate from high-efficiency furnaces or air conditioners can be routed to a gravity drain, a condensate pump discharging to the exterior, or into a dry well — none of which require connection to the building's Plumbing System. Condensate drainage does not always imply a plumbing connection.

subject: HVAC System
rationale: HVAC systems are typically integrated with BMS for scheduling, monitoring, and optimization.
conditions: for centralized monitoring and control
exceptions: small buildings without BMS

Many small and medium commercial buildings (e.g., small retail, standalone restaurants, small offices) do have BMS/BAS systems, while some large residential buildings (e.g., apartment towers) may use simpler thermostatic controls without a centralized BMS. The current exception/scope boundary based on 'commercial and large residential' vs 'small buildings without BMS' is oversimplified and may misclassify actual installations.

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Plumbing systems require a water supply to deliver water to fixtures and appliances.
conditions: Must have adequate pressure and flow rate
exceptions: A Plumbing System does not require a Water Supply System for buildings that are unoccupied shells, storage-only structures, or temporary field outhouses where no water supply is needed or present.

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Plumbing systems require drainage to remove wastewater and maintain sanitation.
conditions: Gravity flow or pumped drainage
exceptions: A Plumbing System does not require a Drainage System if the building uses a composting toilet system or incinerating toilet system where no liquid drainage is produced, or in unoccupied structures with plumbing only for non-wastewater uses.

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Fixtures such as sinks, toilets, and faucets are endpoints where water is used or discharged.
conditions: Code-compliant installation
exceptions: A Plumbing System could exist with only distribution piping and no fixtures (e.g., stub-outs for future tenant fit-out in speculative commercial buildings). The assertion should clarify whether 'requires' means operational vs. installed.

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Water heaters provide hot water to plumbing fixtures and appliances.
applicability: The existing exception already addresses buildings where hot water is not required, but the assertion still asserts requirement for Residential, commercial, institutional. Some commercial buildings (e.g., cold storage warehouses) and certain industrial facilities may have plumbing but no hot water requirement, which the exception covers but the applicability list over-generalizes.
conditions: For hot water supply
exceptions: Buildings where hot water is not required

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Plumbing systems depend on electrical power for pumps, water heaters, and control systems.
conditions: For pumps, water heaters, and controls
exceptions: A simple gravity-fed cold water plumbing system with no pumps, no water heaters, and no electrically operated controls (e.g., a basic outdoor tap fed from a gravity tank) does not depend on an electrical system.

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Plumbing systems often supply water to standpipes and automatic sprinkler systems for fire protection.
conditions: Where combined or separate fire main is provided

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: The plumbing system contains a network of supply pipes that deliver potable water.

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Plumbing systems contain backflow preventers to protect potable water from contamination.
conditions: At cross-connection points
exceptions: Not all cross-connection points require backflow prevention devices in all jurisdictions if there is an air gap, or if the cross-connection is to a non-potable system of equal or higher quality. Some code exceptions exist for certain residential hose bibs or dedicated lawn irrigation systems under specific conditions.

subject: Plumbing System
rationale: Plumbing systems connect to septic tanks for onsite wastewater treatment.
applicability: The condition 'Where municipal sewer is unavailable' is already stated, and the exception covers municipal sewer connections. However, the applicability is 'Rural buildings' but rural buildings may also be on private sewers or shared septic systems. Also, some rural buildings may connect to a holding tank (not a septic tank) or an aerobic treatment unit. The assertion over-specifies septic tank as the only alternative.
conditions: Where municipal sewer is unavailable
exceptions: Buildings connected to municipal sewer

subject: Electrical System
rationale: The electrical system supplies power to all lighting fixtures and controls throughout the building.
applicability: The assertion states applicability is 'all building types', but in buildings with no electrical grid connection (e.g., off-grid cabins, tents, or structures relying solely on natural lighting), the Electrical System as a formal building subsystem may not exist, making the support relationship inapplicable.
conditions: By providing power and control

subject: Electrical System
rationale: HVAC equipment relies on electrical power for operation of compressors, fans, pumps, and control systems.
conditions: By supplying electrical power for motors, compressors, fans, and controls
exceptions: In buildings with fully passive HVAC (e.g., natural ventilation only, no mechanical systems), there is no HVAC System requiring electrical power, so the support relationship does not apply despite the presence of an Electrical System.

subject: Electrical System
rationale: Fire alarm systems require electrical power for detection, notification, and control equipment.
applicability: all building types with fire alarm requirements
conditions: By providing primary and standby power

subject: Electrical System
rationale: Electronic security systems depend on building electrical power for operation.
conditions: By providing power for cameras, readers, locks, and controllers

subject: Fire Suppression System
rationale: Fire pumps boost water pressure to ensure adequate flow at sprinkler heads.
conditions: When municipal water pressure is insufficient
exceptions: May not be needed if gravity tanks or high-pressure mains suffice

subject: Fire Suppression System
rationale: Fire alarms provide detection signals to trigger pre-action or deluge systems and alert occupants.
applicability: All building types with automatic suppression
conditions: For automatic detection and activation
exceptions: Manual-only suppression systems may not require alarms

subject: Fire Suppression System
rationale: Sprinkler heads are the terminal delivery devices that disperse water onto the fire.
applicability: All building types with sprinkler systems
conditions: For water distribution to fire area
exceptions: Alternative suppression systems may use nozzles or gas delivery heads

The assertion 'Fire Suppression System depends_on Sprinkler Head' is incorrect for systems that are not sprinkler-based. Foam suppression systems, clean agent systems (e.g., FM-200, Novec 1230), and CO2 systems do not use sprinkler heads at all—they use specialized nozzles or discharge devices. The dependency should only hold for water-based sprinkler systems, not all fire suppression systems.

subject: Fire Suppression System
rationale: Sprinkler heads are integral sub-components of the suppression system.

subject: Fire Suppression System
rationale: If a fire pump is present, it is a contained sub-component of the suppression system.
conditions: When installed as part of the system
exceptions: Systems without fire pumps do not contain this component

The assertion 'Fire Suppression System contains Fire Pump' is stated with applicability 'High-rise buildings; Large facilities' but fails to acknowledge that even in high-rise buildings, fire pumps may be located in a separate fire pump room and not physically 'contained' within the suppression system as a component assembly. Furthermore, some high-rises use multiple pumps in series or parallel, some in separate buildings—making 'contains' ambiguous for spatial composition.

subject: Fire Suppression System
rationale: The suppression system interfaces with the fire alarm system for detection and activation signals.
applicability: All building types with automatic suppression
conditions: For automatic activation in pre-action and deluge systems
exceptions: Wet-pipe systems may operate independently of alarm signal for water release

subject: Fire Suppression System
rationale: Fire suppression systems often share risers and water supply with standpipe systems for fire department use.
conditions: In buildings with combined standpipe/sprinkler risers

subject: Lift/Elevator System
rationale: Guide rails keep the elevator car and counterweight aligned and prevent swaying
conditions: installed along the hoistway

subject: Lift/Elevator System
rationale: Proper ventilation prevents overheating of equipment and ensures passenger comfort
conditions: required in hoistway and car for air circulation
exceptions: Some smaller or older hydraulic elevators, particularly in low-rise buildings, may have unvented hoistways with no mechanical ventilation system, relying only on natural ventilation or door gaps. This is sometimes permitted under older codes or for low-speed/low-capacity elevators.

subject: Lift/Elevator System
rationale: Elevator hoistways must comply with fire codes including fire-rated enclosures and smoke control
conditions: fire-rated hoistway doors and smoke detection required

subject: Lift/Elevator System
rationale: BMS integration allows remote monitoring, diagnostics, and efficient operation
conditions: for integration and monitoring in modern buildings
exceptions: small buildings may not have BMS integration

subject: Lift/Elevator System
rationale: Adequate lighting is required for maintenance access and passenger safety
conditions: lighting required in hoistway, machine room, and car
exceptions: Some machine-room-less (MRL) elevators do not have a separate machine room, so machine room lighting as a required dependency does not apply. Also, in some older installations, hoistway lighting may be provided by temporary/service lighting rather than a permanent building Lighting System.

subject: Lift/Elevator System
rationale: The counterweight is a core part of the traction elevator system
conditions: for traction elevators
exceptions: hydraulic elevators do not have counterweights

subject: Escalator
rationale: Escalator openings often require sprinklers, smoke curtains, or fire shutters per code.
conditions: building code
exceptions: During fire events, the standard behavior is for escalators to stop automatically via fire alarm interlock, not to 'depend on' the Fire Protection System for their continued operation. In many buildings, escalator power is interlocked with fire alarm for automatic shutdown (ASME A17.1 code requirement in many regions), meaning the escalator actively responds to the fire system rather than depending on it for normal function. The dependency relationship is inverted from what is asserted.

subject: Escalator
rationale: Handrails are part of the escalator system moving in sync with steps.

subject: Escalator
rationale: Escalators can be integrated with BMS for monitoring, diagnostics, and energy management.
applicability: The assertion states that Escalator 'connects_to' BMS, but connection type is ambiguous. Escalators typically provide status monitoring (direction, fault, maintenance mode) to BMS via BACnet or Modbus, but rarely does BMS have bidirectional control over escalator operation (e.g., start/stop) due to safety codes (ASME A17.1/CSA B44). Many escalators in commercial buildings are not connected to BMS at all — they operate on standalone controllers. This needs clearer scope on what 'connects_to' means (monitoring only vs. control) and the prevalence of such integration.
conditions: smart building

subject: Lighting System
rationale: Lighting deters intruders and enables surveillance cameras.
conditions: exterior and perimeter lighting
exceptions: In buildings where lighting and security systems are from different manufacturers without interoperable protocols (e.g., proprietary DALI vs. proprietary security systems), the lighting system may not functionally support the security system even for exterior/perimeter areas.

subject: Lighting System
rationale: Lighting controls often interface with BMS for energy optimization.
applicability: In existing buildings with legacy lighting systems (non-smart), the lighting system typically does not connect to the BMS at all. The condition 'smart or automated buildings' partially covers this, but the assertion does not clarify whether retrofit situations or mixed (partially smart, partially conventional) systems are included.
conditions: smart or automated buildings

subject: Security System
rationale: Perimeter security sensors are installed on building envelope components (doors, windows, walls) to detect breaches.
applicability: The assertion that Security System depends_on Building Envelope 'for mounting sensors on doors and windows' overlooks that many security sensors (e.g., glass-break detectors, motion sensors, vibration sensors) are mounted on walls, ceilings, or interior surfaces, not on the building envelope. The dependency is overstated for interior-mounted sensors.
conditions: for mounting sensors on doors and windows
exceptions: open-plan buildings may rely more on volumetric sensors

subject: Security System
rationale: Security systems draw power from and often integrate with the building's electrical infrastructure.
conditions: for power and wiring
exceptions: battery-powered wireless systems reduce dependence on building wiring

subject: Security System
rationale: Modern security systems often include or integrate with access control (card readers, keypads, biometric scanners).
conditions: when integrated as part of a comprehensive security solution
exceptions: standalone access control may be a separate system

subject: Security System
rationale: Intrusion detection (sensors, contacts, detectors) is a fundamental subsystem within a security system.
applicability: The assertion states Intrusion Detection System is 'contained' by Security System as 'the core detection function,' but intrusion detection can also be a standalone system (e.g., in residential or small commercial settings) that is not a component of a larger security system. The containment relationship is not universally true.
conditions: as the core detection function

subject: Security System
rationale: Security systems often interface with fire alarm systems for coordinated emergency response and monitoring.
conditions: for integrated life safety response
exceptions: some jurisdictions require separation of systems

The assertion that Security System 'connects_to' Fire Alarm System applies only to commercial and institutional buildings, but the exception about jurisdictional separation is more critical than presented. In many jurisdictions (e.g., under NFPA 72 and local codes), security and fire alarm systems must remain electrically supervised and separated, with only limited interface via dry contacts or relays. Direct 'connection' can violate code.

subject: Fire Detection and Alarm System
rationale: Smoke detectors sense smoke particles and are the primary fire detection input devices.
conditions: located in appropriate zones per code

subject: Fire Detection and Alarm System
rationale: Heat detectors activate when temperature rises rapidly or reaches a threshold, suitable for environments with false alarm risks.
conditions: used in areas unsuitable for smoke detectors like kitchens, garages

subject: Fire Detection and Alarm System
rationale: Horns, strobes, speakers, and bells alert occupants to evacuate.
conditions: audible and visual devices

subject: Fire Detection and Alarm System
rationale: The fire alarm system often monitors sprinkler flow switches and tamper switches, and may trigger suppression.
conditions: when fire alarm is integrated with fire suppression
exceptions: buildings without sprinklers

subject: Fire Detection and Alarm System
rationale: The fire alarm system can trigger smoke control sequences to manage smoke migration.
applicability: The assertion states Fire Detection and Alarm System 'supports' Smoke control system, but fails to specify that this is a dedicated fire alarm function (e.g., initiating smoke control sequences via the fire alarm control panel) rather than a general integration with HVAC/BMS. Not all fire alarm systems are capable of supporting smoke control; it requires a specifically listed or certified fire alarm control unit with smoke control functionality per NFPA 92 and UL 864. The condition should specify that only systems specifically configured and listed for smoke control application are included.
conditions: when integrated with HVAC and building management system
exceptions: buildings without smoke control

subject: Building Management System (BMS)
rationale: BMS is heavily dependent on the HVAC system as one of its primary controlled subsystems; without HVAC integration, much of the BMS value is lost.
conditions: for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning control and optimization
exceptions: In small or simple buildings (e.g., standalone retail, small residential), the BMS may not depend on a separate HVAC system because HVAC might be controlled by standalone thermostats or unitary controllers without integration into a centralized BMS.

subject: Building Management System (BMS)
rationale: BMS often integrates lighting control for energy efficiency and occupancy-based scheduling.
conditions: for automated lighting control, scheduling, and daylight harvesting
exceptions: In small residential or basic commercial buildings, lighting control may be manual (switches) or use standalone occupancy sensors without BMS integration, so the BMS does not depend on the Lighting System.

subject: Building Management System (BMS)
rationale: In many buildings, the BMS interfaces with the fire alarm system for life safety monitoring and shutdown sequences.
applicability: commercial, institutional, industrial buildings with fire systems
conditions: for integration and monitoring of fire detection and alarm signals
exceptions: In many jurisdictions, fire alarm systems must be standalone and monitored by a separate Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP) for code compliance; BMS monitoring may be read-only or prohibited entirely by local fire codes, and integration may require a fire alarm interface module, so the BMS does not truly 'depend on' the fire alarm system.

subject: Building Management System (BMS)
rationale: BMS often integrates with security systems to provide centralized facility management.
conditions: for integrated monitoring of doors, CCTV, and intrusion detection

subject: Building Management System (BMS)
rationale: BMS interfaces directly with HVAC equipment for coordinated operation.
applicability: Older HVAC systems using proprietary protocols or pneumatic controls may not support BACnet, Modbus, or similar open protocols, preventing direct BMS connection without gateways or retrofits.
conditions: via BACnet, Modbus, or other protocols for control and monitoring

subject: Building Management System (BMS)
rationale: BMS connects to lighting panels and fixtures for integrated control.
conditions: for automated on/off and dimming control
exceptions: In buildings with simple manual lighting (no automated control), or in residential settings, the BMS does not connect to the lighting system at all.

subject: Building Management System (BMS)
rationale: BMS typically has a connection to the fire alarm panel for status monitoring.
conditions: for monitoring and life safety interlock sequences

subject: Structural Framing System
rationale: A structural framing system must be supported by a proper foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
applicability: The assertion 'Structural Framing System requires Foundation' lacks a condition distinguishing between shallow and deep foundations. Framing systems on deep piles (e.g., in seismic or poor soil conditions) may require specialized foundation integration beyond a generic 'foundation'. Additionally, temporary structural framing (e.g., formwork or scaffolding) does not necessarily require a permanent foundation.
conditions: Load-bearing structural support needed

subject: Structural Framing System
rationale: In many framing systems, load-bearing walls support and transfer vertical loads from the frame.
conditions: Where vertical load transfer is needed
exceptions: In moment-resisting frame systems where columns carry loads

The assertion states 'Structural Framing System requires Load-Bearing Walls' with an exception already noted for moment-resisting frames. However, there are additional exceptions: braced frame systems where lateral loads are resisted by diagonal bracing and vertical loads by columns, and shell or space-frame structures (e.g., geodesic domes) where loads are distributed through the frame without load-bearing walls.

subject: Structural Framing System
rationale: Columns are essential vertical members that support beams and transfer loads to the foundation.
conditions: Vertical support elements needed
exceptions: The assertion 'Structural Framing System requires Column' does not hold for certain structural systems such as flat slab or flat plate systems where loads are transferred directly to columns through thickened slab zones (drop panels) without distinct column elements, or for load-bearing wall structures that use walls instead of columns, and for single-story portal frames where the frame acts as a unified bent.

subject: Structural Framing System
rationale: Beams are the primary horizontal members of a structural framing system, supporting floors and roofs.
conditions: Horizontal spanning required
exceptions: The assertion 'Structural Framing System requires Beam' does not hold for flat plate concrete systems where the slab spans directly to columns without beams, voided slab systems (e.g., bubble deck), or waffle slabs where ribs act as integrated slab stiffeners rather than discrete beams. In timber post-and-beam, balloon framing, or platform framing, the horizontal element may be a joist rather than a beam, and in some prefabricated panelized systems, horizontal members are integrated into floor cassettes.

subject: Structural Framing System
rationale: The framing system supports floor slabs which carry occupancy loads.
applicability: The applicability is 'Multi-story buildings' with condition 'In multi-story buildings', but the statement 'supports Floor Slab' is ambiguous. In a multi-story building, the framing system supports each floor slab, but it also supports floor slabs in single-story buildings (e.g., a single-story commercial building with a raised floor or mezzanine). Additionally, in a slab-on-grade scenario, the slab is supported by the ground/soil, not the structural frame.
conditions: In multi-story buildings

subject: Structural Framing System
rationale: The framing system supports the roof structure and transfers roof loads.
conditions: All buildings with roofs
exceptions: The assertion 'Structural Framing System supports Roof Structure' with applicability 'All building types' has exceptions. In a load-bearing wall or masonry structure, the roof is supported by the walls, not the framing system. In a shell or thin-shell concrete roof structure (e.g., a dome shell), the roof is self-supporting and does not rely on an underlying frame. Similarly, in tensile membrane structures (e.g., fabric roofs with masts and cables), the roof is supported by tension cables and masts, not a structural framing system.

subject: Structural Framing System
rationale: The framing system provides attachment points and support for exterior wall cladding systems.
conditions: Non-load-bearing cladding attached to frame
exceptions: The assertion 'Structural Framing System supports Exterior Wall Cladding' with condition 'Non-load-bearing cladding attached to frame' has exceptions. In systems where cladding is supported directly by foundation or floor slabs (e.g., brick veneer supported on shelf angles attached to the slab edge), the framing system may not directly support the cladding.
