subject: Fire Hydrant Connection
rationale: Hydrant connection provides the water source for sprinklers and standpipes.
applicability: Buildings with automatic sprinklers or standpipes
conditions: Activated during fire events
Supports sprinkler and standpipe systems

subject: Fire Hydrant Connection
rationale: Fire hydrant connections supply water to standpipe systems.
conditions: In buildings with standpipe risers
Properly sized for water flow requirements
exceptions: Not all buildings have standpipes

The assertion states Fire Hydrant Connection 'connects_to Standpipe System' as a general relationship, but in many buildings, the fire hydrant connection (Siamese connection) for standpipes is a separate physical connection from the fire hydrant connection used for sprinkler systems. There are often two distinct fire department connections (FDC) — one for the standpipe system and one for the sprinkler system. The assertion conflates all fire hydrant connections with standpipe connections.

subject: Fire Hydrant Connection
rationale: Hydrant connection may feed the sprinkler system riser.
applicability: The assertion uses 'Fire Hydrant Connection' as a single entity connecting to 'Sprinkler System', but in modern buildings with fire pumps, the fire hydrant connection (FDC) typically feeds into the fire pump suction or discharge manifold, not directly to the sprinkler system. The relationship is indirect — via the fire pump or riser. Additionally, some jurisdictions require the sprinkler FDC to be separate from the standpipe FDC, so the generalized 'connects_to' relationship is ambiguous without specifying the type of connection.
conditions: Fire hydrant is used for sprinkler water supply
Backflow prevention required
exceptions: Some buildings have dedicated fire pumps without hydrant connection

subject: Fire Hydrant Connection
rationale: Prevents contaminated water from flowing back into the water supply.

Must be tested regularly

subject: Fire Hydrant Connection
rationale: The hydrant connection can supply water to a fire pump for boosting pressure.

In tall buildings or low-pressure zones

subject: Fire Pump
rationale: Suction and discharge piping are necessary to move water from the source to the suppression system.
applicability: The assertion states 'Fire Pump requires Piping and Fittings' but there are specialized fire pump configurations such as packaged/containerized fire pump units where piping and fittings come pre-integrated by the manufacturer and may not be a separate field requirement. Additionally, in vertical turbine pump installations, the discharge head piping is integral but suction piping may be a well casing rather than conventional piping.
conditions: for suction and discharge connections

subject: Fire Pump
rationale: Fire pumps supply water at sufficient pressure for fire department hose connections on each floor.
conditions: by providing pressurized water to standpipe risers
exceptions: A fire pump does not support a standpipe system if the standpipe system is served by a gravity tank or by a separate dedicated pressure booster system that bypasses the fire pump. Also, in some high-rise buildings with zone standpipe systems, only certain zone pumps (not the main fire pump) may serve the standpipe.

subject: Fire Pump
rationale: Fire pump controllers typically interface with the fire alarm system to indicate operational status and alarms.
applicability: Older or very basic fire pump installations (e.g., rural or small systems) may not have fire alarm system connectivity; the fire pump controller may only have local status indication with no remote monitoring connection. NFPA 20 does require certain monitoring, but not all installations have a fire alarm system that includes pump monitoring — some connect to a building management system instead.
conditions: for monitoring pump status (run, failure, phase reversal)

subject: Fire Pump
rationale: By code, a backflow preventer is required when a fire pump is connected to a potable water source.
applicability: fire pump systems connected to potable water supplies
conditions: on the discharge side to prevent contamination of water supply

subject: Fire Suppression Riser Room
rationale: A fire suppression riser room houses the risers, valves, and controls for the building's fire suppression system (typically sprinklers). The system is the primary equipment the room exists to serve.
applicability: All buildings with fire suppression riser rooms

The assertion states 'Fire Suppression Riser Room requires Fire Suppression System' which is circular — a riser room is part of the fire suppression system, not something that requires a separate fire suppression system. The riser room houses components of the system; the requirement should be that it contains or is part of a fire suppression system, not that it 'requires' one as a separate entity.
conditions: Active fire protection system

subject: Fire Suppression Riser Room
rationale: Fire pumps are often located in or adjacent to the riser room to boost water pressure for the sprinkler system.
applicability: Buildings with inadequate municipal water pressure
conditions: Building requires pressure boosting for sprinkler system
exceptions: Not all fire suppression riser rooms contain a fire pump. Many buildings with fire sprinkler systems have riser rooms that house only the riser, valves, flow switches, and pressure gauges, but do not include a fire pump. The fire pump is only present when pressure boosting is needed, which is already noted as a condition — but even in high-rise buildings, some have fire pumps located in separate pump rooms, not within the riser room itself.

subject: Fire Suppression Riser Room
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IBC) require fire suppression riser rooms to be enclosed with fire-resistance-rated construction to protect the fire suppression equipment from fire damage.
conditions: Minimum 1-hour fire-resistance rating typical
exceptions: Fire Suppression Riser Rooms do not universally require fire-rated enclosures. In buildings protected with automatic sprinklers throughout (per IBC), the fire rating for the riser room enclosure may be reduced or omitted. Additionally, many code editions exempt sprinklered buildings from requiring a separate fire-rated enclosure for the riser room if the entire building is sprinklered.

subject: Fire Suppression Riser Room
rationale: Devices in the riser room (flow switches, tamper switches) are connected to the building fire alarm system to provide automatic detection of sprinkler activation.
conditions: Flow switches and pressure switches in riser room trigger alarms

subject: Elevator Car
rationale: Guide rails are mounted in the shaft to guide and stabilize the elevator car's vertical movement.
conditions: always required

subject: Elevator Car
rationale: The operating panel inside the car contains floor selection buttons, emergency stop, alarm, and door controls.
conditions: always

subject: Elevator Car
rationale: Handrails along the car walls provide passenger stability and support.
applicability: Handrails in elevator cars are typically required only for larger elevator cars (e.g., those serving as platform lifts or with certain dimensional/accessibility requirements). Small residential elevators or dumbwaiters often do not include handrails. The 'usually' qualifier is appropriate but the assertion could be more precise by noting that handrail requirements are tied to car size and accessibility code requirements (e.g., ASME A17.1/CSA B44).

subject: Elevator Car
rationale: Ventilation openings or fans provide fresh air within the car.

applicability: Not all hoistways/shafts require a dedicated ventilation system for smoke accumulation; very low-rise buildings (e.g., 2-3 stories) with elevators may rely on natural ventilation or be exempt under local codes such as IBC Section 3006. Additionally, dumbwaiters or material lifts in non-combustible environments may not require ventilation.
conditions: to prevent smoke accumulation
exceptions: Hydraulic elevator hoistways with no electrical equipment inside and open venting to outside air may not require a mechanical ventilation system per some local codes.

subject: Hoistway/Shaft
rationale: A pit at the bottom of the hoistway provides space for the car buffer, overspeed governor, and maintenance access.
conditions: below the lowest landing
exceptions: Some elevator types, such as pneumatic vacuum elevators (e.g., PVE) or certain platform lifts intended as accessibility devices, do not have a pit below the lowest landing.

subject: Guide Rails
rationale: Guide rails are often paired with or integrated into handrail systems to provide continuous guidance.
conditions: when used in stairways or ramps

subject: Guide Rails
rationale: Guide rails may connect to guardrail systems to provide fall protection along open edges.

subject: Guide Rails
rationale: Floor-mounted guide rails are anchored directly to or embedded in the floor surface.
conditions: base-mounted guide rails

subject: Elevator Machine/Roomless Controller
rationale: The controller manages the movement and position of the elevator car.
applicability: The assertion states that an 'Elevator Machine/Roomless Controller' requires an 'Elevator Car.' In machine-room-less (MRL) elevator designs, the controller is often mounted inside the hoistway or on the car itself, and it inherently requires an elevator car to function as part of the system. This appears to be a tautology: the controller is part of the elevator system and would never be installed without a car in any real building. The assertion may be technically correct but is trivial and adds no meaningful constraint for domain modeling. It could confuse modelers into thinking there is a separate design choice being constrained.

subject: Counterweight Assembly
rationale: Counterweight assemblies in elevators require guide rails to direct and stabilize vertical movement.
applicability: The assertion states Counterweight Assembly requires Guide Rails for vertical guided movement, but in hydraulic elevators with counterweight arrangements, the counterweight assembly may travel within a framed enclosure without traditional guide rails, or use roller guides instead of sliding guide rails.

rationale: The counterweight assembly is directly connected to the car through the rope system.
applicability: The assertion states Counterweight Assembly connects to Elevator Car via hoist ropes over traction sheave, but in hydraulic traction elevators or roped hydraulic systems, the connection may be via a different mechanical linkage (e.g., direct hydraulic cylinder to counterweight rope arrangement) that does not involve a traction sheave.

exceptions: In certain low-rise traction elevator configurations with a machine-room-less (MRL) design using a drum or winding mechanism instead of a traction sheave, the counterweight assembly and elevator car connect via ropes wound on a drum, not over a traction sheave.

subject: Car Doors
rationale: Car doors on buildings typically use heavy-duty hinges to allow the door to swing open and closed properly.
applicability: The condition 'for hinged door types' is specified, but the assertion does not address car doors that are sliding (e.g., minivan sliding doors) or upward-opening (e.g., garage-style mechanisms on some specialty vehicles). These non-hinged car door types do not use door hinges, so the condition is incomplete.
conditions: for hinged door types

subject: Car Doors
rationale: A structural frame is necessary to support and align the door within the wall opening.
applicability: The assertion applies to 'all building types' but car doors in the context of buildings are typically in parking garages or vehicle entry points, not traditional building doors. The term 'Car Doors' likely refers to vehicular doors on automobiles, which do not use building-style door frames. This appears to be a category error or terminology confusion.

subject: Car Doors
rationale: Weatherstripping seals gaps around the door to prevent air and water infiltration.
applicability: The existing exception notes 'interior doors may not need weatherstripping', but this is incomplete. Even some exterior car doors in certain climates or vehicle types may use gaskets and seals rather than traditional building weatherstripping. The term 'weatherstripping' in automotive contexts typically refers to door seals, which differ from building weatherstripping in material and installation.
conditions: for exterior car doors
exceptions: interior doors may not need weatherstripping

subject: Car Doors
rationale: Many car doors include glazing (windows) for visibility and natural light.
applicability: The assertion and its exception address windows/glazing, but car door windows are typically roll-down or power-operated, requiring window regulators, tracks, and mechanisms that differ significantly from fixed building door glazing. The assertion treats 'Door Glazing' as a simple contained element without acknowledging these additional operational components.
conditions: when door has windows
exceptions: solid doors without windows

subject: Elevator Landing Doors
rationale: Elevator landing doors must provide a fire barrier to prevent fire and smoke spread between floors via the hoistway.

Elevator landing doors in buildings with less than 3 stories or low-rise residential buildings under certain building codes (e.g., IBC exempts buildings under 3 stories or certain R-2 occupancies) may not require fire-rated door assemblies. The assertion as stated is too broad.

subject: Safety Brake/Governor
rationale: Safety brakes clamp onto guide rails to stop the car, so guide rails are essential.
applicability: Assertion states 'Safety Brake/Governor requires Guide Rails' with conditions 'vertical steel rails in hoistway' and applicability 'all elevator types'. The requirement for 'vertical steel rails in hoistway' is not universal across all elevator types.

subject: Hoistway Construction

applicability: The assertion states Hoistway Construction supports Elevator Car via guide rails and hoist ropes, but this conflates two different support mechanisms. subject: Truss/Balustrade Assembly
rationale: The balustrade often serves as the structural backing for a handrail element.
applicability: The assertion does not specify whether structural load-bearing capacity is required from the balustrade for handrail support, nor what constitutes 'supports' — in some jurisdictions the handrail may be independently fixed to the floor or stringer even when visually alongside the balustrade.
conditions: When handrail is mounted on or integrated with balustrade
exceptions: Separate handrail system independent of balustrade

In some designs, the handrail is mounted on the wall adjacent to the balustrade rather than on or integrated with the balustrade assembly itself, meaning the balustrade does not support the handrail even though the handrail is present on the same stair or ramp.

subject: Step Chain and Pallet System
rationale: Guide rails keep the chain and pallets aligned along the intended path.

subject: Step Chain and Pallet System
rationale: Step chain and pallet systems often interface with loading docks for pallet intake and outtake.
applicability: The assertion that Step Chain and Pallet System connects_to Loading Dock only at the warehouse entry/exit point is too narrow. These systems can also connect to loading docks at intermediate points (e.g., cross-docking stations, mezzanine-level loading bays) not limited to entry/exit points. Additionally, 'warehouse; distribution' applicability excludes manufacturing, production, and cold storage contexts where such systems also commonly connect to loading docks.
conditions: at the entry/exit point of the warehouse

subject: Drive Shaft and Sprockets
rationale: Drive shafts and sprocket drives are used to connect to pumps for fluid handling applications.

subject: Landing Platform (Upper/Lower)
rationale: Water accumulation must be managed to prevent deterioration and slip hazards.
applicability: The assertion states that a Landing Platform depends_on a Drainage System only for exterior exposed platforms, but interior platforms (e.g., interior mezzanine landings in covered atriums) may still require drainage from washing or fire sprinkler runoff, which is not addressed. Additionally, the condition 'exterior exposed platforms' does not clarify whether semi-exposed platforms (e.g., under a partial canopy) are included or excluded.
conditions: For exterior exposed platforms

subject: Landing Platform (Upper/Lower)
rationale: Landing platforms provide the threshold and support area for doors at upper/lower levels.
conditions: When platform is located at building entry/exit points
exceptions: The assertion claims that a Landing Platform supports a Door Assembly when located at building entry/exit points. However, there are exceptions: (1) doors that open directly onto a platform but are structurally supported by the adjacent wall frame, not the platform; (2) sliding or pocket doors that are mounted to the building structure rather than resting on the platform; (3) threshold-less doors where the platform acts as a walking surface but does not provide structural support for the door assembly.

subject: Landing Platform (Upper/Lower)
rationale: The platform connects to the main building frame or walls at its perimeter.
conditions: At all points of attachment

subject: Newel (Handrail Base)
rationale: A newel serves as the primary structural anchor supporting the handrail at its base or turning point.
applicability: The assertion states newel depends_on handrail, but many building codes (e.g., IBC) require newels at the base and top of stairs even for wall-mounted handrails or where handrails are not continuous. The dependency direction may be reversed: handrails often depend on newels for structural support, not the other way around.
conditions: newel must be installed at base/end of handrail run
exceptions: continuous handrails without interruption

subject: Newel (Handrail Base)
rationale: The newel provides the primary vertical support and termination point for the handrail.
conditions: newel placed at base, intermediate, and top of stair run
exceptions: wall-mounted handrails do not require newels

In continuous handrail systems (e.g., spiral stairs, curved stairs), intermediate newels may be omitted if the handrail is structurally continuous and brackets provide adequate support. This contradicts the condition that newels must be placed at intermediate points.
For open riser stairs or certain modern designs, the 'top of stair run' newel may be replaced by a handrail return to the wall, eliminating the need for a top newel.

subject: Newel (Handrail Base)
rationale: In many railing designs, newels connect to balusters or infill panels between them.
conditions: when newel is part of a balustrade with balusters between newels
exceptions: glass panel or cable rail systems without balusters

subject: Comb Plate
rationale: A comb plate is typically a perforated steel plate used to connect timber or steel members, so it requires steel beam or similar structural member to function.
conditions: when used as a structural connection component

subject: Comb Plate
rationale: Comb plates are specifically designed to support and reinforce connections between structural members.
conditions: when installed between two or more members
exceptions: if corroded or improperly installed

Comb plates may not support structural connections when the connected members have significantly different coefficients of thermal expansion (e.g., steel-to-timber connections in environments with large temperature fluctuations), as differential movement can loosen the connection over time.

subject: Comb Plate
rationale: Comb plates are used to connect elements within structural frames.
conditions: when used in framed structures

subject: Controller/Panel
rationale: Controller/panel acts as an interface between the BMS and field devices, enabling centralized monitoring and control.
conditions: when the panel serves as a field-level controller or gateway
exceptions: simple standalone panels not integrated into a BMS

subject: Controller/Panel
rationale: Lighting control panels switch dimming and relays based on occupancy, schedule, or daylight sensing.
applicability: The assertion states the panel supports a Lighting Control System when it is a lighting control panel, but this is circular — it offers no substantive information beyond the identity of the panel type. It does not clarify whether this support includes direct load control, DALI/DMX integration, emergency lighting testing, or only simple on/off switching. The assertion as written provides no engineering value.
conditions: when the panel is a lighting control panel

subject: Safety Sensors and Switches
rationale: Integrated safety systems often depend on BMS for alarm logging, notification, and coordinated response.
applicability: The dependency on Building Management System (BMS) is stated for all safety sensors when integrated into building automation, but many modern safety sensors (e.g., IoT-enabled or cloud-connected sensors) integrate with dedicated safety controllers or edge gateways rather than a traditional BMS. This assertion overgeneralizes the integration pathway.
conditions: when sensors are integrated into building automation
exceptions: simple standalone alarms do not require BMS integration

subject: Safety Sensors and Switches
rationale: Fire detection sensors often require integration with the fire alarm system for occupant notification.
conditions: when safety sensors detect smoke, heat, or fire conditions
exceptions: non-fire safety sensors (e.g., motion, door position) do not depend on fire alarm system

subject: Safety Sensors and Switches
rationale: Safety sensors on automatic doors detect obstructions and prevent crushing injuries.
conditions: for safety edge sensors that prevent door closure on obstructions
exceptions: Safety edge sensors for automatic doors in healthcare settings (which is listed as applicable) may be subject to additional requirements per ANSI/BHMA A156.10 and ADA standards, including specific fail-safe and override behaviors that are not captured by a generic 'supports' relationship. In critical access areas (e.g., OR doors), safety edge sensors may have special configurations that modify the dependency.

subject: Safety Sensors and Switches
rationale: Door/window position sensors and motion detectors contribute to intrusion detection functionality.
conditions: when magnetic switches or motion sensors are used for security

subject: Safety Sensors and Switches
rationale: In fire scenarios, smoke sensors connect to HVAC controls for smoke management.
conditions: when smoke sensors trigger HVAC shutdown to prevent smoke spread

subject: Step Demarcation Lighting
rationale: Step lighting along egress routes may need to be tied to emergency backup power.
conditions: if required by building code for egress paths
exceptions: low-height residential stairs not part of egress

Stair treads that are already illuminated by overhead egress lighting (meeting minimum foot-candle requirements) may not require dedicated Step Demarcation Lighting connected to the Emergency Lighting System. In such cases, demarcation lighting is decorative or optional and not emergency-connected.

subject: Escalator Pit
rationale: Water accumulation can damage electrical and mechanical components in the pit.
applicability: The existing exception states 'indoor climate-controlled environments with no moisture risk' but the applicability is limited to 'outdoor escalators; semi-enclosed areas; below-grade installations'. This creates an inconsistency: the exception only applies to indoor environments yet the assertion applicability excludes indoor environments entirely, making the exception effectively moot or contradictory.
conditions: to prevent water accumulation at bottom of pit
exceptions: indoor climate-controlled environments with no moisture risk

subject: Escalator Pit
rationale: Escalator pit is typically a cast-in-place concrete structure that forms part of the building foundation.
conditions: properly poured and cured concrete to form pit enclosure

subject: Escalator Pit
rationale: Prevents groundwater or moisture ingress into the pit which could damage equipment.
applicability: The assertion states 'Escalator Pit depends_on Waterproof Membrane' with the condition 'for pits below grade or exposed to moisture' and applicability 'below-grade pits; exterior installations'. However, waterproofing below-grade pits often requires more than a membrane alone — it may require a full tanking system, drainage board, or sump pump system depending on groundwater levels. A simple waterproof membrane may be insufficient in high water table conditions.
conditions: for pits below grade or exposed to moisture
exceptions: pits in fully interior dry areas

subject: Escalator Pit
rationale: Escalator openings through floors create vertical openings that require fire protection per building codes.
applicability: buildings subject to fire codes with escalator openings
conditions: fire-rated enclosure or fire suppression within or adjacent to pit

subject: Escalator Pit
rationale: The pit houses the lower termination of the escalator truss structure.
conditions: the lower end of the truss rests in the pit

subject: Escalator Pit
rationale: The pit is cast as part of or attached to the building's structural frame and floor system.
conditions: structurally integrated with floor slabs and foundations

subject: Machine Room (Integrated)
rationale: Integrated machine rooms contain mechanical equipment that generates heat and requires ventilation for proper operation and safety.
applicability: All building types with integrated machine rooms
conditions: For heat dissipation from equipment
exceptions: Machine rooms with passive cooling (e.g., naturally ventilated louvered rooms) or equipment that does not generate significant heat (e.g., low-voltage telecom rooms with minimal heat load) may not require a dedicated mechanical ventilation system. Local building codes or equipment manufacturer specifications may accept natural ventilation.

subject: Machine Room (Integrated)
rationale: Machine rooms contain electrical and mechanical equipment that pose fire risks; fire suppression is typically required by building codes.
conditions: Code-compliant type for equipment present

subject: Machine Room (Integrated)
rationale: Machine rooms require adequate lighting for safe operation and maintenance of equipment.
conditions: For maintenance and code compliance

subject: Machine Room (Integrated)
rationale: Machine rooms may contain equipment that produces condensate or requires floor drains for maintenance or leak management.
conditions: For condensate, leaks, or floor washing
exceptions: Not all integrated machine rooms require a dedicated drainage system. Many machine rooms have no floor drains because they house sealed HVAC equipment (e.g., chillers, VRF systems) that does not produce condensate or leaks, and floor washing is not a requirement in all jurisdictions. Adding a floor drain can even be prohibited in some electrical rooms.

subject: Machine Room (Integrated)
rationale: Centralized building automation and control system panels are often placed in the machine room for monitoring mechanical equipment.
exceptions: Small or basic machine rooms in commercial/institutional buildings (e.g., a small fan room or a simple pump room) may not contain a BMS controller. The BMS controller may be located in a central control room or mechanical room rather than within each integrated machine room.

subject: Machine Room (Integrated)
rationale: Elevator machinery housed in the machine room supports the operation of elevators throughout the building.
conditions: By housing elevator/escalator machinery

subject: Escalator Truss
rationale: The truss provides the structural base for mounting balustrades and handrails.

subject: Escalator Truss
rationale: Trusses are typically fabricated from structural steel sections for strength and rigidity.

subject: Escalator Installation
rationale: Building codes typically require fire protection around escalator openings to prevent fire and smoke spread between floors.
conditions: Compliance with local fire codes
may require sprinkler coverage above escalator openings

subject: Escalator Installation
rationale: Handrails provide passenger safety and stability, moving in concert with the steps.
conditions: Must move synchronously with steps
continuous loop design

subject: Escalator Installation
rationale: Balustrades are the side panels that enclose the escalator and support the handrails.
applicability: The assertion states 'contains Balustrade' with 'Glass or metal panel construction' as a condition, but balustrades can also be constructed from other materials (e.g., wood, acrylic, or composite materials) in certain low-rise or custom escalator installations. This condition may be overly restrictive.
conditions: Glass or metal panel construction

subject: Escalator Installation
rationale: Escalator installation supports the building's vertical transportation function alongside elevators.
conditions: Used for continuous movement of people between floors

subject: Escalator Installation
rationale: Motors and drives generate heat requiring ventilation or cooling.
applicability: buildings with enclosed escalator machine rooms
conditions: Adequate ventilation in machine room spaces if enclosed
exceptions: Not required if machine is integrated within truss with open ventilation

subject: Escalator Installation
rationale: The building floor slabs at the upper and lower levels support the escalator truss ends.
conditions: Slab edges at top and bottom openings must support truss end reactions
exceptions: There exist escalator installations where self-supporting truss designs can transfer loads to columns or beams at intermediate points, not requiring slab edge support at both top and bottom openings. This is common in some modern modular escalator designs or when escalators span between independent structural supports.

subject: Railing (Fixed) Adjacent to Escalator
rationale: A railing fixed adjacent to an escalator inherently requires the escalator itself as the primary structure it accompanies.
applicability: The assertion does not specify whether the railing requirement applies to both sides of the escalator or only one side. In many jurisdictions, the requirement is only for the side where the escalator is open to a floor below or where there is an unprotected drop, not universally on any side adjacent to an escalator.
conditions: railing must be installed adjacent to the escalator
exceptions: The assertion may not hold for escalators that are parallel and immediately adjacent to each other (side-by-side escalators). In such configurations, the fixed railing may be omitted or replaced by the escalator balustrade itself, depending on code interpretations.

subject: Escalator Commissioning
rationale: Commissioning can only occur after the escalator system has been properly installed.
applicability: Commissioning may depend on completed electrical systems and safety testing prior to or concurrent with escalator installation completion in some jurisdictions, making the dependency incomplete without additional prerequisites.
conditions: prior completion of installation

subject: Escalator Commissioning
rationale: Commissioning involves calibrating speed sensors, brakes, and control logic.
conditions: before operation
exceptions: In some building types (e.g., residential low-rises with simple escalators), control system calibration may be integrated with the escalator controller and performed as part of installation rather than as a separate commissioning requirement. Also, some jurisdictions allow phased commissioning where calibration occurs after initial operation begins.

subject: Travelator/Moving Walk
rationale: Balustrades form the side barriers of the travelator, guiding passengers and providing safety.
applicability: The condition 'Typically glass or stainless steel' describes a material property rather than a condition under which the assertion holds. A balustrade requirement exists regardless of material. The 'conditions' field appears to conflate a design specification with an actual contextual condition.
conditions: Typically glass or stainless steel

subject: Travelator/Moving Walk
rationale: Comb plates transition passengers smoothly between the moving walkway and fixed floor.
applicability: The condition 'Installed at entry and exit points' describes the location of the comb plate itself rather than a condition under which the assertion applies. The condition should specify the context (e.g., 'When travelator is in public use') rather than restating the component's placement.
conditions: Installed at entry and exit points

subject: Spiral Escalator
rationale: Glass or metal balustrades are needed along the outer edge of the spiral path for safety and aesthetics.

subject: Spiral Escalator
rationale: Comb plates at landings allow steps to smoothly transition into and out of the floor surface.
conditions: at entry and exit points
exceptions: Spiral escalators have a continuous helical path. At the entry and exit points, the spiral curvature may prevent installation of a standard flat comb plate. Some spiral escalator designs use contoured or specially shaped combs, or in certain installations, the comb plate may be absent or integrated differently than in standard escalators.

subject: Spiral Escalator
rationale: Skirt panels run along the sides of the steps to prevent clothing or objects from being caught in the mechanism.
applicability: Spiral escalators often have curved side profiles. A standard flat skirt panel as used in straight escalators may not exist in the same form. Some spiral escalator designs use flexible skirt panels, segmented panels, or may not have a distinct 'Skirt Panel' component at all due to the helical geometry. The assertion is accurate for conventional straight escalators but may not hold for all spiral escalator implementations.

subject: Heavy-Duty/Metro Escalator
rationale: Building codes often require fire-rated enclosures around escalator openings in heavy-use settings
applicability: The assertion states that a Heavy-Duty/Metro Escalator requires a fire-rated enclosure, but this is not universally true even where required by building code. In many jurisdictions (e.g., IBC), escalators in open-air or exterior transit stations, or escalators serving as required means of egress in certain low-rise or sprinklered conditions, may not need a full fire-rated enclosure. The assertion is too broad even with the condition 'where required by building code' because it does not account for the specific conditions under which building codes waive or modify the enclosure requirement.
conditions: where required by building code

subject: Lighting Fixture
rationale: Modern fixtures often depend on switches, dimmers, or automation systems
applicability: The assertion 'Lighting Fixture depends_on Lighting Control System' is stated with conditions 'For dimmable or smart fixtures' and applicability 'commercial; smart buildings', but the assertion itself has no such scoping—the raw relationship 'depends_on' is categorical. This misalignment could cause the unqualified relationship to be interpreted as universally true outside of those contexts, leading to incorrect inferences for residential or simple commercial fixtures.
conditions: For dimmable or smart fixtures
exceptions: Non-dimmable, standalone fixtures do not require controls

In emergency egress lighting, the lighting fixture depends on emergency power (battery or generator) and a local emergency control unit, not on the general Lighting Control System. There are also occupancy-sensor-only fixtures that operate independently of a central control system but are still dimmable.

subject: Lighting Fixture
rationale: Ballasts and LED drivers regulate current to the light source
conditions: For fluorescent, HID, or LED fixtures
exceptions: Incandescent or halogen fixtures have no ballast

Some LED fixtures (e.g., linear strip lights with integrated drivers on a PCB, or corn-cob LED lamps) contain an integrated driver that is not a separable, replaceable 'ballast/driver' component. The assertion 'contains Ballast/Driver' implies a discrete replaceable component, which is not accurate for many integrated LED fixtures where the driver is soldered onto the board.

subject: Lamp / Light Source
rationale: Many lamp types require ballasts or drivers to regulate current.
conditions: For fluorescent or LED fixtures requiring current regulation

subject: Lamp / Light Source
rationale: Artificial light sources can supplement or integrate with natural daylight.
conditions: When used with dimming controls alongside daylight sensors

subject: Lamp / Light Source
rationale: Modern lamps can connect to control systems for scheduling, dimming, and automation.
conditions: For smart or automated building systems

subject: Ballast / Driver
rationale: The ballast/driver is designed to regulate power to a specific lamp type and cannot function without a connected lamp.
applicability: All lighting systems using ballasts or drivers
conditions: Ballast type must match lamp type (e.g., LED, fluorescent, HID)
exceptions: Some drivers are universal or programmable for multiple lamp types

Wireless/non-integrated drivers: In many commercial LED systems, the driver is selected independently of the lamp/light source because modular LED panels and sockets allow lamp replacement without driver replacement (e.g., GU24 or NEMA SSL-7A interfaces). In such systems, the driver does not strictly depend on the lamp.

subject: Ballast / Driver
rationale: Advanced drivers enable integration with building automation and lighting control systems.
applicability: Smart lighting and energy management systems
conditions: When the driver supports dimming, 0-10V, DALI, or other control protocols
exceptions: Non-dimmable or basic ballasts do not support control systems

subject: Ballast / Driver
rationale: The primary function of a ballast/driver is to provide controlled power, protecting the lamp from current surges and thermal damage.
applicability: All lamp types that require external regulation (LED, fluorescent, HID)
conditions: By regulating current and voltage to prevent overdriving
exceptions: Poorly matched or low-quality drivers may fail to protect the lamp

subject: Lighting Control System
rationale: Occupancy sensors detect presence to trigger lighting control actions like on/off or dimming.
applicability: The assertion does not account for jurisdictions that follow newer codes (e.g., 2021 IECC or ASHRAE 90.1-2019) where occupancy sensors are required only in specific space types (e.g., open offices, conference rooms, restrooms) but not for entire lighting control systems in general. The blanket 'requires' wording is too broad.
conditions: automatic dimming or shut-off based on occupancy
exceptions: manually controlled spaces

The assertion states that a Lighting Control System 'requires' an Occupancy Sensor, but there are many valid lighting control strategies (e.g., timeclock scheduling, daylight harvesting alone, or manual dimming without occupancy sensing) that comply with energy codes without any occupancy sensor. In residential applications in particular, occupancy sensors are often optional.

subject: Lighting Control System
rationale: In fire events, lighting controls must override normal operation to ensure safe egress.
conditions: emergency lighting override on fire alarm trigger
exceptions: non-code-compliant installations

subject: Lighting Switch
rationale: The purpose of a lighting switch is to control power to a lighting fixture or set of fixtures.
conditions: as the load being controlled
exceptions: if switch controls an outlet or other device

In commercial and industrial settings, emergency lighting switches, exit sign switches, or fire alarm interface switches control emergency/egress lighting systems that are not 'lighting fixtures' in the traditional sense but rather emergency lighting units with integral batteries or centralized emergency lighting systems.

subject: Occupancy Sensor
rationale: In most installations, occupancy sensors interface with lighting control systems to turn lights on/off based on occupancy.
conditions: Compatible communication protocol (0-10V, DALI, relay, BACnet)
Proper configuration and programming
exceptions: Standalone occupancy sensors with internal relays do not need a separate control system

Some occupancy sensors (e.g., wireless battery-powered sensors using ZigBee/Thread/Matter) may depend on a lighting control system for configuration and data aggregation, but the communication protocols listed (0-10V, DALI, relay, BACnet) exclude modern wireless protocols commonly used in commercial/industrial settings, meaning the assertion's own conditions already create an unstated exception for sensors using non-listed protocols.

subject: Occupancy Sensor
rationale: Occupancy sensors can detect unauthorized presence in secured areas, supporting security and intrusion detection functions.
applicability: The assertion states the sensor 'supports' the security system, but occupancy sensors typically only provide a binary/digital signal (occupied/vacant) and lack the encryption, tamper detection, and supervised signaling required by security-grade alarm systems, so the nature of 'support' is limited to a basic auxiliary input rather than full security integration.
conditions: Integration with alarm and access control systems
Monitoring for unexpected occupancy after hours
exceptions: Basic occupancy sensors may lack security integration capabilities

subject: Daylight Sensor / Photocell
rationale: The photocell needs to interface with a lighting control system to adjust artificial light levels based on daylight readings.
applicability: Daylight sensors/photocells are also commonly used in standalone applications (e.g., exterior lights with integral photocell, simple on/off switching without a lighting control system). The assertion states it 'requires' a lighting control system, which is not universally true.
conditions: Typically requires a compatible DALI, 0-10V, or relay-based control interface

subject: Lighting Control Panel
rationale: The panel controls lighting fixtures; without them there is nothing to control.
conditions: must be compatible with control signals from the panel
exceptions: A lighting control panel does not require a lighting fixture during commissioning, testing, or when used as a spare/backup unit. Panels can be installed and powered up for configuration and programming before any fixtures are connected.

subject: Lighting Control Panel
rationale: Many modern lighting control systems use occupancy sensors for automatic control.
conditions: when configured for occupancy-based control
exceptions: not required for manual-only or scheduled control setups

subject: Lighting Control Panel
rationale: Integration with BMS allows remote monitoring, scheduling, and energy optimization.
conditions: when integrated for centralized control and monitoring
exceptions: standalone panels may operate without BMS integration

subject: Exit Sign
rationale: Exit signs are often part of or connected to the emergency lighting system to remain visible during power failures.
applicability: The assertion states 'Exit Sign depends_on Emergency Lighting System' during power outage, but exit signs in many jurisdictions are required to have their own battery backup or be connected to emergency power directly, not depend on a separate 'Emergency Lighting System' which may refer to egress lighting fixtures. Some exit signs are self-luminous (e.g., tritium) or have dedicated internal batteries, making them independent of any separate emergency lighting system.
conditions: during power outage

subject: Exit Sign
rationale: Some exit sign systems are integrated with fire alarms for testing or emergency activation.
conditions: for automatic testing or integration

subject: Emergency Lighting System
rationale: Exit signs are required by building codes to clearly mark means of egress.
applicability: The condition 'internally or externally illuminated per code' is ambiguous. Exit signs can be internally illuminated (LED, electroluminescent, tritium self-luminous) or externally illuminated (by a dedicated light source), but this condition does not clarify that the assertion applies to exit signs that are part of the emergency lighting system versus exit signs that are separately powered. Some codes allow non-emergency-powered exit signs (e.g., photoluminescent) in certain contexts, and the relationship between the emergency lighting system and the exit sign power source is not addressed.
conditions: internally or externally illuminated per code
exceptions: There are exceptions where emergency lighting is required but exit signs are not. For example, in some jurisdictions, exit signs are not required in spaces that are not normally occupied or in storage areas that nonetheless require emergency egress lighting. Also, certain codes (e.g., IBC, NFPA 101) distinguish between 'means of egress illumination' (emergency lighting) and 'exit signs' as separate requirements with different scopes.

subject: Lighting Conductor / Track
rationale: Track lighting requires compatible fixtures/heads that attach to and draw power from the track.
conditions: compatible track-mounted heads
exceptions: Some track lighting systems come in pre-wired continuous runs where the track itself is the fixture (e.g., linear LED tape installed inside the track channel). In such cases, no separate 'lighting fixture' is mounted onto the track — the track assembly itself serves as the luminaire.

subject: Lighting Diffuser / Lens
rationale: The diffuser/lens requires a light source (bulb, LED, etc.) whose light it diffuses or directs.
conditions: to be positioned behind or within the diffuser
exceptions: Some diffusers are self-illuminating (e.g., electroluminescent panels or edge-lit acrylic with integrated LEDs) where no separate lamp/light source is behind/within the diffuser — the diffuser itself is the light source.

subject: Lighting Diffuser / Lens
rationale: Without a light source, the diffuser has no functional purpose.
conditions: for providing the light that passes through the diffuser
exceptions: In edge-lit or light-guide plate systems, the diffuser does not 'depend on' a discrete lamp/light source behind it; the light source may be along the edge and the diffuser's function is to scatter light from the guide plate, not directly from a lamp.

subject: Lighting Diffuser / Lens
rationale: The lens shields the lamp from dust, moisture, and physical contact.
applicability: The assertion says the diffuser protects_from the lamp/light source, but in many enclosed fixtures the diffuser protects users/objects from the lamp (shatter protection, UV screening, heat), not the lamp itself. The object of protection is ambiguous.
conditions: when installed as a cover or shield
exceptions: open fixtures without lens

subject: Reflector / Baffle / Louver
rationale: Louvers and baffles are often integrated with or positioned relative to lighting fixtures to direct, shield, or diffuse light.
conditions: when used for light control
exceptions: when used purely for acoustic or airflow purposes

subject: Reflector / Baffle / Louver
rationale: A light shelf is a type of reflector that may be combined with or integrated into a louver/baffle assembly.
applicability: commercial and educational buildings with daylight harvesting
conditions: when reflector is designed as part of a light shelf system

subject: Mounting Bracket / Hanger
rationale: Brackets are used to mount lighting fixtures to walls, ceilings, or poles.
applicability: The assertion assumes a single bracket/hanger supports the entire lighting fixture, but many lighting fixtures (e.g., chandeliers, track lights, multi-point pendants) require multiple mounting points or a structural ceiling anchor rather than a single bracket. The assertion is also ambiguous about whether the bracket is surface-mounted, recessed, or flush-mount, which affects load paths and installation code compliance.
conditions: Bracket must be rated for fixture weight and compatible with mounting type
exceptions: The assertion does not hold for integrated LED or 'wafer' style lighting fixtures that are directly fastened to junction boxes via studs or screws, not mounted on a separate bracket or hanger. Also, some fixtures (e.g., surface-mounted strip lights) use a continuous channel or rail system rather than a discrete bracket.

subject: Lighting Circuit / Feeder
rationale: Lighting circuits must accommodate and power control devices that manage lighting operation.
applicability: Daylight harvesting controls require specific photosensor placement and calibration, but the assertion does not account for the fact that not all lighting circuits are suitable for daylight harvesting (e.g., interior corridors without daylight access, or circuits serving spaces with no windows).
conditions: including switches, dimmers, occupancy sensors, daylight harvesting controls

subject: Lighting Circuit / Feeder
rationale: In many configurations, the normal lighting circuit supports the emergency lighting transfer switch or shares raceway/conduit.
conditions: where separate emergency lighting circuits are fed from same or dedicated panel
exceptions: sometimes on separate dedicated emergency circuit

In some jurisdictions (e.g., under NFPA 101 Life Safety Code), emergency lighting is permitted to be supplied by the normal lighting circuit if emergency transfer is provided, or via unit equipment (battery pack) attached to the luminaire rather than a separate circuit. The assertion implies a circuit-level relationship that does not always hold.

subject: Install Lighting Controls
rationale: Lighting controls need lighting fixtures to control; they are the end-devices being operated.
applicability: In retrofit or lighting control upgrade scenarios (e.g., adding occupancy sensors to an existing lighting system), the lighting fixtures already exist, so 'Install Lighting Controls' does not require installation of new lighting fixtures — it requires existing fixtures to be present, not a new fixture installation.
conditions: must be compatible with control system
exceptions: Lighting controls are sometimes integrated into the fixture itself (e.g., smart bulbs with built-in dimming/control), making a separate 'Install Lighting Controls' step unnecessary or not requiring a separate lighting fixture as a prerequisite — the fixture and control are one unit.

subject: Install Emergency Lighting
rationale: Many emergency lighting fixtures integrate exit signs as a combined unit, though they can also be separate.
conditions: when combined fixture/sign units are installed
exceptions: separately installed exit signs may be independent

There exist emergency exit signs that are self-illuminated (e.g., tritium or photoluminescent) which contain no electrical lighting fixture to combine with. These are not 'separately installed exit signs' in the traditional sense and may not constitute a combined fixture/sign unit, yet they still serve the emergency exit sign function without satisfying the 'Install Emergency Lighting contains Emergency Exit Sign' relationship.

subject: Install Emergency Lighting
rationale: Modern emergency lighting systems can be integrated with BMS for remote testing, monitoring, and status reporting.
applicability: The assertion that Install Emergency Lighting connects_to Building Management System (BMS) is stated with applicability 'commercial and institutional buildings', but many emergency lighting systems in existing commercial/institutional buildings are standalone units with self-testing capability (e.g., self-contained emergency luminaires with integral batteries) that do not connect to a BMS. Only centralized emergency lighting systems with remote monitoring heads are typically BMS-connected. This should be scoped to centralized/path-of-egress systems with specified BMS integration.
conditions: if BMS monitoring and testing features are specified

subject: Commission Lighting System
rationale: Commissioning a lighting system inherently requires the lighting fixtures themselves to be present and operational for testing and verification.
conditions: functional lighting system must be installed
exceptions: A lighting system can be commissioned without a lighting fixture if the scope is limited to controls-only commissioning (e.g., relay panels, dimmers, control algorithms) where fixtures are existing or pre-commissioned by others.

subject: Commission Lighting System
rationale: If lighting controls interface with a BMS, commissioning depends on BMS connectivity and programming being in place.
applicability: The assertion may not hold for standalone lighting systems that use local control (e.g., manual switching, standalone timers, or self-contained fixtures with integral sensors) and have no integration with a central BMS. In such cases, the lighting system can be commissioned independently.
conditions: lighting is integrated with central BMS for control and monitoring

subject: Commission Lighting System
rationale: Commissioning depends on occupancy sensors being installed and configured for automated lighting response.
conditions: occupancy-based control is specified
exceptions: An occupancy sensor may not be required for commissioning if the lighting system uses time-clock scheduling, daylight harvesting only, or manual control without occupancy-based logic.

subject: Commission Lighting System
rationale: The commissioning activity contains a structured process of functional performance tests for each lighting zone and control sequence.
conditions: commissioning process includes defined test procedures

subject: Daylighting Integration
rationale: Light shelves help bounce daylight deeper into spaces and reduce glare near window perimeter.
applicability: The applicability lists 'commercial; office; educational buildings' but does not include other building types where light shelves are commonly used, such as libraries, museums, or laboratories. More importantly, light shelves are generally ineffective in buildings with narrow floor plates or deep plans where the shelf cannot reach the ceiling height needed, which is a missing context limitation.
conditions: when deeper daylight penetration is desired
exceptions: not required if solely using top-lighting strategies

subject: Daylighting Integration
rationale: To realize energy savings, daylight harvesting requires sensors and controls that dim or switch electric lights in response to available daylight.
applicability: The applicability includes 'institutional buildings' but excludes residential, healthcare, and hospitality buildings where daylight-responsive controls are also commonly applied and required by energy codes (e.g., ASHRAE 90.1, IECC). The scope is unnecessarily narrow.
conditions: must be integrated with electric lighting systems for dimming or switching
exceptions: manually operated spaces may not need automated controls

Daylight-responsive lighting controls may not be required in spaces where electric lighting is rarely used (e.g., circulation spaces, storage rooms, corridors) or where occupancy sensors already provide off/none switching during daylight hours as a separate control strategy. This is a common exception in energy codes.

subject: Surface-Mount Luminaire
rationale: Can be connected to dimmers, occupancy sensors, or building automation systems.
applicability: The assertion applies only to dimming/smart controls, but not all 'smart buildings' require dimming or smart controls for every luminaire — e.g., occupancy-sensing or daylight-harvesting zones may still use simple switched fixtures. The condition 'when dimming or smart controls are specified' already narrows the scope, yet the applicability tag 'smart buildings' could mislead users into thinking the assertion holds for all luminaires in a smart building.
conditions: when dimming or smart controls are specified
exceptions: simple on/off fixtures without controls

subject: Pendant Luminaire
rationale: Pendant luminaires are commonly used to provide focused task lighting over counters, tables, and work areas.
applicability: The assertion states 'Pendant Luminaire supports Task Lighting' under the given condition, but pendant luminaires can cause glare or shadows on work surfaces if not properly designed (e.g., open-bottom shades vs. opaque shades, light distribution pattern). Many common pendant luminaires are decorative and provide mostly ambient light, not focused task light. The assertion oversimplifies the relationship between pendant luminaires and task lighting.
conditions: when positioned above work surfaces like kitchen islands or desks

subject: Strip Light / Linear Fixture
rationale: Linear fixtures are often placed above work areas to provide focused task illumination.
applicability: The assertion groups commercial, residential, industrial, and retail contexts without distinction. In industrial settings, strip lights for task lighting often need to meet specific luminous efficacy, CRI, and ingress protection (IP) ratings that are not addressed. In residential settings, aesthetic and color temperature requirements differ significantly from retail or industrial.
conditions: When installed over work surfaces, counters, or workbenches
exceptions: Strip lights and linear fixtures often produce harsh glare and uneven illumination, which can be counterproductive for task lighting—especially in residential settings where visual comfort is paramount. Many strip lights lack appropriate diffusers or optics to reduce glare on work surfaces.

Strip lights mounted directly above work surfaces can cause veiling reflections or shadows from the user's own body unless positioned correctly (e.g., at proper offset from the front edge of the counter). The assertion does not account for positioning requirements to avoid such issues.

subject: High-Bay / Low-Bay Luminaire
rationale: May connect to occupancy sensors, daylight harvesting, or building management systems.
applicability: The assertion states that a High-Bay/Low-Bay Luminaire connects to a Lighting Control System when equipped with a dimming/control interface. However, many high-bay/low-bay luminaires are standalone or only have a simple on/off switching function via line-voltage relay control (e.g., via a contactor or occupancy sensor directly), with no dimming or network control interface at all. In those cases, the luminaire does not connect to a Lighting Control System, even though it is still a high-bay/low-bay luminaire. The condition 'if equipped with dimming/control interface' should be clarified to also exclude luminaires that only have simple switching (non-control) wiring.
conditions: if equipped with dimming/control interface

subject: Landscape / Exterior Lighting
rationale: LED landscape lighting fixtures contain drivers to regulate power; older HID fixtures contain ballasts.
conditions: For LED fixtures (driver) or discharge lamps (ballast)
exceptions: Incandescent or halogen fixtures without ballast/driver

subject: Smoke Detector
rationale: Smoke detectors serve as initiating devices for fire alarm systems.
conditions: When interconnected or part of a fire alarm system
exceptions: Standalone battery-operated units may not be connected to a central system

Aspirating smoke detectors (e.g., VESDA systems) used in data centers or clean rooms often connect to a building management system (BMS) rather than directly to a traditional fire alarm system, or they serve as a separate very early warning layer that does not directly trigger the fire alarm system.

subject: Smoke Detector
rationale: Smoke detectors trigger strobes, horns, and speakers throughout the building via the control panel.
conditions: When part of an integrated fire alarm system
exceptions: Standalone units use their own built-in horn/strobe

In some commercial settings, addressable fire alarm systems route detection signals through a control panel (fire alarm control unit, FACU) which then triggers notification appliances. The smoke detector connects to the control panel, not directly to the notification appliance. The assertion implies a direct connection, which may be misleading.

subject: Control Panel / Fire Alarm Control Unit (FACU)
rationale: The FACU controls and requires connection to horns, strobes, speakers, or bells to alert occupants of a fire condition.
applicability: all buildings with fire alarm systems
conditions: for occupant warning
exceptions: In some legacy or limited-purpose fire alarm systems (e.g., single-station smoke alarms in residential occupancies), a Fire Alarm Control Unit may not require a separate Notification Appliance Circuit (NAC) if the notification is integral to the initiating device or if the system uses only voice evacuation from a central point without traditional notification appliances.

subject: Control Panel / Fire Alarm Control Unit (FACU)
rationale: The FACU supports smoke management by initiating fans, dampers, and pressurization sequences upon detection.
applicability: Even in buildings with engineered smoke control, the FACU typically only provides initiating signal input (detection) to the smoke control system, not active control of smoke management equipment (fans, dampers, pressurization). The assertion implies the FACU is the supporting device, but in practice the smoke control system has its own logic panel that receives inputs from the FACU.
conditions: in buildings with engineered smoke control
exceptions: not applicable in buildings without smoke control systems

subject: Voice Evacuation System
rationale: A voice evacuation system needs the fire alarm system to detect fire and trigger the evacuation messages.
applicability: In some jurisdictions, a Voice Evacuation System may be required even in buildings without a full Fire Alarm System (e.g., small buildings with manual fire alarm boxes or stand-alone voice systems tied directly to sprinkler flow switches). The assertion that a Fire Alarm System is universally required may not hold in all code jurisdictions.
conditions: for fire detection and activation
exceptions: In existing buildings undergoing retrofit, a Voice Evacuation System may be added as a standalone emergency communication system without a full Fire Alarm System, provided other detection means are present (e.g., sprinkler monitoring).

subject: Voice Evacuation System
rationale: The voice evacuation system is interconnected with the fire alarm system to receive alarm signals and zone data.
applicability: The connection between Voice Evacuation System and Fire Alarm System can be via a supervised network interface, a dry contact, or a serial data link. The assertion 'connects_to' is vague and does not specify the type or supervision requirements of the connection, which vary by code.
conditions: for signal interface and automatic triggering
exceptions: In some buildings with a combined Fire Alarm/Voice Evacuation system (e.g., a single addressable panel with integrated voice), the systems are not separate entities that 'connect_to' each other—they are the same integrated system.

subject: Conventional Detector Zone Module
rationale: Zone alarm signals may be relayed to a BMS for monitoring.
applicability: The assertion claims a 'Conventional Detector Zone Module' connects to a BMS, but such modules typically connect to a fire alarm control panel (FACP), not directly to a BMS. The BMS connection is via the FACP's outputs/relays as stated in the condition, meaning the zone module itself does not directly connect to the BMS — rather, the FACP acts as intermediary. The assertion wording is misleading about the directness of the connection.
conditions: If integrated via FACP outputs or relays
exceptions: Not all installations include BMS integration

subject: Fire Alarm Control Panel Enclosure
rationale: The enclosure houses the panel that connects to horns, strobes, speakers, etc.
conditions: Via the control panel's output circuits

subject: Backup Battery / Power Supply
rationale: Certain battery chemistries produce hydrogen gas during charging and require ventilation to prevent explosion risk.
conditions: if using lead-acid or vented battery types

subject: Backup Battery / Power Supply
rationale: Backup power systems may need to interface with fire alarm systems for safety shutdown protocols.
applicability: The assertion states Backup Battery/Power Supply 'depends_on' Fire Alarm System, but this dependency is not universal. In many installations, the backup battery operates completely independently of the fire alarm system. The dependency for shutdown during fire events only applies if there is a specific integration (e.g., a battery disconnect switch triggered by the fire alarm), which is not present in most standard backup power installations. The assertion conflates a possible integration with a required dependency.
conditions: for integration and shutdown during fire events

subject: Backup Battery / Power Supply
rationale: Backup battery power supplies are commonly used to keep emergency lighting operational when mains power fails.
applicability: The assertion that Backup Battery/Power Supply 'supports' Emergency Lighting System is true for centralized emergency lighting systems with a common battery bank, but many modern emergency lighting systems use self-contained individual units with their own internal batteries. In those cases, the backup battery/power supply does not support the emergency lighting system as they are independent. The condition 'during power outages' is correct but the relationship type ('supports') may not hold for all emergency lighting configurations.
conditions: during power outages

subject: Backup Battery / Power Supply
rationale: Fire alarm systems often rely on backup batteries to remain operational during power outages for life safety.
applicability: The assertion that Backup Battery/Power Supply 'supports' Fire Alarm System during mains power failure is generally correct, but fire alarm control panels almost always have their own integral backup batteries. So the Backup Battery/Power Supply referenced here (presumably a larger building-level UPS or generator battery) typically does not directly support the fire alarm system — the fire alarm has its own dedicated battery. The relationship may only apply if the fire alarm panel's own battery is insufficient or if it is powered through the building's UPS system.
conditions: during mains power failure

subject: Backup Battery / Power Supply
rationale: Security systems including access control and CCTV typically have backup battery support to remain functional.
applicability: The assertion that Backup Battery/Power Supply 'supports' Security System during power outages is generally correct, but similar to fire alarm systems, many security system panels have their own internal backup batteries. The building-level backup battery/power supply only supports the security system if the security panel is powered through it. This depends on the specific electrical design and is not universally true.
conditions: during power outages

subject: Annunciator Panel (Remote Annunciator)
rationale: The remote annunciator is a peripheral component dependent on the full fire alarm system for its functionality.
applicability: The assertion states Annunciator Panel depends_on Fire Alarm System, but a remote annunciator is actually a component within the fire alarm system, not a downstream dependent. The dependency direction may be inverted—the annunciator is part of the fire alarm system or the fire alarm system provides data to the annunciator, but it's not a separate system that depends on another system. The condition 'annunciator is a subcomponent of overall system' contradicts the 'depends_on' relationship.
conditions: annunciator is a subcomponent of overall system

subject: Annunciator Panel (Remote Annunciator)
rationale: The annunciator may display status of notification appliances but does not directly connect to them.
applicability: The assertion states Annunciator Panel connects_to Notification Appliance, but the condition says 'indirectly through FACP'. An annunciator panel typically outputs visual/audible status information and does not directly connect to notification appliances (horns, strobes). The connection is actually from FACP to notification appliances; the annunciator is a monitoring/display device, not a control device that drives notification circuits.
conditions: indirectly through FACP

subject: Fire Alarm Wiring / Cabling
rationale: Fire alarm wiring provides power and communication to smoke detectors.
applicability: All building types with fire alarm systems

Smoke detectors can also be connected via initiating device circuits (IDC), not exclusively via SLC. The assertion implies a one-to-one relationship between smoke detectors and SLC, but both IDC and SLC are common wiring methods for smoke detectors depending on system size and type (conventional vs. addressable).
conditions: When connected via signaling line circuits (SLC)

subject: Fire Alarm Wiring / Cabling
rationale: Wiring connects heat detectors to the FACP for alarm initiation.
applicability: Heat detectors are commonly connected via initiating device circuits (IDC) in conventional systems, but in addressable systems they are connected via signaling line circuits (SLC). The assertion restricts heat detectors exclusively to IDC, which is only true for conventional (non-addressable) systems.
conditions: When connected via initiating device circuits

subject: Duct Smoke Detector
rationale: The duct smoke detector provides early warning of smoke in the HVAC system, feeding into the broader fire alarm system for occupant notification and building control actions.
applicability: all buildings with fire alarm systems

The assertion states 'Duct Smoke Detector supports Fire Alarm System' applies to 'all buildings with fire alarm systems', but duct smoke detectors serve a different primary purpose (detecting smoke in HVAC ducts to prevent recirculation) than area/spot smoke detectors. In many jurisdictions, duct smoke detectors are not required to initiate a general building fire alarm evacuation signal — they may only initiate HVAC shutdown or send a supervisory signal to the FACP rather than a full alarm. The condition stated ('signal is sent to FACP') conflates supervisory/alarm signals without distinguishing the response type.
conditions: when smoke is detected, signal is sent to FACP

subject: Beam Detector (Projected Beam Smoke Detector)
rationale: In modern buildings, the beam detector may interface with BMS for centralized monitoring and diagnostics.
applicability: The assertion states that a Beam Detector depends on a BMS, but this only applies when the detector is part of an integrated fire alarm system with remote monitoring capabilities. In many jurisdictions, beam detectors are standalone devices connected directly to a fire alarm control panel (FACP) that may have its own local annunciation and reporting without any BMS integration. The dependency on BMS is actually a specific design choice, not a general functional dependency.
conditions: If integrated for remote monitoring
exceptions: Not required in standalone fire alarm systems

Some beam detector models have built-in onboard relays, local sounders, and local LEDs for alarm indication, allowing them to operate as standalone units without any BMS integration whatsoever. Even when connected to a fire alarm panel, the panel itself can provide local monitoring and notifications without a BMS.

subject: Aspiration / Air-Sampling Smoke Detector (ASD)
rationale: ASD provides input signals to the broader fire detection and alarm infrastructure
conditions: Integration with fire alarm system via relays or communication
exceptions: ASD may also support Very Early Smoke Detection Apparatus (VESDA) systems directly without being integrated into a traditional Fire Detection and Alarm System as a sub-system, e.g., when used for property protection in data centers with standalone alerting.

subject: Aspiration / Air-Sampling Smoke Detector (ASD)
rationale: An internal filter removes dust and large particles before air reaches the detection chamber
conditions: Filter must be replaced periodically

subject: Flame Detector
rationale: Flame detectors can initiate fire suppression systems like sprinklers or gas-based suppression.
conditions: by providing early flame detection signals to trigger suppression
exceptions: Flame detectors detect flame signatures (UV/IR) but have no direct role in triggering suppression systems. Suppression systems are typically triggered by dedicated heat detectors, smoke detectors, or sprinkler flow switches, not by flame detectors. Flame detectors primarily serve fire alarm and safety system activation, not suppression release.

subject: Flame Detector
rationale: Flame detectors are connected to the broader fire alarm system infrastructure.
applicability: The assertion states 'all building types' but flame detectors are generally not used in all building types. They are primarily specified for high-hazard industrial applications (e.g., petrochemical, gas turbine enclosures, aircraft hangars) and are rarely found in standard commercial office buildings, residential buildings, or low-hazard occupancies due to cost and nuisance alarm sensitivity.
conditions: via the fire alarm control panel

subject: Interface Relay / Control Module
rationale: Often depends on the BMS for command inputs and integration into overall building automation.
applicability: The assertion states that Interface Relay / Control Module depends_on Building Management System (BMS), but in many building designs, relay/control modules for simple standalone equipment (e.g., unit-level fan control, standalone damper actuators) operate independently without any BMS integration. The dependency only holds when the module is configured for centralized BMS communication (e.g., BACnet, Modbus), not for all automated control scenarios.
conditions: when used for automated control
exceptions: There are battery-powered or wireless relay/control modules used in retrofit scenarios that operate on local scheduling or sensor input (e.g., PIR occupancy) without any BMS backbone. These modules perform automated control but do not depend on a BMS.

subject: Interface Relay / Control Module
rationale: Can support lighting control by switching lighting circuits on/off based on BMS commands.
applicability: The assertion states that Interface Relay / Control Module 'supports' Lighting Control System when used for relay-based lighting switching. However, many relay/control modules only provide dry-contact closure and lack the DALI, 0-10V dimming, or DMX protocols required by modern lighting control systems. Such modules support only simple on/off switching of lighting loads, not actual lighting control system integration.
conditions: when used for relay-based lighting switching

subject: Interface Relay / Control Module
rationale: Interface modules may support fire alarm actions such as equipment shutdown or damper positioning.
conditions: when used for fire/smoke damper control or fan shutdown

subject: Gas Detector (CO / Combustible Gas)
rationale: Combustible gas detection and CO detection often integrate with the building fire alarm system to alert occupants and emergency responders.
applicability: Many gas detectors (especially for CO) are only monitoring devices that produce local alarms and do not have dry contacts or communication modules to interface with a fire alarm panel. The assertion assumes interconnectivity capability that many units lack even in commercial settings.
conditions: when interconnected with fire alarm panel to trigger evacuation
exceptions: standalone detectors not tied to fire alarm

Combustible gas detectors are often required to trigger a separate gas shutoff valve (via a solenoid) rather than (or in addition to) evacuating occupants via the fire alarm system. In many jurisdictions, the primary response to a combustible gas alarm is equipment shutdown, not general building evacuation, which may conflict with fire alarm protocols.

subject: Gas Detector (CO / Combustible Gas)
rationale: Advanced gas detection systems interface with BMS for centralized monitoring, logging, and facility management response.
applicability: In many commercial and industrial installations, gas detectors connect to a dedicated gas monitoring panel or safety system (e.g., a gas detection controller) rather than directly to a general-purpose BMS. Direct BMS integration may be limited to higher-end systems with BACnet or Modbus interfaces, which is not universal even in commercial/industrial settings.
conditions: when gas detection includes remote monitoring and logging capabilities
exceptions: simple standalone residential units

subject: Door Holder / Magnetic Door Release
rationale: Magnetic door holders require a signal from the fire alarm system to release doors upon fire detection.
conditions: for automatic release in case of fire
exceptions: Door holders/magnetic door releases are sometimes released by local smoke detectors directly (not a full fire alarm system), especially in smaller buildings or retrofit applications where a standalone smoke detector powers the release coil. The assertion states a fire alarm system is required, but a local smoke detector can directly trigger release without a central fire alarm panel.

subject: Door Holder / Magnetic Door Release
rationale: A door closer is needed to ensure the door closes automatically when the magnetic holder releases.
applicability: all swinging doors with magnetic holders
conditions: to close the door after release
exceptions: Some magnetic door holders are used on doors that do not require self-closing (e.g., doors held open for convenience in non-fire-rated openings, or doors where automatic closing is done by a spring hinge integrated into the holder itself). In certain configurations, the closer is part of the holder mechanism or a separate closer is omitted intentionally.

subject: Door Holder / Magnetic Door Release
rationale: Magnetic door holders keep fire doors open under normal conditions and release them to close upon fire alarm.
applicability: buildings with rated fire door assemblies

The assertion implies that door holders 'support' fire door assemblies universally, but building codes (e.g., IBC) restrict the use of automatic door holders on fire doors to those tested and listed as part of a fire door assembly. Not all fire doors are permitted to have magnetic holders—only those specifically rated with automatic-closing devices. Additionally, some fire-rated openings (e.g., in hazardous areas) may require doors to remain closed at all times.
conditions: by holding fire doors open during normal operation

subject: Door Holder / Magnetic Door Release
rationale: Standalone magnetic door holders may have integrated or separate smoke detectors to trigger release.
applicability: smaller buildings without full fire alarm systems

The existing exception says 'not required if connected to building fire alarm system with smoke detection' but this is incomplete.
