In such cases, finishing does not depend on curing - finishing partially replaces or delays conventional curing procedures.

subject: Concrete Surface Finishing
rationale: A well-finished surface supports adhesion and uniform application of sealers, epoxies, paints, and other protective coatings.
applicability: The 'supports' relationship direction may be ambiguous. In practice, Protective Coating is applied to finished concrete, meaning Protective Coating depends on Concrete Surface Finishing, not the reverse. The assertion as written (finishing supports coating) could be read as finishing enabling coating, but the depends_on semantics need clarity.
conditions: when applied over finished concrete
exceptions: uncoated exposed concrete

subject: Concrete Grout
rationale: Grout is placed under base plates to create full bearing contact, distribute column loads evenly to the foundation, and prevent uneven settlement.
applicability: The assertion that Concrete Grout supports Column Base Plate is only valid for non-shrink grout used in dry, confined conditions. In wet environments or where shrinkage may occur, the grout may not provide adequate long-term support without proper additives or alternative materials.
conditions: For leveling and load transfer under steel columns
exceptions: Precision shimmed connections without grout

Concrete Grout placed under a base plate does not provide adequate support if the grout thickness exceeds approximately 100 mm (4 inches), as thicker grout layers are prone to cracking and shrinkage, compromising load transfer.

subject: Concrete Grout
rationale: Grout provides a bond between new steel members and existing concrete foundations or walls.
applicability: Concrete Grout connecting to Concrete Foundation for dowel embedment is only valid when the existing concrete surface has been properly prepared (roughened, cleaned, and wetted or primed as specified). Without proper surface preparation, the bond is inadequate.
conditions: When grouting base plates or dowels into existing concrete
exceptions: Concrete Grout does not reliably connect to Concrete Foundation when the ambient temperature is below 4°C (40°F) during placement and curing, unless specialized cold-weather grout and procedures are used.

subject: Concrete Anchor / Embedment
rationale: Concrete anchors/embedments require concrete to be embedded into; they are placed in fresh or hardened concrete.
conditions: Cast-in-place installation

subject: Concrete Anchor / Embedment
rationale: Cast-in-place anchor bolts and embed plates receive welded or bolted steel connections.
conditions: When used as a connection point for steel members

subject: Concrete Anchor / Embedment
rationale: Anchor bolts and embedments must be positioned accurately before concrete pour and held in place during curing.
conditions: For cast-in-place anchors
exceptions: Post-installed anchors do not depend on fresh concrete placement

subject: Concrete Anchor / Embedment
rationale: Anchor bolts transfer loads from steel columns and beams into the concrete foundation.
conditions: When anchor bolt or embed plate is used as a column base connection

subject: Concrete Anchor / Embedment
rationale: Anchors and embedments connect superstructure elements to the concrete foundation.
conditions: When anchors are cast into footings or mat foundations

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: Concrete topping/screed is typically applied over a structural concrete slab to provide a level, finished surface.
conditions: as a base substrate
exceptions: Concrete topping/screed can also be applied over existing ceramic tiles, timber floors, or other rigid substrates with proper preparation (e.g., bonding agents), not exclusively over concrete slabs.

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: Steel or synthetic fiber reinforcement may be required in thicker toppings to prevent cracking.
applicability: Reinforcement mesh in screeds is also required for bonded toppings applied over weak or cracked substrates regardless of thickness, not solely when exceeding 50mm. Additionally, some specifications use fibers (polypropylene or steel) instead of mesh for crack control, so the requirement is not exclusively for 'Reinforcement mesh'.
conditions: when thickness exceeds 50mm
for crack control

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: Expansion joints are needed to control cracking due to temperature changes and shrinkage.
applicability: Expansion joints in screeds are also required to accommodate moisture movement (shrinkage) and not just thermal movement. Additionally, small floor areas with long narrow configurations may also require expansion joints.
conditions: in large floor areas
to accommodate thermal movement

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: Proper curing is essential for concrete topping to achieve design strength and durability.
conditions: after placement
to prevent rapid moisture loss
exceptions: Some modern screed products (e.g., self-levelling compounds, rapid-drying screeds) do not require curing compound as they are formulated differently or are covered by floor finishes before moisture loss becomes critical.

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: In wet areas, a waterproofing layer beneath the screed prevents moisture migration.
applicability: Waterproof membrane is also required under concrete topping/screed over non-wet areas when there is a risk of rising moisture (e.g., ground-bearing slabs without a damp-proof membrane), not exclusively over wet areas like bathrooms or balconies.
conditions: when applied over wet areas
such as bathrooms or balconies

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: Concrete topping provides a smooth, level substrate for final floor finishes.
conditions: such as tiles, timber, vinyl, or carpet

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: Screed is commonly used to encase underfloor heating pipes or cables, providing thermal mass and even heat distribution.
conditions: when embedded within or beneath the screed

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: The topping acts as a sacrificial wear layer, protecting the structural slab from abrasion, impact, and chemical exposure.
conditions: from wear and tear
from chemical attack

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: A thick screed layer can contribute to sound insulation between floors when part of a floating floor system.
applicability: A concrete topping/screed can also improve acoustic insulation through its own mass (mass-loaded impact sound reduction) without acoustic underlay. The current condition implies acoustic underlay is always required, which is not the case in many applications where mass alone provides sufficient acoustic performance.
conditions: when combined with acoustic underlay

subject: Concrete Topping / Screed
rationale: In wet areas, screed is sloped to direct water toward floor drains.
conditions: when falls are incorporated into the screed
exceptions: Concrete topping/screed can connect to a floor drain without falls incorporated into the screed itself if falls are provided in the structural slab or via a pre-sloped drainage board beneath the topping.

subject: Laminated Veneer Lumber (LVL)
rationale: LVL is commonly used as a substitute for solid timber or glulam beams, supporting floor, roof, and deck loads.
conditions: when used as a structural beam element
exceptions: LVL beams require specific end-bearing conditions (minimum bearing length typically 1.5-3.5 inches depending on reaction) and lateral bracing to prevent buckling. Without adequate bearing or bracing, LVL does not support loads as a beam.

LVL is not suitable for beam applications where long-term exposure to moisture or exterior weather conditions exists unless properly protected or treated, as LVL is susceptible to delamination and decay in wet service conditions.

subject: Timber Frame (Heavy Timber / Post-and-Beam)
rationale: A timber frame transfers its loads to the ground through a foundation system; without a proper foundation the structure would settle or fail.
applicability: The assertion states 'requires Foundation' without qualification, but timber frames can be built on continuous strip footings, isolated piers, or slabs-on-grade, which are different foundation types. The assertion is overly generic—it does not specify what type of foundation is required, and some timber structures (e.g., small garden sheds or non-habitable post-and-beam structures) may be permitted on gravel pads or ground screws rather than a formal foundation in some jurisdictions.
conditions: must support heavy vertical loads
must resist lateral forces
exceptions: Temporary timber frame structures (e.g., event pavilions, exhibition halls) or certain engineered timber structures designed for seasonal use may not require a permanent foundation, particularly when designed with ballasted or removable base connections.

subject: Timber Frame (Heavy Timber / Post-and-Beam)
rationale: The timber frame (post-and-beam system) provides the primary vertical support for roof rafters, purlins, and roofing materials.
applicability: all timber frame buildings with roofs
conditions: timber posts and beams carry roof loads

subject: Timber Frame (Heavy Timber / Post-and-Beam)
rationale: Timber frames frequently accommodate SIPs as a compatible, high-performance enclosure system that integrates with the post-and-beam grid.
applicability: modern timber frame buildings with high insulation values
conditions: SIPs are often used as the infill/enclosure system on timber frames
exceptions: traditional stick-framed infill walls may be used instead

subject: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Light timber framing requires a foundation to transfer loads to the ground and provide a level base.
applicability: The assertion states Light Timber Framing 'requires Foundation', but this is only true for load-bearing walls. Non-load-bearing timber stud walls (e.g., infill walls in a concrete or steel frame) do not necessarily require a foundation in the same sense—they may be supported by a slab or structural frame rather than a strip footing or pad foundation. The condition already says 'load-bearing walls' so this may be partially captured, but the wording 'requires Foundation' is categorical and does not account for cases where load-bearing timber walls transfer loads via a ground beam or slab on grade which may not be considered a 'Foundation' in the traditional sense.
conditions: load-bearing walls

subject: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Cavities in timber framing are designed to accommodate insulation for thermal performance.
conditions: thermal performance required
exceptions: The assertion states Light Timber Framing 'depends_on Insulation' when thermal performance is required. However, in some building systems (e.g., structural insulated panels or timber frame with exterior insulated render systems), the insulation is integrated into the panel and is not a separate 'depends_on' dependency in the traditional sense. Additionally, in unoccupied or unconditioned buildings (e.g., sheds, agricultural buildings) where habitation is not expected, no insulation is needed even if listed under 'habitable buildings' applicability. The applicability is broader than the condition.

subject: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Rafters support the roof covering material (tiles, shingles, metal sheets).
applicability: The assertion states Light Timber Framing 'supports Roof Covering' with condition 'directly'. However, in standard construction, roof covering (tiles, shingles, metal sheeting) is not directly supported by rafters—there is typically sarking, battens, counter-battens, or roof decking/sheathing between the rafters and the roof covering. The word 'directly' is misleading as the covering is rarely fixed directly to the timber framing without intermediate layers.
conditions: directly

subject: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Ceiling joists and rafters support ceiling linings such as plasterboard.
conditions: below joists or rafters

subject: Light Timber Framing (Stud Walls, Joists, Rafters)
rationale: Floor joists support the subfloor and finished floor materials.
conditions: above joists
exceptions: The assertion states Floor Finish is supported 'above joists' for Light Timber Framing. However, in typical timber floor construction, there is subflooring/floor decking (plywood, OSB, or tongue-and-groove boards) between the joists and the floor finish. The floor finish (e.g., carpet, tile, hardwood flooring) is not directly supported by the joists but by the subfloor. This is an oversimplification that omits a critical intermediate layer.

subject: Timber Truss
rationale: Timber trusses rely on connectors (nails, bolts, plates) to transfer loads between members
applicability: The assertion does not account for glue-laminated timber trusses (glulam) or other engineered timber truss types where connections are often moment-resisting or integral to the member fabrication, making the dependency on a separate 'Structural Connection' element ambiguous or inapplicable.
conditions: load-bearing application

subject: Timber Truss
rationale: Bottom chord of a truss often supports ceiling drywall or other finishes
conditions: when bottom chord supports ceiling
exceptions: There is an exception where the bottom chord supports a ceiling finish but the truss is part of a scissor truss or raised-heel truss configuration. In these configurations, the bottom chord may be sloped (scissor) or elevated (raised heel), which can change the load path or require additional furring/batten systems, meaning the truss does not directly 'support' the ceiling finish in the conventional sense assumed by this assertion.

subject: Timber Truss
rationale: Trusses transfer forces to load-bearing walls or supports at each end
conditions: at support points
exceptions: trusses supported on columns or beams

The existing exception only mentions columns or beams, but there are other support conditions where trusses do not connect to load-bearing walls, such as trusses supported on steel rafters, portal frames, or masonry piers. Additionally, in balloon-framed construction or pole buildings, trusses may sit on posts rather than walls.

subject: Timber Finishes (Interior Paneling, Trims, Moldings)
rationale: Timber paneling can affect room acoustics; acoustic insulation behind panels may be needed for sound control.
applicability: The assertion does not account for building code variations across jurisdictions. Some local building codes may not require acoustic insulation behind timber paneling even in sound-sensitive areas, or may have different definitions of what constitutes a 'sound-sensitive area' (e.g., some codes differentiate between dwelling units, public corridors, and meeting rooms). The assertion assumes a universal requirement that does not exist in all code jurisdictions.
conditions: When used as wall paneling in sound-sensitive areas
exceptions: Decorative trim and molding do not require acoustic insulation

The existing exception covers decorative trim and molding, but there are additional exceptions not listed. For instance, timber paneling installed over existing drywall that already provides the required acoustic performance would not require additional acoustic insulation. Similarly, if the timber paneling is part of a tested assembly that inherently meets the STC rating without separate acoustic insulation (e.g., a thick solid wood paneling system), no additional insulation is needed.

subject: Timber Stairs and Railings
rationale: Handrails are a mandatory safety component for timber stairs and landings.
conditions: for safety compliance
typically at 865-900mm height per building codes
exceptions: The assertion states 'Timber Stairs and Railings requires Handrail' with conditions specifying 'for safety compliance; typically at 865-900mm height per building codes' and applicability 'all building types'. However, there are exceptions: private staircases in some jurisdictions (e.g., UK Building Regulations for private dwellings) may not require a handrail on one side if the stair width is narrow; also, certain historic buildings or listed structures may be exempt from modern handrail requirements. Additionally, some open-tread or spiral stairs may have different or relaxed handrail requirements depending on local codes.

subject: Timber Stairs and Railings
rationale: Treads are the horizontal components of stair flights that are stepped upon.
conditions: horizontal stepping surface
typically 250-300mm deep

subject: Timber Stairs and Railings
rationale: Risers are the vertical boards between treads in a closed stair design.
conditions: vertical component between treads
typically 150-200mm high
exceptions: The assertion 'Timber Stairs and Railings contains Riser' with applicability 'closed-riser stairs' correctly limits scope, but the condition 'typically 150-200mm high' may not hold for all building types. Commercial/accessible stairs often have stricter riser height maximums (e.g., 178mm or 7 inches in many US codes, sometimes as low as 150mm/6 inches depending on the regulation). Also, open-riser stairs (excluded by scope) still contain risers in the structural sense even if the vertical face is open - the vertical distance between treads is still a riser dimension even if not a physical board.

subject: Timber Stairs and Railings
rationale: Stringers are the inclined load-bearing members that carry treads and risers.
applicability: The assertion 'Timber Stairs and Railings contains Stringer' with applicability 'all timber stairs' is generally correct, but there is a context limitation: not all timber stairs use stringers in the traditional sense. Some modern prefabricated timber stairs use carriage bolts and hanger systems or center-carriage designs rather than side stringers. Additionally, cantilevered timber stairs (treads anchored into a wall) may lack visible stringers on the open side. The assertion may be too absolute for 'all timber stairs'.
conditions: structural side members supporting treads and risers

subject: Timber Stairs and Railings
rationale: Newel posts are the main vertical anchor posts for handrails and balustrades.
applicability: timber stairs with traditional railing systems

The assertion 'Timber Stairs and Railings contains Newel Post' with applicability 'timber stairs with traditional railing systems' is generally correct, but some modern timber stair railing systems use continuous handrail brackets fixed to the wall with no newel posts at all (wall-mounted handrails). Additionally, some glass/steel balustrade systems incorporated into timber stairs may not require newel posts. The assertion should clarify that newel posts are present only in traditional post-to-post or over-the-post railing systems.
conditions: at start and end of stair flights
at landings

subject: Timber Stairs and Railings
rationale: Balusters are the vertical spindles that form the infill of a balustrade.
conditions: vertical infill between handrail and tread/stringer
spaced per building code

subject: Timber Doors and Window Frames
rationale: Weatherstripping is needed to seal gaps and prevent air/water infiltration.
conditions: For energy efficiency and weather resistance
exceptions: Interior doors do not need weatherstripping

External timber doors in protected/covered locations (e.g., recessed entrances, porches) that are not directly exposed to wind-driven rain or drafts may not require weatherstripping while still achieving acceptable energy and weather performance in milder climates.

subject: Timber-Concrete Composite System
rationale: Timber-concrete composite is commonly used for floor slabs, supporting occupancy loads.
conditions: When used in floor systems

subject: Timber-Concrete Composite System
rationale: Can be used for roof decks where stiffness and sound insulation are required.
applicability: The condition 'Where spanning capability and acoustic performance are needed' is incomplete - TCC roof structures can be effective in such scenarios, but acoustic performance in roof structures (sound transmission through roof) is far less commonly a critical design driver compared to floor slabs, where impact sound and inter-tenancy acoustic separation are key requirements.
conditions: Where spanning capability and acoustic performance are needed

subject: Heavy Timber Fireproofing / Encapsulation
rationale: Some heavy timber encapsulation assemblies may incorporate thermal insulation as part of the fire-resistive layering.
conditions: in some encapsulation assemblies

subject: Structural Timber Installation
rationale: Structural timber installation requires a structural framing system (e.g., walls, columns, beams) to support and anchor the timber members.
applicability: The assertion states that Structural Timber Installation 'requires' Structural Framing System, but structural timber installation is itself a type of structural framing system installation, not a separate activity that depends on one. This creates a circular dependency — the timber is the structural framing, not something that requires a separate framing system.
conditions: during installation

subject: Structural Timber Installation
rationale: The timber structure depends on a completed foundation to bear and transfer loads.
conditions: prior to installation
exceptions: Structural Timber Installation does not always depend on a Foundation System prior to installation. Timber can be installed on existing structures (e.g., renovation, roof-only timber framing) where the foundation already exists or is not part of the scope. The dependency is on the foundation being complete, not on the foundation being installed as part of the same project. Additionally, timber may be used in non-foundation-bearing applications like partition walls.

subject: Structural Timber Installation
rationale: Installed timber framing supports roof loads including dead, live, and environmental loads.
conditions: when timber is used as roof framing

subject: Structural Timber Installation
rationale: Timber wall framing provides the substrate and support for interior and exterior wall cladding.
conditions: when timber framing is used for walls

subject: Timber Cladding Installation
rationale: The cladding installation supports the placement and protection of insulation layers in the wall build-up.
applicability: Timber cladding installation itself does not 'support' thermal insulation in the sense of providing structural support or load-bearing capacity for insulation. The assertion conflates the presence of a batten cavity (which can accommodate insulation) with the installation process actively supporting insulation. The cladding installation provides a cavity, but does not mechanically support, retain, or enhance the insulation's performance. The thermal performance depends on the insulation material and its installation, not the cladding.
conditions: When insulation is placed within or behind the batten cavity system
exceptions: Insulation not always present in non-insulated walls

subject: Timber Connection Hardware
rationale: Timber connection hardware provides the structural linkages that hold the timber frame together, transferring loads between members.
applicability: The assertion does not account for alternative connection methods such as traditional joinery (mortise-and-tenon, dovetail, pegged connections) or glued connections, which can support timber frame structures without metal connection hardware. This is particularly relevant in heritage, timber-heavy, or certain engineered timber systems.
conditions: Hardware must be installed at every beam-to-column, beam-to-beam, and column-to-foundation joint
exceptions: The assertion states hardware must be installed at every beam-to-column, beam-to-beam, and column-to-foundation joint, but in timber frame construction, certain joints (e.g., intermediate purlin-to-beam connections or blocking between joists) may be considered secondary and do not require dedicated connection hardware if they are only load-sharing or bridging elements. This over-generalization could lead to unnecessary hardware usage.

subject: Timber Connection Hardware
rationale: Timber connection hardware includes hold-downs, anchor bolts, and post bases that connect the timber structure to the concrete foundation.
applicability: timber buildings with concrete slabs or footings

The assertion does not specify that the connection requires corrosion protection measures (e.g., galvanized or stainless steel hardware, moisture barrier) when timber connection hardware is embedded in or in direct contact with concrete, as concrete's alkalinity and moisture can corrode standard steel hardware over time.
conditions: At the base of timber columns or walls
exceptions: The assertion states that Timber Connection Hardware connects to Concrete Foundation, but many timber-to-concrete connections use a steel base plate or embedded anchor bolts that interface between the hardware and the concrete, rather than the hardware itself directly connecting to the concrete. The hardware often connects to the steel base plate which is then anchored to the concrete.

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Steel columns require a concrete foundation to distribute point loads safely into the ground.
conditions: to transfer vertical loads to ground

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Columns and beams work together to create the structural frame; beams transfer loads to columns.
applicability: Not all steel columns depend on steel beams. In buildings with trusses, space frames, or where columns support only wall loads (e.g., mezzanine columns), beams may not be present or the dependency may be different. The 'depends_on' relationship is too strong for all steel-framed buildings.
conditions: to form the overall frame
when lateral stability is provided by moment connections or braced frames

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Columns provide vertical support for beams at each floor and roof level.
conditions: at beam-to-column connections

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Column loads ultimately support all floor and roof dead and live loads.
conditions: through beams and girders that transfer loads to columns

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Roof loads are transferred through the roof framing to columns.
applicability: all building types with steel roofs
conditions: when columns extend to roof level

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Perimeter columns often support spandrel beams which in turn support cladding panels.
applicability: Even with perimeter columns, exterior wall cladding may be supported by spandrel beams, shelf angles, or floor slabs, and the columns themselves may only provide lateral restraint, not vertical support for the cladding. The assertion oversimplifies the load path.
conditions: when columns are located at the building perimeter
exceptions: curtain wall systems that are self-supporting or floor-slab supported

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Columns terminate at and connect to the foundation.
conditions: via base plates and anchor bolts

subject: Structural Steel Columns
rationale: Column sections are connected end-to-end with bolted or welded splices.
conditions: in multi-story columns where multiple pieces are joined
exceptions: single-story columns

subject: Structural Steel Beams
rationale: Steel beams are horizontal members that typically transfer loads to vertical steel columns.
conditions: as primary vertical support for beams
exceptions: beams may bear on walls or other beams in certain conditions

subject: Structural Steel Beams
rationale: Beams provide attachment points for hanger wires supporting suspended ceilings.
conditions: when ceiling grids are hung from beam bottom flanges
exceptions: direct-attach ceilings or exposed structure designs

subject: Structural Steel Beams
rationale: Girders are larger horizontal members that may support intermediate beams in a floor framing system.
conditions: when beam spans are long and larger primary members are needed to support beams
exceptions: beams may frame directly into columns without girders

subject: Structural Steel Beams
rationale: Beams frame into columns via bolted or welded connections to form the structural frame.
applicability: The assertion states 'connects_to Steel Column' but does not account for connections to other structural elements such as Steel Girders, concrete or masonry walls, or other beams. The connection is described only for beam-to-column scenarios, which is a subset of possible beam connections.
conditions: at beam-to-column moment or shear connections

subject: Steel Trusses
rationale: Trusses need a stable foundation to bear and distribute their weight and imposed loads.
conditions: must support the truss load and transfer to ground
exceptions: In buildings with a transfer structure or podium slab, steel trusses may be supported by intermediate beams or girders rather than a foundation system. The truss load path goes through multiple structural elements before reaching the foundation.

subject: Steel Trusses
rationale: Steel roof trusses directly support the roof covering or the deck that carries the roof membrane.
applicability: The assertion says 'truss is part of roof system' but the existing exception only mentions 'floor trusses'. However, steel trusses used as mezzanine supports or equipment platforms also support non-roof elements and should not be covered under this assertion even if they are not 'floor trusses' per se.
conditions: truss is part of roof system
exceptions: floor trusses

subject: Steel Trusses
rationale: Trusses often support ceiling loads via bottom chord attachments.
applicability: The condition 'ceiling is suspended or attached to bottom chord' is correct for most cases, but steel trusses can also support ceilings via top chord attachments (e.g., in clearspan buildings where ceiling is hung from the top chord or from the truss itself). The statement as written restricts to bottom chord attachment only.
conditions: ceiling is suspended or attached to bottom chord

subject: Steel Trusses
rationale: Trusses connect to columns at bearing points to transfer loads.
conditions: truss ends bear on columns
exceptions: Steel trusses can also connect to steel beams or girders (not just columns), for example when trusses frame into a main girder in a long-span condition. The assertion restricts to columns only.

subject: Steel Girders
rationale: Steel girders require solid concrete foundations to transfer loads to the ground and ensure structural stability.
applicability: The existing exceptions only list 'temporary structures' but fails to exclude steel frame buildings on deep foundations (piles, caissons) or buildings where girders bear on isolated pier foundations rather than a continuous concrete foundation.
conditions: for load-bearing walls
multi-story buildings
exceptions: temporary structures

subject: Steel Girders
rationale: Steel girders span between steel columns to transfer floor and roof loads vertically down the structural frame.
conditions: vertical load-bearing applications
exceptions: single-span truss systems without intermediate columns

subject: Steel Girders
rationale: Steel girders act as primary horizontal members supporting floor slabs and distributing loads to columns.
conditions: composite deck systems
cast-in-place concrete slabs
exceptions: precast planks on bearing walls

Steel girders may support precast concrete planks directly (without a cast-in-place slab or composite deck), which is not listed as an exception. The existing exception only mentions 'precast planks on bearing walls' but not precast planks bearing on steel girders.

subject: Steel Girders
rationale: Steel girders support roof decking materials, transferring dead and live roof loads to the structural frame.
conditions: flat or low-slope roofs
exceptions: arched or tensile roof systems

Steel girders in metal building systems often support purlins which then support roof decking, not the decking directly. The assertion implies direct support of roof decking, but purlin systems create an intermediate framing layer.

subject: Steel Girders
rationale: Steel girders are physically connected to steel columns via bolted or welded connections to form the structural frame.
conditions: at girder-column moment or shear connections
exceptions: truss systems where girders connect to truss chords

subject: Steel Girders
rationale: Secondary steel beams often frame into steel girders, transferring floor loads to the main girders.
conditions: in beam-to-girder framing systems
exceptions: one-way slab systems without secondary beams

The existing exception only covers 'one-way slab systems without secondary beams' but does not account for composite decking systems that span directly between girders without intermediate steel beams (e.g., long-span composite decks), or voided slab systems where girders connect directly to columns without beams.

subject: Steel Bracing Systems
rationale: Steel bracing systems must be anchored to the foundation via connections to transfer lateral loads.
conditions: for load transfer to substructure

subject: Steel Bracing Systems
rationale: Bracing systems are typically integrated with steel columns to create a stable frame.
applicability: Steel bracing systems do not always require a steel column. In some retrofit scenarios, steel braces are added to concrete or masonry frames where the vertical framework is concrete column or concrete wall, not a steel column. The assertion's applicability should note that this holds only for all-steel framed buildings, not for hybrid structures where steel bracing is added to non-steel vertical elements.
conditions: to form the vertical framework

subject: Steel Bracing Systems
rationale: Beams work with columns and bracing to resist lateral and gravity loads.
conditions: to complete the rigid frame
exceptions: Steel bracing systems do not always require a steel beam to complete the rigid frame. In concentrically braced frames (CBFs) with chevron (inverted-V) or X-bracing configurations, the beams are part of the bracing system but the assertion's phrasing 'to complete the rigid frame' is misleading because braced frames are not considered rigid frames (rigid frames rely on moment connections). Many braced frames are designed as simple connections, not rigid frames. Also, in some configurations like knee-braced frames, the brace connects directly to the column and beam flanges near the joint, but the frame is not necessarily 'rigid'.

subject: Steel Base Plates
rationale: Base plates sit on concrete foundations (or piers) to distribute column loads into the substrate.
conditions: for supporting the column load

subject: Steel Base Plates
rationale: Base plates provide a bearing surface that transfers compression, shear, and moment from the steel column to the foundation.
applicability: Steel base plates support steel columns only in the context of pinned or fixed base connections. In moment-resisting frames where base plates are part of a moment connection, the base plate still supports the column but the load transfer mechanism is more complex, involving bending moments in addition to axial load.
conditions: at the column base

subject: Steel Base Plates
rationale: Base plates are welded or bolted to the bottom of steel columns to create a fixed or pinned connection.
conditions: via welding or bolting

subject: Steel Base Plates
rationale: The base plate transfers loads through the anchor bolts and bearing onto the foundation surface.
conditions: via anchor bolts embedded in concrete

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: Steel moment frames rely on steel columns to resist vertical and lateral loads as part of the frame system.
conditions: when vertical load resistance is needed
exceptions: In some steel moment frame designs (e.g., with concrete-filled tube columns or composite construction), the column may be a composite steel-concrete member rather than a pure Steel Column. The condition 'when vertical load resistance is needed' is always true for any column in a moment frame, making it redundant or misleading.

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: Beams are essential horizontal members that work with columns to form the rigid frame.
exceptions: Some steel moment frame systems use reduced beam section (RBS) connections or other beam-to-column connections where the beam might be classified differently or where alternative structural elements (e.g., stub girders, transfer beams with different material specs) could be used. Also, in special cases like 'moment frame with staggered truss', beams may not be present in the conventional sense.

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: The frame must be anchored to a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: The moment frame provides structural support for exterior walls and cladding systems.
applicability: A Steel Moment Frame supports the Building Envelope through its beams and columns, but the assertion oversimplifies. The cladding attachment is typically via girts, sub-framing, or curtain wall systems that are secondary elements, not directly by the moment frame itself. The moment frame provides the structural backing, but the direct support relationship is indirect.
conditions: when cladding is attached to frame

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: A moment frame is composed of columns as primary vertical members.

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: Beams are integral horizontal members of the moment frame system.

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: Steel columns at the base are connected to foundation via base plates and anchor rods.

subject: Steel Moment Frames
rationale: In some designs, moment frames work in conjunction with concentric or eccentric braces.
applicability: The assertion says 'applicability: dual lateral systems' but the condition is 'when dual system is used'. This creates a circular dependency: the assertion only applies to dual systems but also has a condition checking if a dual system is used. Also, Steel Moment Frames do not inherently connect to Bracing Systems in all dual systems; the connection is through the floor/roof diaphragms or shared beams/columns, not typically a direct physical connection between the moment frame and the bracing frame.
conditions: when dual system is used
exceptions: not present in pure moment frame systems

subject: Steel Connections & Fasteners
rationale: Moment connections in steel frames rely on connections to transfer bending moments and resist lateral forces (wind, earthquake).
applicability: The applicability lists 'high-rise buildings' but in many high-rise steel buildings, lateral loads are often resisted by braced frames or core walls (concrete or steel-braced) rather than moment frames alone. Moment frames in very tall buildings can be inefficient due to excessive drift and member sizes. The assertion implies moment frames are the primary lateral system for high-rises, which is not universally true.
conditions: For lateral load resistance

subject: Steel Connections & Fasteners
rationale: Anchor bolts and base plates connect steel columns to concrete footings or foundations.
conditions: At column bases
exceptions: Steel column base plates are typically bolted or welded to anchor rods embedded in concrete, but not all steel-to-concrete connections are 'fasteners' in the sense covered by a 'Steel Connections & Fasteners' category. For instance, base plates with shear lugs, grouted base plates with leveling nuts, or moment-resisting base plates with stiffeners involve more than simple fasteners. Also, in precast concrete foundations or pile caps, the connection mechanism differs from typical bolted/welded fasteners.

subject: Composite Steel Decking
rationale: Composite steel decking requires a concrete topping slab poured over it to form a composite floor system. The concrete and steel deck act together to resist loads.
applicability: The assertion applies only to steel-framed buildings, but composite steel decking with concrete slabs is also used in concrete-framed buildings (where the deck spans between concrete beams or is supported by concrete walls). The applicability scope should be widened or the 'requires' relationship reconsidered for non-steel-frame structures.
conditions: When used as composite system
For composite action to develop

subject: Composite Steel Decking
rationale: Composite decking is typically supported by steel beams or joists. Shear studs are welded through the deck to the beams to create composite action.
applicability: The assertion applies only to steel-framed buildings, but composite decking can also be supported by concrete beams or joists in concrete-framed buildings, not exclusively by steel beams.
conditions: As structural support
For spanning between supports

subject: Composite Steel Decking
rationale: Welded wire mesh or rebar is typically placed in the concrete topping to control shrinkage and temperature cracking and to provide flexural reinforcement.
conditions: In concrete topping
To control cracking
exceptions: Some light-duty applications

Steel fiber-reinforced concrete (SFRC) or macro-synthetic fiber reinforcement can replace traditional welded wire reinforcement mesh in many composite slab applications, making reinforcement mesh not strictly required.

subject: Composite Steel Decking
rationale: The completed composite slab provides a substrate for floor finishes such as tile, carpet, wood flooring, or polished concrete.
conditions: After concrete cures
Once floor assembly is complete

subject: Steel Shear Studs
rationale: Shear studs are embedded in concrete to develop composite action; the concrete resists compression while studs transfer shear.
applicability: The 'depends_on Concrete Slab' condition is stated for composite action, but steel shear studs can also be embedded in lightweight concrete over metal deck or in precast concrete planks with shear pockets; the dependency is not strictly on a conventional 'Concrete Slab' in all cases.
conditions: for composite action in steel-concrete composite systems

subject: Steel Shear Studs
rationale: Shear studs are welded to the top flange of steel beams (typically W-shape or girders) to create a composite section.
conditions: studs are welded to the top flange

subject: Steel Shear Studs
rationale: The concrete must be adequately cured and achieve specified compressive strength before the composite section can resist design loads.
conditions: concrete must reach sufficient strength before composite loading
exceptions: In certain accelerated construction methods (e.g., precast composite systems with dry connections or bolted shear connectors), steel shear studs may not require concrete curing because no wet concrete is placed or curing is not the controlling path. Additionally, some codes allow partial composite action before full curing if studs are designed for it.

subject: Structural Steel Erection
rationale: Steel columns are the fundamental vertical elements that constitute the steel frame.
conditions: as primary vertical load-bearing members

subject: Structural Steel Erection
rationale: Steel beams (wide-flange, I-beams, etc.) form the horizontal framework and floor/roof supports.
conditions: as horizontal load-bearing members

subject: Structural Steel Erection
rationale: Properly cured concrete foundations (footings, piers, grade beams) are necessary to support erected steel.
conditions: cured and ready to receive anchor bolts and base plates

subject: Structural Steel Erection
rationale: Steel guide rails and support beams for elevator systems are installed as part of the steel erection scope.
conditions: within steel-framed elevator shafts

subject: Structural Steel Erection
rationale: Cross-bracing (steel rods, cables, or angles) or moment frames are connected to the steel frame to resist wind and seismic loads.
applicability: While structural steel erection often connects to a bracing system, some steel structures use moment-resisting frames instead of a separate bracing system for lateral stability. In such cases, there is no distinct 'bracing system' to connect to.
conditions: for lateral stability during and after erection

subject: Steel Column & Beam Installation
rationale: Steel columns must be supported by a foundation (concrete footings, pile caps, or grade beams) to transfer loads to the ground.
applicability: All building types with steel structures

The assertion 'requires Foundation' is accurate for most cases, but there is an important context limitation: in some steel structures, columns can be embedded directly into concrete piers or grade beams rather than a continuous foundation. This is common in certain industrial or agricultural buildings where individual pier foundations are used instead of a continuous strip or mat foundation.
conditions: Steel column base plates must be properly anchored to the foundation

subject: Steel Column & Beam Installation
rationale: Grout is used under steel base plates to ensure full bearing and load transfer to concrete foundations.
applicability: All building types with steel structures
conditions: For grouting of base plates and foundation anchorage

subject: Steel Column & Beam Installation
rationale: Steel columns transfer roof loads down to foundations; beams support roof decking.
applicability: All buildings with steel roof framing
conditions: Steel beams and columns form the primary vertical and lateral support system

subject: Steel Column & Beam Installation
rationale: Steel columns and beams are integral to the lateral load-resisting system, supporting braces and moment connections.
applicability: All steel structures requiring lateral stability

The assertion that column and beam installation 'supports Bracing System' is generally correct, but has context limitations: (1) in buildings where bracing is installed simultaneously with the frame (e.g., bolted braced frames erected in pre-assembled sections), the dependency may not follow a strict sequential order; (2) some bracing systems (e.g., tension-only rods) are installed after the main frame is fully erected and plumbed, but they are attached to the frame rather than 'supported' by the installation process itself. The relationship is better described as a prerequisite/sequencing dependency rather than structural support.
conditions: Columns and beams provide attachment points for lateral bracing (cross-bracing, moment frames)

subject: Steel Fireproofing Application
rationale: Steel fireproofing application is performed on structural steel members to provide fire resistance.
conditions: during application process
for fire resistance rating compliance
exceptions: concrete or timber structures

subject: Steel Fireproofing Application
rationale: Proper adhesion of fireproofing materials requires clean, primed steel surfaces.
conditions: before fireproofing material application

subject: Steel Fireproofing Application
rationale: Fireproofing insulates steel from high temperatures, preventing rapid strength loss and collapse.
conditions: during fire events
to maintain structural integrity
exceptions: if fireproofing is damaged or improperly applied

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Light-gauge steel framing requires structural connections (screws, bolts) to join members and transfer loads.
applicability: Not all light-gauge steel framing requires structural connections for load transfer — interior non-load-bearing partitions (e.g., dividing walls in commercial offices) do not transfer significant loads and may use slip-track connections or minimal fastening. The assertion should be scoped to load-bearing walls only.
conditions: for load transfer

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Any steel frame requires a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: to bear vertical loads

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Steel is highly conductive; insulation is critical to prevent thermal bridging and meet thermal performance.
conditions: to meet energy code requirements
exceptions: unconditioned spaces

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Moisture control is critical with steel framing to prevent corrosion and mold.
conditions: in cold climates to prevent condensation within wall cavities
exceptions: hot-humid climates where vapor retarder location differs

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Steel studs provide the substrate and attachment for exterior cladding materials.
conditions: as backup support structure
exceptions: Light-gauge steel framing does not support exterior cladding in all cases — when cladding is directly attached to sheathing (e.g., vinyl siding over foam+sheathing) or when cladding is self-supporting (e.g., structural glass, precast concrete panels that bypass the studs), the stud framing does not act as the backup support. Additionally, curtain wall systems often have their own mullions independent of the steel stud backup.

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Light-gauge steel studs support gypsum board or other interior finishes.
conditions: as substrate for drywall or paneling
exceptions: In some commercial applications, interior finishes are attached to furring channels, hat channels, or directly to structure bypassing the steel studs entirely (e.g., in shaft wall assemblies or when using clip systems for acoustical separation). subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Load-bearing steel stud walls can support roof trusses or rafters.

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Steel studs can support floor joists in multi-story light-gauge construction.
