exceptions: Floor structure support only applies when the steel stud wall is continuous through the floor platform. In platform-framed light-gauge steel construction, the wall below does not directly 'support' the floor — the floor sits on the foundation or a floor joist system with a track. Also, in balloon framing (less common but exists in LGSF), the relationship differs. The assertion is somewhat misstated as 'supports' rather than 'carries load from'.

subject: Light-Gauge Steel Framing
rationale: Light-gauge steel frames require strap bracing, shear walls, or moment frames for lateral stability.
applicability: Not all light-gauge steel framing requires a bracing system — interior non-load-bearing partitions do not require lateral bracing for wind/seismic. Additionally, some LGSF systems use the inherent diaphragm action of sheathing (e.g., plywood/OSB or steel sheet sheathing) rather than a discrete 'bracing system', so the term 'Bracing System' may be ambiguous and could include sheathing itself.
conditions: to resist lateral loads from wind and seismic

subject: Steel Canopies & Canopy Supports
rationale: Canopy supports must be anchored to appropriate foundations (concrete footings or piers) to ensure stability.
applicability: Small, lightweight steel canopy supports (e.g., residential entry canopies less than 10 sq ft) may be surface-mounted or wall-mounted without a separate foundation system, relying on existing slab or wall anchorage.
conditions: for canopy columns and supports
exceptions: Freestanding steel canopies (e.g., in mining or industrial sites) may rest directly on compacted granular pads or rock without a formal 'Foundation System' as defined in building codes. The assertion should note this exception for non-building-site installations.

subject: Steel Canopies & Canopy Supports
rationale: Steel canopies frequently support pendant or surface-mounted lighting fixtures.
applicability: canopies in commercial, public, or walkway areas
conditions: under-canopy or integrated lighting
exceptions: Some steel canopies (e.g., solid metal roof canopies without translucent panels or integrated raceways) do not support any lighting fixtures by design — they are purely weather shelters with no electrical provision.

subject: Steel Stairs & Railings
rationale: Steel stairs require proper foundations or supports at landings and base to distribute loads.
conditions: At base of stair stringers or landings
exceptions: Steel stairs in某些 situations (e.g., freestanding spiral stairs, stairs supported from side walls or beams) do not require a concrete foundation at the base of stringers or landings. They may be supported by steel beams, bearing walls, or other structural elements instead.

subject: Steel Stairs & Railings
rationale: Steel stairs support handrails which are mounted on or adjacent to the stair structure for user safety.
conditions: Always
exceptions: Not all steel stairs and railings include a handrail. Ship stairs, steep stair ladders (e.g., in industrial settings), or very short stair runs (e.g., 1-2 risers) may omit handrails per building code exceptions. Additionally, some stair designs use guardrails without a separate handrail.

subject: Steel Stairs & Railings
rationale: Steel stairs contain stringers (the inclined structural members that support the treads and risers).
conditions: Always
exceptions: Stringers may not be present in certain prefabricated mono-stringer stairs, center-support stairs, or helical stairs where treads are supported by a central column or spiral spine rather than traditional stringers. Also, some stair designs use a single center stringer, but the assertion 'contains Stringer' (implying at least one) is still true - however, some cantilevered stair designs embed treads into walls without any stringers.

subject: Steel Stairs & Railings
rationale: Steel stairs contain treads as the horizontal stepping surface.
conditions: Always

subject: Steel Stairs & Railings
rationale: Steel stairs may contain risers as the vertical face between treads.
conditions: When closed-riser stair design
exceptions: Open-riser stairs do not contain risers

subject: Steel Stairs & Railings
rationale: Steel stairs connect to floor slabs at landings and top/bottom terminations to provide vertical circulation.
conditions: At each landing or floor level
exceptions: Some steel stairs are self-supporting (e.g., freestanding spiral stairs, monumental stairs) and connect to the floor slab only at the base, not at every landing or floor level. Also, mezzanine stairs may connect to steel grating or decking rather than a concrete floor slab.

subject: Steel Roof Trusses & Purlin Systems
rationale: Truss loads ultimately bear on the foundation; settlement or foundation failure will compromise the truss system
applicability: The assertion applies to all permanent buildings, but truss-to-foundation load transfer can also occur through direct ground-bearing columns/posts (e.g., in pole barns or post-frame construction), where walls are not necessarily the intermediate load path. The condition explicitly requires 'walls/columns' but the assertion and applicability imply a broader scope that may not hold for all permanent building types.
conditions: loads from trusses must be transferred through walls/columns to foundations
exceptions: In some building designs, trusses bear directly on foundation-grade beams or ground slabs without intermediate walls or columns (e.g., portal frame buildings with trusses connected directly to pad footings via steel columns that are integral with the truss). The condition 'loads must be transferred through walls/columns' may not cover cases where trusses are directly supported on foundation walls or piers without distinct column elements.

subject: Embedded Steel Anchor Systems
rationale: Embedded steel anchors are mechanically reliant on the surrounding concrete to develop tensile and shear capacity through bond and bearing.
conditions: Anchor rods must be embedded into properly cured concrete
Concrete must have adequate compressive strength (typically ≥ 3000 psi)
Edge distances and embedment depths must meet code requirements
exceptions: May use grout or epoxy in lieu of concrete for retrofits

The assertion states Embedded Steel Anchor Systems requires Concrete, but anchors can also be installed into masonry (e.g., CMU walls) using specialized adhesive or mechanical anchors, provided the masonry has adequate pullout strength. The existing exception only mentions grout or epoxy retrofits, not masonry substrates.

The assertion requires concrete with compressive strength ≥ 3000 psi, but certain embedded anchor systems (e.g., adhesive anchors in lightweight concrete or thin slabs) may require higher strength (≥ 4000 psi) per ACI 318 or manufacturer specifications, making the stated minimum potentially unsafe in those contexts.

subject: Embedded Steel Anchor Systems
rationale: Embedded steel anchors (via base plates) transfer column axial loads, shear, and overturning moments into the concrete foundation.
applicability: Embedded Steel Anchor Systems also support steel column base plates in precast concrete structures and bridge applications, not only in structural steel and industrial buildings. The applicability section is narrower than actual use cases.
conditions: Anchor system must be designed for the column base plate forces
Typically requires leveling nuts and grout for proper load distribution

subject: Embedded Steel Anchor Systems
rationale: The exposed threaded end of the embedded anchor connects to a steel base plate via nuts and washers to transfer loads.
conditions: Base plate holes must align with anchor rods
Leveling nuts and grout are typically required for uniform load transfer
exceptions: The assertion states that leveling nuts and grout are 'typically required' for uniform load transfer. However, in some applications (e.g., direct embedment with base plate cast into concrete or use of high-strength non-shrink grout alternatives), leveling nuts may not be necessary, and grout is not always required (some designs use dry-pack or shims only).

subject: Float Glass
rationale: Float glass is the primary material used for windows, providing transparency and light transmission.
conditions: when installed in window frames

subject: Float Glass
rationale: Float glass can be further processed into tempered or laminated glass for doors.
conditions: when tempered or laminated

subject: Tempered Glass
rationale: Tempered glass provides the necessary strength and safety for shower enclosures.
applicability: The assertion's applicability lists 'commercial locker rooms,' but many commercial locker room showers are gang showers with high-temperature water exposure, where tempered glass may be at higher risk of thermal stress breakage if the glass is not properly heat-soak tested or if large temperature differentials occur.
conditions: when used as frameless glass doors and panels
exceptions: Tempered glass is not universally suitable for all shower enclosure types — for example, curved or bent shower enclosures often require laminated glass or specialized heat-bent tempered glass that may not be available from all fabricators, and the assertion does not account for this.

subject: Insulated Glass Unit (IGU)
rationale: IGU is physically connected to and supported by the surrounding window or curtain wall frame.
applicability: The assertion states the IGU 'connects_to' Window Frame when installed in an opening. However, in many curtain wall or structural glazing systems, the IGU is connected directly to the framing system (mullions/transoms) rather than to a traditional 'Window Frame' as a discrete element. In such cases, the IGU is not connecting to a window frame but to the curtain wall frame.
conditions: when installed in an opening

subject: Insulated Glass Unit (IGU)
rationale: Multiple glass panes with a gas cavity provide better sound attenuation than single glazing.
conditions: when different glass thicknesses or laminated glass are used
with wider cavity

subject: Low-E Coated Glass
rationale: Performance depends on proper SHGC selection matching climate zone and building orientation.
conditions: for energy modeling and code compliance

subject: Frosted Glass
rationale: Frosted glass is often required by building codes to be tempered when used in doors or hazardous locations to ensure safety.
conditions: frosted finish achieved through sandblasting or acid etching
exceptions: when using laminated glass with frosted interlayer

subject: Frosted Glass
rationale: Frosted glass requires a frame or structural support system for installation as a window.
conditions: when used as fixed glazing or operable window
exceptions: when used as free-standing partition without frame

Frosted glass used as a backsplash in kitchens or bathrooms (non-window, non-partition application) does not depend on a window frame. This use case falls outside both 'fixed glazing or operable window' and 'free-standing partition', yet is a common application. An additional exception should be added for these tile-replacement scenarios.

subject: Frosted Glass
rationale: Frosted glass panels are typically held in place with gaskets or sealants within framing systems.
applicability: The assertion 'Frosted Glass connects_to Glazing Gasket' is conditioned on curtain wall or storefront systems, but does not account for structural silicone glazing (SSG) systems where the glass is directly bonded to the frame with structural silicone and no gasket is used. While the existing exception mentions 'structurally glazed with silicone sealant only', this contradicts the core assertion—if structurally glazed, the glass does NOT connect to a glazing gasket. The assertion should either be conditioned to exclude SSG systems entirely, or be rephrased as a conditional connection that is absent in SSG applications.
conditions: when installed in curtain wall or storefront systems
exceptions: when structurally glazed with silicone sealant only

subject: Wired Glass
rationale: Wired glass is commonly installed as vision panels in fire doors to allow visibility while maintaining fire ratings.
applicability: The assertion does not specify which fire door assembly type (e.g., 20-minute, 45-minute, 60-minute, 90-minute) or the required fire-protection rating; wired glass typically only provides up to a 45-minute rating in limited applications and may not satisfy all fire door ratings.
conditions: When used as vision panels in fire doors
exceptions: Wired glass is no longer accepted as a fire-resistive glazing material in many building codes (e.g., IBC) for vision panels in fire door assemblies where fire-rated glazing is required, as it fails to meet modern hose-stream test requirements. It has been widely replaced by ceramic or other fire-rated glazing.

subject: Glass Partition
rationale: A glass partition often incorporates or connects to a glass door for access.
applicability: The assertion assumes glass partitions and glass doors are always compatible for connection, but this may not hold in all contexts. For example, a glass partition might be fixed (non-operable) while a glass door requires framing, hinges, and clearance that the partition's supporting structure may not accommodate. Also, fire-rated glass partitions may have specific requirements about openings that differ from standard glass doors.
conditions: when an opening is needed within the partition

subject: Glass Balustrade
rationale: Building codes typically require a handrail on top of or alongside glass balustrades for safety.
conditions: required by most building codes for fall protection
exceptions: some frameless all-glass systems may be exempt if glass is thick enough and meets code

International Building Code (IBC) and many jurisdictions allow handrail omission for glass balustrades that serve as guardrails in private residences (one- and two-family dwellings) where the drop is less than 30 inches, regardless of glass thickness.

Many building codes exempt glass balustrades in interior applications (e.g., mezzanine overlooks in offices) from handrail requirements if the glass is laminated and meets specific load and deflection criteria per IBC 2407.1.

subject: Glass Balustrade
rationale: The balustrade is physically connected to the floor slab or structure.
conditions: base channel or shoe is bolted to the floor
exceptions: some balustrades are side-fixed to walls

subject: Glass Door
rationale: A glass door must be mounted within a sturdy door frame to remain functional and aligned.
conditions: for structural support
exceptions: Some glass doors (e.g., frameless glass doors, pivot glass doors) can be mounted using only hinges, clamps, or patch fittings directly to the structure without a traditional door frame. The assertion that a glass door always requires a door frame for structural support does not hold for these frameless systems.

subject: Glass Door
rationale: Glass doors must be made of tempered glass to prevent shattering into dangerous shards.
conditions: for safety compliance in most building codes

subject: Glass Door
rationale: Weatherstripping seals gaps around the door to prevent air and water infiltration.
conditions: for exterior doors

subject: Glass Door
rationale: A threshold at the bottom provides a finished transition and helps with sealing.

subject: Glass Door
rationale: The glass is held in place by glazing materials such as gaskets or sealant.

subject: Glass Canopy
rationale: Where the canopy connects to a conditioned building interior, thermal breaks may be needed to prevent heat loss and condensation.
applicability: The assertion 'Glass Canopy requires Thermal Break Assembly' is conditioned on 'For thermally efficient building envelopes', but the existing exception only carves out 'unconditioned canopy spaces'. This does not address other scenarios where thermal breaks may be unnecessary or impractical — e.g., canopies in mild climates with minimal thermal deltas, temporary/seasonal canopies, or canopies with integrated shading that already mitigates thermal bridging. The scope of the existing exception is narrower than the full range of situations where thermal breaks are not required.
conditions: For thermally efficient building envelopes
exceptions: Not required for unconditioned canopy spaces

subject: Glass Skylight
rationale: A glass skylight requires a structural frame (aluminum, steel, or wood) to support and hold the glass in place.
applicability: The exception 'small skylights on low-rise buildings' is vague — there is no threshold for what constitutes 'small' (e.g., area in square feet) or 'low-rise' (number of stories). This ambiguity undermines the exception's enforceability.
conditions: must support dead load of glass and framing
must resist wind uplift
exceptions: small skylights on low-rise buildings

subject: Glass Skylight
rationale: Gaskets and sealants are required to create a watertight seal between the glass and frame.
conditions: must be weather-resistant
must accommodate thermal movement
exceptions: Glazing gaskets are not universally required for glass skylights; some systems use structural silicone glazing or compression-fit EPDM/TPV gaskets integrated into the frame, eliminating the need for a separate glazing gasket component.

subject: Glass Skylight
rationale: Thermal performance of the skylight depends on proper insulation at the curb and frame junctions.
conditions: around skylight curb or frame to prevent thermal bridging
exceptions: unconditioned spaces

subject: Glass Skylight
rationale: The skylight physically connects to the roof deck and framing to transfer loads and provide continuity.
applicability: The assertion says Glass Skylight 'connects_to Roof Structure' for all building types, but in some designs (e.g., curtain wall or monitor-style skylights integrated into a vertical wall assembly), the skylight connects to a wall or vertical frame rather than a roof structure.
conditions: through structural framing or curb

subject: Glass Block
rationale: Glass blocks are typically laid in mortar, which provides structural bonding between blocks.
applicability: Some glass block installations use silicone sealant or epoxy adhesives instead of mortar, particularly in non-load-bearing interior partitions or when using dry-stack systems. The assertion does not account for these alternative methods.
conditions: for setting and bonding glass block units

subject: Glass Block
rationale: Glass blocks expand/contract with temperature changes, so expansion joints at the perimeter prevent cracking.
conditions: at perimeter
to accommodate thermal movement

subject: Glass Block
rationale: Glass block units with air cavities provide some thermal resistance, contributing to building envelope performance.
conditions: when using insulated or hollow glass block units
exceptions: single-glazed blocks without insulation

Glass blocks do not inherently support thermal insulation; they have poor insulating values compared to insulated glazing units. Even insulated hollow blocks provide far less thermal resistance than typical wall assemblies. The assertion overstates the insulating capability.

subject: Glass Block
rationale: Glass blocks are fundamentally made of glass, typically hollow with two pressed-glass halves fused together.

subject: Glass Block
rationale: Glass block panels are often installed within window frames or specially designed aluminum framing systems.
conditions: when used as infill within a framed opening
exceptions: when glass block wall extends from slab to slab without frame

subject: Glass Block
rationale: Glass block has low compressive strength relative to masonry and is not typically used as a primary load-bearing material.
conditions: as primary structural element
exceptions: limited vertical load capacity in low-rise when reinforced

The existing exception allowing limited vertical load capacity in reinforced low-rise applications contradicts the primary assertion that glass block is 'unsuitable_for Load-Bearing Walls'. The assertion should either be softened or the exception should make clear this is a rare, engineered exception with strict limits rather than a general suitability claim.

subject: Spandrel Glass
rationale: Spandrel glass is typically installed within a structural framing system (e.g., curtain wall mullions and transoms) that supports it.
applicability: The assertion states that Spandrel Glass requires a Structural Framing System when used in curtain wall assemblies, but spandrel glass can also be installed in structural silicone glazed (SSG) curtain walls or point-supported glass systems where the glass is directly attached to the structure without a traditional stick framing system. Additionally, spandrel glass in unitized curtain wall systems may use a sub-frame that is integrated into the unit rather than a separate structural framing system.
conditions: when used in curtain wall assemblies

subject: Glass Installation
rationale: Frames provide structural support and mounting points for glass panels.
conditions: For framed glass systems

subject: Glass Installation
rationale: An IGU consists of multiple glass panes with spacer bars and sealants.
conditions: When installing sealed double/triple glazing

subject: Glass Installation
rationale: Glass is mounted into window frames as part of the installation.

subject: Glazing Sealant Application
rationale: Glazing gaskets provide the primary weather seal and compression around glass panels; sealant is often applied over or adjacent to gaskets to ensure airtightness.
conditions: When sealant is applied as part of a curtain wall or structural glazing system

subject: Glass Balustrade Assembly
rationale: The balustrade assembly is anchored to the building's floor structure.
conditions: Base of balustrade must connect to structural slab or floor framing
exceptions: Glass balustrade assemblies in some jurisdictions (e.g., Australia, New Zealand) may be permitted to connect to non-structural substrates such as timber decking or pavers if engineered brackets distribute loads to the structure indirectly, or if the balustrade is independently fixed to side walls or posts rather than the floor structure.

subject: Glass Cutting & Preparation On-Site
rationale: On-site cutting allows glass to be sized precisely for window frames, supporting proper glazing installation.
applicability: Modern window glazing installation typically relies on factory-fabricated windows with precise dimensions. On-site glass cutting introduces dimensional inaccuracies, increased risk of breakage, and voided manufacturer warranties. The assertion overlooks that most window glazing today is done with pre-cut, pre-glazed units delivered from a factory.
conditions: custom-sized windows are required
exceptions: On-site glass cutting is extremely rare in modern construction due to safety regulations (e.g., OSHA fall protection, eye protection), liability concerns, and the prevalence of factory-tempered or laminated glass that cannot be cut on-site. Glass cutting on-site may violate building codes in many jurisdictions that require safety glazing markings and edge finishing only possible in a factory setting.

subject: Glass Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The curtain wall acts as the primary exterior cladding, forming part of the building envelope.
applicability: The assertion does not specify the applicable climate contexts. In extreme climates (e.g., Arctic regions, desert environments with large thermal differentials, or areas with frequent hailstorms), glass curtain wall systems may have significantly reduced performance in supporting the building envelope due to thermal stress, condensation issues, or physical damage that even proper installation and sealing cannot fully mitigate.
conditions: When properly installed and sealed
exceptions: Glass curtain wall installation, even when properly installed and sealed, can fail to support the building envelope during extreme events such as large-magnitude seismic activity beyond design parameters, blast loads from explosions, or impact from windborne debris in tornado/hurricane conditions, leading to breach of the building envelope.

subject: Thermal Insulation
rationale: A vapor barrier prevents moisture from condensing within the insulation layer, which would reduce thermal performance and cause mold.
conditions: In cold climates
Where moisture condensation risk exists
exceptions: In some warm-humid climates vapor barriers may be omitted

The depends_on relationship implies thermal insulation requires a vapor barrier to function. However, in hot-humid climates (Zone 1-2), vapor barriers can trap moisture within assemblies because the dominant vapor drive is inward during air conditioning months, contrary to the cold-climate assumption. This is not covered by the existing exception wording.

subject: Thermal Insulation
rationale: Without air sealing, convective air movement bypasses the insulation, dramatically reducing its effective R-value.
applicability: The assertion 'Thermal Insulation depends_on Air Sealing' for 'optimal performance' is generally correct but lacks important nuance. In some building assemblies (e.g., unvented cathedral ceilings with closed-cell spray foam, or SIPs panels), the air sealing function is inherently integrated into the insulation itself, so it is not a separate dependency in the same sense as needing a distinct air barrier system. The relationship should clarify that this applies to standard framed construction where air sealing is a separate trade/step.
conditions: For optimal performance

subject: Acoustic Insulation
rationale: Many acoustic insulation materials (e.g., mineral wool) also provide thermal resistance, offering dual benefits.
applicability: The existing exception mentions 'some open-cell acoustic foams have low thermal R-value' but fails to note that many acoustic insulation products (e.g., fiberglass acoustic batts) have essentially identical thermal performance to standard thermal batts — thus the insulation is not 'improved' over a thermal-only batt, it is merely equivalent. The word 'improves' implies a positive delta that is not always present.
conditions: when using combined acoustic-thermal batts
exceptions: some open-cell acoustic foams have low thermal R-value

The assertion that 'Acoustic Insulation improves Thermal Insulation' even with the condition 'when using combined acoustic-thermal batts' has a counterexample: mineral wool acoustic batts have similar or slightly lower R-values per inch compared to high-performance rigid foam or spray foam insulation, meaning the acoustic batt does not necessarily 'improve' thermal insulation over standard thermal-only insulation — it may provide equal or less thermal performance depending on comparison baseline.

subject: Cavity Wall Insulation
rationale: Cavity wall insulation is installed within the cavity of a cavity wall; without the wall construction itself, there is no cavity to insulate.
conditions: The cavity must be at least 50mm wide
exceptions: Cavity wall insulation does not strictly require a cavity wall in all cases. There are insulation systems designed for solid walls (e.g., external wall insulation (EWI) or internal wall insulation (IWI)) that are also forms of cavity wall insulation substitutes. However, more precisely: the assertion states 'Cavity Wall Insulation requires Cavity Wall' — this is a tautology by naming convention, but could mislead if interpreted to mean that any building requiring cavity wall insulation must have a cavity wall. Buildings with solid walls can still achieve insulation via other methods, so the assertion is trivially true only if 'Cavity Wall Insulation' is defined as insulation injected into a cavity. The wording could be misinterpreted as a functional requirement rather than a definitional one.

subject: Floor Insulation
rationale: Floor insulation typically requires a vapor barrier to prevent moisture migration from the ground or unheated spaces into the insulation layer, which could reduce thermal performance and cause mold.
conditions: in cold climates
when floor is above unheated space
exceptions: when using closed-cell spray foam insulation

The existing exception already lists closed-cell spray foam, but there are additional exceptions: open-cell spray foam with vapor-permeable air barrier systems, certain rigid foam insulations with sufficient R-value (e.g., polyiso, XPS, EPS above grade) that act as their own vapor retarders, and cases where a vapor barrier is omitted due to moisture risk analysis (e.g., ventilated crawlspaces).

subject: Floor Insulation
rationale: Air sealing is required to prevent air movement through the insulation which would reduce its effective R-value and cause heat loss.
applicability: The assertion states 'Floor Insulation requires Air Sealing' with condition 'before insulation installation' for all building types. However, this does not specify which components need air sealing - rim joists, subfloor penetrations, floor-wall junctions, or all of the above. The scope of air sealing required is undefined, making the assertion ambiguous for practical application.
conditions: before insulation installation

subject: Floor Insulation
rationale: Floor insulation should connect to wall insulation at perimeter junctions to maintain a continuous thermal barrier and prevent thermal bridging.
applicability: The assertion states that floor insulation connects to wall insulation at floor-to-wall junctions for all building types, but this does not apply to slab-on-grade foundations where there is no floor assembly above an unheated space, or to buildings with dropped/separated floor systems that are structurally independent from the walls.
conditions: at floor-to-wall junctions
for continuous thermal envelope

subject: Spray Foam Insulation
rationale: Spray foam insulation often requires a vapor barrier in certain climate zones to prevent moisture accumulation within the assembly.
applicability: The assertion states 'Spray Foam Insulation requires Vapor barrier' but only applies in cold climates and interior-side installation. In warm/hot climates or for exterior installations, the requirement may differ or be reversed (vapor barrier may need to be on the opposite side). Neither condition explicitly excludes warm climates or exterior-side installations, potentially misleading users who apply the assertion outside its intended context.
conditions: In cold climates
When installed on interior side of wall
exceptions: Closed-cell spray foam may act as its own vapor barrier

subject: Rigid Board Insulation
rationale: Rigid board insulation often requires a vapor barrier on the warm-in-winter side to prevent moisture condensation within the wall assembly.
conditions: when installed on interior side in cold climates
when installed on exterior side in warm climates
exceptions: There are exceptions where no separate vapor barrier is needed: (1) when the rigid board insulation itself has sufficient vapor permeance classification (e.g., closed-cell foam with thickness meeting class I or II vapor retarder criteria per IRC), and (2) in climate zones with lesser heating/cooling requirements where codes do not mandate a vapor barrier.

subject: Rigid Board Insulation
rationale: Rigid board insulation can provide a backing surface for certain types of exterior cladding systems.
conditions: when used as a continuous insulation layer on exterior walls
exceptions: when cladding is attached directly through insulation to the structure

subject: Rigid Board Insulation
rationale: Proper integration with flashing systems is required to direct water away from the insulation and building envelope.
conditions: at window and door openings
at roof-to-wall intersections
at base of wall
exceptions: Flashing is not universally required at all these locations when rigid board insulation is used. For example, when rigid board insulation is installed over an existing weather-resistive barrier (WRB) and water-managed assembly that already includes flashing at these penetration points, additional flashing specifically for the insulation layer is not needed. Also, in adhered or fully-bonded insulation systems, the bond layer may seal the perimeter making separate flashing redundant at certain junctions.

subject: Rigid Board Insulation
rationale: Rigid board insulation is installed directly against or between wall framing members.
applicability: The assertion says Rigid Board Insulation 'connects_to Wall Framing' but this is ambiguous. In most assemblies, rigid board insulation is attached through the insulation to the framing (e.g., with long fasteners or cap nails), meaning it physically connects to the framing. However, in many continuous insulation applications, the insulation is attached to sheathing and the framing is a separate structural layer — the insulation does not directly connect to the framing. The term 'connects_to' is too strong and may imply direct attachment that does not always exist.
conditions: when used in wall assemblies

subject: Rigid Board Insulation
rationale: Rigid board insulation is attached to the roof deck in roofing assemblies.
conditions: when used in roofing assemblies
exceptions: On steep-slope roofs, rigid board insulation is typically installed above the roof deck (not connecting to it directly if there is an intervening air gap, slip sheet, or underlayment). Additionally, in some vented roof assemblies for steep-slope roofs, the insulation is placed between rafters or at the ceiling plane rather than against the deck, meaning there is no physical connection to the roof deck.

subject: Batt Insulation
rationale: Batt insulation in exterior walls typically requires a vapor barrier (usually facing) on the warm side to prevent moisture condensation within the insulation.
applicability: Exception states 'Not required in unheated spaces' but this contradicts the main assertion's applicability including 'Residential; Commercial' - unheated spaces such as garages, attics, and crawlspaces are present in both residential and commercial buildings. The exception should be explicitly noted as being within the stated applicability scope.
conditions: When installed in exterior walls in cold climates
exceptions: Not required in unheated spaces or arid climates

subject: Batt Insulation
rationale: Air sealing is required before installing batt insulation to prevent air movement that would reduce thermal performance.
conditions: Always
exceptions: Batt insulation does not inherently require air sealing in all cases. Air sealing is a separate building envelope strategy. While air sealing is always recommended for the overall building envelope, the batt insulation material itself does not 'require' air sealing to function - it can provide thermal resistance even without air sealing, though performance will be reduced. The assertion conflates best practice with a material requirement.

subject: Loose-Fill Insulation
rationale: Loose-fill insulation (e.g., cellulose, fiberglass) typically requires a vapor barrier on the warm side of the wall to prevent condensation within the insulation layer.
conditions: when installed in cold climates
to prevent moisture infiltration
exceptions: vapor-permeable loose-fill insulation types may not require separate vapor barrier

subject: Loose-Fill Insulation
rationale: Loose-fill insulation is susceptible to air movement through the material, which significantly reduces its R-value; an air barrier is essential for performance.
applicability: The assertion states loose-fill insulation 'requires' an air barrier for all building types, but in unconditioned attic spaces where loose-fill insulation is installed above the ceiling plane (attic floor), the air barrier is typically required at the ceiling level (drywall/ceiling membrane) rather than within the insulation itself. The loose-fill material does not itself require an integral air barrier—the assembly does. This context is missing.
conditions: to maintain thermal performance
prevent air leakage
exceptions: some dense-pack installations may reduce need

subject: Insulated Concrete Forms (ICFs)
rationale: ICFs are hollow foam blocks that require concrete to be poured into them to create the structural wall.
conditions: Ready-mix concrete is poured into the ICF forms

subject: Insulated Concrete Forms (ICFs)
rationale: Temporary bracing is essential to prevent ICF wall blowouts and maintain alignment during concrete placement.
conditions: Required during concrete pour and curing to keep walls plumb and aligned

subject: Insulated Concrete Forms (ICFs)
rationale: ICF walls can trap moisture; a vapor barrier may be needed on the exterior side in certain climates.
applicability: The assertion states ICFs 'requires Vapor barrier' but the condition says 'May be required on exterior depending on climate zone'. This indicates it is not a universal requirement — in many climate zones a vapor barrier is not needed or could even be detrimental (e.g., in warm climates where inward vapor drive occurs). The assertion should reflect this conditional nature rather than stating it as a requirement.
conditions: May be required on exterior depending on climate zone

subject: Structural Insulated Panels (SIPs)
rationale: SIPs are panelized elements that typically need a primary structural frame (wood or steel) for load distribution, though they can act as load-bearing wall panels themselves up to certain heights.
conditions: SIPs require a structural frame to transfer loads to foundations
exceptions: Some SIP designs are self-supporting for limited spans

SIPs can be used in post-and-beam or timber frame construction where the SIPs are infill panels that bear directly on the foundation or sill plate, not on an independent structural frame. The existing exception only mentions self-supporting spans, but omits the case where they are infill within a frame that is not a 'structural framing' system in the conventional stud-wall sense.

subject: Structural Insulated Panels (SIPs)
rationale: SIPs must be anchored to a suitable foundation to transfer vertical and lateral loads to the ground.
conditions: Must be level and properly designed for panel loads
exceptions: In panelized foundation systems (e.g., permanent wood foundations or insulated concrete forms used as foundation), SIPs can be integrated into the foundation system itself rather than requiring a separate 'Foundation System' as a prerequisite. Some SIP structures use continuous footing-only designs with thickened edge slabs that serve as both foundation and floor, eliminating the need for a conventional foundation system.

subject: Structural Insulated Panels (SIPs)
rationale: SIP roof panels serve as both structural deck and insulation, supporting the roofing membrane or shingles directly.
conditions: SIP roof panels provide the structural deck for roofing materials

subject: Structural Insulated Panels (SIPs)
rationale: The interior face of SIPs can directly receive gypsum board or other interior finish materials.
applicability: In high-humidity environments (e.g., bathrooms, saunas, indoor pools) or where fire-rated assemblies are required, the interior OSB face of SIPs is NOT a suitable nailing surface for direct drywall application without additional furring strips, a vapor barrier, or a fire-rated underlayment. Direct attachment to OSB in these contexts can lead to moisture damage or fire code violations.
conditions: Interior OSB face provides nailing surface for drywall or paneling

subject: Vapor Retarder
rationale: A vapor retarder often requires a vapor barrier on the opposite side to control moisture migration properly.
conditions: When vapor retarder is used on warm side of assembly
exceptions: In hot-humid climates (e.g., Gulf Coast), vapor retarders are often omitted entirely on the interior side, and a vapor barrier would not be required either. The condition 'When vapor retarder is used on warm side of assembly' does not account for climate-specific exceptions.

subject: Vapor Retarder
rationale: Insulation helps keep the vapor retarder at a temperature above the dew point, preventing condensation.
conditions: To maintain thermal gradient and prevent condensation within assembly
exceptions: In unvented roof assemblies with air-impermeable spray foam insulation, a separate vapor retarder may not be required because the insulation itself acts as the vapor retarder. The assertion does not account for this exception.

subject: Vapor Retarder
rationale: Air leakage can carry moisture past the vapor retarder, reducing its effectiveness.
conditions: To prevent air-transported moisture bypassing the vapor retarder
exceptions: In assemblies using air-impermeable insulation (e.g., closed-cell spray foam), the air sealing function is inherently provided by the insulation itself, so vapor retarder does not strictly depend on separate air sealing. The assertion does not account for this exception.

subject: Vapor Retarder
rationale: Vapor retarder protects structural elements from moisture damage and rot caused by condensation.
applicability: The existing exception mentions hot-humid climates but does not address mixed-humid climates where the warm side may vary seasonally, or cold climates where vapor retarders may be placed on the exterior side of walls in certain designs (e.g., 'smart' vapor retarders).
conditions: When installed on the warm-in-winter side of the insulation
exceptions: In hot-humid climates where vapor retarder may be omitted or placed differently

subject: Vapor Retarder
rationale: Vapor retarder prevents moisture from entering the insulation, maintaining its thermal performance.
conditions: When insulation is within a wall/roof cavity subject to interior humidity

subject: Air Sealing
rationale: Weatherstripping seals gaps around doors and windows to prevent air leakage.
applicability: The assertion states 'Air Sealing requires Weatherstripping' but the condition narrows this to operable components only. However, air sealing encompasses far more than weatherstripping (e.g., caulking, spray foam, gaskets, tape). The title/assertion implies a general dependency that is misleading — weatherstripping is just one air sealing measure for operable joints, not a general requirement for all air sealing.
conditions: Applied to operable building components such as doors and windows
exceptions: Fixed windows and non-operable doors do not require weatherstripping

subject: Bituminous Membrane
rationale: In conventional warm roof assemblies, the bituminous membrane can support insulation placed above it.
conditions: when used as a vapor barrier or base layer beneath insulation
exceptions: inverted roof membrane assembly (IRMA) places insulation above the membrane

subject: Bituminous Membrane
rationale: Flashing details are required to seal membrane terminations and transitions.
applicability: The assertion that Bituminous Membrane requires Flashing does not hold for fully adhered bituminous sheet membranes used as below-grade waterproofing on foundation walls, where the membrane itself is often extended up the wall and terminated with a reglet or surface-sealed termination bar—not conventional flashing. Additionally, some self-adhered bituminous membranes used in plaza deck or planter applications are designed to be terminated with sealant and compression bars rather than metal or membrane flashing. The assertion should be conditioned to distinguish between roofing applications (where edge flashing is typical) and below-grade waterproofing (where termination details differ).
conditions: at edges, penetrations, and terminations

subject: EPDM Membrane
rationale: EPDM membrane is connected to metal, pipe, or preformed flashing details at roof penetrations and perimeter edges.
conditions: at roof edges, penetrations, and terminations
exceptions: EPDM membrane typically connects to flashing via a splice or cover strip, not directly. The membrane itself does not directly 'connect to' flashing in a physical joint sense; rather, flashing is installed over or under the membrane at terminations. This phrasing could mislead about the actual assembly detail.

subject: EPDM Membrane
rationale: EPDM membrane terminates into or laps over roof drain flanges to direct water into the drainage system.
applicability: The assertion applies only to low-slope roofs, which is correctly stated. However, it fails to note that on certain low-slope roof assemblies (e.g., protected membrane/IRMA roofs where insulation is above the membrane), the connection details at drains differ significantly because the membrane is beneath the insulation layer.
conditions: at roof drains and scuppers
exceptions: EPDM membrane does not typically 'connect to' drainage system components directly. At roof drains, a clamping ring or drain bowl assembly secures the membrane; the membrane is sealed to the drain flange, not connected to the drainage pipe system itself. At scuppers, the membrane typically extends into or over the scupper liner, not directly to the drainage system.

subject: PVC/TPO Membrane
rationale: A cover board (e.g., gypsum board or densglass) provides a uniform surface and protects insulation during membrane installation.
applicability: The assertion does not specify which type of cover board (e.g., gypsum, high-density polyiso, wood fiber) is acceptable, and the requirement for a cover board varies significantly by local building codes, wind uplift ratings, and fire rating requirements. The assertion is too broad without these contextual dependencies.
conditions: Used when a separation layer is needed between insulation and membrane
exceptions: May be omitted in some direct-adhered systems

PVC and TPO membranes are often installed directly over polyisocyanurate (polyiso) insulation without a separate cover board in many adhered single-ply systems, as the cover board is only required when using mechanically attached systems or specific insulation types (e.g., perlite). The existing exception mentions 'direct-adhered systems' but the assertion is stated as a hard dependency.

subject: PVC/TPO Membrane
