exceptions: Adhered brick veneer (thin brick) does not require wall ties — it is bonded directly to a substrate. The assertion that 'Brick Veneer requires Wall Tie' is false for adhered veneer systems.

subject: Brick Veneer
rationale: Flashing is required to direct moisture outward through weep holes and protect the structure behind.
conditions: at base of wall, above openings, below windows
exceptions: Adhered thin brick veneer systems may not require flashing at the same locations or in the same manner as anchored veneer, as they are often installed over a waterproofed substrate and do not have a cavity requiring drainage. The assertion assumes a cavity wall configuration.

subject: Brick Veneer
rationale: Brick veneer is a non-loadbearing cladding that depends on a foundation or structural support to carry its weight.
conditions: brick veneer must be supported on a structural foundation or shelf angle

subject: Brick Veneer
rationale: Brick veneer is a key component of the building envelope, providing durability and aesthetics.
conditions: as part of the exterior cladding system

subject: Brick Veneer
rationale: The brick veneer assembly includes the mortar joints that bond the bricks together.
conditions: between brick units
exceptions: Adhered thin brick veneer may use thin-set adhesive rather than conventional mortar joints between units. In some adhered systems, the gap between bricks is filled with grout or adhesive, not traditional mortar.

subject: Brick Veneer
rationale: Brick veneer is not designed to carry structural loads; it is a non-loadbearing facade system.
conditions: brick veneer is a non-structural cladding only

subject: Brick Pillar/Pier
rationale: A brick pillar/pier requires a proper foundation to distribute vertical loads to the ground and prevent settlement or overturning.
conditions: Load-bearing application
exceptions: Non-structural decorative pillars

In some geotechnical conditions (e.g., competent bedrock at shallow depth), a brick pillar/pier can be founded directly on rock without a concrete foundation, particularly in traditional or vernacular construction.

subject: Brick Pillar/Pier
rationale: Bricks are bonded together with mortar to form a monolithic structural element.
conditions: All brick pillars
exceptions: Dry-stack brick systems with special interlocking blocks

subject: Brick Pillar/Pier
rationale: Brick pillars/piers act as vertical supports for beams in framed or load-bearing structures.
conditions: Load-bearing pillar
exceptions: Decorative non-load-bearing pillars

subject: Brick Pillar/Pier
rationale: Pillars can support floor slabs directly or through beams.
conditions: Load-bearing pillar
exceptions: Decorative use only

subject: Brick Pillar/Pier
rationale: Brick piers commonly support roof trusses or roof slabs in masonry buildings.
conditions: Pillar extends to roof level
exceptions: Pillars only supporting intermediate floors

subject: Brick Pillar/Pier
rationale: A brick pier often connects to or bears on a foundation wall or strip footing for load transfer.
conditions: Pillar is part of continuous foundation system
exceptions: Isolated pad footing under pillar

subject: Brick Pillar/Pier
rationale: Tie beams connect pillars at various levels to provide lateral stability and distribute loads.
conditions: Plinth level or roof level tie beam present
exceptions: Very short pillars without tie beams

In some seismic design contexts, tie beams may be absent even at plinth or roof level by design choice (e.g., in low-seismicity regions or where alternative lateral load paths exist). The existing exception only covers 'very short pillars' but not taller pillars in low-seismic zones where tie beams are deliberately omitted.

subject: Brick Coping
rationale: Brick coping is typically laid with mortar to bond bricks and secure the assembly.
conditions: for bonding bricks together

subject: Brick Coping
rationale: Flashing is installed beneath brick coping to direct water away from the wall assembly.
applicability: 'Brick Coping requires Flashing' with condition 'below the coping to prevent water ingress' is generally correct, but there are exceptions. Some modern coping systems are designed as fully waterproofed units with integral drip edges that do not require separate flashing; also, in some climate contexts, flashing may be omitted if the parapet is fully encapsulated.
conditions: below the coping to prevent water ingress

subject: Brick Coping
rationale: Brick coping is most commonly used as a capping on parapet walls.
conditions: brick coping is installed on top of parapet walls

subject: Brick Cavity Wall
rationale: A brick cavity wall requires a concrete foundation to distribute its load evenly and prevent settlement.
conditions: Load-bearing wall
exceptions: Non-load-bearing partitions

subject: Brick Cavity Wall
rationale: Wall ties are essential to connect the inner and outer wythes of a brick cavity wall, providing structural stability.
conditions: All cavity walls

subject: Brick Cavity Wall
rationale: Load-bearing brick cavity walls can support roof loads transferred via wall plates.
conditions: Load-bearing cavity wall
exceptions: Non-load-bearing walls

In buildings where roof loads are transferred via a separate structural frame (e.g., steel or timber frame) that is independent of the masonry, a load-bearing cavity wall does not support the roof structure at all. This is common in industrial and some commercial buildings.

subject: Brick Cavity Wall
rationale: The separated leaves of a cavity wall provide improved sound insulation compared to solid walls.
conditions: Cavity width adequate
Mass of leaves sufficient

subject: Brick Corbelling
rationale: Brick corbelling typically projects from a load-bearing wall to provide structural support for upper elements.
applicability: The assertion states 'Brick Corbelling requires Load-Bearing Wall' but only under the condition 'when used as structural support'. Brick corbelling is decorative in many contexts (e.g., chimney tops, decorative cornices) where it does not serve as structural support but is still brick corbelling. The condition essentially tautologically restates the requirement rather than capturing genuine exceptions.
conditions: when used as structural support

subject: Brick Corbelling
rationale: Mortar is essential for bonding the bricks in a corbelled arrangement, especially for projecting courses.
conditions: for bonding bricks in corbelled courses
exceptions: dry-stack systems

While the assertion correctly notes that dry-stack systems are an existing exception, corbelling in historic lime mortar constructions can also be effectively executed without modern mortar - the bricks may rely purely on gravity and interlocking geometry. Dry-stack is only one type of mortarless system.

subject: Brick Corbelling
rationale: Corbelled brickwork transfers loads down to the foundation; a proper foundation is critical for stability.
applicability: The assertion 'Brick Corbelling depends_on Foundation' for 'overall wall stability' is too sweeping. Small-scale decorative corbelling (e.g., a single brick projecting from a wall) does not create stability dependencies on the foundation. The dependency applies only to substantial corbelled projections that impose significant eccentric loads.
conditions: for overall wall stability

subject: Brick Lintel
rationale: Brick lintels require mortar to bond the bricks together and transfer loads.
conditions: for bedding bricks

subject: Brick Lintel
rationale: The brick lintel sits directly above the window frame, forming a connection.
conditions: when installed above a window opening
exceptions: door openings

In continuous (running) brick lintels that span multiple openings (e.g., a brick band course acting as a lintel over several windows), the same lintel connects to multiple window frames as well as the wall sections between windows, making the one-to-one 'connects_to Window Frame' assertion incomplete.

subject: Brick Lintel
rationale: The brick lintel sits directly above the door frame, forming a connection.
conditions: when installed above a door opening
exceptions: window openings

subject: Brick Lintel
rationale: By definition, a brick lintel is composed of bricks.
conditions: a brick lintel is itself built of bricks

subject: Brickwork Installation
rationale: Brickwork installation fundamentally requires mortar to bond bricks together.
conditions: Fresh mortar must be mixed to correct consistency
exceptions: Thin brick veneer systems (adhered or anchored) may use adhesive or mechanical fasteners instead of traditional mortar, and do not require a mortar bed.

subject: Brickwork Installation
rationale: Bricks are the primary material being installed.
conditions: Bricks must be of appropriate grade and type for the application

subject: Brickwork Installation
rationale: Brickwork requires a stable, level foundation to build upon.
conditions: Must be properly cured and level before brickwork begins
exceptions: Brick veneer over wood-frame or steel-stud structures does not require a concrete foundation; it can be supported on the structural floor slab, shelf angles, or a continuous angle anchored to the frame.
Retaining walls or freestanding brick garden walls can be built on compacted gravel footings or strip footings rather than a full concrete foundation.

subject: Brickwork Installation
rationale: Brickwork interfaces with floor slabs to provide lateral stability.
applicability: Industrial applicability is excluded while it is included in the other assertions, but industrial buildings frequently have brickwork around openings or as architectural cladding that does connect to floor slabs, creating an inconsistency.
conditions: Brickwork must be tied to floor slabs at each floor level
exceptions: In single-story residential construction (which is included in the applicability), there is no upper floor slab for brickwork to connect to, making the assertion inapplicable for that case.

subject: Brick Joint Pointing
rationale: Brick joint pointing requires mortar to fill and seal the joints between bricks.
conditions: for filling joints between bricks

subject: Brick Joint Pointing
rationale: Pointing is the material that fills and contains the mortar joints between bricks.
conditions: the pointing material fills the joint space

subject: Brick Wall Damp-Proofing
rationale: DPC layers are bedded in mortar to integrate them into the brick wall construction.
conditions: For DPC installation during wall construction

subject: Brick Wall Damp-Proofing
rationale: In cavity walls, the DPC bridges the cavity and incorporates weep holes, depending on the cavity design to function.
conditions: For cavity wall DPC systems

subject: Brick Wall Damp-Proofing
rationale: Effective damp-proofing protects interior finishes (plaster, paint, wallpaper) from moisture damage and salt attack.
applicability: The assertion says Brick Wall Damp-Proofing 'supports' Interior Wall Finishes when damp-proofing is effective, but this is overly broad. Effective DPC prevents rising damp, which is necessary but not sufficient for interior wall finishes. For example, interior finishes also require condensation control, surface preparation, and structural soundness. DPC alone does not 'support' finishes in a direct causal sense.
conditions: When damp-proofing is effective

subject: Brick Tying and Wall Starter Installation
rationale: Mortar bonds bricks together and to ties; without it bricks cannot be laid.
applicability: The existing exception mentions 'some engineered systems may use adhesive or mechanical connections,' but this is framed narrowly; in practice, wall starters for brick veneer over steel or wood-framed construction commonly use adjustable masonry ties (seismic ties) that are mechanically fastened to the structure, with no mortar involved at the tie attachment point.
conditions: Type N or Type S mortar typical
Must have proper mix proportions
exceptions: Some engineered systems may use adhesive or mechanical connections

Wall starters are often mechanically anchored (bolted or shot-fired) into existing concrete slabs or foundations before any mortar is applied — the starter itself does not require mortar for its installation, only the bricks that engage with it later.

subject: Brickwork Curing and Protection
rationale: Curing compounds can be applied as an alternative to water curing to retain moisture in freshly laid brickwork.
applicability: The assertion states that brickwork curing and protection requires a curing compound when continuous water curing is not feasible, but fails to account for alternative curing methods such as wet hessian/burlap covering, plastic sheeting, or spray-applied water, which are commonly accepted curing approaches that do not involve curing compounds. This oversimplifies the range of acceptable alternatives to continuous water curing.
conditions: when continuous water curing is not feasible

subject: Standard Hollow CMU
rationale: CMU walls often carry roof loads directly or through roof beams/trusses.
applicability: The assertion states 'Standard Hollow CMU supports Roof Structure' but does not specify critical parameters such as wall height, roof span, seismic zone, wind loads, or CMU thickness/grade. A standard 6-inch hollow CMU may fail under moderate roof loads in certain configurations, while 8-inch or reinforced CMU may be required.
conditions: when used as load-bearing walls
exceptions: In high-seismic regions (e.g., Seismic Design Categories D, E, F), standard hollow CMU acting as load-bearing walls for roof structure typically requires reinforcement (grouted cells and rebar) beyond 'standard hollow CMU' as commonly understood. Unreinforced hollow CMU is often not permitted for structural roof support in these areas per building codes (e.g., IBC, ASCE 7).

subject: Solid CMU
rationale: Solid CMU (concrete masonry units) must be bonded with mortar to form a structural wall assembly.
applicability: Solid CMU does not always require mortar when using surface-bonded (dry-stack) concrete masonry systems, which use a surface bonding cement applied to the faces instead of traditional mortar between courses. Also applies to interlocking dry-stack CMU systems that rely on mechanical interlock.
conditions: for bonding units together

subject: Solid CMU
rationale: Grout is used to fill cores containing reinforcement, bonding the reinforcement to the masonry and increasing compressive strength.
applicability: Grout may also be required in non-reinforced walls for other purposes such as fire ratings, sound transmission control, or increased mass for thermal performance, not solely for reinforcement or structural strength. The condition is under-specified.
conditions: when cells are to be filled for reinforcement or structural strength
exceptions: unreinforced, non-load-bearing walls may not require grout

subject: Solid CMU
rationale: Solid CMU bearing walls support floor and roof structures above.
conditions: when used as load-bearing walls
exceptions: non-load-bearing partitions do not support floor slabs

subject: Solid CMU
rationale: CMU walls can support roof beams, trusses, or slabs.
conditions: when used as load-bearing walls
exceptions: non-load-bearing walls

subject: Solid CMU
rationale: Bond beams are continuous horizontal courses of CMU filled with grout and reinforcement tying the wall together.
conditions: at roof level, floor levels, or as horizontal reinforcement

subject: Lightweight CMU
rationale: Lightweight CMU units are laid with mortar to create a structural wall assembly.
conditions: for bonding units together
exceptions: Dry-stack (surface-bonded) CMU systems do not require conventional mortar between units; they use surface bonding cement applied to both faces. This is a known construction method where lightweight CMU is laid without mortar joints.

subject: Lightweight CMU
rationale: Grout is poured into CMU cells to bond reinforcement and increase structural capacity.
conditions: when reinforcing is required
to fill cells containing rebar
exceptions: partially grouted walls may require grout only in specific cells

In above-grade, non-structural partition walls made of lightweight CMU, grout is generally not required at all even in code-compliant construction, as these walls do not carry structural loads and reinforcing is optional or absent.

subject: Lightweight CMU
rationale: Load-bearing CMU walls support floor and roof structural elements.
applicability: Lightweight CMU has lower compressive strength than normal-weight CMU (typically 1,000-1,900 psi vs 1,900-3,000+ psi). In multi-story buildings with higher floor loads, lightweight CMU may not have sufficient load-bearing capacity to support floor slabs without additional reinforcement or increased wall thickness, limiting this assertion to lower-rise applications or lighter floor systems.
conditions: when used as load-bearing walls
exceptions: Lightweight CMU walls supporting floor slabs must also comply with minimum bearing length requirements (typically 3-4 inches per building codes) and may require bearing plates or bond beams at the slab level. Without these conditions, the wall may not adequately support the floor slab regardless of being load-bearing.

subject: Lightweight CMU
rationale: CMU walls can support roof trusses, joists, or slabs.
conditions: when walls are load-bearing
exceptions: In high-wind or high-seismic regions, lightweight CMU walls supporting roof structures typically require a continuous bond beam at the roof level and specific anchorage to the roof diaphragm. Without detailing these conditions, the assertion may be misleading as the CMU alone does not 'support' the roof without these elements.

subject: Lightweight CMU
rationale: Bond beams tie CMU walls together horizontally and distribute loads.
conditions: at the top of walls or at floor levels
for horizontal structural continuity
exceptions: In non-seismic zones with unreinforced masonry, bond beams are often omitted entirely, yet lightweight CMU walls are still commonly used. The connection is not universal across all CMU wall types.

subject: Ground-Face/Polished CMU
rationale: CMU blocks are typically laid with mortar to create a cohesive wall assembly.
applicability: The assertion 'Ground-Face/Polished CMU depends_on Mortar for bonding CMU units together' does not account for adhered masonry veneer systems where thin-set or epoxy adhesives are used instead of traditional mortar for bonding ground-face or polished CMU to substrates.
conditions: for bonding CMU units together
exceptions: dry-stack applications may use surface bonding

Ground-face and polished CMU units can also be bonded using structural epoxy or acrylic adhesives in specialized applications such as post-installed connections, seismic retrofits, or panelized assemblies where mortar joints are not used.

subject: Split-Face CMU
rationale: Split-face CMU blocks require mortar to be bonded together into a wall assembly.
applicability: Split-Face CMU units can also be stacked dry (without mortar) in certain landscape or non-structural partition applications, so the assertion that mortar is always required regardless of context is too broad. Many thin veneer split-face systems use adhesive rather than mortar.
conditions: for bonding units together

subject: Split-Face CMU
rationale: Grout is poured into CMU cores to bond rebar and blocks together.
conditions: when reinforcing steel is used
to fill cells containing rebar
exceptions: unreinforced walls do not require grout

Grouted cells are not required when post-tensioning is used with unbonded tendons – in such systems, cells are left hollow for tendon installation but are not grouted in the conventional sense. This is a documented exception in reinforced masonry.

subject: Split-Face CMU
rationale: Flashing directs water out of the wall assembly and prevents moisture ingress.
conditions: at base of walls
above openings
at roof intersections

subject: Split-Face CMU
rationale: CMU walls are constructed on and anchored to the building foundation.
applicability: The assertion says 'all CMU walls' connect to foundation at wall base, but this does not account for walls supported on grade beams, slab-on-grade with turned-down footings, or walls that start above foundation (e.g., second-story CMU walls bearing on structural slabs).
conditions: at wall base

subject: Glazed/Faced CMU
rationale: CMU walls require mortar to bond individual blocks together.
conditions: for laying and bonding units
exceptions: Glazed/Faced CMU does not always require mortar — some architectural installations use dry-stack or interlocking CMU systems (e.g., SplitFace or SureBlock) that are laid without mortar. Additionally, thin brick systems adhered to a substrate do not use traditional mortar between units.

subject: Glazed/Faced CMU
rationale: Grout fills cells around rebar to bond steel and masonry.
conditions: when cells are reinforced with rebar
exceptions: non-reinforced walls do not require grout

subject: Glazed/Faced CMU
rationale: CMU walls require a properly designed foundation to distribute loads.
applicability: all building types with CMU walls

Glazed/Faced CMU walls do not always depend on a concrete foundation. In applications with a continuous concrete slab-on-grade, the concrete slab serves as the support rather than a separate concrete foundation element. Also, walls on upper floors depend on the structural floor system (e.g., concrete or steel beams/decks), not a concrete foundation.
conditions: to support the weight of the CMU wall
exceptions: In some retrofit or interior partition applications, glazed/faced CMU can be supported on reinforced concrete bond beams or structural steel channels without a continuous concrete foundation below.

subject: Interlocking/Retaining Wall CMU
rationale: Rebar provides tensile strength that CMU blocks alone lack, critical for withstanding lateral earth pressure.
applicability: Interlocking/Retaining Wall CMU blocks (e.g., Allan Block, Redi-Rock) are often dry-stacked, gravity retaining wall systems that do not use steel rebar at all—they rely on geogrid reinforcement and mass. The assertion applies only to reinforced CMU retaining walls (e.g., conventional grouted CMU), not to mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) segmental retaining wall systems which are a very common form of interlocking retaining wall CMU.
conditions: for structural retaining walls
exceptions: short non-structural decorative walls

Even for structural retaining walls using segmental retaining wall (SRW) units (which are interlocking), steel rebar is typically not required because these systems are designed as un-reinforced gravity walls or use geogrid soil reinforcement instead of internal steel reinforcement.

subject: Interlocking/Retaining Wall CMU
rationale: Waterproofing prevents water penetration through CMU into the retained area.
applicability: Segmental retaining wall (SRW) systems with interlocking CMU blocks typically have joints that are designed to be permeable/drainable, and applying a waterproof membrane to the back face can trap water behind the wall, increasing hydrostatic pressure. For many SRW systems, drainage aggregate and weep pipes are used instead of waterproofing membranes.
conditions: for below-grade walls
for occupied spaces behind wall
exceptions: non-critical landscape walls

Below-grade occupied-space walls (e.g., basement walls) are typically cast-in-place concrete or fully grouted CMU, not interlocking/segmental retaining wall CMU. Interlocking SRW blocks are not designed as waterproofing barriers for habitable spaces—they are gravity or MSE retaining systems. If used in such a scenario, a separate structural wall would already exist, making the membrane requirement applicable to that structural wall rather than the facing blocks.

subject: CMU Bond Beam Block
rationale: CMU bond beam blocks are laid with mortar just like standard CMU blocks to form a continuous wall section.
conditions: for bonding blocks together
exceptions: In specialized dry-stack or surface-bonded CMU systems, bond beam blocks can be stacked without traditional mortar between courses. The mortar requirement is not universal across all CMU construction methods.

subject: CMU Bond Beam Block
rationale: The channel in bond beam blocks is filled with grout to encase the reinforcing steel and create a solid reinforced concrete beam.
applicability: In non-structural or non-seismic applications where the bond beam serves only as a decorative band or crack control, grout may be omitted and only rebar placed dry or the channel left unfilled.
conditions: to fill the bond beam channel after rebar placement

subject: CMU Bond Beam Block
rationale: Bond beam blocks can function as a reinforced lintel course spanning openings to support wall loads above.
conditions: when placed above doors or windows

subject: Aerated Autoclaved Concrete (AAC) Block
rationale: AAC requires autoclaving (steam curing under pressure) to achieve its final strength and properties.
applicability: The assertion states 'requires Steam Curing' but does not account for alternative production methods such as wet-cast AAC or non-autoclaved aerated concrete (NAAC) which use different curing processes and still produce aerated concrete blocks.
conditions: in an autoclave at high pressure and temperature

subject: Aerated Autoclaved Concrete (AAC) Block
rationale: AAC walls require a proper foundation to bear the load and provide a level surface for block laying.
conditions: a level, stable concrete foundation or base

subject: Aerated Autoclaved Concrete (AAC) Block
rationale: AAC's porous structure provides excellent thermal insulation, reducing heating and cooling loads.
applicability: The assertion does not account for moisture exposure: AAC blocks can absorb significant moisture, which drastically reduces their thermal insulation performance (R-value can drop by 50% or more when wet). This limitation should be noted for applicability in humid or wet environments.
conditions: by virtue of its cellular structure containing air pockets

subject: CMU Lintel Block
rationale: CMU lintel blocks are laid with mortar to bond them to adjacent masonry units and provide structural integrity.
conditions: for bonding and bedding

subject: CMU Lintel Block
rationale: Lintel blocks are essentially bond beam blocks used specifically above openings; they depend on the same grouting and reinforcement detailing.
conditions: when used in conjunction with bond beam courses at the same level
exceptions: standalone lintel installations

subject: CMU Corner Block
rationale: CMU corner blocks require mortar to bond with adjacent blocks and form a structurally sound corner.
applicability: The assertion states 'CMU Corner Block requires Mortar' applies to load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls, but CMU corner blocks are typically manufactured as interlocking units (e.g., with tongue-and-groove or other mechanical interlock profiles) that allow dry-stacking without mortar even in some load-bearing applications beyond the cited exception. The 'Dry-stacked CMU systems' exception is listed but is overly narrow — many modular interlocking corner block systems can be laid without mortar in non-load-bearing or even low-load-bearing walls.
conditions: For bonding and laying the block
exceptions: Dry-stacked CMU systems

subject: CMU Corner Block
rationale: Grout is poured into CMU cells to bond rebar and block, creating composite structural action.
conditions: When reinforcing cells with rebar
For solid grouted walls
exceptions: Unreinforced masonry
Partially grouted walls in low-seismic areas

The assertion does not account for surface-bonded CMU construction (e.g., surface bonding cement applied to both faces of a dry-stacked wall) where corner blocks may be part of a reinforced wall system that uses surface bonding for structural integrity rather than conventional grouting of individual cells.

subject: CMU Half Block / Stretcher Block
rationale: CMU half blocks must be bonded with mortar to create a solid, stable wall assembly.
applicability: The assertion states that CMU Half Block / Stretcher Block 'requires' mortar, but the existing exception already acknowledges dry-stack interlocking systems. However, the assertion does not account for surface-bonded CMU construction (e.g., using surface bonding cement on dry-stacked blocks), which is a distinct method where mortar is not used between blocks but structural integrity is achieved via a cementitious coating. This is not covered by the 'dry-stack interlocking' exception since surface-bonded blocks may not be interlocking.
conditions: for joining blocks together
for structural integrity
exceptions: dry-stack systems where interlocking blocks are used

subject: Horizontal Joint Reinforcement
rationale: Horizontal joint reinforcement is embedded in mortar joints to bond with the masonry.
applicability: The assertion states that horizontal joint reinforcement requires mortar, but welded wire reinforcement (WWR) used in masonry is typically embedded in mortar of the bed joint — however, pre-stressed or post-tensioned horizontal reinforcement may be placed in bond beams or hollow cores without being embedded in mortar. Additionally, in some reinforced masonry systems, horizontal reinforcement is placed in grouted bond beams where grout rather than mortar provides the embedment.
conditions: for embedment in bed joints

subject: Vertical Rebar in CMU
rationale: Vertical rebar in CMU must be encased in grout to bond with the masonry and develop composite action.
conditions: When filling cells containing vertical rebar
exceptions: When vertical rebar is placed in bond beam cells or other horizontally reinforced cells that are filled with grout, the assertion still holds, but there are cases where vertical rebar is intentionally left ungrouted for later tensioning (post-tensioned CMU) or for non-structural applications such as temporary construction. In those scenarios, concrete grout is not immediately required.

subject: Vertical Rebar in CMU
rationale: Vertical rebar typically terminates in or is lapped with bond beam reinforcement at each level.
applicability: The assertion only describes the connection at floor or roof levels but does not address that vertical rebar in CMU also connects to other elements at intermediate points, such as lintels above openings, or at the foundation connection at the base level.
conditions: At floor or roof levels
exceptions: In buildings with a concrete or steel podium, the vertical rebar at the transition between the CMU wall and the podium floor level typically connects to dowels or embed plates rather than a bond beam unless a bond beam is explicitly designed at that level.

subject: CMU Control Joint / Expansion Joint Material
rationale: The material fills an expansion joint gap; the joint opening must be provided in the masonry assembly.
conditions: when used as expansion joint material

subject: CMU Washout Access / Cleanout
rationale: Cleanouts are necessary to remove debris before grout is placed in CMU cores. Grout is the material being placed.
conditions: During grouting operations
exceptions: In some construction sequences, cleanouts are installed and used before any grouting takes place (e.g., for inspection or debris removal), so the dependency on grouting operations does not always hold—cleanout access may exist independently of grouting.

subject: CMU Wall Ties / Anchors
rationale: Wall ties are set in mortar joints to achieve proper anchorage.
applicability: The assertion states CMU wall ties/anchors 'requires mortar', but in reinforced CMU construction with grout-filled cells, wall ties can be embedded in grout rather than mortar. Also, some code-approved mechanical anchors (e.g., screw-type or expansion anchors) are designed for post-installed applications into cured CMU and do not require mortar embedding at all. The condition 'for embedding tie ends in mortar joints' already narrows the scope, but the assertion statement itself is overly broad and should be conditioned to clarify that it applies only to ties embedded in mortar joints, not to mechanical or grout-embedded anchors.
conditions: For embedding tie ends in mortar joints

subject: CMU Wall Assembly (grouted & reinforced)
rationale: Grouting provides structural continuity and bonds reinforcement to masonry.
applicability: The assertion states that grouted and reinforced CMU wall assembly requires grout, but the condition already specifies 'for grouted assemblies'. This creates a tautology — the assertion itself defines the assembly type by requiring grout, yet the condition also says it's for grouted assemblies. The condition should describe the context (e.g., when reinforcement is present) rather than restating the assembly type.
conditions: for grouted assemblies
cells are filled after reinforcement placement

subject: CMU Wall Assembly (grouted & reinforced)
rationale: Mortar is essential for bedding and bonding CMU blocks into a structural assembly.
conditions: for bonding CMU units together

subject: CMU Wall Assembly (grouted & reinforced)
rationale: The CMU wall assembly must be supported by a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: load-bearing support
must be properly designed and cured

subject: CMU Wall Assembly (grouted & reinforced)
rationale: Load-bearing CMU walls can support roof framing members.
applicability: The assertion states that a grouted and reinforced CMU wall assembly supports a roof structure when load-bearing, but does not account for the case where a bond beam or concrete topping slab is required at the roof level to properly distribute loads. Without a bond beam at the roof level, the assembly may not adequately support the roof structure even if nominally load-bearing.
conditions: when wall is load-bearing

subject: CMU Wall Assembly (grouted & reinforced)
rationale: CMU walls can support floor slabs or joists in multi-story construction.
applicability: The assertion that a grouted and reinforced CMU wall supports floor structure in multi-story buildings does not account for necessary additional conditions such as bond beams at floor levels, minimum reinforcement requirements for diaphragm connections, or the need for proper bearing details (e.g., shelf angles or floor hangers). A grouted CMU wall alone, without these additional elements, may not be sufficient to support floor structures.
conditions: when wall is load-bearing
multi-story buildings

subject: CMU Wall Assembly (grouted & reinforced)
rationale: Bond beams provide horizontal reinforcement and distribute loads across the wall.
conditions: for horizontal structural continuity
at floor/roof levels and top of walls
exceptions: The assertion states that a grouted and reinforced CMU wall assembly requires a bond beam for horizontal structural continuity at floor/roof levels and top of walls. However, some engineered CMU wall designs achieve horizontal continuity through horizontal joint reinforcement (truss-type or ladder-type) placed in mortar joints at specific spacing, without the need for a full bond beam at every floor level. This is a recognized alternative in many building code jurisdictions per TMS 402/602.

subject: CMU Cavity Wall Assembly
rationale: Grout fills CMU cores around reinforcement to create a solid structural section.
conditions: When reinforcing cores
When bond beams are used
exceptions: Dry-stacked, non-grouted assemblies

subject: CMU Cavity Wall Assembly
rationale: The cavity between CMU wythes is typically filled with rigid or batt insulation to meet thermal code requirements.
applicability: all building types requiring thermal envelope

rationale: Grout fills cores to bond reinforcement and blocks

While generally true for grouted cells, in practice: (1) low-lift grouting vs high-lift grouting have different consolidation/placement conditions and after placement some voids may exist despite best efforts (honeycombing or incomplete fill), (2) in high-lift grouting, there can be 'grout dropout' where grout flows out of unintended openings (blowouts) resulting in incomplete cores, and (3) in partially grouted CMU construction, many cores are intentionally left empty - the assertion could be misinterpreted as claiming all cores contain grout after placement. rationale: The partition's bottom track is anchored to the floor slab.
applicability: The assertion states Gypsum Board Wall Partition 'connects_to Floor Slab' at the bottom track. However, in many construction scenarios, the bottom track is connected to a concrete floor slab or a wood/steel subfloor, but not necessarily directly to the 'Floor Slab' itself. For example, when there is a raised access floor, a structural topping slab, or when the gypsum partition sits on a metal deck, the connection is not directly to the structural floor slab. Also, in seismic or deflection-track assemblies, the bottom track may be intentionally not rigidly connected to the floor slab to allow for movement.
conditions: at the bottom track

subject: Gypsum Board Soffit
rationale: Joint compound is needed to tape and finish gypsum board joints.
applicability: Joint compound is used for finishing joints and screw heads, but the assertion does not specify the type of joint compound. For example, setting-type joint compound (hot mud) requires different mixing/application than drying-type compound, and UK/Ireland typically use a different approach (scrim tape + multi-finish plaster). The assertion also omits the fact that on some metal-framed soffits in commercial settings, mesh tape and specific joint compounds are required for fire-rated assemblies.
conditions: for finishing joints and screw heads

subject: Gypsum Board Soffit
rationale: Corner beads protect and reinforce external corners of gypsum board assemblies.
applicability: Corner beads are required for external corners of gypsum board soffits, but this is dependent on the type of corner bead used (e.g., paper-faced metal bead, vinyl bead, or no-coat/trimless systems). Some modern corner bead systems (e.g., No-Coat, Trim-Tex) require specific techniques or proprietary compounds. Additionally, in certain commercial applications with metal stud framing, L-bean or J-bead might be used instead of traditional corner beads at specific junction conditions.
conditions: for external corners of soffit

subject: Gypsum Board Soffit
rationale: Soffits often provide a mounting surface for recessed or surface-mounted lighting.
conditions: when soffit is designed to house recessed lighting
exceptions: A gypsum board soffit designed to house recessed lighting requires specific fire-rating considerations. For example, fire-rated soffit assemblies often require IC-rated (insulation contact) fixtures or specific clearance requirements. The assertion does not account for the fact that conventional non-IC-rated recessed lights cannot be used in insulated soffits or fire-rated assemblies without creating a fire hazard and code violation (NEC 410.116 and IRC building code requirements).

subject: Gypsum Board Bulkhead
rationale: Gypsum board bulkheads are typically attached to metal stud framing for structural support.
applicability: The assertion is limited to wall bulkheads but gypsum board bulkheads used as ceiling soffits may be supported by furring strips or direct attachment to structure rather than metal stud framing.
conditions: When installed as a wall bulkhead

subject: Gypsum Board Bulkhead
rationale: Corner beads protect and finish external corners of gypsum board.
conditions: At external corners of the bulkhead
exceptions: If no external corners exist

subject: Gypsum Board Bulkhead
rationale: Bulkheads often house or support lighting fixtures in dropped ceiling transitions.
applicability: The assertion states the bulkhead 'supports' a lighting fixture, but typical gypsum board bulkheads provide enclosure or housing for lighting, not structural support for the fixture's weight unless specially reinforced. A standard gypsum board soffit cannot support a light fixture's weight directly.
conditions: When bulkhead is designed as a soffit for recessed or mounted lighting

subject: Gypsum Board Chase Wall
rationale: Gypsum board chase walls are typically constructed using metal stud framing to create the hollow chase cavity for concealing pipes, ducts, or conduits.
conditions: when used as a non-load-bearing partition
exceptions: Gypsum board chase walls can also be constructed with wood stud framing (e.g., 2x4 or 2x6 wood studs) in residential or light commercial construction where non-load-bearing chase walls are needed. The assertion that metal stud framing is required is incorrect for these contexts.

subject: Gypsum Board Furring/Liner System
rationale: The furring system creates a cavity that can accommodate acoustic insulation batts, improving sound transmission class (STC) ratings.
applicability: The assertion applies only when the furring/liner system is used as part of a partition assembly. When used as a ceiling furring/liner system, the cavity may be oriented differently (e.g., above ceiling tiles) and acoustic insulation may need different support mechanisms (e.g., mesh, wire) rather than relying on the furring channels.
conditions: When cavity is filled with insulation
exceptions: In theaters and performance spaces, furring/liner systems may be intentionally decoupled (e.g., double-stud or staggered-stud assemblies) rather than relying on a simple furring/liner system. A standard furring/liner system with cavity insulation alone may not achieve the required STC ratings for theater separation walls between auditorium and backstage or between adjacent theaters.

subject: Gypsum Board Shaft Wall Assembly
rationale: Acoustic sealant prevents sound transmission through gaps in the shaft wall assembly.
applicability: Sound-sensitive occupancies like hotels, hospitals, residential
conditions: at perimeter joints and penetrations

subject: Gypsum Board Shaft Wall Assembly
rationale: The shaft wall assembly depends on the floor slab for anchoring the top and bottom J-runners.
conditions: for vertical support and anchorage of J-runners at each floor level

subject: Gypsum Board Shaft Wall Assembly
rationale: The assembly is used to create fire-rated enclosures around stairwells.
conditions: when used as rated separation around stairwells
exceptions: The assertion states the assembly 'contains' a Stairwell Enclosure, but a shaft wall assembly is the enclosure construction itself, not a component within it. The stairwell enclosure is the space/room being enclosed by the shaft wall assembly, not a contained element. This is a semantic/relationship misclassification - the proper relation would be that the shaft wall assembly is used as (or constitutes) the stairwell enclosure, rather than containing it.

subject: Gypsum Board Shaft Wall Assembly
rationale: Fire dampers are installed where ducts penetrate the shaft wall to maintain the fire rating.
conditions: at duct penetrations through the shaft wall

subject: Gypsum Board Joint Tape and Compound
rationale: Joint compound is the material used to embed the tape and build up finish coats over joints and fasteners.
conditions: for bedding tape and finishing coats

subject: Drywall Taping and Finishing
rationale: Tape (paper or mesh) is essential to reinforce joints and prevent cracking.
applicability: The assertion assumes standard gypsum drywall taping. It does not account for situations where the joint treatment uses a different system (e.g., European-style skim-coat, or metal lath and plaster), where tape is not used or a different type of reinforcing is applied.
conditions: for reinforcing joints between drywall panels
exceptions: Drywall taping and finishing does not always require drywall tape when using alternative methods such as veneer plaster systems (one-coat or two-coat plaster over drywall) or when using setting-type joint compounds that can be applied without tape for certain small repairs or when using mesh tape alternatives. Additionally, some adhesive-backed fiberglass mesh tapes are considered part of the process but technically the assertion conflates the material with the activity.

subject: Drywall Taping and Finishing
rationale: Taping and finishing cannot begin until drywall panels are installed and fastened to the framing.
conditions: drywall panels must be properly hung and fastened first
exceptions: Drywall taping and finishing does not strictly depend on completed drywall installation in all cases. In some renovation or repair work, taping and finishing can be performed on existing drywall that was previously installed, or on partial installations where some panels are hung and then finished before others are installed in a separate area.

subject: Drywall Installation and Hanging
rationale: Joint compound is essential for taping and finishing seams between drywall panels.
conditions: Finishing joints and fasteners
exceptions: Exposed/industrial look

Joint compound is not required for drywall installation when using certain adhesive-only fastening systems (e.g., glue-up applications) where joints are butted without finishing, or in temporary/construction drywall used as formwork or backing that is later covered.

subject: Drywall Installation and Hanging
rationale: Tape is embedded in joint compound to prevent cracks at panel seams.
conditions: Reinforcing joints
exceptions: Drywall tape is not required when using certain 'tape-free' joint compound systems (e.g., fiber-reinforced mud that bridges gaps without tape), for butt joints in certain non-critical applications, or when using mesh tape alternatives that may actually be considered 'tape' but the assertion lacks clarity on tape type (paper vs. mesh vs. fiberglass). Also, in some adhesive-only or structural applications joints are not taped.

subject: Drywall Installation and Hanging
rationale: Corner beads are installed at outside corners to provide a straight, durable edge.
conditions: Protecting external corners
exceptions: Rounded corner systems

subject: Drywall Installation and Hanging
rationale: Insulation is often installed within wall cavities before drywall is hung, especially for exterior walls.
applicability: The assertion states that Drywall Installation requires Insulation with conditions 'Thermal or acoustic performance required' and applicability 'Exterior walls; Acoustic-rated walls', but this conflates the requirement for insulation as a separate system. In many code jurisdictions, exterior walls require a continuous air barrier and vapor retarder which are separate from insulation; the drywall itself does not 'require' the insulation to be present at the time of hanging — insulation can be installed after drywall in some systems (e.g., dense-pack cellulose in closed cavities). The sequence dependency is not entirely correct as a strict requirement for the drywall installation process.
conditions: Thermal or acoustic performance required
exceptions: Uninsulated interior partitions (non-acoustic)

subject: Drywall Installation and Hanging
rationale: Plumbing pipes and fixtures within walls must be installed before drywall enclosure.
conditions: Plumbing in walls
exceptions: No plumbing in wall cavities

In fire-rated wall assemblies, plumbing rough-in must be approved by the assembly listing, and sometimes plumbing is furred out or placed in a separate chase — the drywall may be installed before plumbing in those cases. Additionally, in retrofits where walls are opened, drywall installation may precede plumbing rough-in if pipes are surface-mounted or in exposed systems.

subject: Drywall Installation and Hanging
rationale: Drywall is commonly used for finished ceilings and supports the application of ceiling paint or texture.
conditions: Drywall ceiling installation
exceptions: Suspended ceiling systems

subject: Drywall Sanding and Surface Preparation
rationale: Joint tape is embedded in compound to prevent cracking at drywall seams.
conditions: for reinforcing joints between drywall panels
exceptions: In certain industrial applications such as partition walls that will receive heavy-duty paneling or cladding without finishing, drywall tape is not required before sanding and surface preparation.

subject: Drywall Sanding and Surface Preparation
rationale: Sanding and surface preparation can only begin after drywall panels are installed and secured.
conditions: drywall panels must be properly hung and fastened
exceptions: In remodeling or repair scenarios where skim-coating over existing painted drywall, sanding and surface preparation can occur without preceding drywall installation. The dependency is only valid for new construction.

subject: Drywall Trim/Accessory Installation
rationale: Corner beads are a primary accessory that protects and finishes drywall corners.
applicability: The assertion states that Drywall Trim/Accessory Installation requires Corner Beads when exposed outside corners exist. However, corner beads are just one type of trim for outside corners; other methods exist such as metal bullnose corner beads, paper-faced metal corner beads, vinyl corner beads, and even hand-taped outside corners with no bead. The assertion may need to clarify that a trim/accessory for corner protection is required, but not necessarily a traditional 'corner bead' specifically.
conditions: exposed outside corners exist
exceptions: rounded corner systems that use optional trim

subject: Drywall Trim/Accessory Installation
rationale: Tape reinforces joints between drywall panels.
conditions: for flat joints and inside corners

subject: Lime Mortar
rationale: Lime mortar and lime plaster are often used together as a compatible, breathable system.
applicability: The assertion 'Lime Mortar connects_to Lime Plaster' assumes a direct physical connection, but in many historic building systems, lime mortar is used for masonry joints while lime plaster is applied to wall surfaces; they may not physically connect if there is an intervening material layer (e.g., stone or brick) between them, or if the plaster is applied over a different substrate.
conditions: when used in compatible building systems
exceptions: Lime mortar may not connect to lime plaster if the plaster is applied over a lath or a modern substrate (e.g., gypsum backing), or if a damp-proof course or separation layer is present between the mortar joint and the plaster surface.

subject: Fireproof Mortar
rationale: Fireproof mortar can be troweled or sprayed onto steel beams and columns to provide fire resistance by insulating the steel from heat.
applicability: The assertion states 'Fireproof Mortar protects Structural Steel', but the applicability context is limited to buildings. Structural steel in bridges, industrial chimneys, petrochemical plants, tunnels, or marine environments may have different fireproofing approaches and standards, and fireproof mortar may not be suitable or permitted in those contexts.
conditions: When applied as fireproofing coating or encasement
exceptions: Spray-applied fireproofing is more common for large steel members

Under sustained fire exposure beyond its material rating (typically 2-4 hours depending on thickness and formulation), fireproof mortar can spall, crack, or delaminate, causing loss of protection. There is no exception addressing fire duration limits or fire severity classes (e.g., hydrocarbon vs. cellulosic fires).

Fireproof mortar does not protect structural steel when applied over existing heavy rust, mill scale, or oil/grease contamination unless the steel surface is properly prepared (e.g., abrasive blasting, primer application). The assertion lacks an exception for inadequate surface preparation.

subject: Scratch Coat Mortar
rationale: Scratch coat is embedded into metal lath to create a strong mechanical bond and support the overall stucco system.
conditions: when used as a base for stucco over framed walls

subject: Stucco Mortar
rationale: Metal lath provides a mechanical key for stucco mortar to adhere to when applied over wood framing or sheathing.
conditions: For application over wood frame construction
exceptions: Not needed when applied directly to masonry surfaces

subject: Stucco Mortar
rationale: Stucco mortar is mechanically keyed into metal lath, connecting the mortar to the structural framing.
applicability: The assertion that Stucco Mortar connects_to Metal Lath in frame construction lacks specificity. In frame construction, there is typically a weather-resistant barrier (building paper or house wrap) and metal lath (or other lath) installed over that. The stucco mortar does not directly 'connect_to' the metal lath in a structural sense — it is applied to and embeds around the lath. The nature of the connection (mechanical bond through embedment) is not clarified, which could lead to misinterpretation of the relationship.
conditions: In frame construction
exceptions: In steel frame construction, the stucco application system differs. For steel frame, a different lath attachment method (self-furring lath with clips or screws) is often required, and the connection semantics between stucco mortar and lath may differ due to the differing substrate and attachment mechanisms. The assertion does not account for this difference between wood and steel frame.

subject: Repair Mortar
rationale: Proper surface preparation (cleaning, profiling, dampening) is critical for bond.
applicability: The assertion states that Repair Mortar requires surface preparation prior to application, but does not specify what type of surface preparation (e.g., cleaning, priming, roughening) or account for scenarios where the substrate is already prepared (e.g., fresh concrete with adequate bond). Additionally, some repair mortars are self-bonding or designed for application without mechanical preparation.
conditions: Prior to mortar application

subject: Repair Mortar
rationale: Proper curing ensures strength development and durability.
applicability: The assertion specifies curing is required for cementitious mortars, but the 'conditions' field only covers 'after application for cementitious mortars' without noting that some modern repair mortars (e.g., polymer-modified, rapid-setting) may have different or no curing requirements, or that curing requirements vary by ambient temperature and humidity.
conditions: After application for cementitious mortars

subject: Mortar Bed
rationale: Mortar beds serve as a supportive base layer directly beneath tile flooring, holding tiles in place.
conditions: when used as a setting bed for ceramic, porcelain, or stone tiles
exceptions: Thin-set mortar (not a mortar bed) is the standard setting method for many modern tile installations, especially large-format tiles. A thick mortar bed is not always required or used; thin-set directly over a suitable substrate (e.g., concrete slab, plywood with underlayment) is common and can support tile flooring without any mortar bed.

subject: Mortar Bed
rationale: Mortar beds are typically interrupted by or connect to expansion joints to allow for thermal and moisture movement.
conditions: in large floor areas to accommodate movement
exceptions: small installations may not require expansion joints

The assertion applies only to large areas and already mentions small installations may not require expansion joints. However, the concrete subfloor or slab beneath the mortar bed typically has its own control/expansion joints that are independent of the tile/mortar assembly. The mortar bed does not 'connect to' those structural expansion joints; rather, movement joints in the tile assembly should be aligned with them. The wording 'connects_to' is misleading.

subject: Mortar Joint
rationale: Mortar joint requires brick (or other masonry units) to form a wall; mortar binds bricks together.
conditions: Proper mixing ratio of cement, sand, and water

subject: Mortar Mixing
rationale: Mortar mixing supports plastering activities by providing the plaster material.
applicability: Mortar mixing is not universally suitable for all plastering applications. Plastering often requires specific binders (e.g., gypsum-based plaster, lime plaster) that differ from standard cement mortars. The assertion does not distinguish between cement mortar plastering and other plaster types (e.g., gypsum plaster, clay plaster, lime plaster), which have fundamentally different mixing requirements.
conditions: When mortar is used for plaster

subject: Mortar Mixing
rationale: Properly mixed mortar supports pointing work in masonry restoration.
applicability: Pointing requires mortar with specific properties (e.g., lower strength than the masonry units, appropriate color, specific joint profile compatibility, and often lime-based mixes for historic masonry). Generic mortar mixing may not accommodate these specialized requirements, particularly for color matching, water absorption matching, and strength compatibility with existing masonry.
conditions: When mortar is used for repointing joints
exceptions: When repointing historic or heritage masonry, specially formulated lime-based mortars are often required with specific mixing procedures (e.g., slaking, longer soaking times) that differ significantly from standard mortar mixing. The assertion does not account for this exception.

subject: Pointing
rationale: Pointing is the process of applying mortar to the joints of masonry; mortar is the essential material used.
conditions: when repointing existing masonry
exceptions: In dry stone construction or ashlar stonework with no mortar, there is no pointing at all in the sense of a mortar joint. However, if someone were to 'point' such a wall (e.g., repointing a historic dry stone wall), no mortar would be used — it would be re-set with stone chips or gravel instead. This contradicts the assertion that pointing requires mortar.

subject: Pointing
rationale: Pointing is the finishing layer of the mortar joint itself; it constitutes the visible face of the joint.

subject: Tile Adhesive/Thinset
rationale: Thinset adhesive is the primary medium that transfers loads from the tile to the substrate and holds the tile in place.
conditions: Used as the bonding layer between substrate and tile
exceptions: Tile adhesive/thinset does not support tile installation on flexible substrates (e.g., wood flooring over joists with deflection > L/360) unless an uncoupling or crack isolation membrane is used. The adhesive itself provides no structural support against movement.

subject: Caulk
rationale: Caulk forms a water-resistant barrier at joints, preventing water infiltration into building assemblies.
conditions: When applied to exterior joints and penetrations
exceptions: Not suitable for submerged conditions unless specified

The assertion claims caulk 'supports' waterproofing in general terms, but many standard caulks (e.g., basic acrylic latex) are not waterproof and will degrade with prolonged moisture exposure. Only specific types like silicone or polyurethane caulk actually provide waterproofing. The condition 'exterior joints and penetrations' does not guarantee waterproofing capability - a material-specific exception exists.

subject: Caulk
rationale: Standard caulk is not designed to carry structural loads; it is strictly a sealing/filling material, not an adhesive for load-bearing connections.
conditions: When load-bearing capacity is required
exceptions: Structural sealants exist for specialty glazing applications

The existing exception mentions structural sealants for specialty glazing, but there are also high-strength construction adhesives and epoxy-based products that are technically caulk-like (dispensed from tubes, applied with caulk guns) and are rated for structural load-bearing connections in certain applications (e.g., anchoring bolts, bonding structural elements). These blur the line and should be noted as exceptions.

subject: Expansion Joint Sealant
rationale: Expansion joint sealant is specifically designed to be installed within expansion joints; without the joint itself, the sealant has no purpose.
applicability: The assertion states that Expansion Joint Sealant 'requires' an Expansion Joint, but Expansion Joint Sealant is also used for other joint types such as control joints, construction joints, and isolation joints in some applications. The assertion incorrectly implies that an expansion joint is the only context where this sealant is used.
conditions: For proper installation and sealing of joints

subject: Expansion Joint Sealant
rationale: Expansion joint sealant prevents water, air, and moisture intrusion through the building envelope at movement joints.
conditions: At exterior joints
When properly installed and maintained
exceptions: Expansion Joint Sealant protects the building envelope only if the sealant is compatible with the adjacent substrates and designed for exterior exposure (UV-resistant, weatherproof). Many standard interior-grade sealants used at expansion joints will fail when exposed to weather, so the assertion does not hold for all sealants labeled as expansion joint sealant.

subject: Expansion Joint Sealant
rationale: Sealant prevents moisture and air leakage from damaging interior wall, floor, and ceiling finishes.
conditions: When used at interior expansion joints
exceptions: The assertion states that Expansion Joint Sealant 'protects' interior finishes, but some expansion joint sealants (e.g., those that are hard or non-elastic after curing) can instead cause damage to interior finishes if the joint moves, by transferring stress to adjacent materials rather than accommodating movement. Additionally, certain sealants may stain or react with interior finishes.

subject: Glazing Sealant
rationale: The sealant bonds the glass to the window or curtain wall frame.
applicability: In structural glazing systems, the glazing sealant (structural silicone) connects to the glass panel and the framing via a structural bond, but in many curtain wall systems there is also a pressure plate or cap that mediates the connection. The assertion 'connects_to Window Frame' oversimplifies as the sealant may connect to an intermediate extrusion (pressure plate, gasket, or setting block) rather than directly to the window frame member. Additionally, in captured (non-structural) glazing systems, the sealant may only act as a weatherseal between glass and gasket, not a direct structural connection to the frame.

subject: Roofing Sealant/Lap Cement
rationale: Sealant/lap cement is used to bond and waterproof flashing elements at roof penetrations and perimeters.
conditions: At joints and terminations
Sealing edges

subject: Roofing Sealant/Lap Cement
rationale: The entire roofing system, including sealant joints, depends on a stable and sound roof deck.
conditions: Load-bearing capacity adequate

subject: Epoxy Adhesive
rationale: Epoxy adhesion depends critically on surface preparation such as grinding, shot-blasting, or acid-etching.
applicability: The assertion 'Epoxy Adhesive depends_on Surface Preparation' is overly broad. Epoxy adhesives vary widely — some are specifically formulated for low-prep or 'damp-surface' applications (e.g., Sikadur 32 Hi-Mod for concrete bonding), where extensive surface preparation like grinding or acid-etching is not required. While surface preparation generally improves bond strength, a universal dependency is misleading.

subject: Epoxy Adhesive
rationale: Epoxy adhesives bond rebar into concrete for structural anchoring and can also coat rebar to support corrosion resistance.
conditions: When used as epoxy-coated rebar or epoxy anchoring adhesive
exceptions: Epoxy adhesive does not reliably support rebar bonding when temperatures exceed the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the epoxy during curing or service. For example, many standard epoxy adhesives soften or creep at sustained temperatures above 60–80°C, compromising bond strength to rebar.

Epoxy adhesive does not support Steel Reinforcement Bars in wet or saturated substrate conditions for many standard formulations unless specifically rated as 'moisture-tolerant' or 'damp-cure' epoxy. Standard epoxies require dry surfaces for proper adhesion to rebar.

subject: Carpet Adhesive
rationale: Carpet adhesive is the bonding agent that holds carpet flooring in place on the subfloor.
applicability: All building types with carpeted floors
conditions: Applied evenly and at correct coverage rate
exceptions: Carpet adhesive does not support carpet flooring that is installed using stretch-in or tackless methods (e.g., with carpet tack strips and padding), which is a common installation approach for residential wall-to-wall carpet. In such cases, no adhesive is used at all.

Carpet adhesive may off-gas VOCs during and after installation, making it unsuitable or restricted in sensitive environments such as hospitals, cleanrooms, or buildings pursuing low-VOC certifications (e.g., LEED v4 EQ credits) without special low-VOC adhesive products.

subject: Panel/Drywall Adhesive
rationale: Vapor barriers can create a separation layer that prevents adhesive from bonding directly to the framing, reducing effectiveness.
applicability: Exterior wall assemblies with vapor retarders

The assertion only covers conflict between panel/drywall adhesive and vapor barriers. It does not address common scenarios where the vapor barrier is used on the warm side of the wall (interior) rather than between framing and drywall, or where the vapor barrier is a paint/coating rather than a membrane. In those cases, the adhesive may not conflict at all.
conditions: When vapor barrier is placed between framing and drywall, limiting direct contact
exceptions: Some adhesives are formulated to bond through certain building wraps or membranes

In assemblies where a double-layer of drywall or a resilient channel is used between framing and drywall, the vapor barrier may not be in direct contact with the adhesive, so the conflict may not arise. The assertion does not account for this construction detail.

Some vapor barriers (e.g., certain Class II or III vapor retarders like kraft paper facing) are vapor-permeable and may bond acceptably with panel/drywall adhesives without conflict, unlike Class I vapor barriers (e.g., polyethylene sheeting). The assertion treats all vapor barriers as equivalent.

subject: Fully-Adhered Membrane
rationale: The membrane protects the underlying roof deck from water intrusion and weather exposure.
applicability: protect_from relationship is ambiguous in direction. Does the membrane protect the roof deck (e.g., from UV/weather), or does the membrane protect the building from the roof deck? The assertion lacks clarity on what threat the membrane protects the deck from.

subject: Fully-Adhered Membrane
rationale: The membrane protects insulation layers from water damage when placed above them.
conditions: insulation is below membrane in assembly
exceptions: inverted roof membrane assemblies place insulation above

subject: Fully-Adhered Membrane
rationale: Proper surface preparation is critical for achieving a reliable bond.
conditions: substrate must be smooth
free of debris
free of moisture
free of contaminants
exceptions: Some self-adhered membranes are designed for application to damp or green concrete substrates (e.g., certain peel-and-stick membranes used in below-grade waterproofing), so 'free of moisture' is not universally required.

subject: Fully-Adhered Membrane
rationale: Flashing components are required at all terminations, penetrations, and edges to ensure continuity of the waterproofing system.
applicability: The requirement for flashing specifically at roof edges, penetrations, and walls is correct for roofing applications, but in waterproofing applications (e.g., below-grade or plaza deck), the term 'flashing' may not apply in the same way — instead, terminations are detailed with sealants, termination bars, or liquid-applied details.
conditions: at roof edges
at penetrations
at walls

subject: Fully-Adhered Membrane
rationale: The membrane is often applied over roof insulation boards in conventional roof assemblies.
conditions: in insulated roof assemblies
exceptions: uninsulated structures

subject: Mechanically-Fastened Membrane
rationale: Termination bars, edge metal, and flashings are required to secure the membrane edges and provide watertight terminations.
conditions: At perimeter and penetrations

subject: Self-Adhered Membrane
rationale: The membrane provides a continuous waterproof barrier that protects the roof structure.
conditions: When used as a roof underlayment or primary waterproofing layer
exceptions: Self-adhered membranes, even as underlayment, are often not permitted for direct exposure to UV on steep-slope roofs for extended periods before the final roof covering is installed. Some products have strict UV exposure limits (e.g., 30–90 days), after which the membrane degrades, so the assertion 'supports Roof Assembly' fails if UV exposure exceeds product limits.

subject: Self-Adhered Membrane
rationale: Water diverted by the membrane must be directed to the drainage system.
applicability: The assertion specifies 'connects_to Drainage System' but does not clarify whether this refers to mechanical connection (the membrane physically laps into the drain tile) or functional connection (water flows from membrane to drainage). In many systems, the membrane terminates above the drainage board/footing drain rather than physically connecting to the drain tile; water simply drains by gravity. This distinction matters for design documentation and detailing.
conditions: In below-grade applications, the membrane ties into the drainage board and drain tile system
exceptions: In vertical wall applications without below-grade water table concerns

In below-grade applications where a positive-side waterproofing system uses fluid-applied or sheet membrane that wraps the footing rather than tying into a drainage board/drain tile (e.g., blindside waterproofing against a shored wall), the self-adhered membrane does not connect to a drainage system in the manner described — it may bond directly to the structure with no drainage layer.

subject: Torch-Applied Membrane
rationale: The membrane can be installed to hold insulation in place and protect it from weather exposure.
applicability: Torch-applied membranes cannot be used over all insulation boards — they are incompatible with polystyrene (EPS/XPS) insulation unless a thermal barrier or cover board is used, because the torch flame can melt or ignite polystyrene foam. The assertion does not specify this critical restriction.
conditions: when installed over insulation boards
exceptions: Torch-applied membranes cannot be installed over insulation boards when wind speeds exceed manufacturer recommendations (typically >15-20 mph) or in wet/rainy conditions, as the torch operation becomes unsafe and adhesion is compromised.

subject: Torch-Applied Membrane
rationale: Standing water can degrade the membrane over time; proper drainage is required for long-term performance.
applicability: The assertion does not specify that the requirement for a roof drainage system is subject to local building code minimums (e.g., number of drains, scupper sizing, slope requirements per IBC). Simply stating 'requires Roof Drainage System' is too vague — some low-slope roofs may use gutters, interior drains, or scuppers with specific sizing requirements.
conditions: to prevent ponding water on the membrane

subject: Protection Board / Cover Board
rationale: A primary function of protection board is to shield waterproofing membranes from physical damage, UV radiation, and traffic.
applicability: The assertion states Protection Board protects from Waterproof Membrane, but protection boards are designed to protect the membrane from physical damage (traffic, hail, UV), not to protect FROM the membrane. If waterproof membrane is present below, no protection from it is needed. The direction of protection is reversed - the membrane is what needs protection from above. Additionally, in green roof assemblies, a root barrier or drainage layer typically serves as the protective layer, not necessarily a protection board.
conditions: When used as a cover board over membrane

subject: Protection Board / Cover Board
rationale: Protection boards can shield insulation boards from mechanical damage during and after installation.
conditions: When installed above insulation in a roof assembly

subject: Protection Board / Cover Board
rationale: The cover board is installed directly on or over the roof membrane in many roofing systems.
conditions: In multi-ply or built-up roofing assemblies

subject: Membrane Flashing / Flashing Strips
rationale: Membrane flashing strips are installed on roof decks as a base substrate.
conditions: for proper installation

subject: Membrane Flashing / Flashing Strips
rationale: Flashing strips work as an integrated component with the primary roof membrane to seal edges and penetrations.
conditions: as compatible material
for overlapping installation
exceptions: Membrane flashing does not always require roof membrane as a separate component — in some systems (e.g., self-adhering flashing tapes used on exposed deck edges, or metal flashing used without membrane tie-in), the flashing itself serves as the primary weatherproofing and is not overlapped with a separate roof membrane layer.

subject: Roof Membrane Adhesive / Bonding Agent
rationale: The adhesive serves to bond the membrane to the substrate; it depends on the membrane being present.
applicability: Some roof membranes use self-adhered backing or heat-welded seams (e.g., TPO, PVC, modified bitumen torching) that do not require a separate liquid adhesive or bonding agent. The assertion 'depends_on Roof Membrane Adhesive / Bonding Agent' is false for these membrane types.

exceptions: Fully adhered single-ply membranes (e.g., certain EPDM or TPO systems) may use a bonding adhesive, but mechanically attached or ballasted roof assemblies do not use an adhesive/bonding agent between the membrane and substrate.

subject: Roof Drain / Drain Flashing Assembly
rationale: The drain flashing must integrate with and be sealed to the roof membrane to prevent leakage.
conditions: for proper flashing integration

subject: Roof Drain / Drain Flashing Assembly
rationale: The drain assembly is installed through the roof deck which provides structural support.
applicability: The assertion states Roof Deck is required as 'structural substrate' for all roof types, but in some retrofit or re-roofing scenarios over existing roofs, the drain flashing assembly is installed directly over an existing roof surface without exposing or using the original structural deck as a substrate. Also, some roof systems (e.g., structural standing seam metal roofs) may not have a continuous structural deck beneath the drain location.
conditions: as structural substrate

subject: Roof Drain / Drain Flashing Assembly
rationale: Insulation is typically installed around the drain sump and flashing to maintain thermal continuity.
conditions: above or below deck depending on system design

subject: Roof Drain / Drain Flashing Assembly
rationale: The drain assembly removes standing water, preventing structural decay, rot, or corrosion.
conditions: from water ponding and moisture intrusion

subject: Roof Drain / Drain Flashing Assembly
rationale: By removing water, the drain protects insulation from becoming wet and losing thermal performance.
conditions: from water saturation and degradation

subject: Roof Drain / Drain Flashing Assembly
rationale: Standing water can degrade membrane seams and materials over time; drainage prevents this.
applicability: The assertion states that the drain flashing assembly protects the Roof Membrane from hydrostatic pressure and ponding damage for 'all membrane roofs', but in some PMR/IRMA systems, the drain assembly typically passes through the insulation layer and the membrane below, and it is primarily the drain body and clamping ring (not the flashing assembly per se) that provide this protection. Also, on fully adhered EPDM or TPO roofs with pre-manufactured boot systems, the flashing is often a prefabricated accessory and its protective role varies by design.
conditions: from hydrostatic pressure and ponding damage

subject: Edge Metal / Fascia Flashing
rationale: Edge metal/fascia flashing must be attached to a solid roof deck substrate at the roof perimeter.
applicability: All building types with sloped roofs

The assertion states Edge Metal/Fascia Flashing requires Roof Deck, but in some retrofit or re-roofing scenarios, fascia flashing may be installed directly over existing roofing material (e.g., built-up roofs or existing shingle layers) without exposing the original roof deck. This limits the universal applicability.
conditions: Must be structurally sound and provide proper nailing surface

subject: Edge Metal / Fascia Flashing
rationale: Underlayment provides secondary water barrier that integrates with edge flashing.

subject: Edge Metal / Fascia Flashing
rationale: Fascia flashing often terminates into or above gutters to direct water runoff.

conditions: Gutters are typically installed below or integrated with fascia flashing
exceptions: Buildings in arid climates may omit gutters; fascia flashing still required

Buildings with internal gutter systems (e.g., concealed or built-in gutters behind parapet walls) may not require a visible gutter system integrated with fascia flashing, even in non-arid climates. The existing exception only covers arid climates.

subject: Edge Metal / Fascia Flashing
rationale: Fascia flashing profiles often incorporate a drip edge projection to shed water away from the wall.
conditions: Many fascia flashing profiles include an integrated drip edge at the bottom lip
exceptions: Some fascia flashings are separate from drip edge profiles

subject: Pipe Penetration Boot / Pipe Flashing

The 'requires Roof Membrane' condition does not hold for all roof penetration scenarios.
conditions: when installed on a roof penetration

subject: Pipe Penetration Boot / Pipe Flashing
rationale: The roof deck provides the structural substrate into/onto which the penetration and boot are secured.
applicability: The assertion 'Pipe Penetration Boot / Pipe Flashing requires Roof Deck' is marked as applicable to all roofing systems. However, in wall-penetration scenarios (e.g., a pipe exiting through a sidewall rather than through the roof deck), the boot/flashing does not require a roof deck. The condition only holds when the penetration is specifically through the roof plane.

subject: Pipe Penetration Boot / Pipe Flashing
rationale: The base of the boot is integrated with (lapped into) the roof membrane.

subject: Expansion Joint Cover (Roof)
rationale: Expansion joint covers require adjacent roof membrane to terminate properly and be flashed into the joint cover system to maintain waterproofing.
applicability: The assertion conflates 'requires Roof Membrane' as a directional dependency — the expansion joint cover is typically installed after the membrane, and it's more accurate to say the membrane extends up to or under the cover rather than the cover requiring the membrane. The installation sequence and functional dependency may be reversed in practice.

subject: Expansion Joint Cover (Roof)
rationale: Where a roof expansion joint meets a roof curb for equipment, the cover must transition properly to the curb flashing.
