applicability: All buildings with fire alarm systems
conditions: For automatic actuation during fire events

subject: Smoke Damper
rationale: Smoke detectors provide the detection input that triggers smoke damper closure.
applicability: Buildings with automatic smoke management systems

Smoke dampers in some jurisdictions can be closed manually or via a remote control station without requiring automatic smoke detection or fire alarm activation. The assertion assumes automatic closing response as the only scenario, which may not cover manual/remote operation cases.
conditions: For automatic closing response
exceptions: May also be activated by fire alarm system alone

subject: Smoke Damper
rationale: Smoke dampers are integral components of HVAC duct systems, depending on the HVAC layout for proper placement and zoning.
conditions: For physical integration and air handling context

subject: Smoke Damper
rationale: Smoke dampers are key components that close off or open duct paths to direct smoke flow during fire events.
applicability: Buildings with engineered smoke control systems
conditions: In smoke management zones

subject: Smoke Damper
rationale: Smoke dampers are physically installed within duct sections, typically at barrier penetrations.
applicability: Smoke dampers also connect to walls, floors, and partitions at barrier penetrations — not exclusively to ductwork. The assertion that it connects to ductwork 'at duct penetrations through barriers' is correct for those cases, but smoke dampers can also be installed without connecting to ductwork (e.g., in a wall between two spaces without ducted connections).
conditions: At duct penetrations through barriers

subject: Backdraft Damper
rationale: The damper interfaces directly with ductwork as an in-line or end-of-line component.
conditions: installed within or at the termination of duct sections
exceptions: Backdraft dampers installed directly at an exterior wall louver without any intervening duct section (e.g., mounted in a wall opening with no duct attached) do not connect to ductwork even though they are within or at termination of a duct system. The condition should account for this null-duct case.

subject: Duct-Mounted Access Door
rationale: A duct-mounted access door is physically installed on ductwork to provide access.
conditions: must be installed within HVAC duct system
exceptions: A duct-mounted access door might be installed on equipment casings (e.g., AHU, rooftop unit) that are not classified as ductwork but are still part of the air distribution path. This creates an exception where Ductwork is not the requiring element.

subject: Duct-Mounted Access Door
rationale: The access door serves HVAC duct systems for inspection and maintenance.
applicability: all building types with mechanical ventilation
conditions: must be part of a mechanical ventilation or air distribution system

subject: Duct-Mounted Access Door
rationale: Thermal integrity of the duct system must be maintained around the access door.
applicability: buildings with insulated ductwork for thermal efficiency

The dependency on Duct Insulation is stated as conditional (if duct is externally insulated), but the existing exception only covers 'uninsulated duct systems'. There is a gap: ducts that are internally insulated (lined) do not require Duct Insulation as a separate element on the exterior, yet the condition does not address this scenario. The assertion should clarify that 'externally insulated' is the specific trigger.
conditions: if duct is externally insulated, access door must accommodate or be insulated
exceptions: uninsulated duct systems

subject: Duct Takeoff Fitting
rationale: A duct takeoff fitting is part of an HVAC system's ductwork.
applicability: The condition 'As part of air distribution network' is ambiguous — a duct takeoff could be part of an exhaust or outdoor air duct network that is not part of a mechanical HVAC system but rather a standalone ventilation system. The assertion should clarify whether it applies only to supply-side takeoffs or also to return/exhaust takeoffs.
conditions: As part of air distribution network
exceptions: In some configurations, a duct takeoff fitting may serve a non-HVAC purpose such as exhaust-only or transfer air paths that do not involve a conditioned HVAC system (e.g., gravity ventilation, split systems with no central air handler). The assertion that it always requires an HVAC System may be too broad.

subject: Duct Takeoff Fitting
rationale: Many takeoff fittings are designed to accept a manual or balancing damper for airflow regulation.
conditions: When branch airflow adjustment is needed
exceptions: Not present in constant-volume systems without dampers

subject: Duct Transition & Reducer
rationale: Duct transitions and reducers are components of ductwork systems and require ductwork to function.
conditions: for air distribution systems

subject: Duct Transition & Reducer
rationale: Duct transitions and reducers are part of HVAC air distribution.
conditions: for conditioned air delivery

subject: Duct Transition & Reducer
rationale: Duct transitions often connect to AHUs to transition duct sizes.
conditions: when connected to central HVAC

subject: Duct Sealing (Mastic/Tape)
rationale: Duct sealing is applied directly to ductwork (supply and return) to seal joints, seams, and connections; without ductwork there is nothing to seal.
applicability: The assertion states applicability is 'All HVAC systems with ducts,' but duct sealing with mastic/tape is only appropriate for supply and return ducts in conditioned or semi-conditioned spaces. It is not applicable to certain specialized duct systems such as exhaust-only ducts, combustion air ducts, or ducts embedded in concrete slabs, where other sealing methods or materials are required by code (e.g., IMC 2018 Section 603.9 for duct penetration seals may differ).
conditions: Must have accessible duct joints and seams
exceptions: Mastic or tape-based duct sealing is not the required method for all duct types. For example, certain flexible duct connections require mechanical fastening (clamps, straps) in addition to or instead of mastic/tape per manufacturer instructions and building codes (e.g., UL 181 listed tapes/mastics for flexible ducts). Also, fibrous glass ductboard systems typically require closure systems per SMACNA standards that may differ from standard mastic/tape application.

subject: Ductwork Pressure Testing
rationale: Ductwork pressure testing cannot be conducted without an existing ductwork system to test.
applicability: all HVAC systems with ducted air distribution
conditions: pressure testing must be performed on installed ductwork

subject: Ductwork Installation Coordination
rationale: The coordination process includes placement and access provisions for balancing and control dampers.
applicability: The assertion states that 'Ductwork Installation Coordination' contains a 'Volume Control Damper' as a general rule for all building types, but this is not universally true. Volume control dampers are typically used in larger or zoned HVAC systems, but in many simple residential or small commercial duct systems, volume control dampers may be absent entirely — balancing is instead done at the register/grille or via simple manual dampers at branch take-offs. The assertion should be scoped to building types where zoned or multi-zone air distribution is present, not all building types.

subject: Diffuser & Grille Installation
rationale: Diffusers and grilles must be connected to supply and return ductwork to deliver or extract air.
conditions: For all forced-air HVAC installations
exceptions: In some forced-air HVAC installations, ductless mini-split systems use diffusers/grilles directly on the indoor unit without separate ductwork. The assertion that diffuser & grille installation requires ductwork does not hold for ductless forced-air systems.

subject: Diffuser & Grille Installation
rationale: The AHU supplies conditioned air that ultimately reaches the diffusers; without it, diffusers have no air to distribute.
applicability: The assertion uses a 'depends_on' relationship which implies a direct installation dependency, but in practice diffusers and grilles are physically attached to ductwork or terminal boxes, not directly to the AHU. The dependency on the AHU is indirect (through the duct system) and the assertion overstates the directness of the relationship.
conditions: For systems with mechanical ventilation
exceptions: In systems with mechanical ventilation where the AHU is remote, diffuser and grille installation depends on the ductwork connecting to the AHU, but the actual dependency chain is on the duct system rather than directly on the AHU. A diffuser can be installed even if the AHU is not yet on-site, as long as the ductwork connecting to it is in place.

subject: Duct-Mounted Humidifier
rationale: A duct-mounted humidifier must be installed directly into the HVAC ductwork to introduce moisture into the air stream.
applicability: All HVAC systems with forced air distribution
conditions: Must be connected to HVAC air handling unit
exceptions: A duct-mounted humidifier does not strictly require ductwork if it is installed in a dedicated air handler cabinet or plenum that is not traditional ductwork but still part of the forced air system. Additionally, duct-mounted humidifiers are sometimes installed directly on the supply plenum of a furnace, which may be considered part of the unit rather than separate ductwork.

subject: VAV Box Duct Connection
rationale: Flexible duct is commonly used to connect VAV box outlets to terminal diffusers.
applicability: The assertion only lists 'Commercial; Institutional' as applicability, but VAV box duct connections in residential or light commercial settings may have different requirements or code restrictions regarding flexible duct lengths and fire ratings.
conditions: For connecting VAV box to diffusers
Typically spiral wire-reinforced
exceptions: When hard duct is specified instead

The assertion states 'requires Flexible Duct' but the existing exception already notes 'When hard duct is specified instead.' This means flexible duct is not always required; the assertion should be reframed to reflect that flexible duct is typical but not mandatory, with an explicit condition clarifying when hard duct is allowed.

subject: Plenum Box
rationale: Plenum boxes are typically connected to ductwork to distribute conditioned air from the main HVAC system to diffusers.
applicability: A plenum box can be used as a junction box without connecting to ductwork on one side (e.g., connecting directly to a diffuser with a flexible duct connector or being mounted directly to a plenum ceiling without hard duct connections). The assertion treats ductwork as a universal requirement.
conditions: For connection to HVAC system

subject: Plenum Box
rationale: A plenum box depends on an active HVAC system (air handler/furnace) that supplies heated or cooled air through it.
conditions: For air supply source

subject: Plenum Box
rationale: In fire-rated ceilings or walls, a plenum box may require fire dampers to maintain fire separation integrity.
conditions: Where plenum box penetrates fire-rated assembly
exceptions: If the plenum box does not penetrate a fire-rated assembly (e.g., it is installed within the same fire compartment or below a non-fire-rated ceiling), a fire damper is not required. The condition already implies the need for it, but the 'depends_on' relationship may be too strong—it depends on the condition, but the condition itself is not always present.

subject: Plenum Box
rationale: Plenum boxes often contain internal or external insulation lining to prevent condensation, reduce noise, and maintain air temperature.
applicability: Not all plenum boxes contain insulation. Some are uninsulated depending on the application (e.g., where condensation is not a concern or where the plenum box is located in conditioned space). Internal insulation is application-specific.
conditions: For thermal and acoustic purposes

subject: Plenum Box
rationale: The plenum box must be anchored to the building's structural slab or beams via hangers.
conditions: For suspension and anchorage

subject: Kitchen Exhaust Duct
rationale: Kitchen exhaust ducts in commercial settings must be protected by an automatic fire suppression system (wet chemical) due to grease fire risk.
applicability: The assertion does not account for jurisdictions that adopt IMC (International Mechanical Code) instead of or in addition to NFPA 96. Under IMC Section 506, grease duct construction and clearance requirements differ, and the dependency on fire suppression may be interpreted differently. The assertion is scoped to 'NFPA 96 compliant' but many commercial kitchens also must meet IMC requirements which could alter this dependency.
conditions: for commercial kitchen exhaust ducts
exceptions: residential systems without auto-suppression

subject: Kitchen Exhaust Duct
rationale: Insulation prevents condensation and heat loss; required for energy code compliance in some cases.
applicability: ducts in attics or exterior walls
conditions: where duct passes through unconditioned spaces or requires condensation control
exceptions: short ducts within conditioned envelope

The assertion states that Kitchen Exhaust Duct depends_on Duct Insulation for condensation control, but NFPA 96 grease ducts are typically constructed of welded steel or stainless steel and are not insulated for condensation control like typical HVAC ducts. Grease duct insulation (when required) is usually for fire resistance rating (e.g., 1-hour or 2-hour fire rating) or for clearance reduction, not for condensation control. Condensation in grease ducts is generally managed by maintaining a minimum slope to drain and providing cleanouts, not by insulation.

subject: Laboratory Exhaust Duct
rationale: Fire dampers may be required at penetrations of fire-rated walls, though some codes prohibit dampers in hazardous exhaust ducts.
conditions: duct penetration of fire-rated barriers
exceptions: lab exhaust systems where dampers are prohibited per code

The assertion itself already lists an exception: 'lab exhaust systems where dampers are prohibited per code'. However, there are additional important exceptions not captured. For instance, many codes (e.g., IMC, NFPA 45, and IBC) explicitly prohibit fire dampers in hazardous exhaust duct systems serving fume hoods or chemical labs because dampers could accumulate corrosive residues, fail to close properly, or create a fire/explosion hazard. Also, exceptions exist for duct penetrations of fire-rated barriers where the duct is enclosed in a fire-rated shaft, where shaft enclosure serves as the fire barrier without requiring an in-duct damper.

subject: Pipework Routing
rationale: Insulation is required around routed pipes for thermal efficiency and condensation control.
conditions: when thermal control or condensation prevention is needed
exceptions: uninsulated systems in non-critical areas

subject: Pipework Routing
rationale: Pipework routing is the physical backbone that enables the plumbing system to deliver water and remove waste.
conditions: for water supply and drainage

subject: Pipework Routing
rationale: Routing of pipes enables the distribution of heating and cooling media throughout the building.
conditions: for chilled water, hot water, and steam distribution

subject: Pipework Routing
rationale: Fire sprinkler pipe routing directly supports fire safety infrastructure.
conditions: for sprinkler and standpipe networks
exceptions: In some jurisdictions, fire suppression systems may use non-metallic piping (e.g., CPVC) with different routing requirements (e.g., clearance from heat sources, specific hanger spacing) that differ from metallic pipe routing generalities. This exception is not captured.

subject: Pipework Routing
rationale: Routed pipes terminate at sinks, toilets, showers, and other fixtures.
applicability: The assertion 'Pipework Routing connects_to Plumbing Fixtures' is vague about what 'connects_to' means — does it cover routing to the fixture rough-in only, or does it include the final connection (which may be flexible supply lines, not rigid pipe routing)? In practice, the final connection to fixtures is often made with flexible hoses (e.g., faucet supply lines), not rigid pipe routing.
conditions: in water supply and drainage systems

subject: Pipework Jointing and Connection
rationale: Pipework jointing connects all sections of plumbing, enabling water distribution and waste removal.
conditions: for water supply and drainage

subject: Pipework Jointing and Connection
rationale: Reliable joints are critical for HVAC pipe networks carrying heating/cooling fluids.
applicability: For HVAC chilled water and refrigerant piping, many specialized jointing methods (e.g., brazing for refrigerant lines, grooved couplings for large chilled water) have specific pressure and temperature constraints. The assertion does not account for the fact that some pipework jointing methods (e.g., solvent welding for PVC) are unsuitable for refrigerant piping due to pressure and chemical compatibility issues. The blanket 'supports' statement may overstate the scope of compatibility.
conditions: for chilled water and refrigerant piping

subject: Pipework Jointing and Connection
rationale: Sprinkler systems depend on securely jointed pipework to deliver water to fire control points.
conditions: for sprinkler and standpipe networks

subject: Pipework Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Testing and commissioning is performed on installed pipework systems.
conditions: Prior to testing
exceptions: Pipework testing and commissioning may occur in phases (e.g., sectional testing before full installation is complete), where full Pipework Installation is not yet finished but partial testing is still valid. The depends_on relationship may not hold for interim or staged testing.

subject: Pipework Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Supports must be in place before testing can proceed.
conditions: Must be properly installed

subject: Pipework Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Drainage pipework testing is part of the overall plumbing commissioning.
conditions: When testing drainage pipework

subject: Pipework Penetrations and Firestopping
rationale: Firestop sealants are essential for sealing gaps around pipes passing through fire-rated walls and floors to maintain fire-resistance ratings.
applicability: The assertion does not account for penetrations by metal pipes (e.g., copper, steel) which have different firestopping requirements, often involving mineral wool or firestop pillows rather than sealant alone, depending on the pipe material and annular space.
conditions: When pipe penetrations pass through fire-rated assemblies
exceptions: Firestop sealant alone is insufficient for plastic pipes (e.g., PVC, CPVC, PEX) passing through fire-rated assemblies, as fire can melt the pipe and create an opening even if sealant is present. These require specifically listed firestop devices or intumescent wraps/collars that collapse and seal the pipe when it softens.

subject: Pipework Penetrations and Firestopping
rationale: Pipe insulation may be required for thermal performance, but specialized firestop-rated insulation or coverings may be needed where pipes penetrate fire-rated assemblies.
conditions: Where pipes carry hot or cold fluids and pass through fire-rated assemblies

subject: Hot Water Pipework
rationale: To maintain hot water circulation and ensure prompt delivery at fixtures, a circulation pump is typically required.
conditions: In recirculating hot water systems

subject: Hot Water Pipework
rationale: Insulation is necessary around hot water pipes to retain heat, improve energy efficiency, and prevent burns.
conditions: To minimize heat loss and prevent condensation

subject: Hot Water Pipework
rationale: Hot and cold pipes run close together can cause unwanted heat transfer (thermally bridging), requiring insulation separation.
applicability: The 'conflicts_with' relationship may not apply in all building contexts. For example, in some mechanical room layouts or specific plumbing configurations (e.g., manifold systems), hot and cold water pipes are intentionally run close together in a shared chase. The conflict only arises where thermal interference is a concern, which depends on pipe material, fluid temperatures, ambient conditions, and distance of separation.
conditions: When improperly separated or insulated

subject: Cold Water Pipework
rationale: Prevents contaminated water from flowing back into the clean water supply.
applicability: Backflow prevention devices are required only at specific points of connection (cross-connections) where there is a risk of backflow contamination, not universally on all cold water pipework. The assertion is overly broad — it implies all cold water pipework requires backflow prevention, which is not accurate for interior distribution piping that has no cross-connection risk.
conditions: Required by plumbing codes to protect potable water supply
exceptions: Temporary construction water lines or hose bibbs with atmospheric vacuum breakers are a specific case, but many cold water pipe runs within a building (e.g., pipes inside walls feeding a sink) do not individually require a dedicated backflow prevention device — the device is typically at the service entrance or at the fixture/equipment level where a cross-connection exists.

subject: Cold Water Pipework
rationale: Insulation prevents freezing and condensation on cold water pipes.
conditions: In unheated spaces
In cold climates where freezing is a risk
exceptions: In interior conditioned spaces where freezing is not a concern

In climate zones where freezing is not a risk (e.g., tropical or subtropical climates), pipe insulation on cold water pipes in unheated spaces is primarily for condensation control rather than freeze protection. However, even in such climates, insulation may still be required by energy codes to prevent heat gain and condensation — but the stated condition 'In cold climates where freezing is a risk' wrongly suggests insulation is only needed in cold climates.

subject: Cold Water Pipework
rationale: Cold water pipework supplies the water heater, which then distributes hot water.
conditions: Cold water feeds into water heaters to produce hot water

subject: Cold Water Pipework
rationale: Cold water pipework delivers potable cold water to all plumbing fixtures in the building.
applicability: Not all plumbing fixtures require cold water — some fixtures (e.g., urinals, dishwashers in some configurations, certain faucets that only receive hot water) do not have a cold water supply connection. Additionally, some fixtures like waterless urinals have no water supply at all.
conditions: Toilets, faucets, showers, sinks, bidets, etc.

subject: Cold Water Pipework
rationale: Cold water pipework may extend to exterior hose bibs and irrigation connections.
conditions: Where landscape irrigation is fed from the building supply
exceptions: Many jurisdictions require a backflow prevention device (e.g., reduced pressure zone assembly) on irrigation systems fed from the building supply due to cross-connection hazards. This is a critical regulatory requirement that should be explicitly noted as an exception or additional condition rather than implied as a simple supply relationship.

subject: Cold Water Pipework
rationale: Cold water pipework connects to the water heater inlet to supply water for heating.

subject: Cold Water Pipework
rationale: Drain valves and connection to the drainage system allow emptying of cold water pipes for repairs or freeze prevention.
conditions: For draining pipes during maintenance or winterization

subject: Heating Pipework
rationale: Heating pipework requires a heat source to convey heated fluid from.
conditions: System must generate hot water or steam
exceptions: District heating systems receive heat from a central plant via heat exchangers, not from an on-site boiler or heat pump. The pipework still requires a heat source, but that source may be external (district heating network) rather than a boiler/heat pump on the premises.

subject: Heating Pipework
rationale: A pump is needed to circulate water through the pipework.
conditions: Hydronic heating systems
exceptions: Gravity-fed systems

Steam heating systems (one-pipe or two-pipe steam) do not require a circulation pump; steam moves by pressure differential and condensate returns by gravity or via a condensate return pump which is functionally different from a circulation pump. The existing exception for gravity-fed systems does not cover this distinction.

subject: Heating Pipework
rationale: Insulation is essential for thermal efficiency and freeze protection.
applicability: All heating pipework in cold or unconditioned spaces

The applicability says 'All heating pipework in cold or unconditioned spaces' but the assertion condition says 'To reduce heat loss and prevent freezing'. For pipework carrying fluids above freezing temperatures (e.g., high-temperature hot water), freezing prevention may not be a concern, only heat loss. The dual-purpose condition conflates two distinct requirements.
conditions: To reduce heat loss and prevent freezing
exceptions: Uninsulated pipework in unconditioned spaces may cause energy loss

subject: Heating Pipework
rationale: An expansion vessel accommodates thermal expansion of water.
conditions: Closed-loop hydronic systems
exceptions: Open-vented systems use an expansion tank instead

Some closed-loop hydronic systems use a pressure-reducing valve and air separator instead of an expansion vessel (e.g., very small systems or systems with a different pressurization method like nitrogen cushion tanks). The assertion should account for alternative pressurization methods.

subject: Sanitary Drainage Pipework
rationale: Sanitary fixtures are the point of entry for waste into the drainage pipework.
applicability: Sanitary drainage pipework is required for any building that collects and removes wastewater, but sanitary fixtures are not the only source — industrial process drains, laundry equipment, and certain mechanical equipment drains also connect to sanitary drainage systems. The assertion as stated (requiring 'Sanitary Fixtures') is too narrow and may omit legitimate connections.
conditions: Such as toilets, sinks, urinals, showers, floor drains
exceptions: In certain buildings (e.g., temporary construction sites, some industrial facilities), sanitary drainage pipework may exist to receive only greywater or blackwater from non-traditional sources (e.g., portable toilet connections, chemical toilets) that are not conventional 'Sanitary Fixtures' as listed. These are still valid connections but the assertion would not cover them.

subject: Sanitary Drainage Pipework
rationale: The drainage pipework physically connects to each sanitary fixture.
applicability: The assertion states each fixture is connected via branch pipes and traps, but in some jurisdictions or designs, certain fixtures (e.g., floor drains in specific applications, or fixtures with integral traps) may not require a separate trap or may connect differently. Additionally, some fixtures like emergency showers or certain laboratory fixtures may drain indirectly (air gap) rather than directly via branch pipes with traps.
conditions: Each fixture is connected via branch pipes and traps

subject: Vented and Overflow Pipework
rationale: Vented and overflow pipework must be connected to a water supply system to function as overflow for cisterns or tanks.
applicability: The assertion states 'Vented and Overflow Pipework requires Water Supply System' under the condition 'When used as overflow pipework for water storage cisterns' and applicability 'all buildings with water storage'. However, overflow pipework does not always require a connection to a water supply system — for example, in some jurisdictions, overflow pipes from rainwater harvesting tanks or greywater storage tanks may discharge to drainage or to a soakaway without being connected to a mains water supply. The condition only mentions cisterns but does not specify that the cistern must be supplied by a water supply system (it could be a tank fed by rainwater, tankered water, or well water).
conditions: When used as overflow pipework for water storage cisterns

subject: Fire Suppression Pipework
rationale: Fire pumps boost water pressure to ensure adequate flow through the pipework system.
conditions: when municipal water pressure is insufficient
exceptions: gravity-fed systems with sufficient head pressure
Existing exception lists gravity-fed systems only, but systems using on-site pressure tanks or pumped tanks without municipal connection are also valid exceptions where no fire pump is needed.

subject: Fire Suppression Pipework
rationale: Backflow preventers are required by code to stop fire suppression water from flowing back into the potable water system.
applicability: all buildings connected to municipal water
conditions: to prevent contamination of potable water supply
exceptions: Systems using a dedicated non-potable water supply such as a tank, reservoir, or natural water source with no municipal potable connection do not require a backflow preventer.

subject: Fire Suppression Pipework
rationale: Sprinkler heads are the terminal devices that distribute water from the pipework system during a fire.
conditions: installed at specified spacing and coverage areas

subject: Fire Suppression Pipework
rationale: Fire alarm systems provide detection and trigger activation of suppression systems.
applicability: Many wet-pipe automatic sprinkler systems activate mechanically via heat-sensitive fusible links or glass bulbs without requiring an electrical fire alarm system to initiate water flow. The fire alarm may be needed for occupant notification but not for suppression pipework function itself.
conditions: for automatic activation in fire events
exceptions: manual-only systems

subject: Fire Suppression Pipework
rationale: Standpipe systems rely on fire suppression pipework to deliver water to hose connections on each floor.
conditions: in buildings over a certain height or as required by code

subject: Fire Suppression Pipework
rationale: By controlling or extinguishing fires early, the pipework system helps protect the structural frame from fire damage.
applicability: all buildings with fire suppression systems
conditions: when activated during a fire event

subject: Gas Pipework
rationale: Ventilation is critical to disperse any potential gas leaks, preventing accumulation of explosive gas mixtures.
conditions: Areas housing gas appliances and pipework joints must be adequately ventilated
exceptions: Outdoor or fully open-sided installations

In sealed combustion or direct-vent appliances (e.g., balanced flue boilers), the appliance draws combustion air directly from outside and does not rely on indoor ventilation. In such installations, the gas pipework joint area may not need ventilation to the same standard as open-flue appliances, creating an exception to the general dependency.

subject: Gas Pipework
rationale: The building structure provides the physical pathways and mounting surfaces for gas pipework installation.
conditions: Pipework must be routed through walls, floors, and ceilings; structural load paths must be considered
exceptions: Gas pipework may be surface-mounted on walls using exposed pipe clips or brackets without being routed through the building structure at all. In such cases, the pipework does not depend on walls/ceilings for routing and the structural load path consideration is minimal. This is common in retrofits, basements, and external meter box installations.

subject: Pipework Identification and Labeling
rationale: Physical labels may be coordinated with digital identification in BMS or BIM models.
conditions: when labels are integrated with digital twins or BIM

subject: Refrigerant Pipework
rationale: Insulation on refrigerant pipes prevents condensation, reduces thermal losses, and protects against frost.
conditions: For suction lines and cold pipes to prevent condensation and improve efficiency

subject: Refrigerant Pipework
rationale: Pipework connects condenser coil to other system components.

subject: Pipework Corrosion Protection
rationale: Pipework corrosion protection relies on applying protective coatings such as epoxy, polyethylene, or zinc coatings to metal pipe surfaces
applicability: all building types with metal pipework

The assertion requires protective coating for all external pipe surfaces, but indoor exposed metal pipes in dry, conditioned spaces (e.g., interior plumbing risers in office buildings) typically do not require corrosion-protective coating as the risk of atmospheric corrosion is negligible.
conditions: for external pipe surfaces
for buried pipes
exceptions: Protective coating is not universally required for all buried pipes — non-metallic pipes such as PVC, HDPE, or ABS do not require protective coating against corrosion, though the assertion conditions state 'for buried pipes' without restricting to metallic pipes.

Stainless steel pipes (e.g., 304 or 316 grades) exposed externally or buried typically do not require additional protective coating as their chromium oxide layer provides inherent corrosion resistance, yet the assertion requires protective coating for all metal pipework.

subject: Pipework Corrosion Protection
rationale: Insulation helps prevent moisture accumulation that can lead to external corrosion on pipes
conditions: to prevent condensation-induced corrosion
for temperature-controlled pipes
exceptions: Pipe insulation is not required for condensation-induced corrosion prevention on pipes that are not temperature-controlled (e.g., ambient-temperature drainage pipes carrying cold water but not chilled enough to cause condensation below dew point), yet the condition 'for temperature-controlled pipes' may be misinterpreted — many pipes that are not actively temperature-controlled can still condense moisture.

subject: Cable Trunking and Raceways
rationale: Trunking and raceways are fundamental components of structured cable management.
conditions: for organizing and routing cables neatly

subject: Cable Trunking and Raceways
rationale: Cable trunking facilitates the physical distribution of electrical power throughout a building.
applicability: The assertion does not specify voltage or current limitations. In many electrical codes (e.g., NEC, IEC), trunking and raceways used for power cables must meet specific fire rating, IP rating, and segregation-from-data-cables requirements. Without these conditions, the assertion is too broad.
conditions: by providing pathways for power distribution cables

subject: Underfloor Duct and Cellular Floor Systems
rationale: Underfloor duct systems are typically embedded in or placed on top of structural slabs; the slab provides the primary structural support.
applicability: The assertion 'Underfloor Duct and Cellular Floor Systems depends_on Structural Slab' assumes the structural slab is always present, but in some building types (e.g., buildings with raised access floors on a structural frame without a full slab, or buildings with timber/concrete joist systems where the 'slab' is not a distinct structural element) there may be no conventional structural slab as the primary support. The dependency should be scoped to buildings with concrete or steel frame and a poured slab.
conditions: must be designed to accommodate duct layouts
load-bearing capacity must support duct and floor system
exceptions: Underfloor duct systems may also be installed in or atop a concrete topping slab on a precast hollow-core plank system. In such cases, the 'structural slab' might be a precast plank (which is not a conventional poured structural slab), yet the duct system still depends on it. This is an exception where the definition of 'structural slab' is ambiguous.

subject: Firestopping and Cable Transit Seals
rationale: In some designs, firestopping penetrations may be monitored or coordinated with fire alarm zones, though not a direct physical connection.
applicability: The condition 'in buildings where firestop penetrations require fire alarm monitoring or detection' is extremely narrow and atypical. Most building codes (e.g., IBC, NFPA 101) require firestopping of penetrations but do not mandate electronic monitoring or connection to the fire alarm system. The assertion is only valid in the rare context of 'intumescent firestop systems with integrated alarm signalling' or 'firestop monitoring systems' — a very small subset of applications. The general applicability ('commercial; industrial') is therefore misleadingly broad.
conditions: in buildings where firestop penetrations require fire alarm monitoring or detection

subject: Cable Pulling and Installation Activity
rationale: Cable pulling is a prerequisite activity that enables subsequent termination and connection of cables to equipment.
applicability: The assertion assumes a linear sequential workflow (pull first, then terminate). However, in many real-world installation projects, multiple cables are pulled first as a batch, and termination occurs later in a separate phase, often by different trades (e.g., pullers vs. terminator/connector technicians). Pulling does not always 'support' termination directly; it merely makes cables available at both ends. The causal dependency is weaker than the term 'supports' implies.
conditions: after cables are pulled and before final connection
exceptions: In many structured cabling installations, cable termination (connector installation) occurs before pulling, especially for factory-terminated or pre-terminated fiber/copper cable assemblies. In such cases, the pulling activity does not support termination — the termination is done prior to and independently of pulling.

subject: Cable Termination and Connection Activity
rationale: Fire alarm systems rely on properly terminated cables for sensors and control signals.
applicability: Fire detection and alarm systems have distinct cable types (e.g., fire-rated, circuits requiring end-of-line monitoring, addressable loop cables) that differ from general cable termination. The assertion implies any generic 'cable termination' activity supports fire alarm systems, but fire alarm cabling requires specific fire-resistant cabling and supervised terminations that standard cable termination may not satisfy. Additionally, fire alarm cabling often requires specialized terminations per NFPA 72 or BS 5839 that general electricians may not be qualified to perform.
conditions: fire alarm cabling is terminated

subject: Cable Termination and Connection Activity
rationale: Lighting systems depend on cable termination to receive power and control signals.
applicability: Lighting control systems often use low-voltage control wiring (e.g., DALI, 0-10V, KNX) in addition to power circuits. The assertion only mentions 'lighting circuits are terminated' which typically refers to mains voltage power circuits, but many modern lighting control systems require termination of control/data cables (e.g., DALI bus wiring, DMX, sensor cables) that are distinct from standard lighting circuits. Without including these control cable terminations, the assertion may be incomplete.
conditions: lighting circuits are terminated

subject: Cable Testing and Commissioning Activity
rationale: Cable testing is a prerequisite activity within the broader electrical system commissioning process.

subject: Cable Dressing and Management Activity
rationale: Proper cable dressing facilitates subsequent testing by ensuring cables are organized and accessible.
applicability: The assertion assumes cable dressing is always completed before testing and commissioning begins. In many projects, cable dressing is an iterative process — some dressing is done, then partial testing, then more dressing. The linear 'supports' relationship may not hold in such overlapping workflows.
conditions: well-dressed cables enable effective testing and commissioning
exceptions: If cables are dressed but then disturbed or damaged during testing/commissioning (e.g., by pulling, bending, or accessing termination points), the dressing may no longer support the activity effectively. Also, if cable testing requires temporary removal of dressing (e.g., to access connectors), the dressing activity may actually hinder rather than support testing.

subject: Wire (Conductors) per AWG Size
rationale: AWG conductors are the physical pathways delivering electricity throughout a building.
applicability: The assertion assumes AWG sizing is universally applicable, but many building electrical distribution systems use conductors sized in kcmil (thousands of circular mils) rather than AWG for larger feeders and service entrance conductors (above 4/0 AWG). AWG scale tops out at 4/0, so larger conductors commonly used in distribution systems are specified in kcmil, not AWG.
conditions: Wires of appropriate AWG sizes carry power from source to loads

subject: Wire (Conductors) per AWG Size
rationale: Branch circuit wiring per AWG supplies lighting loads.
applicability: Same kcmil limitation applies: for large lighting systems (e.g., sports field lighting, industrial high-bay lighting), feeder conductors to lighting panelboards or lighting distribution centers may be sized in kcmil rather than AWG.
conditions: AWG conductors supply power to lighting fixtures

subject: Armored (BX/AC) and Metal-Clad Cable
rationale: MC cable is commonly run to lighting fixtures in commercial and industrial settings.
conditions: when used for lighting circuits

subject: Non-Metallic (NM/Romex) Cable
rationale: NM cable commonly supplies power to lighting fixtures in residential construction.
conditions: when used as branch circuit wiring for lights
exceptions: NM cable cannot be used as a support means for a lighting fixture. The National Electrical Code (NEC 314.27) requires fixtures to be supported independently of the wiring method. NM cable is not rated for mechanical support of fixtures.

subject: Service Entrance and Feeder Cabling
rationale: A dedicated electrical room provides space and clearance for safe installation.
conditions: for housing service entrance equipment
exceptions: small residential may use exterior-mounted service panel

subject: Service Entrance and Feeder Cabling
rationale: Feeder cabling provides necessary power for building lighting circuits.
applicability: The assertion states that Service Entrance and Feeder Cabling 'supports' Lighting System 'when feeder supplies lighting panel'. However, feeder cabling also frequently supplies non-lighting loads (e.g., mechanical equipment, receptacles, elevators) from the same service entrance, and the assertion does not capture that the cabling supports those other systems as well. This is a context limitation because the relationship is stated as if the primary support is to lighting, whereas in many buildings the feeder cabling supports multiple distribution panels for various purposes.
conditions: when feeder supplies lighting panel

subject: Fire Sprinkler Piping
rationale: A fire pump boosts water pressure to ensure sprinklers function properly.
applicability: The assertion states 'Fire Sprinkler Piping requires Fire Pump' when municipal water pressure is insufficient, but this is not universally true. In many jurisdictions, fire sprinkler systems can rely on elevated tanks, gravity tanks, or booster pumps that are not classified as 'Fire Pumps' per NFPA 20. Additionally, some systems use pressure tanks (NFPA 13) that eliminate the need for a fire pump entirely. The term 'Fire Pump' has a specific meaning (NFPA 20 listed assembly) that is narrower than any pump providing pressure.
conditions: when municipal water pressure is insufficient

subject: Fire Sprinkler Piping
rationale: Sprinkler heads are the terminal devices that discharge water when activated.
conditions: installed at designed spacing and coverage

subject: Fire Sprinkler Piping
rationale: Prevents contaminated water from flowing back into the potable water system.
applicability: all buildings connected to potable water supply

The assertion 'Fire Sprinkler Piping requires Backflow Preventer' conditioned on local codes is accurate, but it misses an important exception: backflow preventers are not required where the system is supplied by a dedicated fire protection water supply (e.g., a private well, tank, or reservoir not connected to a potable water system). The assertion's applicability says 'all buildings connected to potable water supply,' which partially addresses this, but the condition should explicitly exclude non-potable supplies rather than relying only on local code triggers.
conditions: required by local codes

subject: Fire Sprinkler Piping
rationale: Sprinkler system depends on the fire alarm system to signal activation and supervisory conditions.
conditions: for monitoring flow switches and tamper switches

subject: Fire Sprinkler Piping
rationale: Sprinkler piping may interconnect with standpipe risers for fire department use.
conditions: in buildings with combined systems

subject: Sprinkler Control Valve
rationale: The valve may interface with fire alarm for automatic activation and monitoring of flow switches and tamper switches.
applicability: The assertion states 'Sprinkler Control Valve depends_on Fire Alarm System', but in many jurisdictions (e.g., NFPA 13-compliant systems), sprinkler control valves (e.g., OS&Y gate valves) are mechanical valves that do not require electrical power or a fire alarm system to function. They can be manually operated. The dependency on a fire alarm system is only applicable to certain electrically supervised valve types (e.g., butterfly valves with tamper switches) or where the valve's status is monitored by the fire alarm - not for the valve's basic operation.
conditions: Electrical power and control wiring must be intact

subject: Sprinkler Control Valve
rationale: Tamper switches on control valves send a supervisory signal if the valve is partially or fully closed.
conditions: Wired to fire alarm panel
exceptions: The assertion states 'Sprinkler Control Valve depends_on Tamper Switch' but there are many sprinkler control valves that do not have tamper switches at all - e.g., small systems, older installations, or valves where local manual supervision is used instead. The dependency only applies when the valve is electrically supervised via a tamper switch wired to the fire alarm panel.

subject: Sprinkler Control Valve
rationale: Sprinkler control valves are typically installed on sprinkler risers where the system connects to the water supply.
conditions: Located at sprinkler riser assemblies

subject: Sprinkler Control Valve
rationale: The control valve connects to flow switches that detect water movement when sprinklers activate.
conditions: Installed downstream of the valve
exceptions: The assertion 'Sprinkler Control Valve connects_to Flow Switch' with condition 'Installed downstream of the valve' is not universally true. In many sprinkler system configurations, the flow switch is installed upstream of the control valve (e.g., on the riser before the main control valve) or on a separate branch. The flow switch location relative to the valve depends on the specific system design and what the flow switch is monitoring.

subject: Fire Sprinkler Pump
rationale: The fire alarm system monitors pump status and signals faults to the building management or fire department.
applicability: All sprinkler systems monitored by fire alarm

The assertion states that a Fire Sprinkler Pump 'depends_on' a Fire Alarm System, but in many jurisdictions, fire pumps can start via pressure drop alone (e.g., from a jockey pump controller) without a fire alarm signal. The dependency is often on the fire alarm for supervisory/status monitoring rather than for pump operation itself.
conditions: Pump run status, power failure, and phase reversal signals must be transmitted
exceptions: In some configurations, the fire alarm system monitors the pump (run status, power failure, phase reversal) but the pump can operate independently of the fire alarm system—e.g., via local manual start or automatic pressure switch start. The assertion implies a hard operational dependency that is not universally true.

subject: Fire Sprinkler Pump
rationale: Diesel engines require combustion air and must exhaust fumes safely.
applicability: The assertion says 'Fire Sprinkler Pump depends_on Ventilation System' but this dependency is room-specific (diesel engine rooms), not a dependency of the pump itself. Diesel fire pump controllers/engines require ventilation, but electric fire pumps do not depend on the ventilation system at all. The title is misleadingly broad.
conditions: For diesel engine rooms: combustion air and exhaust ventilation needed
exceptions: Electric pump rooms require less ventilation

subject: Fire Sprinkler Pump
rationale: Fire pumps often supply both sprinkler and standpipe risers in high-rise buildings.
conditions: Combined sprinkler/standpipe systems require pump to serve both
exceptions: Separate standpipe pumps may exist

subject: Fire Sprinkler Pump
rationale: The fire pump enables effective fire suppression by delivering water at adequate pressure.
applicability: Buildings with fire suppression demands exceeding municipal water pressure
conditions: Any water-based fire suppression system needing pressure boost

subject: Fire Sprinkler Pump
rationale: The pump is physically connected to suction piping from the water source and discharge piping to the sprinkler system.
conditions: Properly sized suction and discharge piping per NFPA 20

subject: Sprinkler Water Supply Connection
rationale: Backflow preventers protect potable water supply from contamination by sprinkler system water.
conditions: required by plumbing codes
exceptions: In some jurisdictions, a backflow preventer is not required if the sprinkler system is supplied by a dedicated fire protection water supply (e.g., a储水 tank or natural water source) rather than a potable water connection, as cross-connection risk does not exist.

subject: Sprinkler Water Supply Connection
rationale: A fire pump may be connected downstream to boost pressure from the water supply connection.
applicability: In many configurations, especially where the fire pump takes suction directly from a public water main or a dedicated storage tank, the sprinkler water supply connection feeds the pump suction rather than 'connecting to' the pump output. The phrasing 'connects_to' is ambiguous and could be misinterpreted as a direct connection at the discharge side.
conditions: when pressure from source is insufficient

subject: Sprinkler Water Supply Connection
rationale: Flow switches may be part of the connection or riser assembly to detect water flow and trigger alarms.
conditions: for alarm initiation
exceptions: In dry-pipe or pre-action sprinkler systems, a flow switch may be located on the system side (downstream of the dry-pipe valve) rather than being directly 'contained' in the water supply connection itself. The flow switch in such systems is not integral to the water supply connection riser but is part of the distribution piping.

In very small or residential sprinkler systems, a flow switch may be omitted entirely if alarm initiation is achieved through other means (e.g., pressure switches or water motor gongs), especially in systems with fewer than a certain number of sprinkler heads per code allowances.

subject: Sprinkler System Riser
rationale: Building codes typically require a backflow preventer on the sprinkler riser to protect the public water supply from contamination.
applicability: Backflow preventers are not universally required on sprinkler risers in all jurisdictions or system types. For example, some jurisdictions may allow a double-check valve assembly or reduced pressure zone (RPZ) device instead of a dedicated 'backflow preventer' as a separate component, or may have different requirements based on the water source (e.g., non-potable sources). Additionally, in some dry-pipe or pre-action systems, the backflow prevention requirements may differ.
conditions: to prevent contamination of potable water

subject: Sprinkler System Riser
rationale: A flow switch is typically installed on the riser to detect water flow and trigger the fire alarm.
applicability: Flow switches are not required on all sprinkler risers. They are typically required on wet-pipe systems for alarm initiation, but in dry-pipe or pre-action systems, the detection and alarm may be provided by other devices such as pressure switches or release panels. Flow switches may also be omitted on very small systems or in certain configurations where the riser serves only a limited area.

subject: Sprinkler System Riser
rationale: A tamper switch monitors the position of the riser control valve and signals if it is closed.
applicability: Tamper switches are required on control valves, not universally on the riser itself. While the main control valve at the riser typically requires a tamper switch, a riser is not synonymous with a valve. If the riser is defined as the vertical pipe assembly, the tamper switch is actually a requirement on the control valve (gate valve or butterfly valve) that is part of or adjacent to the riser, not on the riser as a pipe. The assertion is ambiguous and may misrepresent what the tamper switch is physically attached to.

subject: Sprinkler System Riser
rationale: The riser's flow and tamper switches connect to the fire alarm system for monitoring.
applicability: Not all sprinkler risers are connected to a fire alarm system for monitoring. Smaller systems or those in jurisdictions with less stringent code adoptions may use local alarms only (e.g., mechanical water motor gong) without electrical monitoring by a fire alarm system. Additionally, in very simple configurations, the flow switch or pressure switch may activate a local bell without a full fire alarm system involvement.
conditions: for monitoring and alarm activation

subject: Sprinkler System Riser
rationale: The riser supports the entire sprinkler system by providing the pressurized water supply to all branch lines and sprinkler heads.

subject: Sprinkler Flow Switch
rationale: Flow switches are typically installed on the sprinkler riser or branch lines.
conditions: Installed in proper orientation (arrow direction)
exceptions: Flow switches can also be installed on the main supply line downstream of the riser, such as on floor-level branch lines in large multi-story buildings where zone-based flow detection is required. In such cases, the flow switch does not directly connect to the Sprinkler System Riser but to a branch line or feed main.

In certain configurations, such as with a floor control valve assembly, the flow switch is installed on the branch line downstream of the control valve, not directly on the riser. This is a common exception in multi-story buildings where each floor has its own flow detection.

subject: Sprinkler Tamper Switch
rationale: The tamper switch detects if a sprinkler system valve is closed or partially closed, preventing the sprinkler system from being rendered inoperative without notice.
applicability: all buildings with fire sprinkler systems

The assertion applies to all buildings with fire sprinkler systems, but not all sprinkler systems have tamper switches. Smaller systems (e.g., those with a single valve that is not concealed) or older systems may lack tamper switches entirely. The assertion should be scoped to systems that actually include a tamper switch.
conditions: when valve is partially or fully closed unintentionally

subject: Sprinkler Tamper Switch
rationale: The tamper switch is typically connected as a supervisory device on the fire alarm system.
conditions: as a supervised initiating device

subject: Sprinkler Escutcheon
rationale: A sprinkler escutcheon is a metal ring or plate that fits around a sprinkler head to cover the gap between the ceiling and the sprinkler head. It requires the sprinkler head to function.
applicability: all building types with fire sprinkler systems

Escutcheons are not required for sprinkler heads in concealed spaces (above drop ceilings) or in walls where no escutcheon is specified by code. Many sprinkler heads in plenum spaces or unfinished areas do not use escutcheons.
conditions: for proper coverage and water distribution

subject: Sprinkler Escutcheon
rationale: Escutcheons provide a neat, finished look around sprinkler heads in ceilings.
applicability: all building types with finished ceilings
conditions: by providing a clean, finished appearance around sprinkler penetration

subject: Sprinkler Escutcheon
rationale: The escutcheon is a ring that encircles/girts the sprinkler head where it protrudes through the ceiling.
applicability: A sprinkler escutcheon does not contain the sprinkler head in the sense of enclosing or holding it. The escutcheon is a ring that fits around the sprinkler head; 'contains' is ambiguous and may imply the head is inside the escutcheon, which is not the intended relationship.
conditions: the escutcheon surrounds and frames the sprinkler head

subject: Sprinkler Escutcheon
rationale: The escutcheon is physically attached to or presses against the sprinkler head assembly.
conditions: mechanically fitted around the sprinkler base or neck

subject: Sprinkler Head Guard
rationale: A sprinkler head guard is an accessory mounted on a sprinkler head; it requires an underlying sprinkler system and sprinkler head to function.
conditions: Sprinkler head guard is installed on sprinkler heads

subject: Sprinkler Head Guard
rationale: The guard is mounted directly onto the sprinkler head.
applicability: The condition states 'Guard is specifically designed for the sprinkler head model', but universal or adjustable sprinkler head guards exist that can fit multiple head models. In such cases, the guard does not require a specific head model—it requires a sprinkler head but not one of a specifically matching model.
conditions: Guard is specifically designed for the sprinkler head model

subject: Fire Sprinkler System Type
rationale: Sprinkler heads are the discharge components that distribute water onto a fire.
exceptions: A fire sprinkler system type (e.g., deluge, pre-action, foam-water) can exist as a design specification or classification without physical sprinkler heads having been installed yet. The assertion conflates the design/type with physical components.

subject: Fire Sprinkler System Type
rationale: Many sprinkler systems are tied to fire alarms for waterflow detection and notification.
applicability: The assertion states that Fire Sprinkler System Type requires a Fire Alarm System, listing conditions for flow switches and pre-action systems. However, wet pipe systems do not necessarily require a fire alarm system in all jurisdictions; they may only require local waterflow alarms (bells) rather than a full fire alarm system. The conditions listed are incomplete.
conditions: flow switches activated
pre-action systems

subject: Fire Sprinkler System Type
rationale: The system physically contains pipes, fittings, hangers, and brackets as integral components.
applicability: The assertion states that Fire Sprinkler System Type 'contains' Piping and Fittings. While physical sprinkler systems contain piping and fittings, the 'Fire Sprinkler System Type' is a classification or design parameter (e.g., wet, dry, pre-action, deluge), not an assembly that physically contains components. This confuses the type/classification with the physical system.

subject: Fire Sprinkler System Type
rationale: When water pressure is insufficient, a fire pump is needed to boost pressure to sprinkler heads.
conditions: inadequate municipal water pressure
exceptions: The assertion states Fire Sprinkler System Type depends_on Fire Pump with conditions of inadequate municipal pressure and applicability limited to high-rise and large industrial. However, some sprinkler system types (e.g., NFPA 13R systems in residential buildings up to 4 stories) may not require a fire pump even in those scenarios if the municipal supply is adequate at the topmost sprinkler.

subject: Fire Sprinkler System Type
rationale: Backflow preventers protect potable water supply from contamination by sprinkler system water.
applicability: The assertion states Fire Sprinkler System Type depends_on Backflow Prevention Devices without any conditions. While backflow prevention is commonly required, some sprinkler system types (e.g., dry pipe systems supplied from a dedicated fire pump drawing from a private tank/pond) may not require a backflow preventer because there is no cross-connection with the potable water supply.

subject: Sprinkler System Room
rationale: Backflow preventer is required to protect potable water supply from contamination by sprinkler system water.
conditions: installed on water supply line
exceptions: In buildings with a backflow preventer located outdoors (e.g., in a vault or pit), the Sprinkler System Room does not depend on an indoor Backflow Preventer. The dependence only exists when the backflow preventer is physically located within or immediately adjacent to the sprinkler room.

subject: Sprinkler System Room
rationale: A floor drain is required to handle water discharge from system testing, draining, or accidental leakage.
conditions: floor drain required
exceptions: Sprinkler System Rooms in existing buildings with slab-on-grade construction may not require a separate floor drain if drainage is achieved through a trench drain, sump pit with pump, or if the room is in a seismic zone where floor drains are prohibited to prevent gas backflow.

subject: Sprinkler Pipe Insulation
rationale: A vapor barrier or vapor retarder is needed to prevent moisture from condensing on cold pipes and saturating the insulation.
conditions: For cold pipe applications to prevent condensation
exceptions: Closed-cell foam insulation may have integral vapor retarder

In dry/arid environments (e.g., desert climates with very low ambient humidity), condensation is unlikely to form on cold sprinkler pipes, so a vapor barrier may not be necessary. The assertion only notes humid environments as applicability, but does not acknowledge that in non-humid conditions the vapor barrier requirement may be absent.

If the sprinkler pipe is located within a conditioned, temperature-controlled space (e.g., interior of a building with HVAC maintaining dew point above pipe surface temperature), condensation risk may be mitigated without a vapor barrier being strictly required.

subject: Sprinkler Installation and Testing
rationale: Sprinkler systems require a reliable water source (municipal, tank, or reservoir) to function during fire events.
applicability: The assertion does not address fire sprinkler systems supplied by dedicated fire pumps drawing from wells, lakes, or storage tanks where the 'Water Supply System' is the fire protection system itself, not a separate municipal or building water supply system.
conditions: Adequate water pressure and flow rate must be available
exceptions: Temporary water supply via fire department connections during testing

Standalone residential sprinkler systems in single-family dwellings often use a dedicated residential sprinkler riser and do not have a separate 'Water Supply System' as a distinct external system dependency; the domestic water service serves as the supply. The assertion assumes an external Water Supply System always exists as a separate entity.

subject: Sprinkler Installation and Testing
rationale: Fire pumps boost water pressure to meet sprinkler system demand when natural pressure is inadequate.
conditions: Where municipal water pressure is insufficient
exceptions: Buildings where gravity tanks or high street pressure provide adequate flow

subject: Sprinkler Installation and Testing
rationale: Sprinkler heads are the discharge devices that activate when heat triggers them.
conditions: Must be selected based on occupancy hazard classification

subject: Sprinkler Installation and Testing
rationale: Backflow preventers stop non-potable water from flowing back into the public water supply.
applicability: all buildings connected to municipal water
conditions: Required by local plumbing codes to prevent contamination of potable water
exceptions: Systems supplied by dedicated fire protection water tanks only

Backflow prevention is not universally required for all buildings connected to municipal water. Some jurisdictions exempt systems with fire department connections where a reduced pressure zone (RPZ) device would impair fire flow, and instead require a check valve assembly or double-check detector assembly which is not a full 'Backflow Prevention Device' as commonly defined.

subject: Sprinkler Installation and Testing
rationale: Sprinkler system status is electrically monitored and annunciated through the fire alarm system.
conditions: Flow switches and tamper switches must be connected to the fire alarm panel
exceptions: Very small residential systems may use local bells only

subject: Gypsum Board Panels
rationale: Corner beads protect vulnerable external corners and provide a straight edge for finishing.
conditions: at external corners
exceptions: some trimless systems or rounded corners may use alternative profiles

subject: Gypsum Board Panels
rationale: Insulation is often placed within wall cavities behind gypsum board for thermal and acoustic performance.
conditions: when used as interior wall finish in exterior walls or between sound-rated assemblies
exceptions: interior non-rated partitions may not require insulation

subject: Metal Stud Framing
rationale: Insulation is placed within metal stud cavities for thermal and sound control.
conditions: thermal and acoustic performance requirements
exceptions: unconditioned spaces may not require insulation

subject: Metal Stud Framing
rationale: Metal stud framing supports exterior cladding materials such as brick veneer, metal panels, or EIFS.
conditions: exterior wall applications
exceptions: load-bearing cladding systems may be self-supporting

subject: Metal Stud Framing
rationale: The cavities between metal studs contain insulation materials for thermal and acoustic control.
applicability: The assertion 'Metal Stud Framing contains Insulation' with condition 'within stud cavities' is overly broad. In commercial metal stud applications (e.g., curtain wall systems, exterior insulation finish systems), insulation is often placed exterior to the stud framing (continuous insulation / ci) rather than within stud cavities. The assertion fails to capture that insulation location depends on thermal bridging strategy and code requirements.
conditions: within stud cavities

subject: Metal Stud Framing
rationale: Metal stud framing connects to the floor structure through the anchored bottom track.
conditions: via bottom track anchored to floor

subject: Joint Compound (Mud)
rationale: Joint compound is used to embed and cover corner beads, creating smooth, durable external corners.
applicability: The assertion states 'Joint Compound connects_to Corner Beads' but does not distinguish between paper-faced and metal corner beads. Metal corner beads often require a different joint compound formulation (setting-type compound) for the initial coat to prevent rust discoloration through the paper face, whereas paper-faced beads can use standard drying-type compound throughout.
conditions: At external corners of drywall assemblies
exceptions: Vinyl corner beads typically require adhesive (not joint compound) for attachment to the substrate; joint compound is only used for the finish coats over the bead, not for the initial bonding/connection. The assertion 'connects_to' implies the compound is the joining agent, which is incorrect for vinyl beads.

subject: Drywall Fasteners (Screws/Nails)
rationale: Tape is applied over joints and fasteners to prevent cracking, though fasteners themselves work without tape functionally.
conditions: for reinforcing joints between drywall panels
exceptions: Drywall fasteners (screws/nails) are used to attach drywall panels to studs/framing, not to reinforce joints between panels. The described function 'reinforcing joints between drywall panels' is actually the role of drywall tape (and joint compound), not the fasteners. Fasteners and tape serve independent functions - fasteners secure panels to framing, tape covers the joints between panels. A fastener does not physically or functionally 'depend on' tape.

subject: Drywall Cutting and Fitting
rationale: Proper cutting and fitting is a prerequisite for subsequent taping, mudding, and finishing operations.
conditions: after cutting and fitting is complete

subject: Drywall Cutting and Fitting
rationale: Drywall panels protect insulation material from physical disturbance and help hold it in place within wall cavities.
conditions: after installation

subject: Taping and Bedding
rationale: Paper or mesh tape is embedded in joint compound to bridge and reinforce the joints between drywall sheets.
applicability: all buildings with gypsum board walls
conditions: for reinforcing joints between drywall panels

subject: Taping and Bedding
rationale: Taping and bedding cannot proceed until drywall panels are hung, fastened, and joints are properly gapped.
applicability: all buildings with gypsum board walls
conditions: drywall panels must be properly fastened and aligned

subject: Taping and Bedding
rationale: Metal or vinyl corner beads are installed at outside corners and are covered as part of the taping and bedding process.
applicability: all buildings with gypsum board walls
conditions: at external corners of drywall assembly
exceptions: Corner beads are not required at internal corners of drywall assembly — only at external corners. The applicability says 'all buildings with gypsum board walls' but the condition already specifies 'at external corners.' This is consistent. However, there are exceptions: some systems use concealed (no-bead) corner finishing techniques, such as 'butted' or 'taped' corners without metal or vinyl beads for certain architectural finishes.

subject: Panel Hanging and Fastening
rationale: Panel fastening systems must work in conjunction with movement joints to allow for dimensional changes.
applicability: The assertion states that 'Panel Hanging and Fastening connects_to Movement joints' under the condition of accommodating thermal expansion and contraction, but this is only one type of movement joint. Movement joints also accommodate structural movement (e.g., differential settlement, wind load deflection, seismic movement) which are not related to thermal expansion/contraction of panels at meeting points. The condition should also reference structural and seismic movement, or the assertion should be scoped specifically to thermal movement joints.
conditions: Where panels meet to accommodate thermal expansion and contraction

subject: Mudding and Finishing
rationale: Mudding requires drywall tape (paper or mesh) to reinforce joints between drywall panels.
applicability: The assertion 'requires Drywall Tape' could be misinterpreted because the term 'Drywall Tape' may include both paper tape and self-adhesive mesh tape, which have different application methods and may or may not require a bed coat of mud. This ambiguity limits the precision of the assertion.
conditions: Joint compound application
exceptions: There are alternative methods for mudding joints that do not require drywall tape, such as using mesh tape (which is a different product from standard paper drywall tape) or, in some very specific repair contexts, using joint compound alone for small cracks or holes (e.g., patch repairs under 2 inches). Additionally, mesh tape is often used instead of paper tape for certain applications.

subject: Mudding and Finishing
rationale: Mudding and finishing cannot begin until drywall panels are properly hung.

subject: Mudding and Finishing
rationale: Corner beads must be installed at outside corners to provide a straight edge; mudding covers and embeds them.
applicability: The condition 'Exterior corners present' is ambiguous — it could refer to outside (external) corners of drywall, which typically require corner beads, or it could be misinterpreted as exterior building corners. A clearer condition would be 'outside corners of drywall assembly are present'.
conditions: Exterior corners present

subject: Mudding and Finishing
rationale: Properly finished drywall provides the smooth substrate required for painting.

subject: Mudding and Finishing
rationale: Mudding includes embedding tape into the joint compound at seams.

subject: Water-Resistant (Greenboard) Drywall
rationale: Joints between greenboard panels need to be taped and finished with joint compound.
conditions: For finishing joints and seams
exceptions: Greenboard drywall does not always require joint compound for finishing joints — it is typically used with cement board (e.g., in tile backer applications) where thinset mortar or special adhesives are used instead of standard drywall joint compound. Greenboard is often used as a tile substrate, and in wet areas, standard joint compound is not appropriate; instead, cement-based or polymer-modified setting materials are required.

subject: Water-Resistant (Greenboard) Drywall
rationale: Joint tape is used with compound to create seamless finished walls.
conditions: For reinforcing joints
exceptions: In wet areas where greenboard is used as tile backer (e.g., behind shower surrounds), standard paper drywall tape is not recommended because it lacks moisture resistance. Fiberglass mesh tape is typically specified instead for greenboard joints in damp environments. Additionally, if greenboard is used with a waterproofing membrane system, taped joints may be handled differently per the membrane manufacturer's instructions.

subject: Water-Resistant (Greenboard) Drywall
rationale: In certain applications, a vapor barrier may be needed behind greenboard to prevent moisture migration.
conditions: In exterior walls or cold climates

subject: Water-Resistant (Greenboard) Drywall
rationale: Greenboard encloses insulation within wall cavities.
conditions: When installed as interior wall cladding over insulated cavities

subject: Water-Resistant (Greenboard) Drywall
rationale: By resisting moisture, greenboard helps protect the underlying framing from moisture damage.
conditions: From incidental moisture exposure
exceptions: Greenboard does not 'protect' structural framing from incidental moisture exposure in a meaningful way. While the paper facing is moisture-resistant, greenboard is not a water barrier — it will still allow moisture vapor transmission and can wick water through cut edges or fastener penetrations. True protection of framing from moisture requires a dedicated weather-resistive barrier (house wrap, building paper, or fluid-applied membrane), not greenboard. Asserting that greenboard 'protects' framing overstates its capability.

subject: Fire-Rated (Type X) Drywall
rationale: Tape reinforces joints and helps maintain fire integrity.
applicability: The assertion is missing the critical context that this requirement depends on the specific UL fire-rated assembly design. Many fire-rated assemblies have explicit listing numbers with specific materials, and not all require tape at every joint — some use only compound, or specific fire-rated sealants at certain joints (e.g., head-of-wall joints).
conditions: Typically paper or fiberglass mesh tape used at joints
exceptions: Fire-rated Type X drywall does not always require drywall tape at all joints — for example, fire-rated assemblies often require specific listed systems (UL designs) that may call for joint compound without tape, or proprietary systems where the tape is not needed for the full fire rating. Additionally, in some non-rated repairs, skip-taping may be used. The assertion that tape is always required is an overstatement.

subject: Sound-Insulating (Acoustic) Drywall
rationale: Acoustic sealant is required to seal gaps and prevent sound flanking paths, essential for acoustic performance.
applicability: The applicability is specified as 'All building types', but sound-insulating drywall systems and their sealing requirements vary significantly by building code and occupancy type (e.g., healthcare facilities, schools, and residential buildings may have different fire-rating and acoustic requirements that modify how joints/penetrations must be sealed). Additionally, seismic-rated buildings often require flexible sealants or different detailing than standard acoustic sealant.
conditions: At all joints, edges, and penetrations

subject: Sound-Insulating (Acoustic) Drywall
rationale: Acoustic performance is only as good as the weakest link; walls must connect to acoustic-rated doors for full isolation.
conditions: For complete room-in-room acoustic isolation

subject: Mold-Resistant Drywall
rationale: In cold climates, vapor retarders prevent moisture migration that could compromise even mold-resistant drywall.
conditions: In cold climates to prevent condensation within walls
exceptions: Not required in warm climates or on interior side of insulation

subject: Mold-Resistant Drywall
rationale: Like standard drywall, mold-resistant drywall provides a substrate for wall finishes.
applicability: Some mold-resistant drywall products have fiberglass facers or non-paper surfaces that are not compatible with standard wallpaper adhesives or may require specific primers/application methods. The existing exception about 'specific primers' is too narrow—it should also address wallpaper adhesion and paint compatibility issues.
conditions: Paint, primer, or wallpaper can be applied
exceptions: Some mold-resistant drywall types may require specific primers

subject: Mold-Resistant Drywall
rationale: Mold-resistant drywall is a finish material, not a structural element, and cannot be used for load-bearing purposes.
conditions: Mold-resistant drywall does not provide structural load capacity

subject: Shaftliner Drywall
rationale: Shaftliner panels form the fire-rated enclosure around stairwells.
applicability: The assertion claims shaftliner drywall 'supports' stairwell enclosure, but in stair pressurization shafts, shaftliner is used as a fire-resistant membrane within the shaft wall assembly, not as a structural support element for the enclosure itself. The intended meaning may be that it forms a fire-rated boundary for the enclosure, not structural support.
conditions: When used in stair pressurization shafts
exceptions: Shaftliner drywall (typically a lightweight, non-structural gypsum board for elevator/mechanical shafts) is not designed to support stairwell enclosures structurally. It is a non-loadbearing infill panel, not a structural supporting element for an enclosure assembly.

subject: Exterior Gypsum Sheathing
rationale: Exterior gypsum sheathing requires a structural frame (wood studs, steel studs) to be attached to.
conditions: For vertical support and attachment

subject: Exterior Gypsum Sheathing
rationale: Gypsum sheathing provides a flat, rigid surface that supports the exterior cladding system (e.g., siding, stucco, EIFS).
conditions: When used as a substrate for cladding attachment
