subject: Residential Units
rationale: Residential units require a structural frame (load-bearing walls, columns, slabs) to support floors, walls, and roofs.
conditions: when part of a multi-story building
exceptions: A single-story residential building (e.g., a ranch-style house) that is part of a larger multi-story building complex (e.g., a podium-style apartment building) would still require a structural frame, but the condition only triggers for multi-story buildings. Conversely, a multi-story residential unit made of load-bearing masonry or CLT panels may not have a 'Structural Frame' in the traditional sense (beam/column system), yet still be structurally sound.

subject: Residential Units
rationale: Residential units require heating, ventilation, and air conditioning to maintain indoor comfort and air quality.
conditions: in climates requiring heating or cooling
exceptions: naturally ventilated designs in mild climates

The existing exception already covers naturally ventilated designs in mild climates, but there is an additional exception: residential units designed as 'unconditioned' spaces (e.g., seasonal cabins, sunrooms, enclosed porches used as sleeping quarters in warm climates) that lack mechanical heating/cooling but are still occupied as residential units. These would not require an HVAC system.

subject: Residential Units
rationale: Residential units require potable water supply and wastewater drainage for kitchens, bathrooms, and laundry.

subject: Residential Units
rationale: Residential units require electrical wiring, outlets, lighting, and power for appliances and devices.
exceptions: Off-grid residential units (e.g., tiny houses, remote cabins) that operate entirely on solar photovoltaic with battery storage and no connection to an electrical grid or conventional electrical system technically have an electrical power system but it may not be classified as a building 'Electrical System' in the traditional sense. Additionally, some very basic dwellings (e.g., primitive huts, traditional structures in developing regions) may have no electrical system at all.

subject: Residential Units
rationale: Residential units depend on soundproofing between units and from exterior noise for livability.
conditions: in multi-unit buildings or noise-sensitive areas

subject: Residential Units
rationale: Residential units depend on insulation in walls, roof, and floors to reduce energy loss.
conditions: in climates with temperature extremes
exceptions: Residential buildings in very hot climates (e.g., desert regions) may require thermal insulation to keep heat out, but the condition 'in climates with temperature extremes' is ambiguous — does it include climates that are extremely hot but not cold? The assertion might be read as only applying where both hot and cold extremes occur. Additionally, unconditioned residential buildings (e.g., screened porches used as sleeping areas, seasonal structures) in extreme climates would not require thermal insulation.

subject: Common Amenity Spaces
rationale: Common amenity spaces (lounges, gyms, pools, etc.) need HVAC to maintain comfortable indoor air quality and temperature.
conditions: for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning
exceptions: Unconditioned amenity spaces such as unenclosed rooftop terraces, open-air courtyards, or naturally ventilated pergolas may not require an HVAC system, yet the assertion lacks a condition to exclude these cases.

subject: Common Amenity Spaces
rationale: Amenity spaces require adequate lighting for safety, wayfinding, and usability.
conditions: for general illumination and task lighting
exceptions: Amenity spaces that rely solely on natural daylighting and are only used during daytime (e.g., sunrooms, solariums, open-air pavilions) may not require a general illumination or task lighting system, yet the assertion does not account for this.

subject: Common Amenity Spaces
rationale: Many amenity spaces (fitness centers, pools, kitchens) rely on water supply and drainage.
conditions: if amenity includes restrooms, kitchenettes, or wet areas

subject: Common Amenity Spaces
rationale: Amenity spaces with heavy equipment or water features depend on adequate structural support.
conditions: for floor load capacity, especially for pools, gyms, or roof terraces

subject: Common Amenity Spaces
rationale: Common amenity spaces often require keycard or fob access to ensure only residents/tenants use them.
conditions: for access control to restrict amenity use to authorized residents/users

subject: Common Amenity Spaces
rationale: Sound control is important in amenity spaces to avoid disturbing adjacent residents and to ensure user comfort.
applicability: The assertion treats acoustic treatment as a general requirement for noise-sensitive amenity spaces but does not address building code minimums (e.g., IBC STC ratings, or local noise ordinances) which may impose specific performance criteria beyond generic acoustic treatment.
conditions: for noise-sensitive amenity spaces like libraries, quiet lounges, or media rooms

subject: Laundry Facilities
rationale: Laundry facilities need hot and cold water supply and wastewater drainage to operate washing machines and sinks.
applicability: all building types with laundry facilities
conditions: for water supply and drainage

subject: Laundry Facilities
rationale: Washing machines, dryers, irons, and lighting all require electrical power.
applicability: all building types with laundry facilities
conditions: for powering washing machines, dryers, and lighting

subject: Laundry Facilities
rationale: Laundry dryers produce hot, moist air that must be vented to prevent mold, corrosion, and moisture damage.
applicability: all building types with laundry facilities
conditions: for moisture and heat removal from dryers and washer-extractors
exceptions: condenser dryers that do not require external venting

The existing exception mentions condenser dryers that do not require external venting, but there are also ventless heat pump dryers that recirculate air and require no external venting. The exception should be broadened to include heat pump dryers or the assertion needs to be updated.

subject: Laundry Facilities
rationale: Floor drains help manage water spills, leaks, and floor cleaning in wet laundry areas.
applicability: commercial laundry facilities, multi-family laundry rooms
conditions: for overflow protection and floor washing
exceptions: Floor drains in laundry rooms are not required universally even in commercial settings if the room is on an upper floor above occupied spaces and local codes do not mandate them. Some jurisdictions allow washing machine pan/drip trays with drain connections in lieu of a floor drain.

subject: Laundry Facilities
rationale: Washing machines require connection to the building's water supply via dedicated hose bibs or valves.
applicability: all building types with laundry facilities
conditions: for hot and cold water connection to washing machines

subject: Laundry Facilities
rationale: Carpet absorbs water, harbors mold, and is damaged by bleach and detergents; hard flooring is required.
applicability: all building types with laundry facilities
conditions: due to moisture, bleach, and staining risk

subject: Mail and Package Rooms
rationale: Mail rooms require adequate lighting for reading addresses, sorting, and safe movement.
applicability: The assertion states Mail and Package Rooms 'requires' Lighting System, but small or very basic package rooms (e.g., a simple locked cabinet or drop-box in a lobby) may not have or need a dedicated lighting system if ambient hallway lighting is sufficient. This is a context limitation where a separate/dedicated lighting system may not be required.
conditions: For occupant visibility and safety

subject: Mail and Package Rooms
rationale: Interior mail rooms need mechanical ventilation for air quality.
conditions: If the room is interior without exterior windows
exceptions: Rooms with natural ventilation may not require mechanical ventilation

subject: Mail and Package Rooms
rationale: Mail rooms often need restricted access to prevent theft and vandalism.
conditions: For secure access by authorized personnel and residents
exceptions: Small buildings may rely on a locked building door only

The existing exception mentions small buildings may rely on a locked building door only, but there are additional exceptions not captured: buildings with package lockers (e.g., Amazon Hub, Luxer) that have integrated access control on the locker itself rather than a room-level access control system, or buildings where package delivery personnel have temporary building access codes negating the need for a separate room access system.

subject: Corridors and Circulation
rationale: Handrails are required along at least one side of egress corridors per IBC and accessibility standards.
conditions: in corridors serving as means of egress
where required by accessibility codes
exceptions: very short corridors less than 3m

Corridors serving as a means of egress that are less than the minimum width threshold for requiring two handrails (e.g., under 48 inches in some codes, or corridors where only one side is required) may not require handrails on both sides. Also, fire-rated corridors that are part of a horizontal exit may have different handrail requirements.

subject: Corridors and Circulation
rationale: Corridors connect to stairwells to enable vertical circulation and egress.
conditions: for multi-level buildings
exceptions: The assertion lacks exceptions for open-plan buildings where exit passageways or 'horizontal exits' may be used instead of stairs for means of egress, and for single-story buildings where exit doors to the exterior replace stair connections. Also does not account for mezzanines or buildings where exit discharge is directly to exterior at grade.

subject: Corridors and Circulation
rationale: Corridor ceilings contain sprinkler heads as part of fire suppression systems.
conditions: in buildings with fire sprinkler systems
exceptions: Not all corridors in sprinklered buildings contain sprinkler heads. Building codes allow sprinkler omissions in certain corridors, such as those less than 4 ft wide, dead-end corridors of limited length, corridors that are part of 'un-sprinklered' spaces, corridors where the ceiling is of a type that does not require sprinkler coverage (e.g., open gratings), or corridors in buildings with alternative compliance paths.

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: The structural frame is the skeleton that supports the core and shell.
conditions: for vertical load bearing
exceptions: Some building types (e.g., single-story warehouses, agricultural barns, or certain tensile membrane structures) may use load-bearing walls or other systems instead of a dedicated structural frame for vertical load bearing. The assertion overstates necessity of a 'Structural Frame' as distinct from other vertical load-bearing strategies.

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: Foundations are essential for any building core and shell to remain stable.
conditions: to transfer loads to ground
exceptions: Temporary or relocatable buildings on shallow grade beams or ground slabs (e.g., modular portable buildings) may not require a dedicated 'Foundation System' in the traditional sense to transfer loads to ground, especially if placed on compacted ground or gravel pads.

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: The roof is part of the building envelope which is a key component of the core and shell.
conditions: to provide weather enclosure
exceptions: In arid or desert climates, or for open-air structures (e.g., covered parking, pavilions, certain industrial facilities), a Roof System may not be required to provide weather enclosure since the building is intentionally designed without full enclosure or rainfall is negligible.

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: Waterproofing protects the core and shell from moisture ingress.
conditions: for below-grade and wet areas

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: Elevator shafts are integral to the building core design.
applicability: The assertion applies only to multi-story buildings, but even among those, buildings with only 2-3 stories may use ramps or be served by platform lifts rather than a full 'Elevator System' as defined in building codes.
conditions: for vertical transportation in multi-story buildings

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: Elevator shafts are typically contained within the building core.
conditions: as part of vertical core
exceptions: Multi-story buildings may have elevators without a dedicated 'Elevator Shaft' (e.g., glass-enclosed external elevators, hydraulic elevators with hoistway inside stairwell), or may use platform lifts that do not require a shaft at all.

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: Stairwells are contained within the core area.
conditions: as part of vertical core

subject: Building Core and Shell
rationale: Public restrooms are often part of the core design.
conditions: on each floor
exceptions: Very small floor plates (e.g., small retail kiosks, small offices) in commercial/institutional/public buildings may not have a public restroom on each floor, relying instead on consolidated restrooms on select floors or nearby shared facilities.

subject: Residential Unit Interior Finishes
rationale: Wall finishes require structural backing (studs or furring) to be attached.
conditions: for wall finishes like drywall, paneling, or tile backer board
exceptions: load-bearing masonry walls may not need additional framing for finish

In many jurisdictions, furring strips attached directly to masonry or concrete walls are considered an acceptable substrate for drywall and do not constitute full 'Wall Framing'. This is a common alternative method not accounted for in the assertion or its existing exception.

subject: Residential Unit Interior Finishes
rationale: Wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be in place before drywall or paneling is applied.
conditions: before wall and ceiling finishes are installed
exceptions: In residential renovations or additions where ceiling finishes are installed but walls are left unfinished (e.g., open-concept exposed structure or 'industrial' style), electrical rough-in is still complete but interior finishes are partially applied. The assertion implies all interior finishes require electrical rough-in, but some finishes like ceiling-only work may proceed without new wall electrical rough-in.

subject: Residential Unit Interior Finishes
rationale: Pipes and drains must be installed within walls prior to closing them with finishes.
conditions: before wall finishes in bathrooms and kitchens

subject: Residential Unit Interior Finishes
rationale: Interior finishes often rely on insulation being in place for energy code compliance and comfort.
conditions: for thermal and acoustic performance behind finishes
exceptions: in unconditioned spaces where insulation is not required

subject: Residential Unit Interior Finishes
rationale: Moisture control layers behind finishes depend on proper sequencing before finish application.
applicability: Vapor barrier requirements vary significantly by climate zone (e.g., Class I, II, or III vapor retarders per IRC). In some climate zones or specific wall assemblies (e.g., certain warm-humid climates), vapor barriers are not recommended or may be prohibited. The assertion and its exception do not address this geographic/climatic dependency.
conditions: in exterior walls or moisture-prone areas
exceptions: in dry interior partition walls where no vapor barrier is needed

subject: Residential Unit Interior Finishes
rationale: Wall finishes are a primary subcategory of interior finishes.
conditions: including drywall, paint, wallpaper, tile, wood paneling, or plaster

subject: Residential Unit Interior Finishes
rationale: Ceiling finishes are a primary subcategory of interior finishes.
conditions: including painted drywall, acoustic tiles, suspended grid ceilings, or wood

subject: Unit Kitchen Systems
rationale: Unit kitchen systems require water supply and drainage piping to function for sinks, dishwashers, etc.
applicability: all building types with kitchen units
conditions: for water supply and drainage
exceptions: Food trucks, mobile kitchens, and temporary cooking setups (e.g., event catering tents) with Unit Kitchen Systems do not require permanent Plumbing System connections; they rely on portable water tanks and waste collection instead.

subject: Unit Kitchen Systems
rationale: Kitchen units require electrical power for lighting, outlets, and appliances like refrigerators, ovens, and dishwashers.
applicability: all building types with kitchen units
conditions: for power supply to appliances
exceptions: Gas-powered kitchen appliances (e.g., gas stoves/ovens) in Unit Kitchen Systems do not require an Electrical System for their primary power; they use gas combustion. The assertion is too broad as it implies all appliances require electrical power.

subject: Unit Kitchen Systems
rationale: Proper ventilation (range hoods, exhaust fans) is required to remove airborne grease, smoke, odors, and excess heat from cooking.
applicability: all building types with kitchen units
conditions: for exhaust of cooking fumes, smoke, and heat
exceptions: Outdoor kitchens or well-ventilated open-air cooking areas with Unit Kitchen Systems may not require a dedicated mechanical Ventilation System; natural ventilation suffices.

subject: Unit Kitchen Systems
rationale: Unit kitchen systems are composed of base cabinets, wall cabinets, and tall cabinets for storage.
applicability: all building types with kitchen units
exceptions: Some minimalist kitchen designs or commercial kitchens (e.g., in fast-food chains) may use open shelving, stainless steel counters, or equipment racks instead of traditional Kitchen Cabinetry. The assertion states Unit Kitchen Systems 'contains' Kitchen Cabinetry as a universal part, which is not always true.

subject: Unit Kitchen Systems
rationale: Countertops form the primary work surface of a unit kitchen system.
applicability: all building types with kitchen units
exceptions: Some commercial kitchens use stainless steel worktables or equipment-integrated surfaces rather than a distinct Countertop. Also, modular or compact kitchenettes may integrate sink and cooktop directly without a separate countertop surface.

subject: Unit Bathroom Systems
rationale: Bathrooms require ventilation to prevent mold, moisture buildup, and remove odors.
conditions: mechanical or natural ventilation to control humidity and odors
exceptions: Bathrooms in mobile vehicles (e.g., RVs, boats, aircraft lavatories) often lack dedicated mechanical or natural ventilation systems meeting building code definitions, yet they functionally include bathroom units.

subject: Unit Bathroom Systems
rationale: Hot water is essential for shower and sink functionality.
conditions: for hot water supply to shower, sink, and bath fixtures
exceptions: buildings with central hot water system

subject: Unit Bathroom Systems
rationale: Waterproofing prevents moisture damage to underlying structure and adjacent spaces.
conditions: applied to floors and wet walls

subject: Unit Bathroom Systems
rationale: Bathtubs are included in some but not all unit bathrooms.
conditions: optional luxury or family bathroom
exceptions: Bathtubs are not present in bathrooms in certain cultures/regions where shower-only bathrooms are the norm (e.g., many modern Japanese bathrooms, some European renovations replacing tubs with walk-in showers).

subject: Unit Bathroom Systems
rationale: Mirrors are standard above lavatories in unit bathrooms.
conditions: above sink or vanity
exceptions: Utility bathrooms, half-baths (powder rooms), or accessible/WC-only bathrooms may lack a mirror — these are still valid bathroom units (e.g., small WC with only a toilet and sink). Also, temporary/portable bathroom units (construction site toilets, event porta-potties) often do not include mirrors.

subject: Unit Bathroom Systems
rationale: Lighting is necessary for safe and functional bathroom use.
conditions: ambient and task lighting above mirror
exceptions: Utility bathrooms, half-baths (powder rooms without showers), or very small accessible WCs may have no overhead dedicated lighting fixture — relying on ambient light from adjacent spaces or a simple vent light combo that may not qualify as a dedicated 'Lighting Fixture' in the same sense.

subject: Common Kitchen and Dining Systems
rationale: Fire codes typically require fire suppression (e.g., Ansul system) over cooking equipment in commercial kitchens.
applicability: The assertion states that Common Kitchen and Dining Systems requires Fire Suppression System 'for cooking areas with grease-producing equipment' in commercial/institutional settings, but this conflates building system requirements with fire code requirements. Fire suppression systems (hood suppression systems per NFPA 96) are required specifically for commercial cooking operations that produce grease-laden vapors (deep fryers, griddles, ranges), not all grease-producing equipment (e.g., residential-style ovens with minimal grease output may not trigger the requirement). Additionally, many smaller commercial kitchens (e.g., coffee shops with only a microwave and toaster) do not have grease-producing cooking equipment and would not require a fire suppression system under most codes.
conditions: for cooking areas with grease-producing equipment

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: HVAC systems need ductwork to distribute conditioned air to different zones.
conditions: For air distribution throughout the building
exceptions: Hydronic systems may not require ductwork

The assertion 'HVAC Systems requires Ductwork' has an existing exception for hydronic systems, but there are additional exceptions not covered: ductless mini-split systems, through-wall PTAC units, window units, and VRF systems that use refrigerant piping to fan coil units without ductwork. The assertion should also note that ductless systems are a common exception in both commercial and residential contexts.

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: AHUs condition and circulate air as a core component of central HVAC systems.
conditions: For central HVAC systems
exceptions: Split systems may use separate indoor units

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: Chillers provide chilled water for cooling coils in larger HVAC installations.
conditions: For cooling in large-scale systems
exceptions: Smaller systems may use direct expansion (DX) cooling

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: Boilers generate hot water or steam for heating coils and radiators.
conditions: For heating in hydronic systems
exceptions: Electric resistance or heat pump systems may not require boilers

The assertion 'HVAC Systems requires Boiler' conditions specify 'For heating in hydronic systems', but the existing exception mentions heat pump systems may not require boilers. However, heat pumps themselves may still be part of a hydronic system (water-to-water heat pumps supplying hydronic distribution). The exception should be clarified to distinguish between air-source heat pumps and hydronic heat pump systems that might still use a boiler as backup.

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: Refrigerant piping connects compressors, condensers, and evaporators in refrigeration cycles.
conditions: For DX and VRF systems
exceptions: Hydronic systems do not require refrigerant piping

The assertion 'HVAC Systems requires Refrigerant Piping' does not account for emerging low-GWP refrigerant alternatives and refrigerant-free cooling technologies such as evaporative cooling, which do not require refrigerant piping. Additionally, chilled beam systems use water-based cooling without refrigerant piping.

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: Insulation minimizes energy losses from ducts and pipes carrying conditioned air or water.
conditions: For ductwork and piping to reduce heat loss/gain
exceptions: Unconditioned spaces with no thermal requirements

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: Filters remove particulates from air to protect equipment and occupants.
conditions: For maintaining indoor air quality
exceptions: Basic systems may have minimal filtration

The assertion 'HVAC Systems requires Air Filter' with applicability 'All building types' does not account for simple exhaust-only ventilation systems (e.g., bathroom exhaust fans in residential, parking garage ventilation) that do not have air filters. These are HVAC-adjacent systems but do not include filtration.

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: The building envelope's insulation, glazing, and airtightness determine heating and cooling loads that HVAC must overcome.
conditions: For thermal load calculations and system sizing

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: Pumps circulate heating or cooling fluid through pipes and coils.
applicability: The assertion 'HVAC Systems contains Pumps' is scoped to hydronic systems, but the phrasing says 'contains Pumps' without qualification in the main assertion text. The applicability correctly limits to 'Hydronic HVAC systems', but the assertion title is overly broad and could mislead users who do not read the fine print.
conditions: In hydronic systems for circulating water/glycol
exceptions: All-air systems without hydronic loops

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: HVAC systems interface with plumbing for water supply and drainage.
conditions: For condensate drainage, boiler water supply, and cooling tower makeup water
exceptions: All-air DX systems have minimal plumbing connections

The assertion 'HVAC Systems connects_to Plumbing System' states conditions involving condensate drainage, boiler water supply, and cooling tower makeup water. However, there are additional plumbing connections missed: humidifier water supply, chilled water system makeup water, and water-source heat pump loop water treatment. These should be noted or the exception scope adjusted.

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: HVAC equipment is powered by and controlled through the building's electrical system.
conditions: For power supply and control wiring

subject: HVAC Systems
rationale: HVAC ducts include fire dampers, and systems may be used for smoke evacuation and pressurization.
conditions: For smoke control, fire dampers, and interface with fire alarm
exceptions: Buildings without mechanical smoke control

subject: Plumbing and Drainage Systems
rationale: Plumbing systems need a water source to function.
conditions: for supplying fresh water to fixtures

subject: Plumbing and Drainage Systems
rationale: Fixtures like toilets, sinks, and showers are endpoints of the plumbing system.
conditions: for functional use of plumbing system

subject: Plumbing and Drainage Systems
rationale: Backflow preventers protect water quality by stopping reverse flow.
applicability: all buildings with potable water connections

Backflow prevention is not universally required on all potable water connections — specific local codes determine where backflow prevention is needed (e.g., based on hazard level, cross-connection risk). Some jurisdictions permit certain low-hazard connections without backflow prevention devices.
conditions: to prevent contamination of potable water

subject: Plumbing and Drainage Systems
rationale: Water heaters are typically included as part of the plumbing system.
conditions: when part of the domestic hot water system
exceptions: buildings without hot water

Even in buildings with hot water, water heaters may not be 'contained' within the Plumbing and Drainage System scope — in some buildings, water heaters are considered part of the mechanical/HVAC system or are separate packaged units (e.g., point-of-use heaters at fixtures) that may belong to a different system boundary.

subject: Plumbing and Drainage Systems
rationale: Stormwater piping often connects to the plumbing drainage network.
conditions: when roof drains and stormwater piping are part of building plumbing

subject: Electrical and Lighting Systems
rationale: Electrical systems provide power to HVAC equipment such as compressors, fans, and controls.
exceptions: In buildings with fully mechanical (non-electric) HVAC systems — such as those using steam radiators with no electrical blowers, controls, or thermostats — the electrical system may provide only minimal power for ignition or nothing at all, not meaningful 'support'.

subject: Electrical and Lighting Systems
rationale: Cameras, card readers, alarms, and security panels require electrical power.

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Fire alarm systems provide early warning, which is essential for life safety and activation of other fire protection systems.
applicability: The assertion states that Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems 'requires' a Fire Alarm System, but in many code jurisdictions, a fire alarm system is only required when the total occupant load exceeds a certain threshold (e.g., 300 in IBC) or for specific occupancy classifications. Small occupancies may have no such requirement.
conditions: for early detection of fire

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Automatic sprinkler systems are the primary active fire suppression system in most modern buildings.
conditions: where required by code for fire suppression
exceptions: some historic buildings may have alternatives

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Standpipes provide water supply connections for fire department hose lines in tall buildings.
conditions: in buildings over a certain height or with large floor areas
exceptions: low-rise buildings may not require standpipes

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Emergency lighting ensures safe evacuation when normal lighting fails during a fire.
conditions: for illumination of egress paths during power failure

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Exit signs guide occupants to safety during evacuation.
conditions: to clearly mark means of egress

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Fire suppression systems require adequate water pressure and volume to function effectively.
applicability: buildings with wet fire suppression systems

Sprinkler systems and standpipe systems may depend on a water supply, but fire hose connections can also be connected to standpipe systems that are fed from a fire department connection (FDC) without requiring a permanent dedicated water supply system. Also, some jurisdictions allow stored-water or tank-based systems that are separate from the building's main water supply system.
conditions: for sprinklers
standpipes
and fire hose connections

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Fire pumps boost water pressure to ensure sprinklers and standpipes operate correctly.
conditions: when municipal water pressure is insufficient for sprinkler systems
exceptions: buildings with adequate municipal water pressure

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Smoke control systems manage smoke movement to maintain tenable egress paths.
conditions: in atria
covered malls
and high-rise buildings
exceptions: small buildings without smoke control requirements

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Smoke detectors are key components that sense combustion products and trigger alarms.
conditions: for automatic fire detection

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Heat detectors activate at a fixed temperature or rate-of-rise, suited for dusty or steamy environments.
conditions: in areas where smoke detectors may cause false alarms

subject: Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems
rationale: Notification appliances alert occupants of a fire emergency through audible and visual signals.
applicability: all building types with fire alarm systems
conditions: including horns
strobes
and speakers

subject: Security and Access Control Systems
rationale: Access control systems depend on compatible door hardware such as electric strikes, magnetic locks, and panic hardware to physically secure entries.
applicability: The assertion states a dependency on 'Door Hardware' but does not specify which types of door hardware (e.g., electric strikes, magnetic locks, panic hardware, automatic operators). Some electrified doors may use different hardware types that have different integration requirements with access control.
conditions: Electrified doors

subject: Security and Access Control Systems
rationale: Access control systems must interface with fire alarm systems to unlock doors on fire alarm activation for safe egress.
conditions: Life safety integration required by code

subject: Security and Access Control Systems
rationale: Environmental controls may be needed for sensitive electronic components in extreme temperatures or humidity.
conditions: Outdoor or unconditioned environments
exceptions: Climate-controlled indoor environments only

The assertion states a dependency on HVAC System for outdoor or unconditioned environments, but the existing exception already covers climate-controlled indoor environments. However, there is a missing exception: access control components in outdoor/unconditioned environments may use standalone weatherproof enclosures with local heating/cooling (e.g., thermostatically controlled heaters) that do not depend on the building's main HVAC system.

subject: Security and Access Control Systems
rationale: Integration with intrusion detection allows arming/disarming based on access control status and cross-event triggering.
applicability: The assertion states 'connects_to Intrusion Detection System' but does not specify the nature of the connection (e.g., hardwired, network-based, dry contact relays). In older systems or simple configurations, the connection may be through alarm output relays rather than a true integrated platform connection.
conditions: Integrated security platform

subject: Vertical Transportation Systems
rationale: Guide rails mounted in the hoistway keep the elevator car and counterweight aligned during travel.
applicability: Assertion states 'Vertical Transportation Systems requires Guide Rails' with condition 'for elevator cars and counterweights'. However, many vertical transportation systems do not use guide rails: escalators use track systems (not guide rails), moving walks use pallets on rollers, dumbwaiters may use cables without rails, and pneumatic vacuum elevators use air pressure in a tube with no rails. The statement is overly broad even with the condition attached.
conditions: for elevator cars and counterweights

subject: Vertical Transportation Systems
rationale: Vertical transportation depends on fire-rated shaft enclosures, smoke detectors, and firefighter recall systems for life safety.
applicability: The dependency on Fire Protection System is stated for 'firefighter elevator operation' and 'smoke control in hoistways', but these are distinct requirements. Firefighter elevator operation typically requires fire-rated shafts, firefighter's control panels, and emergency power — not necessarily a direct dependency on the building's Fire Protection System (which includes sprinklers and alarms). Smoke control in hoistways may depend on HVAC/smoke management systems rather than the fire suppression system. The assertion conflates 'fire protection' broadly with specific fire-safety subsystems.
conditions: for firefighter elevator operation, smoke control in hoistways

subject: Vertical Transportation Systems
rationale: Modern vertical transportation often integrates with the BMS for traffic management, monitoring, and energy efficiency.
conditions: for group scheduling, destination dispatch, energy optimization
exceptions: standalone control systems in simpler buildings

The assertion states that Vertical Transportation Systems 'depends_on Building Management System (BMS)' but already includes an exception for 'standalone control systems in simpler buildings'. However, even in commercial, institutional, and high-rise residential buildings, elevators may operate independently via their own dedicated elevator controller with no BMS integration — particularly for older buildings, systems installed before BMS modernization, or properties where the elevator OEM's proprietary system operates standalone. The existing exception should be expanded or more clearly scoped.

subject: Exterior Common Areas
rationale: Signage helps users navigate exterior common areas and identify entrances, amenities, and paths.
applicability: The dependency direction is questionable: Exterior Common Areas typically include signage as a component or sub-system, rather than 'depending on' signage. Signage is usually part of the common area scope, not a prerequisite that common areas depend on.
conditions: for wayfinding and identification

subject: Data and Telecommunications Infrastructure
rationale: Modern security systems (CCTV, access control, intrusion detection) depend on the data network for transmission and centralized monitoring.
applicability: The assertion may not hold in residential contexts where many security systems (e.g., Ring, SimpliSafe) use wireless cellular or dedicated low-power RF protocols rather than relying on the building's structured data and telecommunications infrastructure. The existing exception for standalone non-networked systems does not capture this distinction.
conditions: IP cameras
networked access readers
exceptions: standalone non-networked systems

subject: Loading and Service Areas
rationale: Loading areas containing combustible materials need sprinklers and fire extinguishers per code.
applicability: The assertion conflates 'depends_on Fire Protection System' with a condition listing sprinklers and fire extinguishers. The existing exception only covers warm humid climates but should also cover this case.

rationale: Full-height partitions typically require attachment to the overhead ceiling or structure.

exceptions: partial-height partitions

subject: Subculture Boundary Partition System
rationale: Acoustic insulation is needed to prevent sound transmission between different subculture zones.
applicability: The assertion covers multi-tenant commercial, residential, and educational, but omits healthcare facilities (e.g., hospitals, clinics) where acoustic isolation between subcultures (e.g., patient rooms, treatment areas) is frequently required by code and is a critical design consideration.

subject: Subculture Boundary Acoustic Barrier
rationale: Sealant is critical to prevent sound leakage around barrier edges.
applicability: The assertion states 'Subculture Boundary Acoustic Barrier requires Acoustic Sealant at all joints and perimeter edges', but this may not hold in all contexts. Some acoustic barrier systems use pre-gasketed joints, compression seals, or interlocking edge treatments that do not require additional acoustic sealant. Additionally, certain fire-rated acoustic assemblies may require intumescent products instead of standard acoustic sealant.
conditions: at all joints and perimeter edges to prevent flanking noise
exceptions: There is an apparent typo: 'Subculture' is likely intended to be 'Subsurface' or 'Subfloor' — 'Subculture' is not a recognized building construction term for acoustic barriers. If the product or system is actually named 'Subculture' this is an unusual/non-standard term that should be clarified.

subject: Subculture Boundary Threshold
rationale: A boundary threshold requires a stable foundation to be anchored and remain in place.
conditions: when installed as a permanent structure

subject: Subculture Boundary Threshold
rationale: Subculture boundary thresholds are often mounted against or integrated into structural walls for support.
conditions: when integrated into a partition system

subject: Subculture Boundary Threshold
rationale: A subculture boundary threshold in a doorway is typically installed as part of or adjacent to the door frame assembly.
applicability: The assertion states 'Subculture Boundary Threshold requires Door Frame' when used as a door threshold. However, many thresholds (especially for exterior doors) are installed independently of the door frame, or the door frame is installed on top of the threshold. Some sliding door systems integrate the threshold into the frame assembly in a different relationship.
conditions: when used as a door threshold

subject: Subculture Boundary Threshold
rationale: The threshold provides a sealing surface and support for the bottom edge of the door leaf when closed.
conditions: when used as a bottom door threshold
exceptions: The assertion states 'Subculture Boundary Threshold supports Door Leaf' when used as a bottom door threshold. However, for sliding doors, the door leaf typically rides on tracks or rollers within the threshold or header, and the threshold primarily provides guidance rather than vertical support. For sliding doors, the weight is typically carried by the header track, not the bottom threshold.

subject: Subculture Boundary Threshold
rationale: The threshold interfaces with weatherstripping on the door bottom to create a continuous seal.
applicability: The assertion states 'Subculture Boundary Threshold connects_to Weatherstripping' at exterior locations. While thresholds do interface with weatherstripping, the exact connection type varies: some thresholds have pre-formed grooves for weatherstripping, others require adhesive-applied weatherstripping, and still others use a compression fit. Not all thresholds have a direct connection — weatherstripping may be attached to the door leaf or frame rather than the threshold itself.
conditions: when installed at exterior locations

subject: Subculture Boundary Air Barrier
rationale: The air barrier system at the subculture boundary connects to the foundation or slab edge to complete the envelope seal.
conditions: at foundation-to-wall transition

subject: Subculture Boundary Air Barrier
rationale: Flashing components are contained within the air barrier assembly at critical transitions and penetrations.
conditions: at penetrations and transitions
exceptions: In many continuous air barrier systems (e.g., fluid-applied membranes, fully adhered sheet membranes), the flashing is integrated into or part of the air barrier assembly itself rather than being a separate component contained within it. The assertion that Subculture Boundary Air Barrier 'contains' Flashing suggests a part-whole relationship that may not hold in systems where flashing is a separate, adjacent component that overlaps with but is not contained by the air barrier.

subject: Subculture Boundary Thermal Insulation
rationale: Subculture boundary thermal insulation is installed at the subculture boundary (the interface between conditioned space and ground/outside), so a defined subculture boundary is required.
applicability: All building types with conditioned basements or slabs-on-grade
conditions: To define the thermal boundary of the building
exceptions: In conditioned basements where interior insulation is used (e.g., interior rigid foam or batt insulation), the subculture boundary thermal insulation does not require a subculture boundary — the interior insulation itself defines the thermal boundary. This assertion incorrectly states the insulation requires the boundary, when in some designs the boundary is established by other assemblies.

subject: Subculture Boundary Thermal Insulation
rationale: Below-grade insulation depends on proper waterproofing to prevent moisture penetration and maintain thermal performance.
conditions: Applied on the exterior side of the insulation
For below-grade applications
exceptions: May not be needed if closed-cell foam insulation is used in non-hydrostatic conditions

subject: Subculture Boundary Thermal Insulation
rationale: Subculture boundary insulation must connect to the wall insulation above to create a continuous thermal envelope.
applicability: The connection between Subculture Boundary Thermal Insulation and Wall Insulation may not apply in buildings with a monolithic slab-on-grade and no foundation wall transition (e.g., frost-protected shallow foundations where insulation is continuous from slab to wall without a distinct boundary).
conditions: At the transition between foundation wall and above-grade wall

subject: Subculture Boundary Thermal Insulation
rationale: Insulation at the subculture boundary ties into slab edge insulation to maintain thermal continuity.
conditions: At slab-on-grade constructions
exceptions: In uninsulated slab-on-grade constructions (e.g., unconditioned garages, storage sheds, or slabs in mild climates that do not require edge insulation per code), there is no Slab Edge Insulation to connect to, so this assertion does not hold.

subject: Subculture Boundary Control Zone
rationale: Adequate lighting is critical for boundary legibility, surveillance, and safety in zones where different subcultures interact.
applicability: All building types with nighttime operation

The condition 'nighttime visibility and safety' is anthropocentric (human visual comfort), but a subculture boundary control zone may be for biological/industrial processes (e.g., sterile culture growth) where lighting is needed for monitoring/inspection rather than visibility, or may not need lighting at all if the process is automated and light-sensitive. This mismatch between the stated purpose and actual functional needs limits the assertion's validity.
conditions: For nighttime visibility and safety
exceptions: The assertion claims the dependency holds for 'all building types with nighttime operation,' but a Subculture Boundary Control Zone may rely on natural daylight infiltration (e.g., through skylights or windows) rather than an artificial Lighting System, negating the dependency on a dedicated lighting system in some designs.

subject: Subculture Boundary Glazing System
rationale: The system includes framing components to support and seal the glass panels.

subject: Subculture Boundary Glazing System
rationale: To prevent thermal bridging and condensation, a thermal break is often needed in the frame.
conditions: when required by energy code or in conditioned spaces

subject: Subculture Boundary Glazing System
rationale: Proper waterproofing at the perimeter is critical to prevent water intrusion at the system boundaries.
conditions: at perimeter interfaces with adjacent construction

subject: Subculture Boundary Glazing System
rationale: The system is physically anchored to the building's primary structural frame at floors, columns, or walls.
applicability: The assertion 'Subculture Boundary Glazing System connects_to Building Structure' lacks conditions. A glazing system connects to the building structure in specific ways (at anchor points, via sub-framing, etc.), and the connection details vary significantly by system type (curtain wall vs. storefront vs. window wall). Without conditions specifying connection type or method, this is overly broad.

subject: Subculture Boundary Expansion Joint
rationale: The joint gap can be a thermal bridge; insulation must be placed within or behind the joint assembly to maintain thermal continuity.
conditions: In exterior walls or roofs within conditioned spaces
exceptions: Structural (non-thermal) expansion joints in interior conditioned walls (e.g., seismic or movement joints in concrete shear walls) commonly omit thermal insulation because they address structural movement rather than thermal bridging, yet they still qualify as 'subculture boundary expansion joints' in exterior walls within conditioned spaces.

subject: Subculture Boundary Sealing
rationale: Subculture boundary sealing is typically applied at the connection between foundation walls and the building structure above.
applicability: The assertion states that Subculture Boundary Sealing connects to Foundation Wall 'at the interface between foundation and superstructure', but this is ambiguous — it could refer to the top of the foundation wall (bearing the superstructure) or the base. Additionally, many buildings with foundations have no distinct 'subculture boundary sealing' element (e.g., monolithic pours, insulated concrete forms where the seal is integrated). The applicability claim 'all buildings with foundations' is overly broad.
conditions: at the interface between foundation and superstructure
exceptions: In buildings with step foundations or sloped sites, the subculture boundary sealing may connect to a stepped foundation wall or retaining wall rather than a single continuous foundation wall, making the assertion as stated inaccurate.

subject: Subculture Boundary Sealing
rationale: The sealing is applied at the perimeter joint where the slab meets the wall system.
conditions: at slab perimeter and penetrations

subject: Neighborhood Entry Portal
rationale: Neighborhood Entry Portals typically need access control to manage who enters the community.
conditions: for entry authorization
exceptions: There exist Neighborhood Entry Portals that are purely aesthetic or symbolic (e.g., monument signs, archways) in residential neighborhoods that do not control vehicular or pedestrian entry at all, and thus have no need for an Access Control System.

subject: Neighborhood Entry Portal
rationale: The portal must be integrated with the roadway approach and exit.
conditions: for vehicle entry and exit lanes

subject: Neighborhood Identifier Signage
rationale: Neighborhood identifier signage serves as a landmark in a broader wayfinding strategy, helping residents and visitors orient themselves.
applicability: Neighborhood Identifier Signage may not support Wayfinding System effectively in very large or high-density neighborhoods where a single sign at entry points is insufficient for navigation, or where visitors rely on digital/mobile wayfinding rather than static signage.
conditions: when placed at neighborhood entry points or intersections
exceptions: In neighborhoods with restricted access (gated communities with security checkpoints), entry-point signage may be positioned after security barriers or be obscured, reducing its wayfinding utility for non-residents such as delivery drivers or emergency services.

subject: Neighborhood Street/Aisle
rationale: Street lighting is essential for safe navigation and security in neighborhood streets and aisles.
conditions: for nighttime visibility and safety
exceptions: A Neighborhood Street/Aisle in a remote area with no utility infrastructure (e.g., a seasonal road in a national park or a very low-density rural subdivision) may not require a formal lighting system, as nighttime visibility may be provided by other means (e.g., vehicle headlights, moonlight) or the road may not be used at night.

subject: Neighborhood Street/Aisle
rationale: Proper drainage is required to keep the street/aisle functional during and after rainfall.
conditions: to manage runoff and prevent flooding
exceptions: A short neighborhood aisle serving only a few properties on flat terrain with permeable soil may not require a formal stormwater drainage system because natural infiltration is sufficient to prevent flooding.

subject: Neighborhood Plaza/Hub
rationale: Walkable access via pathways is fundamental to a plaza's function as a gathering space.
conditions: connecting to surrounding streets and buildings
exceptions: A Neighborhood Plaza/Hub located in a pedestrian-only zone (e.g., a fully car-free district or pedestrian mall) may have no surrounding streets to connect to, making the requirement for pedestrian pathways connecting to surrounding streets impossible or nonsensical.

subject: Neighborhood Plaza/Hub
rationale: Trash and recycling bins are needed to maintain cleanliness in the public space.
applicability: In temporary or pop-up neighborhood plazas/hubs (e.g., seasonal plaza events, one-day street closures), requiring a permanent Waste Receptacle may be excessive or impractical; portable waste collection solutions may suffice and the assertion does not account for temporary installations.

subject: Neighborhood Plaza/Hub
rationale: Shade elements are often contained within plazas for sun protection.
applicability: In climates with predominantly overcast or cool conditions (e.g., Nordic/Baltic regions), the requirement for a Shade Structure may be unnecessary or counterproductive as it could reduce already limited sunlight and make the plaza less inviting.
conditions: pergolas, awnings, canopies
exceptions: In very small neighborhood plazas/hubs (e.g., less than ~20 sqm pocket parks or corner plazas), a Shade Structure such as a pergola, awning, or canopy may not fit physically or may cause overshadowing issues for adjacent properties or plantings. The assertion does not consider spatial constraints.

subject: Neighborhood Subzone
rationale: Functional neighborhoods require potable water distribution for residential and commercial use.
applicability: The dependency on a 'Water Supply System' is stated as conditional on 'potable water needed for occupants' but many Neighborhood Subzones (e.g., industrial zones, warehouse districts, seasonal event zones) may not have occupants needing potable water yet still exist as valid subzones. The assertion does not account for these non-occupant subzone types.
conditions: potable water needed for occupants
exceptions: A Neighborhood Subzone could be served by decentralized water sources (e.g., private wells, rainwater harvesting, trucked-in water) rather than a 'Water Supply System' as typically understood in civil engineering (a centralized piped network). The assertion assumes a centralized infrastructure model.

subject: Neighborhood Subzone
rationale: Proper drainage is required to prevent flooding and manage runoff within the subzone.
conditions: precipitation management needed
exceptions: arid regions with minimal rainfall

subject: Neighborhood Subzone
rationale: Lighting is required for pedestrian safety, traffic visibility, and security after dark.
conditions: nighttime visibility and safety needed
exceptions: unlit rural subzones

A Neighborhood Subzone that is only used during daytime hours (e.g., a daytime market zone, a park that closes at dusk) may not require street lighting for the vast majority of its use period. The condition 'nighttime visibility and safety needed' is assumed but not all subzones operate at night.

subject: Neighborhood Subzone
rationale: Sidewalks and paths are required for safe pedestrian movement within the subzone.
applicability: The assertion applies to 'walkable neighborhood design' but the existing exception for 'car-only subzones' is an oversimplification. Many subzones are mixed-mode (e.g., pedestrian-priority but allowing service vehicles) or have walkways that are not formal 'Pedestrian Walkway' infrastructure (e.g., shared streets, woonerfs, dirt paths). The binary distinction misses these gradations.
conditions: walkable neighborhood design
exceptions: car-only subzones

subject: Neighborhood Lighting Zone
rationale: Controls enable adaptive lighting based on time of day, occupancy, or ambient light.
applicability: The existing exception mentions 'manually operated zones' but the assertion's conditions are 'for automated operation, scheduling, and dimming'. This creates ambiguity: if manual operation is excepted, does the assertion still hold that a lighting zone *requires* a control system? Manual zones would have no control system, contradicting the core assertion.
conditions: for automated operation, scheduling, and dimming
exceptions: manually operated zones

subject: Neighborhood Signage Installation
rationale: Neighborhood signage directly supports navigation and wayfinding.
applicability: The assertion assumes signage installation inherently supports wayfinding, but poorly designed, cluttered, or inconsistent signage can confuse rather than aid wayfinding, undermining the claimed support.
conditions: by providing clear directional information to visitors and residents

subject: Neighborhood Signage Installation
rationale: Signage installation often connects with pedestrian circulation routes.
conditions: when signage is positioned along walkways for wayfinding

subject: Neighborhood Signage Installation
rationale: Signage may connect to street lighting for visibility or share installation infrastructure.
conditions: when illuminated signage is used or signage needs nighttime visibility

subject: Neighborhood Acoustic Treatment Installation
rationale: Acoustic panels are often the core element of a neighborhood acoustic treatment installation.
applicability: The assertion states that 'Neighborhood Acoustic Treatment Installation contains Acoustic Panel' as primary treatment components, applicable to all building types. However, acoustic treatment installation in a neighborhood context (e.g., outdoor noise barriers, traffic noise mitigation) typically uses materials like sound barriers, earth berms, vegetation, or specialized outdoor acoustic structures — not interior-grade Acoustic Panels, which are designed for indoor room acoustics (e.g., recording studios, offices, auditoriums). Acoustic panels are generally unsuitable for outdoor or neighborhood-scale installations due to weather exposure, vandalism risks, and different acoustic requirements.
conditions: As primary treatment components

subject: Neighborhood Lighting Commissioning
rationale: Neighborhood lighting commissioning requires a lighting control system to properly manage and automate lighting operations.
conditions: For automated scheduling and dimming

subject: Neighborhood Lighting Commissioning
rationale: Occupancy sensors help optimize energy use by detecting presence and adjusting lighting.
conditions: For adaptive lighting control

subject: Neighborhood Lighting Commissioning
rationale: Functional testing is a key element within the commissioning process.
conditions: As a core commissioning activity

subject: Setback Zone
rationale: Permanent building structures are generally prohibited within required setback zones; only limited encroachments are typically permitted.
applicability: The assertion does not account for boundary walls, fences, retaining walls, or steps/stairs that are often permitted within setback zones and are considered structures in many building codes. This omission limits the assertion's accuracy.
conditions: within the required setback zone
exceptions: projections such as eaves, balconies, bay windows may be allowed to encroach

The assertion states Setback Zone is 'unsuitable for Building Structure' but the existing exceptions already allow projections (eaves, balconies, bay windows) which are part of building structures in many codes. This is a contradiction—the assertion is too absolute given the encroachments already listed.

subject: Perimeter Buffer
rationale: Perimeter buffers (like vestibules, sunspaces, or buffer zones) often rely on thermal insulation to reduce heat transfer between conditioned interior and unconditioned exterior spaces.
applicability: The applicability listing includes residential buildings, but in many residential contexts (e.g., attached garages, enclosed porches, mudrooms acting as buffers), thermal insulation is not required by code if the buffer space is unconditioned. The assertion as stated implies a universal requirement that does not hold across all residential typologies.
conditions: when acting as a climate transition zone
exceptions: A perimeter buffer acting as a climate transition zone does not require thermal insulation if it is an unconditioned, unheated buffer space (e.g., a sunroom, enclosed porch, or air-lock vestibule) where thermal insulation would be thermally unnecessary or structurally impractical. Many energy codes (e.g., IECC) exempt unconditioned buffer spaces from insulation requirements provided they are not intended for occupancy.

subject: Perimeter Buffer
rationale: Perimeter buffer spaces depend on air barrier systems to prevent uncontrolled airflow and maintain the intended buffer function.
conditions: to maintain separation between conditioned and unconditioned zones
exceptions: A perimeter buffer does not depend on an air barrier in all cases. For example, an uninsulated, unconditioned perimeter buffer (like a seasonal sunroom or a screened porch enclosure) may not include or require an air barrier at all, as the buffer itself is not intended to maintain a conditioned environment and may intentionally allow air exchange with the exterior.

subject: Perimeter Buffer
rationale: To maintain the buffer's effectiveness, weather stripping is needed at penetrations to limit air leakage.
applicability: The assertion applies weather stripping at door and window openings in the buffer zone, but does not account for non-operable windows or fixed glazing in the buffer zone, which do not require weather stripping. This over-generalizes the requirement.
conditions: at door and window openings in the buffer zone

subject: Perimeter Buffer
rationale: A common example of a perimeter buffer is an entry vestibule, which is contained within the buffer zone and provides an airlock function.
conditions: when designed as an enclosed transition space

subject: Building Envelope Line
rationale: The building envelope line defines the boundary between conditioned and unconditioned space; thermal insulation is typically required along this line to reduce heat transfer.
applicability: The assertion states that a Building Envelope Line requires a Thermal Insulation Layer for energy efficient building operation, but not all commercial or institutional buildings require thermal insulation in the envelope line itself (e.g., curtain wall systems on unconditioned atriums or enclosed parking garages within commercial buildings may not include insulation in the envelope line). The exception list only covers unconditioned buildings like sheds, missing other conditioned building sub-types where parts of the envelope may legitimately omit insulation.
conditions: for energy efficient building operation
exceptions: unconditioned buildings like sheds

subject: Building Envelope Line
rationale: The envelope line relies on the structural frame to hold it in place and transfer loads.
applicability: all building types with rigid envelope

The assertion states Building Envelope Line depends_on Structural Framing System for all building types with rigid envelope, but there are cases where the envelope is directly supported by the foundation or structural walls (e.g., load-bearing masonry or concrete walls) without a separate structural framing system. In such buildings, the envelope line depends on the structural wall system, not a 'Structural Framing System' (typically implying beams and columns).
conditions: to support envelope materials
exceptions: tent or membrane structures where envelope is self-supporting

subject: Building Envelope Line
rationale: The building envelope line intersects with the foundation at grade and below-grade walls.
applicability: all buildings with below-grade walls or slabs

The assertion states Building Envelope Line connects_to Foundation System at the base, but in buildings with raised floors, crawl spaces, or podium slabs, the envelope line at the base may connect to a slab-on-grade or a structural deck rather than a foundation system directly. The existing exception for piles is too narrow and does not cover these common conditions.
conditions: at the base of the envelope line
exceptions: buildings on piles where envelope starts above grade

subject: Adjacent Road Right-of-Way Edge
rationale: The adjacent road right-of-way edge delineates the boundary of the right-of-way which contains the road pavement area.
applicability: The condition 'when the right-of-way is improved' is ambiguous — it does not specify what constitutes 'improved' (e.g., paved, fully developed, contains utilities). Different jurisdictions define 'improved right-of-way' differently, which could lead to inconsistent application.
conditions: when the right-of-way is improved
exceptions: Even on improved rights-of-way, the road pavement may not always extend to the full ROW boundary — there are cases where the pavement is set back (e.g., with landscaped verges or shoulders between pavement and ROW edge). The assertion that Adjacent Road Right-of-Way Edge *contains* Road Pavement is too strong in such cases.

subject: Adjacent Road Right-of-Way Edge
rationale: Curbs and gutters are typically located within the right-of-way adjacent to the road edge.
conditions: when curbs are present
exceptions: rural roads without curbs

subject: Adjacent Road Right-of-Way Edge

conditions: when stormwater infrastructure is present
exceptions: Stormwater drainage systems are not always located at the right-of-way edge. In many urban and suburban configurations, stormwater infrastructure (e.g., catch basins, pipes, swales) may be located within the roadway, under the pavement, in medians, or in easements beyond the ROW. Locating it strictly at the ROW edge is an oversimplification.

subject: Boundary Marker / Survey Monument
rationale: Permanent survey monuments often require a concrete footing or foundation to prevent movement and maintain positional accuracy over time.
conditions: for permanent monuments
where ground is soft or unstable
exceptions: temporary markers may use stakes only

Even for permanent monuments in soft/unstable ground, concrete foundations may not be required if bedrock is encountered at shallow depth; monuments can be set directly into competent bedrock without concrete.

subject: Fence or Wall Foundation
rationale: Waterproofing protects the foundation from moisture ingress that can cause freeze-thaw damage.
conditions: for below-grade walls
in habitable spaces
exceptions: simple garden walls

Retaining walls, which are listed as an applicability, often have drainage systems (e.g., gravel backfill, weep holes, drain pipes) rather than a waterproof membrane. A waterproof membrane on a retaining wall can trap hydrostatic pressure behind the wall, leading to structural failure. The standard approach is to provide drainage, not waterproofing.

subject: Train Station Platform
rationale: Adequate illumination is necessary for passenger safety, wayfinding, and operations.
conditions: during hours of darkness or low visibility

subject: Train Station Platform
rationale: Signs indicating train lines, directions, exits, and schedules are essential for passenger navigation.

subject: Train Station Platform
rationale: Proper drainage prevents water accumulation, ice hazards, and structural damage.
conditions: outdoor or uncovered platforms
exceptions: fully enclosed underground platforms

This creates a logical inconsistency: the exception for underground platforms is unnecessary because the scope already restricts to outdoor stations. Additionally, the condition says 'outdoor or uncovered platforms' but applicability says 'outdoor train stations' — these are slightly different scopes (station vs. platform), creating ambiguity.

subject: Light Rail / Tram Stop
rationale: A tram/light rail stop requires a boarding platform for passengers to safely board and alight from the vehicle.
conditions: passenger boarding and alighting
exceptions: Light rail / tram stops at grade-level in shared streets or pedestrian zones may not have a raised platform; passengers board from the street surface level. subject: Light Rail / Tram Stop
rationale: Modern light rail stops require digital displays showing next train arrival times for passenger convenience.
conditions: when real-time data is available
exceptions: stops with only static schedules

subject: Light Rail / Tram Stop
rationale: Many light rail stops require ticket vending machines for passengers to purchase fare media.
conditions: proof-of-payment or paid fare zones
exceptions: fare-free systems or systems using mobile ticketing only

Some proof-of-payment transit systems use onboard fare validation (validators inside the tram) rather than requiring a ticket vending machine at the stop itself. Passengers purchase or validate tickets upon entering the vehicle, making a stop-level ticket vending machine optional.

subject: Light Rail / Tram Stop
rationale: Proper drainage is required to prevent water accumulation on platforms and tracks, ensuring safety and operation.
conditions: prevent platform flooding and standing water

subject: Light Rail / Tram Stop
rationale: The stop contains designated waiting areas for passengers.
exceptions: Very small or minimal stops (e.g., a single pole with a sign, often called a 'flag stop' or 'request stop') do not contain a waiting area. Many rural or low-ridership tram stops consist of only a signpost with no shelter, bench, or defined waiting area.

subject: Light Rail / Tram Stop
rationale: The stop connects to pedestrian pathways for access from surrounding areas.
exceptions: Some light rail / tram stops are designed as island platforms between tracks with pedestrian crosswalks at grade level rather than dedicated pedestrian walkways. In these cases, passengers cross the tracks directly rather than using a separated walkway.

subject: Subway / Metro Entrance
rationale: Subway/metro entrances require ticket vending or fare collection equipment for passengers to purchase access.
conditions: for paid-access systems
exceptions: Many metro systems (e.g., Vancouver SkyTrain, some European light rail) use proof-of-payment or fare gates that do not use freestanding ticket vending machines at every entrance; fare validation may be done via validators or card readers instead of a full Ticket Vending Machine.

subject: Subway / Metro Entrance
rationale: Subway entrances typically require stairways to descend from street level to platform level.
exceptions: Metro entrances may be at-grade with direct street access (e.g., surface-level stations) or served by elevators alone; a stairway is not strictly required in all cases.

subject: Subway / Metro Entrance
rationale: Escalators provide high-volume vertical circulation for passengers entering and exiting subway stations.
conditions: for high-capacity stations
when vertical rise exceeds ~3m
exceptions: Even in high-capacity stations with vertical rise over 3m, elevators may serve as the primary vertical circulation instead of escalators, or escalators may be present but not strictly required by code if alternative means exist.

subject: Subway / Metro Entrance
rationale: Entrances require adequate lighting for safety, security, and wayfinding, especially when transitioning from daylight.

subject: Subway / Metro Entrance
rationale: Subway entrances connected to underground networks depend on ventilation to manage air quality and smoke control.
conditions: for underground stations

subject: Subway / Metro Entrance
rationale: Below-grade entrances depend on drainage to prevent water ingress during rain or flooding events.
conditions: in flood-prone areas
for below-grade entrances

rationale: Handrails are required on stairways and ramps for passenger safety and code compliance.

conditions: on stairs and ramps

subject: Taxi Stand / Ride-Share Pick-up Zone

subject: Taxi Stand / Ride-Share Pick-up Zone
rationale: Proper stormwater drainage prevents ponding in the vehicle waiting and loading areas.
exceptions: A taxi stand / ride-share pick-up zone that is located in a covered or indoor area (e.g., airport arrivals hall, parking garage) with existing building drainage (e.g., floor drains, roof drainage) does not require a dedicated drainage system specific to the zone. The zone simply relies on the general building drainage.

subject: Taxi Stand / Ride-Share Pick-up Zone

conditions: when implemented

subject: Bicycle Parking Facility
rationale: Bicycle parking facilities need physical racks or stands to park and secure bicycles.

exceptions: Bicycle parking facilities can include wall-mounted hooks, racks integrated into furniture, or vertical storage systems that are not standard 'Bicycle Racks' as typically defined (e.g., Sheffield stands, wave racks). subject: Bicycle Parking Facility
rationale: Some bicycle parking facilities include a repair station with tools and an air pump.
conditions: in larger or premium facilities
exceptions: basic facilities

subject: Pedestrian Bridge / Skywalk Connection
rationale: Lighting ensures visibility and safety for pedestrians, especially during nighttime or in covered/enclosed skywalks.
applicability: all pedestrian bridges and skywalks used at night or in enclosed conditions
conditions: Must provide adequate illumination for safe passage
Must comply with egress lighting codes

The existing exception says 'short, naturally well-lit bridges in temperate climates may rely solely on daylight', but the applicability scope says 'all pedestrian bridges and skywalks used at night or in enclosed conditions'. A bridge used at night but that is naturally well-lit under moonlight or well-lit by adjacent urban lighting may still be safe without a dedicated lighting system, yet this exception is not captured.

subject: Pedestrian Bridge / Skywalk Connection

subject: Pedestrian Bridge / Skywalk Connection
rationale: Expansion joints allow the structure to accommodate thermal expansion, contraction, and minor seismic movements without damage.

Typical expansion joints handle thermal expansion/contraction, while seismic movements require specialized seismic joints or gaps that are designed differently (larger displacements, different detailing). A standard expansion joint is not designed for seismic movement demands.
conditions: Required for bridges longer than certain length thresholds
