subject: Integrated Display Casework
rationale: Display casework must be integrated with the building's fire suppression (sprinklers, clean agent) for fire safety, and casework design must not obstruct sprinkler coverage.
applicability: The dependency 'Integrated Display Casework depends_on Fire Suppression System' is stated as applicable to all building types, but in many jurisdictions display casework is not required to have integrated fire suppression unless it exceeds certain size, volume, or material thresholds. Small or open display units often rely on the building's ambient fire suppression system rather than a dedicated one, and building codes (e.g., IBC) do not universally mandate a direct dependency relationship.
conditions: For compliance with building codes and protection of contents
exceptions: In heritage or museum contexts, integrated display casework may use specialized fire suppression (e.g., inert gas systems) that is distinct from a generic 'Fire Suppression System' and may not be classified as depending on the building's main fire suppression system. There are also scenarios where casework with small enclosed volumes uses standalone suppression (e.g., Novec or FM-200 cylinders) that do not connect to the building's primary fire suppression infrastructure.

subject: Integrated Display Casework
rationale: Integrated display casework often contains built-in LED strips, spotlights, or fiber-optic lighting within the casework structure.
applicability: The 'contains' relationship implies a part-whole or composition relationship, but an Integrated Lighting System may be a separate prefabricated component mounted onto or into the casework rather than being inherently 'contained by' it. Many display casework systems have modular, plug-in lighting tracks that are not physically integral to the casework structure and can be swapped or removed independently.
conditions: When specified with built-in lighting
exceptions: Casework relying on external lighting only

subject: Integrated Display Casework
rationale: Freestanding or floor-mounted display casework transfers loads to the floor structure below.
conditions: For floor-supported or freestanding casework
exceptions: Entirely wall-hung casework without floor contact

The assertion states that floor-supported casework connects_to Floor Structure. However, casework mounted on raised access floors (common in commercial/museum environments) may connect to the raised floor panels or support pedestals rather than the structural floor slab. In seismic zones, casework may be connected to walls or ceiling structures for bracing instead of the floor structure even when floor-supported.

subject: Project Resource Kiosk
rationale: The kiosk may connect to a BMS for data sharing and centralized management, but this is not always the case.
applicability: The assertion that a Project Resource Kiosk connects to a BMS may be limited in scope to only certain types of BMS protocols (e.g., BACnet, Modbus) and may not hold for proprietary or legacy BMS systems without additional middleware. The existing exception mentions standalone kiosks without integration, but does not address BMS protocol compatibility limitations.
conditions: if integrated for centralized monitoring and resource tracking
exceptions: standalone kiosks without integration

subject: Community Broadcast Booth
rationale: Temperature and ventilation control is necessary for electronic equipment and occupant comfort in an enclosed booth.
applicability: The assertion states that a Community Broadcast Booth requires an HVAC System, but this may not apply to broadcast booths that are purely passive or unoccupied (e.g., automated relay booths that generate no heat and have no occupants).

exceptions: The low-noise condition may conflict with standard HVAC equipment (compressors, fans, blowers) that inherently produce noise. If the booth uses a passive ventilation system (e.g., natural convection or a heat sink with no moving parts), an HVAC system may still be required for temperature control but could be impossible to implement without violating the low-noise condition.

subject: Community Broadcast Booth

subject: Market Hall / Enclosure
rationale: Enclosed market requires a roof to protect goods and people from rain/sun.

exceptions: A Market Hall with enclosure may not require a roof if the market is designed as an open-air covered market (e.g., a market square with permanent stalls that have their own individual awnings or a tensile structure that is not technically a 'roof' in building code terms). subject: Market Hall / Enclosure

subject: Market Hall / Enclosure
rationale: Floor drains and waste water removal needed for sanitation.

exceptions: A market hall with food stalls and wet cleaning may not require a formal Drainage System if it uses a temporary/mobile setup (e.g., weekend farmers market in a parking lot) where cleaning water is collected manually or drains into municipal stormwater grates, or if it uses portable containment systems.

subject: Individual Shop Stall / Kiosk
rationale: Lighting is needed to illuminate the stall interior and products for customers.
applicability: The assertion assumes all kiosks/stalls are indoor or covered, but many outdoor market stalls in public spaces (e.g., street food kiosks, farmers market tents) operate solely during daylight hours and have no electrical supply available. The existing exception for 'daylight-only temporary stalls' is too narrow — it only covers 'temporary' stalls, but many permanent outdoor kiosks in pedestrian zones also lack integrated lighting systems and rely on ambient street lighting or natural light.
conditions: for product visibility
for safe operation in low light
exceptions: daylight-only temporary stalls

Kiosks that are part of a larger shared retail environment (e.g., pop-up kiosks inside a mall atrium) may rely on the host building's ambient lighting rather than having their own dedicated lighting system. The assertion does not account for this scenario where the lighting requirement is satisfied by the surrounding space rather than by an independent system belonging to the stall/kiosk itself.

subject: Market Stall Partition System
rationale: A market stall partition system depends on a structural frame (e.g., aluminum or steel framing) to support its panels and maintain stability.
applicability: The assertion only covers freestanding market stall partition systems, but in many commercial and temporary market setups, partition systems are attached to or integrated with structural frames (e.g., bolted to columns, hung from overhead beams). For attached/integrated systems, the dependency on a structural frame is even more direct and fundamental, not less. The condition 'when freestanding' may actually describe a case where dependency is reduced (self-supporting), yet the assertion claims dependency exists. This inverts the likely relationship.
conditions: when the partition system is freestanding
exceptions: A freestanding market stall partition system (e.g., a heavy self-supporting modular display wall) may be designed to be structurally independent of the building's primary frame, instead relying on its own base, weight, or ground anchors. exceptions: Outdoor covered walkways or exterior circulation aisles in commercial contexts may not require the same type of floor finish as interior spaces, as weather-resistant surface treatment (e.g., broom-finished concrete) may serve a different function than an interior floor finish.

subject: Shared Customer Circulation Aisle

conditions: in climate-controlled retail environments
for temperature-sensitive merchandise

applicability: Fire suppression requirements for refuse enclosures vary significantly by jurisdiction and are typically tied to the building's occupancy classification, the proximity to exits, and the enclosure size. subject: Market Fire Suppression System

rationale: Some market suppression systems include storage tanks for water or specialized suppression agents.

conditions: Where water or chemical agent storage is required

subject: Market Fire Suppression System

In practice, workflow typically goes from clean to soiled (one direction), so the connection may be a one-way pass-through or hatch rather than a two-way connection, which changes the architectural planning requirement.

In small or single-corridor healthcare facilities (e.g., small rural clinics), soiled and clean utility rooms may be combined into a single room or separated only by a counter or partition, with workflow managed by time separation rather than physical connection. subject: Sterilization / Autoclave Room

The dependency on a drainage system is not universal across all pharmaceutical applications.

In some laboratory settings, small benchtop autoclaves may be located in a room that already falls under the coverage of a general building fire suppression system, and the autoclave itself may not introduce a fire hazard requiring a dedicated or specially rated Fire Suppression System dependency. The existing exception about sprinkler temperature ratings is noted, but the assertion of dependency itself may not hold for smaller units that do not significantly elevate ambient temperature or fire risk.

rationale: The terrace roof must be supported by a load-bearing structural slab (concrete or composite deck) capable of carrying both dead and live loads.
applicability: The assertion states that Shared Terrace Roof 'depends_on Structural Slab' under conditions of 'dead load of terrace finish; live load of occupants'. However, some terrace roof assemblies are designed as lightweight or cold-formed steel framing systems over structural steel beams, not cast-in-place or precast concrete slabs. In such systems, the decking (e.g., metal deck, wood sheathing) rather than a structural slab provides the substrate. The 'Structural Slab' dependency is not universally applicable to all building types.
conditions: dead load of terrace finish
live load of occupants

subject: Unit Entry Alcove
rationale: A Unit Entry Alcove by definition is an entry transition space; it requires a door to separate the alcove from the unit interior and/or exterior.
conditions: Unit Entry Alcove must provide access to a dwelling unit
exceptions: In residential multifamily buildings, an alcove may serve as an entry without a physical door (e.g., open-plan lobby entries or 'doorless' foyers in accessible units). Building codes (e.g., IBC 1008) permit means of egress without a door where the alcove opens directly into the unit. Also, exterior entry alcoves may use a storm door or screen door context rather than a 'Door' as a building element.

subject: Unit Entry Alcove
rationale: Entry alcoves need artificial lighting for safe entry/exit and to create a welcoming transition space.
applicability: The condition 'enclosed or has limited natural light' is ambiguous—there is no objective definition of 'limited natural light.' An alcove with borrowed light from an adjacent room or with translucent panels may not require an artificial lighting fixture. The assertion should specify criteria (e.g., minimum daylight factor or distance to a window).
conditions: Unit Entry Alcove is enclosed or has limited natural light

subject: Unit Entry Alcove
rationale: The alcove requires finished interior wall surfaces (paint, paneling, etc.) as a habitable transition space.
exceptions: An exterior, unenclosed unit entry alcove (e.g., a covered porch or stoop with exposed rough framing) may not require a wall finish such as paint or wallcovering. Also, in utility or service areas (e.g., janitor closets leading to a unit), a wall finish may be omitted per budget class or building type.

subject: Unit Entry Alcove
rationale: A durable floor finish (tile, hardwood, LVT) is needed in the entry alcove to withstand traffic and dirt.
exceptions: Exterior unit entry alcoves (e.g., uncovered concrete stoops or landings) may use exterior-rated materials (e.g., exposed concrete, brick, or stone) that are not considered a 'Floor Finish' in the typical interior sense. The assertion should exclude exterior or semi-exposed alcoves.

subject: Unit Entry Alcove
rationale: The alcove depends on the surrounding structural walls to define its boundaries and provide spatial enclosure.
exceptions: In light-frame wood or metal stud construction, a Unit Entry Alcove may be supported by non-structural partition walls or shear walls that differ from a 'Structural Wall' element (i.e., a load-bearing wall). In open-plan designs, the alcove may be defined by columns or partial-height screens with no structural wall dependency at all.

subject: Concrete Frame Structure
rationale: Concrete frame structures rest on foundations (e.g., footings, piles) that distribute loads to the soil.
applicability: The assertion 'Concrete Frame Structure depends_on Foundation System' with condition 'For load transfer to ground' is stated as applicable to 'all building types', but concrete frame structures are not used in all building types (e.g., light timber residential, tent structures, earthbag buildings). The assertion itself is correct for buildings that have a concrete frame structure, but the applicability should be scoped to building types that actually use concrete frames, not 'all building types'.
conditions: For load transfer to ground

subject: Concrete Frame Structure
rationale: Concrete frames (columns and beams) carry and transfer loads from floor slabs to the foundation.
applicability: The assertion states applicability 'all building types' but 'Concrete Frame Structure supports Floor Slab' is only relevant to buildings that actually contain a concrete frame structure. Many building types (e.g., load-bearing masonry, timber frame, steel frame) do not have concrete frames, so 'all building types' is too broad.
conditions: Typically cast monolithically or connected via beams

subject: Concrete Frame Structure
rationale: The frame supports the roof and transfers its loads (dead, live, environmental) downward.
applicability: Applicability to 'all building types' is overbroad. Concrete Frame Structure only exists in buildings with concrete frames; the assertion is not applicable to buildings without concrete frames.

subject: Concrete Frame Structure
rationale: Concrete frames often support curtain walls or infill wall panels that are attached to the structural frame.
applicability: Applicability stated as 'all building types' but this relation only applies to buildings with concrete frames and non-load-bearing infill walls. Buildings without concrete frames, or where cladding is load-bearing, are outside scope.
conditions: When walls are non-load-bearing infill

subject: Concrete Frame Structure
rationale: Concrete frames are often combined with shear walls to form dual systems that resist lateral forces.
conditions: For lateral load resistance in seismic or wind design
exceptions: The assertion states 'Concrete Frame Structure connects_to Shear Wall' for lateral load resistance, but in many seismic designs concrete frames are designed as moment-resisting frames specifically to avoid shear walls. Additionally, in low-rise buildings or low-seismic zones, shear walls may not be required even if the building has a concrete frame. The assertion should note that this is an optional connection, not a mandatory one.

subject: Integrated Planter Bench
rationale: Proper drainage is required to prevent waterlogging and root rot in the planter portion.
applicability: all building types with integrated planters
conditions: if integrated planter includes live plants
exceptions: Some integrated planter bench designs use self-contained sub-irrigation planters (SIPs) or capillary wicking systems that capture and recirculate water, making a separate drainage layer redundant. For such planter types, water is managed through internal wicking, so no dedicated drainage layer below the soil is required.

If the integrated planter uses artificial or preserved (not live) plants but still has a planting medium that requires moisture management, the assertion's condition says 'includes live plants' — but even with live plants, certain green roof or planter technologies (e.g., pre-vegetated mats with integrated drainage fabric) may already incorporate drainage into the product itself, making a separate layer unnecessary.

subject: Integrated Planter Bench
rationale: Protects the building structure from moisture damage due to irrigation and rainwater in the planter.
applicability: built-in or structural integrated planter benches
conditions: when planter is integrated into building structure
exceptions: freestanding movable planters

If the planter is integrated into below-grade or concrete slab-on-grade construction where the structure itself is inherently water-resistant (e.g., waterproof concrete, post-tensioned slabs with no penetration risk), a separate waterproof membrane may not be required by code or necessity, depending on jurisdiction and local building codes.

Some proprietary integrated planter systems feature pre-manufactured waterproof liners (e.g., rubber or HDPE basin inserts) that serve as the waterproofing layer; in such cases adding a separate 'waterproof membrane' beyond the factory-installed liner would be redundant and may violate the product warranty.

subject: Integrated Planter Bench
rationale: Sustained plant health may require an irrigation supply unless plants are drought-tolerant.
conditions: if live plants are used and manual watering is not feasible
exceptions: rain-fed or drought-tolerant plantings

subject: In-Slab Hydronic Heating
rationale: In-slab hydronic heating is embedded within a concrete slab, so a concrete slab is necessary to encase the tubing.
conditions: When used in new construction or retrofit with slab-on-grade or suspended slab
exceptions: In-slab hydronic heating is sometimes installed in timber subfloor constructions with a poured concrete or gypsum screed on top, not in a concrete slab itself. The 'requires Concrete Slab' condition is not strictly necessary in these retrofit or lightweight construction scenarios.

subject: Construction of Frame and Slabs
rationale: Concrete is the primary material for frames and slabs.
conditions: for monolithic slabs and beams

subject: Construction of Frame and Slabs
rationale: Slabs provide the structural base for floor toppings and finishes.
applicability: The assertion is limited by the fact that 'supports Floor Finish' is ambiguous—it could mean structural load support (which the slab inherently provides) or physical compatibility (such as surface flatness and curing requirements). For certain floor finishes like thin-set tile or epoxy coatings, the slab may need additional surface preparation, curing time beyond initial cure, or moisture mitigation before the finish can be applied.
conditions: after slab cures
exceptions: The assertion that 'Construction of Frame and Slabs supports Floor Finish' after slab cure has exceptions for industrial floors where floor finishes are applied directly to the structural slab without a separate topping, or for exposed concrete floors that serve as the final finish (polished concrete). In these cases, the frame/slab construction itself is the floor finish, not a separate 'Floor Finish' being supported.

subject: Rammed Earth Infill Panel
rationale: Rammed earth infill panels are non-load-bearing and require a structural frame (wood, steel, or concrete) to carry building loads.
applicability: The assertion does not account for hybrid systems where rammed earth panels provide partial lateral load resistance while a frame handles vertical loads (e.g., in seismic regions). The binary 'requires a Structural Frame' vs. 'self-supporting' framing misses intermediate structural roles.
conditions: Must have a load-bearing frame to support vertical loads
exceptions: Can be self-supporting if designed as a structural wall system

subject: Rammed Earth Infill Panel
rationale: Rammed earth infill panels require a proper foundation to transfer loads and avoid moisture wicking from the ground.
conditions: Must have a continuous strip or reinforced concrete footing

subject: Installation of Lattice Screens
rationale: Lattice screens commonly serve as a support structure for climbing vegetation.
applicability: Lattice screens designed for climbing plants require adequate structural support (weight of mature vines, water retention in foliage) and appropriate species selection. Not all climbing plants are suitable for all lattice materials (e.g., heavy wisteria on lightweight plastic lattice may fail).
conditions: Lattice screens are designed as trellis for vines and greenery
exceptions: Lattice screens may not support climbing plants if they are mounted flush against a wall without an air gap, as vines require airflow and space to twine around the lattice structure.

subject: Commissioning of Ventilation Shafts
rationale: Fire dampers within ventilation shafts must be tested and verified during commissioning to ensure they operate correctly.
applicability: The assertion assumes fire dampers are always required in ventilation shafts serving fire-rated compartments, but in some jurisdictions, fire-rated shafts (e.g., dedicated smoke exhaust shafts) may use fire-rated construction instead of dampers, or grease ducts in commercial kitchens have different requirements. Additionally, the condition does not account for shafts that only serve non-fire-rated compartments.
conditions: if shafts serve fire-rated compartments

subject: Commissioning of Ventilation Shafts
rationale: Commissioning includes verifying communication and data exchange between shaft components and the BMS.
applicability: The assertion states ventilation shaft commissioning connects to BMS for remote monitoring and control, but many existing ventilation shafts are commissioned with standalone control systems or simple on/off control without BMS integration, especially in older buildings or smaller facilities where BMS is not present.
conditions: for remote monitoring and control

subject: Road Base Course
rationale: The performance of the base course depends on proper subgrade preparation including grading, compaction, and moisture control.
applicability: The assertion states 'depends_on Subgrade Preparation' with the condition 'Must be graded and compacted to specified density', but in some road construction methods (e.g., full-depth asphalt pavement on poor subgrade with geotextile stabilization), the base course may be placed directly on the subgrade without the subgrade itself being compacted to full road-base specification — the base course and geotextile bridge the weak subgrade. This is common in low-volume roads and temporary roads.
conditions: Must be graded and compacted to specified density

subject: Road Base Course
rationale: Base course materials require proper drainage to prevent water accumulation that can weaken the structure.
applicability: The assertion states 'requires Drainage System' with condition 'In areas with high water table or rainfall', but even in areas with low water table and low rainfall, road base courses can fail due to capillary rise, frost heave, or surface infiltration from occasional storms. A drainage system (e.g., edge drains, underdrains, or permeable base) is often required or beneficial across all climate zones, not only those with high water table or rainfall.
conditions: In areas with high water table or rainfall

subject: Asphalt Wearing Surface
rationale: The existing surface must be cleaned and prepared prior to placing the wearing surface for proper bonding.
conditions: before application

subject: Concrete Curb
rationale: Curbs channel stormwater toward catch basins and drains.
applicability: The assertion states that concrete curb supports roadway drainage system when it includes gutters or drainage inlets. However, concrete curbs without gutters or inlets (e.g., standard barrier curbs) still play a role in drainage by channeling water along the roadway edge. The condition 'when curb includes gutters or drainage inlets' may be too narrow — even plain concrete curbs contribute to drainage management through water conveyance and containment.
conditions: When curb includes gutters or drainage inlets

subject: Road Pavement Structure
rationale: Proper drainage is critical to prevent water accumulation, which weakens pavement layers and subgrade.
conditions: adequate subsurface and surface drainage
exceptions: The assertion states that Road Pavement Structure depends_on Drainage System, but the relationship is more accurately bidirectional: poor pavement design (e.g., impermeable surface, inadequate crossfall) can also overload or cause failure of the drainage system. Therefore, Drainage System also depends on Road Pavement Structure in certain contexts, making the unidirectional 'depends_on' an oversimplification.

subject: Road Pavement Structure
rationale: The pavement structure connects laterally to shoulders for edge support and drainage.

subject: Road Gutter
rationale: Road gutters depend on downstream drainage systems (pipes, catch basins, outfalls) to convey collected water away.
conditions: connection to stormwater network
exceptions: if gutter discharges directly to infiltration or retention area

subject: Road Shoulder
rationale: A road shoulder requires proper drainage to prevent water from seeping into the pavement structure and causing damage.
conditions: to prevent water accumulation
exceptions: In arid or desert regions with very low rainfall, road shoulders may not require a drainage system at all, as water accumulation is negligible.

subject: Road Shoulder
rationale: Proper subgrade compaction and preparation is required to ensure the shoulder can support vehicle loads without settling.
conditions: for stability

subject: Road Shoulder
rationale: Shoulders can support pedestrian movement where dedicated sidewalks are not available.
conditions: in rural areas without sidewalks
when designated for pedestrian use

subject: Traffic Signage
rationale: Traffic signage helps users navigate from point A to point B, forming a critical part of the overall wayfinding system.
applicability: All building types with vehicular or pedestrian traffic
conditions: When consistently designed and placed along decision points
exceptions: Traffic signage may hinder wayfinding when it creates information overload or clutter, particularly in complex urban environments or dense campus settings where excessive signage confuses rather than guides.

subject: Traffic Signage
rationale: Traffic signage works in conjunction with pavement markings (lane lines, arrows, stop bars) to create a complete guidance system.
applicability: All building sites with roads or parking lots
conditions: Signage and pavement markings should be coordinated for consistent guidance

subject: Road Pavement Marking
rationale: Road pavement markings are applied on top of the road surface, which itself requires a stable base and subbase to prevent cracking and deformation that would distort markings.
applicability: If this assertion is meant to convey that pavement marking can only be applied after the full pavement structure (including base/subbase) is in place, this is true only in the sense that any pavement marking requires a completed pavement structure. But the direct dependency and 'proper load distribution' reasoning is misleading since markings do not distribute loads.
conditions: for proper load distribution

subject: Road Pavement Marking
rationale: The pavement surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris, oil, or existing markings for proper adhesion.
conditions: before marking application

subject: Road Pavement Marking
rationale: Marked crosswalks indicate where pedestrians should cross and alert drivers to yield.
conditions: at signalized and unsignalized intersections

subject: Road Pavement Marking
rationale: Edge line markings delineate the boundary between the traveled lane and the shoulder.
conditions: via edge lines

subject: Road Drainage Inlet
rationale: The inlet is the entry point that feeds the larger roadway drainage network, supporting overall stormwater management.
applicability: The assertion is extremely generic — a road drainage inlet (e.g., curb inlet, grate inlet, combo inlet) typically supports a roadway drainage system, but this relationship may vary by context. In some systems, inlets are part of a stormwater management system rather than strictly a 'roadway drainage system', or they may serve other functions like pedestrian safety grading. Additionally, 'supports' is vague and could mean structural support, hydraulic support, or functional support.

subject: Underground Stormwater Drainage Pipe
rationale: Filter fabric prevents fine soil particles from entering the pipe system while allowing water passage.
conditions: in areas with fine-grained soils to prevent soil migration
exceptions: not needed in well-graded granular soils

subject: Underground Stormwater Drainage Pipe
rationale: Installation of underground pipes requires excavation of trenches for placement.
applicability: The assertion says underground stormwater drainage pipe depends on trench excavation, with the exception for trenchless methods. However, in shallow depth applications or where ground conditions (e.g., soft soils, high water table) make open-cut impractical or unsafe, trenchless methods are the primary option, not merely an exception. The assertion assumes open-cut as default which may not always be appropriate.
conditions: during construction phase
exceptions: trenchless methods like directional drilling may be used instead

subject: Pedestrian Crosswalk
rationale: Crosswalks are part of an accessible pedestrian route per ADA guidelines.
conditions: When combined with curb ramps and detectable warnings
exceptions: Pedestrian crosswalks that are mid-block or uncontrolled crossings often lack curb ramps or detectable warnings, yet they are still intended to support accessible routes per ADA requirements. The assertion's condition 'When combined with curb ramps and detectable warnings' creates an exception where crosswalks without these elements (e.g., due to delayed installation, temporary crossings, or non-compliant legacy infrastructure) would not support an accessible route, even though ADA scoping requires accessible routes at all pedestrian crossings.

subject: Road Subgrade Preparation
rationale: Subgrade performance depends on adequate drainage to prevent water accumulation and weakening of the soil.
applicability: The 'depends_on' relationship is not universally true even in the stated conditions. Subgrade preparation may depend on drainage systems in wet climates, but in many low-lying areas, alternative solutions like wicking drains, subgrade stabilization with lime/cement, or engineered fills can be used instead of or in addition to a conventional drainage system. The assertion overstates the dependency as a direct depends_on relationship when drainage may be only one of several possible prerequisites.
conditions: In areas with high water table or poor natural drainage

subject: Road Subgrade Preparation
rationale: Geotextiles provide separation, filtration, and reinforcement for weak subgrades.
conditions: When subgrade soil is weak or soft
exceptions: Even when subgrade soil is weak or soft, geotextile fabric is not always required. Alternatives such as soil stabilization with lime, cement, or fly ash, or mechanical stabilization through compaction and granular replacement (e.g., imported borrow material) are valid approaches that eliminate the need for geotextile fabric in many soft ground and swampy area road constructions.

subject: Road Subgrade Preparation
rationale: The subgrade is the foundation that supports the entire pavement structure and traffic loads.
conditions: All cases

subject: Road Base Installation
rationale: Geotextile fabric is often placed between subgrade and base to separate materials and improve drainage and stability.
conditions: When subgrade soil is weak or wet
exceptions: May be omitted if subgrade is stable, well-draining soil

subject: Road Base Installation
rationale: Edge restraints such as curbs or edging help contain the base material and prevent spreading under load.
conditions: On sloped sites or where lateral movement is a concern
exceptions: May not be needed on flat, contained areas

subject: Road Base Installation
rationale: Proper drainage (e.g., culverts, French drains, underdrains) is often necessary to prevent water accumulation in the base layer.
applicability: The applicability only mentions 'roads in wet climates; low-lying areas' but does not cover roads in climates with seasonal freeze-thaw cycles, where subsurface drainage before base installation is also critical to prevent frost heave.
conditions: In areas with high water table or poor drainage

subject: Road Markings Application
rationale: Markings are applied onto the pavement surface.
conditions: As the surface receiving markings

subject: Road Markings Application
rationale: Markings often complement and reinforce traffic signs.
applicability: The assertion uses 'connects_to' which implies a physical linkage, but road markings and traffic signage are separate physical elements that do not connect to each other. Even at intersections, markings on the road surface do not physically connect to signage mounted on posts or overhead structures.
conditions: At intersections and regulatory zones

subject: Speed Bump Installation
rationale: Speed bumps are installed on top of or embedded into roadway pavement to function as traffic calming devices.
applicability: The assertion covers 'Private driveways' in its applicability, but speed bumps on private driveways are often installed on unpaved surfaces (e.g., gravel driveways), and the existing exception for 'Unpaved roads' may not properly address this scenario since driveways are not 'roads'. The exception should explicitly include unpaved driveways.
conditions: Speed bumps must be installed on an existing paved surface
exceptions: Unpaved roads

subject: Speed Bump Installation
rationale: Warning signs alert drivers to the presence of speed bumps ahead to ensure safety and regulatory compliance.
conditions: Speed bumps require warning signs per traffic regulations

subject: Speed Bump Installation
rationale: Speed bumps can alter runoff patterns; drainage channels or gaps are required to prevent ponding.
conditions: Speed bumps should not obstruct water flow; drainage provisions needed
exceptions: Modular or temporary speed bumps (e.g., rubber speed bumps bolted to the surface) are often installed without dedicated drainage provisions, as water can flow around or under them. The assertion that drainage provisions are needed for 'All installations' does not hold for such installations.

subject: T-Junction Corridor
rationale: Corridors require air circulation; the T-junction geometry can create air stagnation zones needing proper HVAC design.
conditions: Ventilation to meet occupancy load
Temperature and humidity control
exceptions: Naturally ventilated corridors in mild climates

subject: T-Junction Corridor
rationale: The corridor's enclosing structure (walls, ceiling) depends on the building's structural frame.
conditions: Must support corridor walls and ceiling above

subject: T-Junction Corridor
rationale: The T-junction geometry inherently supports wayfinding by offering a clear branch point for directional choices.
applicability: The assertion that T-Junction Corridor supports a Wayfinding System assumes the corridor is part of a larger pathfinding strategy. In purely utilitarian or service corridors (e.g., back-of-house in retail), wayfinding may not be a design concern, and the corridor would not 'support' a wayfinding system in any meaningful sense.
conditions: When designed with clear sightlines and landmarks at the junction

subject: T-Junction Corridor
rationale: Corridors typically contain fire extinguisher cabinets positioned for easy access during egress.
conditions: Mounted along corridor walls per code spacing

subject: T-Junction Corridor
rationale: T-junction corridors commonly connect egress stairwells to main circulation paths.
conditions: At end of one or both corridor branches
Must maintain egress path continuity
exceptions: A T-Junction Corridor does not necessarily connect to a Stairwell. In single-story buildings, in buildings with only ramps or elevators as egress, or where the corridor terminates at an exit door to the exterior, there is no stairwell connection. The current assertion implies stairwell connection is a general characteristic rather than a design option.

subject: T-Junction Corridor
rationale: Accessibility codes often require handrails along corridors, especially at change-of-direction points like T-junctions.
conditions: On at least one side of corridor per accessibility code
May be required on both sides in healthcare settings
exceptions: Very short corridors may be exempt per local codes

subject: T-Junction Wall Intersection
rationale: T-junction wall intersections require structural framing (studs, columns, or wall framing) to connect the intersecting wall to the continuous wall, providing load transfer and lateral stability.
conditions: When walls meet at a T-junction
exceptions: In wood-light frame construction, T-junction wall intersections (load-bearing) do not require 'Structural Framing' elements like beams or columns — the intersecting wall simply nails into the continuous wall's studs with standard blocking or backing. The assertion incorrectly implies a dedicated structural frame element is needed.

subject: T-Junction Wall Intersection
rationale: The T-junction wall intersection ultimately connects to the foundation, transferring loads from both wall segments into the substructure.
conditions: Both the continuous and intersecting walls bear on the foundation
exceptions: Non-load-bearing partitions on slab

In cold-formed steel (CFS) or light-gauge steel framing, a T-junction wall intersection does not 'connect_to Foundation' as a direct structural connection; the intersecting wall's bottom track simply terminates at the face of the continuous wall's bottom track. There is no continuous load path to the foundation through the intersection itself — the load transfers through the continuous wall.

subject: T-Junction Door Assembly
rationale: A T-Junction door assembly requires at least one door leaf to open/close the opening at the junction.
conditions: hinged or pivoted operation

subject: T-Junction Door Assembly
rationale: A door frame is needed to support the door leaf within the T-junction wall opening.
conditions: structural support at junction

subject: T-Junction Door Assembly
rationale: Often required by code for fire doors at T-junctions to ensure self-closing.
conditions: fire-rated assemblies
automatic closing required
exceptions: Not all fire-rated T-junction door assemblies require a door closer. Some fire-rated assemblies use self-closing hinges or sliding fire doors with integrated closing mechanisms instead of a separate door closer device.

subject: T-Junction Door Assembly
rationale: The T-junction door assembly contains the door leaf as its primary movable component.

subject: T-Junction Door Assembly
rationale: The assembly contains the door frame that anchors into the T-junction wall opening.

subject: T-Junction Door Assembly
rationale: A threshold may be contained at the bottom of the door opening at the T-junction.
applicability: A threshold may be absent even in exterior or fire-rated applications if the assembly is designed with a bottom seal integrated into the door leaf or frame, or in certain accessibility-compliant designs where thresholds are minimized or eliminated.
conditions: exterior or fire-rated application

subject: T-Junction Corner Guard
rationale: The guard is mounted at the T-junction of walls, so a wall surface is necessary.
applicability: All building types with T-junction wall corners

The assertion assumes T-junction corner guards are always wall-mounted, but T-junction corners can also occur at ceiling junctions (between wall and ceiling planes) where the guard would be mounted on the ceiling rather than a wall. Additionally, T-junctions can occur in other contexts like floor-to-wall junctions or column-to-beam junctions where the 'wall' terminology is imprecise.
conditions: T-junction corner guard requires a wall to be mounted on at the junction corner

subject: T-Junction Ceiling Transition
rationale: T-junction transitions may contain integration points for HVAC components.
applicability: The assertion assumes that an integrated ceiling design in a commercial context always includes an HVAC diffuser at a T-junction ceiling transition. However, many modern commercial ceiling designs use displacement ventilation, chilled beams, or underfloor air distribution (UFAD) systems where diffusers are not located in the ceiling at all. In these systems, the T-junction ceiling transition would not contain an HVAC diffuser even under 'integrated ceiling design'.
conditions: when integrated ceiling design
exceptions: non-integrated layouts

There are commercial environments such as cleanrooms, server rooms, or laboratories where T-junction ceiling transitions contain specialized filtration housings (HEPA boxes) or perforated ceiling panels rather than standard HVAC diffusers. These are functional exceptions where the element at the transition is not a conventional diffuser.

subject: T-Junction Ceiling Transition
rationale: Lighting fixtures are often integrated into or mounted through ceiling transitions.
conditions: when ceiling integrates lighting
exceptions: separate lighting system

In corridors with emergency lighting requirements, the T-junction ceiling transition may contain an emergency lighting unit (battery-backed egress light) rather than a standard lighting fixture. Additionally, in some designs, the transition area may house a smoke detector or sprinkler head instead of a lighting fixture, even though the ceiling integrates lighting elsewhere.

subject: T-Junction Ceiling Transition
rationale: T-junctions often occur where corridor ceilings meet room ceilings.
applicability: The assertion states that T-Junction Ceiling Transition connects_to Corridor Ceiling at corridor intersections, applicable to commercial and institutional buildings. However, in open-plan commercial layouts (e.g., modern offices with no dedicated corridors, or 'corridorless' floor plans where circulation space is part of the open area), there is no distinct Corridor Ceiling element to connect to, even though a T-junction ceiling condition may still exist at the junction of two ceiling planes.
conditions: at corridor intersections
exceptions: single-room ceilings without corridors

subject: T-Junction Floor Transition
rationale: A T-junction floor transition connects different floor finishes or flooring materials at a T-shaped junction.
applicability: A T-junction transition does not inherently 'connect to' a Floor Finish as a direct relationship. It is a transition strip installed at the junction between two floor finishes of different materials at the same height. The assertion phrasing is ambiguous about what 'connects_to Floor Finish' means—it could imply the T-junction is a type of floor finish or that it connects two floor finishes. The intended semantics are unclear.
conditions: transition between different flooring materials
exceptions: T-junction transitions are not used where both flooring materials are of the same type (e.g., carpet-to-carpet) or where a seam is hidden under a wall or partition. The condition 'transition between different flooring materials' is stated but does not cover the exception where the flooring materials are of the same type at the same level.

subject: T-Junction Signage Location
rationale: Signage may require illumination to be legible in dark corridors or during power failure.
conditions: For low-light or emergency conditions
exceptions: Well-lit environments with natural daylight

subject: T-Junction Signage Location
rationale: Individual T-junction signs are part of a coordinated wayfinding system for consistency.
applicability: The assertion requires that T-junction signs match building-wide signage standards, but this may not hold in contexts where the building has multiple independent tenancies (e.g., a multi-tenant commercial building) where each tenant's wayfinding signage is governed by separate standards or local codes. In such cases, the T-junction sign may be required to match only the tenant's signage system, not a single building-wide standard.
conditions: T-junction sign must match building-wide signage standards

subject: T-Junction Handrail Termination
rationale: A T-Junction Handrail Termination is a specific fitting attached to a handrail where it terminates at a T-junction (i.e., where one handrail meets another perpendicularly), so it requires a handrail as the primary structural element it connects to.
conditions: at T-junction configuration
exceptions: At a T-junction where the continuing run has a handrail already on the opposite side, terminating the handrail at the T-junction may be acceptable because the user can transfer to the other handrail. This is a common building code exception in jurisdictions following IBC or EN 1991-1-1.

subject: T-Junction Wall Framing
rationale: T-junction wall framing structurally supports the intersecting partition wall, connecting it to the main wall.
conditions: When forming an interior wall layout

subject: T-Junction Wall Framing
rationale: The wall cavity formed at the T-junction contains thermal or acoustic insulation material within the framed spaces.
conditions: When the T-junction wall assembly is insulated

subject: T-Junction Drywall Finishing
rationale: Tape is required to reinforce the joint where the intersecting wall meets the perpendicular wall at a T-junction.
conditions: paper or mesh tape

subject: T-Junction Drywall Finishing
rationale: External corners at T-junction intersections typically require metal or vinyl corner bead for durability and straight edges.
conditions: for external corners at T-junctions
exceptions: internal corner T-junctions do not require corner bead

subject: T-Junction Drywall Finishing
rationale: T-junction finishing depends on proper metal stud framing to provide a stable substrate and backing for drywall attachment.

conditions: for embedment or base foundation

Additionally, removable bollards often use a metal sleeve set in asphalt without concrete.

subject: Bike Path Bollard
rationale: Bollards are physically anchored into the path pavement or adjacent ground.
conditions: through bolting or embedment into the path surface
exceptions: Some bollards are installed on the edge of or adjacent to the path (e.g., in a planter or on a curb), not directly connecting to the pavement surface. They may also be installed on a separate concrete pad or plinth that does not touch the bike path pavement.

subject: Bicycle Storage Room
rationale: A bicycle storage room requires racks to hold bicycles in an organized manner.
applicability: All buildings with bicycle storage rooms
conditions: For storing bicycles securely
exceptions: A bicycle storage room could use wall hooks, vertical storage racks, or stacked parking systems that are not technically 'bicycle racks' (typically floor-mounted rail/stand designs). In smaller rooms, wall-mounted hooks are common and more space-efficient.

subject: Bicycle Storage Room
rationale: Security measures like CCTV or access control help protect stored bicycles.
applicability: Public or shared bicycle storage rooms
conditions: To prevent theft
exceptions: A bicycle storage room may rely on the building's general security system (e.g., lobby access control, CCTV covering the corridor) rather than a dedicated Security System specifically for the bicycle storage room. This would satisfy the theft prevention intent without requiring an explicit 'Security System' as a separate system for the room.

subject: Bicycle Storage Room
rationale: Some bicycle storage rooms include a repair stand or air pump for user convenience.
applicability: Larger or well-equipped bicycle storage rooms
conditions: Optional amenity for maintenance
exceptions: A bicycle storage room could provide a bicycle pump, tire repair kit, or vending machine with spare tubes without including a full 'Bicycle Repair Station' (typically a fixed stand with tools). A repair station is a specific, space-consuming amenity that many well-equipped rooms opt not to include, offering smaller mobile repair kits instead.

subject: Bicycle Wash Station
rationale: Water runoff from washing must be drained to prevent flooding and contamination.
conditions: floor drain or trench drain
connection to sewer or greywater system
exceptions: Portable bicycle wash stations (e.g., mobile pop-up units used at events) do not require a permanent drainage system — they often capture wash water in a contained basin or sump for later disposal, with no floor drain, trench drain, or sewer connection.

subject: Bicycle Wash Station
rationale: Wash stations are typically located adjacent to bicycle parking for user convenience.
conditions: nearby proximity for user convenience
exceptions: A bicycle wash station positioned adjacent to a stormwater drain, environmental buffer zone, or waterway may need to be placed away from the bicycle parking area to prevent runoff contamination near where bicycles are parked — proximity is not always desirable for environmental reasons.

subject: Bicycle Wash Station
rationale: The station must be connected to building plumbing for water supply and drainage.
conditions: water supply and drainage connection
exceptions: Self-contained bicycle wash stations with integrated water tanks and holding tanks for wastewater do not require connection to a building's plumbing system for either water supply or drainage.

subject: Construct Bike Path Pavement
rationale: A stable subgrade is essential before any pavement construction can proceed.
conditions: must be compacted and stable
exceptions: if existing subgrade is already adequate

subject: Construct Bike Path Pavement
rationale: Geotextile separates subgrade from base course to prevent contamination and improve drainage.
applicability: The applicability is 'paths on poor soil' but the condition says 'when subgrade soils are weak or prone to mixing'. The exception covers 'if subgrade is well-draining and strong'. However, there is no mention of other contexts like organic soils, expansive clays, or permafrost where geotextile might also be beneficial or required, nor does it address surface erosion control which is a distinct use case for geotextile.
conditions: when subgrade soils are weak or prone to mixing
exceptions: if subgrade is well-draining and strong

subject: Construct Bike Path Pavement
rationale: Proper drainage is critical to prevent water damage and extend pavement life.
applicability: The applicability is 'all bike paths' but drainage system requirements depend on climate, topography, and soil type. In arid regions with well-draining soils and no frost, a formal drainage system may not be necessary. Similarly, elevated boardwalk-style bike paths over wetlands may use alternative water management approaches. The assertion should note context where drainage is truly required vs. where simple grading suffices.
conditions: to prevent water accumulation on or under pavement

subject: Install Bike Path Bollards
rationale: Signage mounted on or near bollards provides instructions to path users.
applicability: The applicability field limits this to 'Trailheads, path entrances', but the assertion itself uses the broad 'Install Bike Path Bollards' label without qualification, which could cause the relationship to be applied incorrectly to bollard installations in other settings such as parking lots, sidewalks, or roadway medians where signage relationships differ.
conditions: Bollards often paired with regulatory or wayfinding signs
exceptions: Some installations use bollards alone without signs

The existing exception notes that some installations use bollards alone without signs, but this is listed as an exception rather than a proper conditional dependency. In many municipal standards, bollards are installed purely as physical barriers with no requirement for co-located signage (e.g., bollards used solely to prevent vehicle access on pedestrian-only paths).

subject: Children's Playroom
rationale: Proper ventilation maintains indoor air quality and reduces spread of illness among children.
applicability: The assertion states 'requires Ventilation System' but the condition only mentions 'adequate fresh air supply required' — this conflates a performance requirement (fresh air supply) with a specific system type (mechanical ventilation). In many climates and building designs, fresh air can be supplied via operable windows and natural ventilation without a dedicated mechanical ventilation system. The assertion should either specify 'mechanical ventilation system' if that is intended, or rephrase to match the condition.
conditions: Adequate fresh air supply required for occupied spaces

subject: Children's Playroom
rationale: Unanchored furniture can tip onto children causing serious injury.
conditions: Bookshelves, dressers, and play equipment must be secured to walls

subject: Children's Playroom
rationale: Connection to outdoor area allows easy transition between indoor and outdoor play.
conditions: Direct access or visual connection to outdoor space preferred

subject: Child-Height Door Hardware
rationale: Child-height door hardware must be mounted on a door to function as a door handle or latch.
applicability: The phrase 'Standard door installation' is vague and may include fire-rated doors where altering hardware height or adding child-height hardware could violate fire rating certifications. In such cases, child-height hardware may not be permissible regardless of dependency on the door.
conditions: Standard door installation

subject: Child-Height Door Hardware
rationale: The door frame houses the strike plate that the latch engages with for proper closure.
conditions: Proper alignment with door strike plate
exceptions: Child-height door hardware does not necessarily depend on a door frame for installations on non-swinging doors such as sliding barn doors or accordion-fold doors, which may have hardware mounted directly to the door panel without a standard strike plate or frame interaction.

subject: Child-Height Door Hardware
rationale: A door closer may be connected to ensure the door closes properly after a child opens it, as children may not fully close doors.
conditions: Automatic door closure required by code

subject: Children's Toilet Room
rationale: Toilet rooms require ventilation to maintain indoor air quality and prevent mold.
applicability: In many jurisdictions (e.g., IBC, IPC), children's toilet rooms in residential childcare facilities with only one or two children may use an adjacent general toilet room with ventilation rather than a dedicated ventilation system. The assertion does not account for very small facilities where shared ventilation suffices.
conditions: mechanical or natural ventilation to control odors and humidity

subject: Children's Toilet Room
rationale: Fixtures require fresh water supply for flushing and handwashing.
conditions: hot and cold water to washbasins, cold water to toilets

subject: Children's Toilet Room
rationale: A functional children's toilet room must contain toilet paper dispensers accessible to children.
conditions: mounted within reach of child users
exceptions: Toilet paper dispensers may be omitted in diapering-only changing areas within a children's toilet room, as the primary function is diaper changing (requiring wipes, not toilet paper). This applies especially to rooms serving exclusively non-toilet-trained toddlers.

subject: Children's Toilet Room
rationale: Hand hygiene requires soap dispensers within children's reach.
conditions: mounted at child height
exceptions: Some facilities use combination soap-and-waterless-sanitizer stations where the primary dispenser is a wall-mounted sanitizer unit, and a separate soap dispenser is not required if a hands-free sanitizer dispenser at child height is provided instead. This is common in lower-cost childcare settings.

subject: Children's Toilet Room
rationale: Children's toilet rooms in facilities serving very young children often include changing tables.
conditions: if the facility serves toddlers or infants
exceptions: not required if age range is exclusively older children

subject: Guardrail/Barrier System for Children
rationale: A handrail or top rail is an integral component of the guardrail system for children to grip.
conditions: top rail of guardrail system

subject: Guardrail/Barrier System for Children
rationale: The guardrail system connects to the floor slab or deck structure at its base for anchorage.
applicability: The assertion states Guardrail/Barrier System for Children 'connects_to Floor Structure' at the base of the guardrail. However, many child guardrail/barrier systems (e.g., portable safety gates, crib rails, stair barrier gates) do not connect to a floor structure at all—they are pressure-mounted or hardware-mounted to walls/doorframes, not to a floor structure. This assertion may only apply to built-in/permanent guardrails, not to all children's barrier systems.
conditions: at the base of the guardrail

subject: Indoor Children's Garden/Courtyard
rationale: Plants require regular watering, so an integrated irrigation or drip system is necessary for maintenance.
applicability: An indoor children's garden/courtyard that uses only hand-watering or self-watering planters with no in-ground irrigation does not require a formal Irrigation System. The assertion assumes permanent irrigation infrastructure, but small or container-based gardens may not need this.
conditions: for watering plants

subject: Indoor Children's Garden/Courtyard
rationale: Proper drainage (floor drains, sloped surfaces, gravel beds) prevents water pooling and structural damage.
applicability: The condition says 'if open to sky' but the assertion title says 'Indoor' Children's Garden/Courtyard. An indoor space is by definition not open to the sky, making the rain component of this condition contradictory or inapplicable. The drainage requirement should be based solely on irrigation water handling, not rain.
conditions: to handle excess water from irrigation and rain if open to sky

subject: Indoor Children's Garden/Courtyard
rationale: To protect the building structure from moisture damage due to soil beds, irrigation, and humidity.
applicability: The assertion specifies waterproof membrane at floor and wall junctions where soil and water are present, but 'all building types' includes existing buildings with raised planter boxes on waterproof trays or prefabricated self-contained garden units that may not require membrane at structural wall junctions.
conditions: at floor and wall junctions where soil and water are present

subject: Indoor Children's Garden/Courtyard
rationale: Plants and soil can produce CO2, humidity, and organic odors; proper ventilation is needed for air quality.
conditions: to prevent CO2 buildup and control odors from soil and plants

subject: Child-Zone Acoustic Treatment
rationale: Acoustic ceiling tiles are a standard component in achieving acoustic treatment in children's zones.
applicability: The existing exception only mentions full-height walls with acoustic finish, but does not cover other common alternatives such as acoustic baffles, clouds, or stretched fabric systems that are frequently used for overhead sound absorption in lieu of ceiling tiles, especially in modern childcare design.
conditions: For overhead sound absorption
exceptions: If full-height walls with acoustic finish are used instead

Acoustic Ceiling Tiles require a suspended ceiling grid system, which may conflict with fire sprinkler head placement requirements in childcare centers. Sprinkler heads must be positioned below the ceiling tiles for proper coverage, creating a trade-off situation where the acoustic treatment could be compromised or additional coordination is needed.

subject: Child-Zone Acoustic Treatment
rationale: Child-zone acoustic treatment depends on acoustic insulation within wall and floor assemblies to block sound transmission between rooms.
conditions: Within wall and floor cavities

subject: Child Activity Room Partition
rationale: A child activity room partition is typically a non-load-bearing partition, but if it's structural, it would require a structural wall system or framing.
conditions: load-bearing partition
exceptions: non-load-bearing demountable partition

subject: Child Activity Room Partition
rationale: Full-height partitions depend on ceiling system for top support and finish integration.
applicability: The assertion lists applicability as 'all', which is overly broad. Even for full-height partitions, the dependence on the ceiling system may vary by jurisdiction, building code edition (e.g., IBC vs. NFPA), and whether the ceiling is rated or non-rated. A blanket 'all' applicability fails to account for these regulatory variations.
conditions: full-height partition
exceptions: partial-height partitions

A full-height partition in a child activity room may still not depend on the ceiling system if it is a freestanding full-height partition that is structurally independent (e.g., self-supporting with its own framing and not braced by the ceiling). The existing exception only covers partial-height partitions.

subject: Mount Child-Height Door Hardware
rationale: Mounting child-height door hardware requires a door to mount onto.
conditions: child-height installation
exceptions: Child-height door hardware may be mounted on existing full-height doors without requiring a new 'Door' — the assertion implies a new Door must be provided when only the hardware is being added. Retrofit installations are common.

subject: Mount Child-Height Door Hardware
rationale: The door frame provides structural support and alignment for mounting hardware at a child-accessible height.
conditions: child-height installation

subject: Install Guardrails with Child-Safe Spacing
rationale: Guardrails are the primary component being installed; the activity inherently requires guardrail system components.
applicability: The assertion states 'requires Guardrail' but 'Guardrail' is referenced as a prerequisite without clarifying that 'Install Guardrails with Child-Safe Spacing' is itself a type of guardrail installation. This creates a circular dependency or an unclear prerequisite hierarchy — it may mean a standard guardrail must be installed first and then modified for child-safety, or that child-safe spacing is an additional feature. The precondition is ambiguous.
conditions: child-safe spacing regulations must be followed

subject: Install Guardrails with Child-Safe Spacing
rationale: Guardrails connect to the floor structure at the edge of elevated surfaces.
conditions: guardrails must be at the edge of the floor or balcony
exceptions: The assertion states guardrails with child-safe spacing always connect to a floor structure, but there are exceptions where such guardrails may be attached to a wall (e.g., stairway wall-mounted handrails/guardrails) or to posts embedded in the ground (e.g., playground perimeter fencing). The 'connects_to Floor Structure' is not universally true.

subject: Install Acoustic Treatment in Children's Zones
rationale: Acoustic ceiling tiles are a primary component used to absorb sound and reduce noise levels in children's zones.
applicability: The assertion states 'requires Acoustic Ceiling Tiles' but this is overly prescriptive. Acoustic treatment in children's zones may also be achieved through ceiling-mounted acoustic baffles, clouds, or stretched fabric systems, which are not 'tiles' in the traditional sense. The requirement should be broader than just tiles.
conditions: in children's zones such as daycare rooms, play areas, or school classrooms
exceptions: In many existing daycare and classroom environments, ceilings are not accessible for tile installation (e.g., concrete slab ceilings, high ceilings, or historic buildings with decorative ceilings). In such cases, acoustic treatment must be achieved through wall panels, freestanding absorbers, or ceiling-mounted baffles rather than tiles.

subject: Install Acoustic Treatment in Children's Zones
rationale: Wall panels help reduce reverberation and control noise in active children's environments.
conditions: where wall surfaces are available and within reach of children's activity areas
exceptions: Some children's zones (e.g., active play areas, gymnasiums, or indoor gross-motor spaces) may require impact-resistant acoustic solutions rather than standard acoustic wall panels, which can be damaged by balls or active play.

subject: Age-Appropriate Signage System
rationale: Signage must be adequately lit to be readable, especially for users with visual impairments.
conditions: for visibility and legibility
exceptions: self-illuminated or backlit signs may reduce dependency on ambient lighting

subject: Carnival Structure / Enclosure
rationale: A carnival structure/enclosure typically needs a structural frame to maintain its shape and support cladding.
applicability: The assertion uses 'Carnival Structure / Enclosure' as a subject but the existing exception only covers 'carnival tents'. The assertion may not apply to all carnival structure types (e.g., inflatable structures, tensile fabric structures, demountable stages) that might have alternative structural systems not fitting the definition of a 'Structural Frame'. The assertion's scope is unclear regarding non-frame structural systems common in temporary/portable carnival buildings.
conditions: When serving as a permanent structure
exceptions: Temporary carnival tents may not require a permanent structural frame

subject: Carnival Stage / Performance Platform
rationale: Performers need to be visible; lighting sets the atmosphere.
applicability: The assertion assumes a traditional stage lighting system is required, but does not account for alternative lighting solutions such as portable battery-powered LED lighting, festival string lights, or other non-permanent lighting setups that could provide visibility and visual effects for a carnival/performance platform without a dedicated Stage Lighting System.
conditions: for visibility and visual effects
exceptions: daytime-only performances with sufficient natural light

subject: Ticket Booth / Entry Kiosk
rationale: Many ticket booths incorporate or are adjacent to queue management elements like stanchions or railings.
applicability: The assertion is limited to 'high-traffic venues' but does not specify venue type. In some high-traffic contexts (e.g., transit fare gates, stadium turnstiles), the entry kiosk is a simple ticket validator with no queue management logic whatsoever — queue management is handled by separate barriers, staff, or digital signage systems.
conditions: for high-traffic venues
exceptions: In high-traffic venues that use staggered entry times or reservation-based access (e.g., museums with timed tickets), queue management is handled upstream (online booking) and the kiosk itself may not contain or operate any queue management system — it merely validates pre-assigned entry slots.

subject: Carnival Game Booth Structure
rationale: A Carnival Game Booth Structure needs a frame to stand and support roof, walls, and game equipment.
applicability: Small carnival game booths (e.g., ring toss, balloon darts) often use lightweight collapsible frames or tables that do not require a dedicated structural frame. The assertion may overstate necessity.
conditions: load-bearing support needed

subject: Carnival Game Booth Structure
rationale: The structure supports string lights or mounted lamps for visibility and attraction.
conditions: evening operation
exceptions: Battery-operated or self-illuminating lighting fixtures (e.g., LED string lights with internal power) do not require structural support from the booth frame; they can be freestanding or attached to adjacent structures.

subject: Concession Stand / Food Counter
rationale: Fire codes typically require fire suppression (e.g., Ansul system) over cooking equipment.
applicability: The assertion does not address whether the fire suppression system requirement varies based on the type of cooking equipment (e.g., deep fryers vs. grills vs. induction cooktops) or the volume/scale of food preparation. Some small, non-grease-producing cooking appliances (e.g., panini presses, microwaves for popcorn) may not trigger the same code requirements.
conditions: for kitchen/cooking areas with grease-producing appliances
exceptions: pre-packaged food sales only, no cooking

subject: Ride Foundation / Anchor
rationale: Proper drainage around the foundation prevents water accumulation and soil erosion.
conditions: For outdoor ride foundations exposed to water
exceptions: Ride foundations or anchors in permafrost or arid environments (e.g., desert rides) may not require a drainage system, as water does not accumulate or drainage is handled by natural percolation.

subject: Carnival Sound System
rationale: Safe cable routing is needed for safety and reliability.
applicability: The assertion states Carnival Sound System requires Cable Management System, but the condition 'Trip hazard prevention essential in public areas' suggests this is only required when trip hazards are a concern. In controlled backstage areas, private events, or spaces where no public foot traffic occurs, a cable management system may not be necessary — e.g., a carnival sound system set up in a fenced-off equipment zone.
conditions: Trip hazard prevention essential in public areas
exceptions: There are exceptions where a cable management system is not required even with trip hazard concerns: (1) when cables are run overhead through rigging or truss systems rather than on the ground, (2) when the sound system is battery-powered and wireless (no cables exist), or (3) when cables are buried in temporary trench covers or recessed floor channels that are flush with the walking surface.

subject: Carnival Seating / Spectator Area
rationale: Accessibility codes mandate wheelchair-accessible seating and companion seating within spectator areas.
applicability: The assertion requires 'Accessible Seating Area' for all Carnival Seating / Spectator Areas, but many smaller or temporary carnival/spectator venues (e.g., temporary bleachers at a small community event, standing-room-only spectator areas, or very small venues under a certain capacity threshold) are explicitly exempt from ADA accessible seating requirements under applicable local codes.
conditions: per ADA and local accessibility codes

subject: Carnival Seating / Spectator Area
rationale: Handrails are required by building codes along stairways and ramps for spectator safety.
applicability: The assertion states 'all public venues' but handrail requirements for stairs and ramps in seating areas are governed by specific codes (IBC, ADA, local amendments) that may have different thresholds for when handrails are required based on the number of risers, slope of ramp, or occupancy type. Some jurisdictions may not require handrails on both sides, or may have different height/grasp requirements.
conditions: along stairs and ramps within the seating area
exceptions: Handrails are not required along stairs or ramps that serve only a single riser (i.e., a single step) or have very low rise (e.g., less than 6 inches) per most building codes, even within seating areas. Additionally, some temporary or portable seating structures may have alternative compliance paths that exempt handrails.

subject: Carnival Flooring / Decking
rationale: Outdoor carnival decking requires adequate drainage to prevent water accumulation, slip hazards, and material degradation.
applicability: The existing exception says 'Interior only installations with no water exposure', but this is potentially misleading for 'Wet areas' listed in applicability. Wet areas (e.g., shower surrounds, pool decks, laundry rooms) typically require drainage by building code regardless of decking material. However, many Carnival decking products are not rated for standing water or continuous wet exposure — they may be slip-resistant but require proper slope and drainage as a site requirement. The wording 'requires Drainage System' could be misinterpreted as a product-integrated drainage requirement versus a site drainage requirement.
conditions: For outdoor or marine decking applications to prevent water pooling
exceptions: Interior only installations with no water exposure

subject: Carnival Utilities Distribution
rationale: Water is essential for drinking, cleaning, food service, and restroom facilities at carnivals.
applicability: The assertion applies specifically to 'carnivals, theme parks, temporary events' but does not clarify whether very small or pop-up carnivals (e.g., a single-day street fair with a few food stalls) have the same requirement. Small-scale events may not have a formal water supply system.
conditions: for sanitation, food preparation, and cooling
exceptions: A carnival may rely entirely on tankered water (delivered by truck) rather than a dedicated Water Supply System with permanent infrastructure. In such cases, utility distribution still occurs but does not 'require' a Water Supply System in the sense of a fixed piped network.

subject: Carnival Utilities Distribution
rationale: Surface-level utilities can create tripping hazards and obstruct foot traffic.
conditions: when cables or pipes cross pathways without proper covers or bridging
exceptions: when buried or covered with protective ramps

The assertion states that utilities distribution conflicts with pedestrian walkways when cables/pipes cross pathways without covers. However, some utilities (e.g., overhead electrical cables) may cross above walkways at sufficient height and never conflict with pedestrian traffic, even without covers or bridging.

subject: Install Carnival Flooring / Decking
rationale: The installation depends on the structural framing being in place and sufficiently cured/stable.
conditions: completed and inspected

subject: Install Carnival Flooring / Decking
rationale: The decking system connects to stair assemblies for access to/from the decked area.
applicability: The assertion states that Install Carnival Flooring/Decking connects_to Stair 'required for access'. However, the connection between decking and stairs is typically a direct structural connection (the stair stringer attaches to the deck framing/joists, not to the flooring/decking surface itself). The decking (the walking surface material) does not directly 'connect to' a stair in a construction sequencing sense - the stair structure connects to the deck framing. This seems to describe a relationship at the wrong level of detail.
conditions: required for access

subject: Install Carnival Flooring / Decking
rationale: Where raised, the decking connects to handrails or guardrails for safety compliance.
applicability: The assertion states that installing Carnival Flooring/Decking connects to Handrail 'if elevated above 30 inches'. However, building codes (IBC, IRC, NFPA) typically require handrails on stairs and guardrails on decks/raised surfaces. The 30-inch threshold is associated with guardrails (fall protection), not handrails. Handrails are required for stairs regardless of elevation, while guardrails (not handrails) are required for decks elevated above 30 inches. This conflates handrails and guardrails.
conditions: if elevated above 30 inches

subject: Build Carnival Stage Platform
rationale: Power supply and distribution for lighting, sound systems, and other equipment.
applicability: The assertion states 'Build Carnival Stage Platform depends_on Electrical Distribution System' but the condition 'if stage uses lighting, sound, or power equipment' and applicability 'stages with AV equipment' are redundant with the existing exception 'unpowered stages'. The condition and applicability essentially restate the exception, suggesting the assertion's core statement is too broad — it implies all Build Carnival Stage Platform depend on Electrical Distribution System, but the condition and exception carve out most non-AV or unpowered stages. The dependency should be scoped more precisely to avoid confusion.
conditions: if stage uses lighting, sound, or power equipment
exceptions: unpowered stages

subject: Install Ticket Booth / Kiosk
rationale: A ticket kiosk supports organized queuing for customer service at transportation hubs, events, or attractions.
conditions: high-traffic venues

subject: Install Concession Stand Equipment
rationale: Sinks, ice machines, and beverage dispensers need water supply and drainage.
conditions: for water supply and drainage

subject: Install Concession Stand Equipment
rationale: Cooking equipment requires exhaust hoods and the space needs ventilation.
conditions: for kitchen ventilation and space conditioning

subject: Install Concession Stand Equipment
rationale: Commercial cooking requires fire suppression per code.
conditions: if cooking equipment is installed

subject: Set Up Carnival Game Booths
rationale: A physical structure/frame is required to house and organize the carnival game.
conditions: For any carnival game booth setup
exceptions: Some carnival game booths are set up indoors or in venues where a separate 'Carnival Game Booth Structure' is not used — e.g., a school gymnasium event using existing wall partitions or simply taping lines on the floor. The assertion does not account for such environments.

subject: Install Ride Anchors / Foundations
rationale: Concrete foundations provide the structural base needed to anchor ride equipment securely.
applicability: all building types with ride installations

The assertion does not specify what types of 'ride installations' it covers. Different ride categories (roller coasters, water rides, dark rides, children's rides, simulators) have vastly different structural load and anchorage requirements, and some may not need a concrete foundation at all. The blanket applicability to 'all building types with ride installations' is overly broad without distinguishing ride types.
conditions: for load-bearing capacity

subject: Quiet Back Finish Materials
rationale: To prevent flanking noise paths, acoustic sealants are needed around the perimeter of quiet back finish panels.
applicability: The dependency 'Quiet Back Finish Materials depends_on Acoustic Sealant' is limited to 'At joints and edges' but does not specify which materials are included in 'Quiet Back Finish Materials' — different finish materials (e.g., drywall, plywood, acoustic panels) may have different sealant requirements or may not require acoustic sealant at all.
conditions: At joints and edges

subject: Sound-Attenuating Partition
rationale: Gypsum boards form the surface layers of the partition, providing mass and fire resistance.
conditions: as facing layers
exceptions: some specialized partitions may use alternate facings like plywood or metal panels

subject: Sound-Attenuating Partition
rationale: The partition assembly contains acoustic insulation within its cavity as a core component.
conditions: inside the stud cavity
