subject: Breakfast Room / Dining Hall
rationale: Kitchen fire suppression systems (e.g., Ansul systems) are required by code to protect against grease fires.
applicability: The assertion applies Fire Suppression System dependency to 'all commercial kitchens', but the item type is Breakfast Room / Dining Hall, not a kitchen. A dining hall may or may not have a cooking area with grease-prone equipment (e.g., it could be a serving-only dining hall with food prepared off-site). The condition should clarify that this only applies when the dining hall contains a cooking kitchen within its scope, not merely because it is adjacent to one.
conditions: for cooking areas with grease-prone equipment

subject: Breakfast Room / Dining Hall
rationale: Proper ambient and task lighting is required for food preparation, dining, and cleaning.
conditions: for safe and pleasant dining environment

subject: Breakfast Room / Dining Hall
rationale: Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning is needed to maintain comfortable temperatures and air quality for diners and staff.
conditions: for thermal comfort and air quality

subject: Breakfast Room / Dining Hall
rationale: Large dining halls often require acoustic panels or sound-absorbing materials to manage reverberation and noise levels.
conditions: for noise control in large dining spaces
exceptions: small breakfast rooms

subject: Commercial Kitchen
rationale: Required by fire codes (NFPA 96) for commercial cooking operations to suppress grease fires.
applicability: The assertion does not differentiate between types of fire suppression (wet chemical vs. dry chemical vs. CO2). Different cooking equipment types and local codes may mandate specific suppression agents. The assertion as stated implies a generic 'Fire Suppression System' without acknowledging this variability.
conditions: for cooking equipment
exceptions: Residential-style cooking equipment in a commercial setting (e.g., a standard residential range in a small bed-and-breakfast kitchen) may not require a commercial-grade fire suppression system. Some jurisdictions allow residential-type equipment and corresponding suppression requirements under certain conditions. This is an exception to the blanket assertion.

subject: Interior Corridor
rationale: Interior corridors have limited or no natural daylight, requiring artificial lighting for safe navigation and egress.
conditions: for occupant safety and wayfinding
exceptions: emergency lighting only during power outages

Interior corridors that are not occupied (e.g., utility corridors, mechanical access corridors) may not require general lighting fixtures for occupant safety/wayfinding since they are not regularly traversed by occupants, yet the assertion applies to 'all building types' with no such exception.

subject: Interior Corridor
rationale: Accessibility standards require handrails in certain corridors for occupant support.
conditions: on at least one side when corridor width exceeds certain dimensions or serves accessible routes
exceptions: residential corridors not serving as accessible routes

Corridors with very short length (e.g., less than 6 feet) serving as passage between two rooms may not require handrails even in public buildings, as they function more as door openings than traversable corridors. The assertion lacks any minimum length threshold for handrail requirement.

subject: Interior Corridor
rationale: Corridor floors must withstand heavy foot traffic and meet slip resistance and fire-rating requirements.
conditions: slip-resistant, durable, and cleanable
exceptions: Industrial/service corridors (e.g., in factories or warehouses) may require specialized floor finishes (e.g., chemical-resistant, heavy-duty) that differ significantly from the slip-resistant/cleanable finishes used in occupied spaces. Additionally, unfinished concrete floors may meet durability requirements without additional 'floor finish' products. This affects the 'all building types' applicability.

subject: Interior Corridor
rationale: The corridor is an architectural space that relies on the building's structural frame for its physical existence.
conditions: to support corridor floor and walls

subject: Interior Corridor
rationale: Fire extinguishers are commonly mounted in recessed cabinets within corridor walls for easy access.
conditions: as required by code at intervals along the corridor
exceptions: Fire extinguisher cabinets are not universally required by code at intervals along corridors in all commercial/institutional buildings. Many newer building codes (e.g., IBC) allow for fire extinguishers on wall brackets without recessed cabinets, and some corridors may be too narrow to accommodate a recessed cabinet. The assertion conflates the presence of fire extinguishers with the specific requirement for a cabinet.

subject: Interior Corridor
rationale: Corridors typically lead to stairwells for vertical movement between floors.
conditions: for vertical circulation and egress
exceptions: In single-story multi-story buildings (e.g., a two-story building with only one story occupied), corridors on the single occupied floor may not connect to stairwells. Also, some multi-story buildings use ramps or elevators as the only means of vertical circulation on certain floors, and corridors connecting only to elevators without a stairwell connection are possible in buildings with a single exit stair.

subject: Interior Corridor
rationale: Corridors provide access to elevator banks for vertical transportation.
exceptions: In multi-story buildings where elevators open directly into a corridor without a distinct lobby (common in smaller buildings or existing retrofits where space is limited), the corridor connects to the elevator hoistway or elevator bank without an intervening 'Elevator Lobby' space. The assertion should account for cases where no distinct lobby exists.

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: A guest bathroom requires a toilet as a core fixture.
conditions: for primary sanitation function

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: Mechanical or natural ventilation is critical to prevent mold and moisture buildup.
conditions: to control humidity and odors
exceptions: if window provides natural ventilation

The existing exception only mentions natural ventilation via a window, but an exhaust-only mechanical ventilation system (e.g., a passive vent stack or a heat recovery ventilator) that is not a traditional 'Ventilation System' could also suffice. Also, in some climates/designs, an open-air bathroom or a bathroom with louvered door and no dedicated fan might meet code requirements without a traditional mechanical ventilation system.

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: No bathroom can function without hot/cold water supply and waste drainage.
conditions: for water supply and drainage

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: A mirror is standard in a guest bathroom for user convenience.
conditions: for grooming and checking appearance

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: A functional drainage system is critical for sanitation.
conditions: for waste water removal from sink and toilet

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: The bathroom depends on a reliable water supply.
conditions: providing hot and cold water to fixtures

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: Lighting and ventilation rely on electrical supply.
conditions: for powering lights, vent fan, and possibly outlets

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: A guest bathroom contains a toilet as a primary fixture.
exceptions: A Guest Bathroom does not universally contain a toilet. In some commercial guest bathrooms (e.g., a bathroom with only a urinal, or a powder room with only a sink), there may be no toilet present. Some guest bathrooms are also designed as accessible unisex bathrooms with only a sink and grab bars but no toilet.

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: A mirror is typically installed above the sink.

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: Hand soap dispenser is standard in a guest bathroom.

subject: Guest Bathroom
rationale: Carpet in a bathroom absorbs moisture, promotes mold, and is unsanitary.
applicability: The assertion that Guest Bathroom conflicts with Carpet Flooring is too broad. Modern water-resistant and waterproof carpet materials (e.g., marine-grade carpet, luxury waterproof carpet tiles) are used in some commercial restrooms and high-end residential guest bathrooms where moisture is properly managed. Also, in dry climates with well-ventilated bathrooms, textile floor coverings are sometimes used successfully.
conditions: due to moisture and hygiene concerns

subject: Guestroom HVAC Terminal Unit
rationale: Air filters are required to clean recirculated or fresh air and protect the coil and fan.

subject: Guestroom HVAC Terminal Unit
rationale: The terminal unit often depends on a BMS for remote monitoring, scheduling, and energy optimization.
conditions: centrally controlled hotel

subject: Guestroom Door & Lock System
rationale: A door frame is structurally required to mount and support the door and lock system.
applicability: The assertion does not specify that the door frame is required only for hinged/pivoting door types. For sliding or pocket door systems (sometimes used in guestrooms for space efficiency), a door frame as traditionally understood (with jambs and stop) may not be required, or the frame is integrated differently into the wall assembly.
conditions: guestroom installation

subject: Guestroom Door & Lock System
rationale: Hinges are required for the door leaf to swing and align properly with the lock strike.
conditions: swinging door type
exceptions: Some guestroom doors use pivot hinges that are fundamentally different from standard butt hinges. The assertion should clarify whether 'Door Hinge' includes pivot hinges or is limited to traditional butt hinges. Additionally, sliding doors for guestrooms do not use hinges at all, which contradicts the condition 'swinging door type' if that condition is interpreted broadly.

subject: Guestroom Door & Lock System
rationale: Many guestroom doors depend on a door closer to ensure the door self-closes and latches properly.
conditions: automatic closing required
fire code compliance

subject: Built-in Wardrobe
rationale: Built-in wardrobes are typically attached to an existing structural wall for support.
applicability: The assertion states that a built-in wardrobe depends_on a structural wall, but in many residential contexts, built-in wardrobes can be installed against non-structural partition walls (e.g., timber stud walls, metal furring channels) or even as freestanding units that are not attached to any wall. The condition 'load-bearing or non-load-bearing wall for attachment' acknowledges a wall is needed, but the dependency should be on any wall (or partition), not specifically a 'Structural Wall' as defined in structural engineering.
conditions: load-bearing or non-load-bearing wall for attachment

subject: Guestroom Window Assembly
rationale: A guestroom window assembly requires a window frame to provide structural support and housing for the glazing.
conditions: for structural support

subject: Guestroom Window Assembly
rationale: Operable guestroom windows require a sash to hold the glazing and allow opening/closing.
conditions: if operable window type
exceptions: fixed windows do not require a sash

subject: Guestroom Window Assembly
rationale: Weatherstripping is required around the window assembly to seal gaps and improve energy efficiency and comfort.
conditions: to prevent air and water infiltration
exceptions: Weatherstripping is not universally required for all guestroom windows. Some interior or non-weather-exposed windows (e.g., windows between a conditioned corridor and a guestroom, or interior light wells) may not require weatherstripping as there is no air/water infiltration concern. The applicability includes 'residential' where basement or garage windows that are not directly exposed to exterior conditions may also omit weatherstripping.

subject: Guestroom Window Assembly
rationale: Flashing is required to direct water away from the window opening and prevent water damage to the wall assembly.
applicability: Window flashing is required for water drainage, but the assertion lacks specificity about what type of flashing is needed (head flashing, jamb flashing, sill flashing, or pan flashing). In many residential and hotel applications, less than full-perimeter flashing is installed depending on climate zone and wall assembly type. In some IBC-compliant construction, a sill pan alone may satisfy code without full-perimeter flashing.
conditions: for water drainage above and around window opening

subject: Guestroom Window Assembly
rationale: The window assembly must interface with the exterior wall cladding for a continuous building envelope.
applicability: The assertion states Guestroom Window Assembly depends_on Exterior Wall Cladding, but the dependency direction may be inaccurate. In typical construction sequencing, the window assembly is installed before the exterior wall cladding (the cladding overlaps or butts against the window frame). The window assembly does not depend on cladding being present; rather, cladding is installed after windows. Additionally, in some curtain wall or storefront systems, the window assembly and cladding are integrated into a single system.
conditions: for integration into building envelope

subject: Guestroom Window Assembly
rationale: The window assembly connects to the interior wall finish (e.g., drywall, trim) at the window reveal.
conditions: at the interior perimeter of the window opening
exceptions: Guestroom Window Assembly does not always connect to Interior Wall Finishes. For example, if the window is in a pre-finished panelized wall system or in a bathroom with tile backer board, the interior wall finish may be applied directly over the window frame or a separate trim piece is used. Also, some window installations have a drywall return (drywall wrapped into the window opening) where the window connects to the rough framing rather than to the wall finish.

subject: Electrical Room
rationale: Electrical rooms must be fire-rated enclosures per building codes to prevent fire spread.
conditions: to contain fire risk from electrical equipment
exceptions: In many jurisdictions, small electrical rooms (e.g., serving a single dwelling unit or containing only a panelboard) do not require a fire-rated enclosure. For example, the NEC and IBC typically exempt electrical rooms under a certain size or with a fire-resistance rating of the wall they are installed in, or they may only require a 1-hour rating rather than a full fire-rated enclosure depending on the building type and room size.

subject: Electrical Room
rationale: Smoke detectors and fire alarm devices are required in electrical rooms.
conditions: for early warning of electrical fires
exceptions: Small electrical rooms or closets that contain only a lighting panelboard or service disconnect (e.g., in a residential or small commercial setting) are typically not required to have a dedicated fire detection and alarm system. Codes like IBC/NFPA 72 generally require fire detection in larger electrical rooms, electrical equipment rooms, or rooms with critical or high-voltage equipment, but not in every small electrical closet.

subject: Mechanical Room
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IBC) require fire-rated separation for mechanical rooms containing fuel-burning equipment or serving as critical building infrastructure.
applicability: Commercial, industrial, multi-family residential, institutional buildings
conditions: Mechanical rooms typically require fire-resistance rated construction per building code
exceptions: Small residential mechanical closets may have reduced requirements

subject: Mechanical Room
rationale: Mechanical equipment such as boilers, chillers, and pumps depend on building plumbing connections.
applicability: The assertion 'Mechanical Room depends_on Plumbing System' is not universally true. A mechanical room may contain only air-handling equipment, boilers, or chillers with no plumbing connections (e.g., a dedicated electrical mechanical room for VAV boxes or a mechanical penthouse with only ducted air equipment and no water-based systems). In such cases, there is no dependency on the plumbing system at all. The condition lists supply water, chilled water, hot water, and drainage, but these are not present in every mechanical room.
conditions: For equipment supply water, chilled water, hot water, and drainage connections

subject: Sprinkler Riser Room
rationale: A sprinkler riser room contains the sprinkler riser and often the fire pump to pressurize the system.
applicability: Not all sprinkler riser rooms require a fire pump. A fire pump is only needed when the available water supply pressure and flow are insufficient to meet sprinkler demand (e.g., tall buildings). Many sprinkler systems operate on municipal water pressure alone without a fire pump.
conditions: when sprinkler system requires pressure boosting

subject: Sprinkler Riser Room
rationale: Floor drains or drainage is needed for testing, draining, and potential water discharge.
exceptions: A sprinkler riser room does not universally require a dedicated drainage system. NFPA 13 requires a floor drain or other means of disposing of water from system testing and drainage, but not every jurisdiction or design includes a formal drainage system — a simple drain connection or hose bib to a nearby plumbing fixture may be sufficient.

subject: Sprinkler Riser Room
rationale: Sprinkler riser rooms require fire-rated walls, doors, and enclosures per building codes.
applicability: While many codes require fire-resistance-rated enclosures for sprinkler riser rooms, the requirements vary by building type, occupancy, and local code adoption. In some smaller buildings or those protected by an automatic sprinkler system throughout, the riser room may not be required to be fire-rated (e.g., NFPA 13 does not always mandate a fire-rated enclosure; IBC 2018 Section 903.2 exceptions may apply).

subject: Sprinkler Riser Room
rationale: Monitoring and alarm initiation depends on integration with the building fire alarm system.
applicability: A sprinkler riser room does not universally depend on a fire alarm system. In buildings without a required fire alarm system (e.g., small buildings not triggering smoke/heat detection requirements), sprinklers may be monitored by a sprinkler flow switch/tamper switch alone connected directly to a central station or local bell without a full fire alarm system.

subject: Sprinkler Riser Room
rationale: A backflow preventer is often installed in the riser room to protect the potable water supply.
applicability: Not every sprinkler riser room contains a backflow preventer. A backflow preventer is required only when the sprinkler system is connected to a potable water supply AND there is a cross-connection hazard. In systems supplied from a non-potable source (e.g., dedicated fire storage tank raw water), backflow preventers may be omitted. Additionally, some backflow preventers are installed outdoors or in separate vaults, not in the riser room.

subject: Sprinkler Riser Room
rationale: The room's equipment connects electrically to the building fire alarm system.
applicability: A sprinkler riser room does not universally 'connect_to' a fire alarm system. The connection is via flow switches, tamper switches, and pressure switches — not the room itself. In buildings without a fire alarm system, these switches may connect to a local bell or a central station communicator rather than to a fire alarm system.

subject: Elevator Machine Room
rationale: Ventilation is required to dissipate heat from motors and controllers and maintain ambient temperature within equipment specifications.
exceptions: Many jurisdictions allow machine-room-less (MRL) elevators, which have no dedicated machine room and thus no ventilation system requirement for a machine room.

subject: Elevator Machine Room
rationale: Machine rooms require fire-rated construction per building and elevator codes (typically 1-hour or 2-hour fire rating).

subject: Elevator Machine Room
rationale: The machine room must be connected to the building fire alarm system for recall and shutdown functions.
exceptions: Machine-room-less (MRL) elevators do not have a separate machine room, so the dependency on a fire alarm system for the machine room does not apply.

subject: Passenger Elevator
rationale: Traditional traction elevators require a machine room housing the motor, controller, and drive equipment.
conditions: for traction elevators
exceptions: machine-room-less (MRL) elevator designs do not require a separate machine room

The assertion states 'Passenger Elevator requires Elevator Machine Room' for traction elevators, but the existing exception already notes that machine-room-less (MRL) traction elevators exist. MRL elevators are still traction elevators (using geared or gearless traction machines mounted in the hoistway), so the 'conditions: for traction elevators' scope does not exclude them. This means the assertion as stated is false for MRL traction elevators, which are a subset of the stated condition.

subject: Passenger Elevator
rationale: The car is the enclosed cabin that carries passengers between floors.
conditions: for transporting passengers

subject: Passenger Elevator
rationale: Steel guide rails mounted in the hoistway keep the car and counterweight aligned during travel.
conditions: for vertical guidance

subject: Passenger Elevator
rationale: Ventilation is needed in the hoistway and machine room for heat dissipation from equipment and for air quality.
conditions: for hoistway and machine room

subject: Passenger Elevator
rationale: Elevators interface with fire alarm systems for automatic recall to designated floors during fire emergencies.
applicability: all buildings with fire alarm systems

The condition 'for fire emergency recall operation' and applicability 'all buildings with fire alarm systems' may be overly broad. Fire recall operation of elevators depends on the fire alarm system, but in some jurisdictions or smaller buildings, the elevator may have its own dedicated smoke/heat detectors for recall without depending on the building-wide Fire Alarm System. Additionally, buildings without fire alarm systems (e.g., some very small buildings) might still have passenger elevators, making the applicability condition self-limiting but incomplete.
conditions: for fire emergency recall operation

subject: Passenger Elevator
rationale: The car interior typically contains handrails for passenger stability during travel.
conditions: for passenger support

subject: Fire Alarm System
rationale: Smoke detectors sense smoke particles and trigger the alarm system for early warning.
conditions: strategically placed per code
exceptions: In some detached one- and two-family dwellings, smoke alarms (not connected to a fire alarm system) are standalone devices, and a full fire alarm system with smoke detectors may not be required at all. The assertion conflates 'smoke alarm' with 'smoke detector connected to a fire alarm system'.

subject: Fire Alarm System
rationale: Heat detectors activate when temperatures rise rapidly, suitable for environments prone to steam or smoke-like conditions.
conditions: used in areas where smoke detectors may cause nuisance alarms (kitchens, boiler rooms)

subject: Fire Alarm System
rationale: Notification appliances (audible and visual) alert building occupants of a fire emergency.
conditions: includes horns, strobes, speakers
must comply with ADA audibility/visibility requirements
exceptions: The assertion says Notification Appliance is required with applicability 'all buildings', but in very small buildings or certain existing buildings undergoing minor alterations, code may not require additional notification appliances if existing occupant notification is adequate. Some codes also allow for 'visible only' or 'audible only' exceptions depending on occupancy.

subject: Sprinkler System
rationale: Sprinkler heads are the terminal devices that activate and discharge water when heat is detected.
conditions: Appropriate temperature rating and coverage pattern

subject: Sprinkler System
rationale: Sprinkler systems are typically connected to a fire alarm system for flow alarms, tamper switches, and notification.
conditions: Interface for monitoring and alarm activation
exceptions: Small residential sprinkler systems (e.g., NFPA 13D systems in one- and two-family dwellings) often use flow switches or water motor gongs rather than a full fire alarm system. Many local codes allow exceptions for fire alarm interface when the sprinkler system is in a small residential occupancy.

subject: Sprinkler System
rationale: In many buildings, the sprinkler system shares the riser and water supply with the standpipe system for fire department use.
conditions: Combined systems in high-rise or large buildings
exceptions: Not required in all buildings

subject: Sprinkler System
rationale: A backflow preventer ensures fire protection water does not contaminate the domestic water supply.
applicability: All building types connected to municipal water
conditions: Required by plumbing codes to prevent contamination of potable water supply
exceptions: May not be needed if using a dedicated non-potable water source

Some jurisdictions allow reduced backflow prevention or no backflow prevention when the sprinkler system is supplied from a dedicated fire service line with no cross-connections to potable uses (e.g., using a double check valve assembly rather than a reduced pressure principle assembly, or exemptions permitted by local amendments). The existing exception only mentions non-potable source, but does not cover this scenario.

subject: Sprinkler System
rationale: A fire pump boosts water pressure to ensure sprinkler heads have adequate flow and coverage.
applicability: High-rise buildings, large warehouses, industrial facilities
conditions: When municipal water pressure is insufficient to meet system demand
exceptions: Not needed if adequate pressure exists from city main or gravity tank

subject: Plumbing Distribution System
rationale: Hot water distribution is a key function of the plumbing system.
conditions: if hot water is required by building program
exceptions: buildings without hot water demand

subject: Plumbing Distribution System
rationale: Plumbing risers and runs require structural support and designated pathways.
conditions: chases, shafts, and penetrations must be coordinated

subject: Plumbing Distribution System
rationale: The distribution system delivers water to and removes waste from sinks, toilets, showers, etc.
conditions: supply and drainage connections must be provided

subject: Plumbing Distribution System
rationale: Plumbing distribution often provides water supply to fire sprinkler systems.
conditions: when combined with fire sprinkler standpipes
exceptions: buildings without fire sprinklers

The assertion states plumbing distribution supports fire suppression when combined with standpipes, but there are cases where fire suppression systems are fed from a dedicated fire pump and tank that are entirely separate from the building's plumbing distribution system, even in buildings with fire sprinklers. The plumbing distribution may not support the fire suppression system in these configurations.

subject: Plumbing Distribution System
rationale: Plumbing provides water for humidifiers, cooling towers, and drainage for condensate.
conditions: when providing makeup water or condensate drainage
exceptions: The assertion says plumbing distribution supports HVAC for makeup water or condensate drainage, but in many buildings HVAC systems use closed-loop chilled water systems that require no makeup water connection to plumbing, and condensate from air handlers may be routed to a dedicated drainage system or to the exterior rather than to the plumbing distribution system.

subject: Plumbing Distribution System
rationale: Backflow preventers protect potable water from contamination.
conditions: required by code at cross-connection points

subject: Plumbing Distribution System
rationale: Insulation prevents heat loss, condensation, and freezing.
conditions: required for hot water pipes and cold pipes in unconditioned spaces
exceptions: temperate climate buildings with interior-only pipe runs

The assertion states pipe insulation is required for hot water pipes and cold pipes in unconditioned spaces, but in some building types (e.g., certain industrial/process applications, or in hot climates where piping heat loss is not a concern for certain hot water systems, or where hot water recirculation is not employed), insulation may be omitted on hot water pipes based on energy code exceptions or alternative compliance paths.

subject: Lighting Fixture Package
rationale: Advanced fixtures connect to control networks via 0-10V, DALI, or wireless protocols.
applicability: The condition 'when fixtures include dimming or addressable control interfaces' may be incomplete: some fixture packages connect to lighting control systems via relay or contactor interfaces (e.g., for simple load shedding or emergency lighting control) even if the fixtures themselves are not dimming or addressable individually.
conditions: when fixtures include dimming or addressable control interfaces
exceptions: simple on/off non-dimmable fixtures

Fixture packages that are line-voltage switched (e.g., via a contactor) and do not contain dimming or addressable drivers still 'connect to' a lighting control system at the panel level. This contradicts the existing exception which only covers 'simple on/off non-dimmable fixtures' — but even those can connect to a control system if relay-controlled.

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: An electrical room provides space, ventilation, and access for the main distribution equipment and panels.
conditions: for housing main distribution equipment
exceptions: small residential systems may use wall-mounted panels

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: The electrical distribution system supplies power to all lighting fixtures throughout the building.
applicability: The assertion claims the Electrical Distribution System 'supports' the Lighting System 'by providing power and control' for 'all buildings'. However, not all lighting systems require 'control' from the electrical distribution system — many lighting systems have integral or distributed controls (e.g., fixture-integrated sensors, Bluetooth mesh controls, PoE switches) that are not directly part of the main electrical distribution. Additionally, emergency lighting often has its own dedicated battery backup or is fed from a separate emergency distribution system. The assertion oversimplifies the relationship for all building types.
conditions: by providing power and control

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning equipment requires electrical power for operation of motors, compressors, and control systems.
applicability: The assertion states Electrical Distribution System supports HVAC System 'by providing power for fans, compressors, and controls' for 'all buildings with HVAC'. This is overly broad — in many modern buildings, HVAC systems include heat pumps, VRF systems, or dedicated outdoor air systems (DOAS) that may have their own dedicated electrical sub-panels or separate power feeds. Additionally, package terminal units (PTACs) often plug into standard receptacles rather than being directly served by the main electrical distribution. The assertion should clarify the level of electrical distribution hierarchy involved.
conditions: by providing power for fans, compressors, and controls

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: Fire alarm systems require reliable electrical power for detection, notification, and control functions.
applicability: all buildings with fire alarm systems
conditions: by providing dedicated power supply
exceptions: The assertion states that the Electrical Distribution System 'supports' the Fire Alarm System 'by providing dedicated power supply'. However, in many jurisdictions (e.g., NFPA 72 compliance), fire alarm systems are required to have a secondary or standby power source (typically batteries or a separate generator) that is not part of the main electrical distribution system. Additionally, some fire alarm systems use addressable loops with power drawn from the fire alarm control panel itself, not directly from the building's electrical distribution. The 'dedicated power supply' phrasing may imply the main distribution when it should also cover emergency/standby sources.

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: Security cameras, access control readers, and alarm systems rely on the electrical distribution system for power.
applicability: The assertion claims Electrical Distribution System supports Security and Access Control Systems 'by providing power and data connectivity' for 'commercial; institutional; high-end residential'. However, many modern security and access control devices (e.g., wireless locks, battery-powered sensors, PoE cameras) receive both power and data over structured cabling (e.g., Cat6 PoE) which is typically part of the low-voltage/telecommunications infrastructure, not the building's main electrical distribution system. The assertion conflates the electrical power distribution system with the low-voltage/data distribution infrastructure.
conditions: by providing power and data connectivity

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: UPS systems connect to the distribution system to provide conditioned, uninterrupted power to critical loads.
conditions: for critical load protection
exceptions: buildings without critical systems

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: Water pipes near electrical components create shock hazards and corrosion risks; building codes mandate separation distances.
conditions: when water pipes are placed too close to electrical conduits
exceptions: when proper separation distances are maintained

subject: Electrical Distribution System
rationale: Structural steel can become energized if faults occur; it must be properly bonded to the grounding system to avoid hazards.
conditions: if not properly bonded for grounding
exceptions: when intentional bonding connections are made

subject: Guestroom Bed Base & Headboard
rationale: A guestroom bed base requires a structural bed frame to support the mattress, box spring, and headboard assembly.
applicability: The assertion applies only to traditional bed configurations. For platform beds or beds with integrated headboard/base systems (e.g., Murphy beds, loft beds, or certain Scandinavian designs), a separate bed frame is not required as the headboard and base are self-supporting or wall-mounted.
conditions: for structural support of mattress and bedding

subject: Lobby Seating Group
rationale: Adequate lighting is essential for the lobby seating area to be functional and welcoming.
conditions: general ambient and task lighting for visibility and comfort
exceptions: A lobby seating group may not require a lighting system if placed in a naturally well-lit atrium or open-air lobby where daylight provides sufficient ambient lighting and no task lighting is needed (e.g., seating is purely decorative or for brief waiting).

subject: Lobby Seating Group
rationale: Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning are needed for occupant comfort in the seating area.
conditions: thermal comfort for occupants
exceptions: In unconditioned interior spaces (e.g., naturally ventilated lobbies in temperate climates or transitional buffer zones), the seating group may not depend on an HVAC system at all, relying instead on passive ventilation and natural thermal comfort.

subject: Lobby Seating Group
rationale: Lobby seating is often positioned in visual or physical proximity to the reception desk.
applicability: The assertion assumes a typical lobby layout, but many lobbies have seating groups that are intentionally separated from the reception desk (e.g., a quiet waiting area around a corner, or seating near elevators while the desk is at the entrance). In those configurations, the seating group does not directly connect to the reception desk.
conditions: in typical lobby layout

subject: Exterior Signage
rationale: Illuminated signage requires lighting components such as LEDs, neon, or fluorescent lamps.
applicability: The assertion is limited to commercial, retail, and public buildings. However, exterior signage in certain contexts like temporary event signage (festivals, fairs) or construction site signage may also be illuminated but falls outside the stated applicability scope, yet the condition (illuminated signage) is general.
conditions: If signage is internally or externally illuminated
exceptions: Non-illuminated signage does not require lighting fixtures

Some exterior signage uses self-illuminating technologies (e.g., electroluminescent panels, fiber-optic edge-lit acrylic, LED-embedded materials) that are integrated into the sign itself and do not require a separate Lighting Fixture component. The assertion assumes illumination always comes from an external or separate fixture.

subject: Exterior Signage
rationale: Freestanding signage requires a concrete footing or foundation for stability.
conditions: For freestanding or monument signage
exceptions: Wall-mounted signage

Freestanding signage on existing paved surfaces (e.g., parking lots) may use surface-mounted anchors or ballast-block support instead of a full foundation system. Additionally, temporary freestanding signage (e.g., A-frame or sandwich board signs) does not require any foundation system.

subject: Exterior Signage
rationale: Exterior signage is a key component of building wayfinding, helping visitors locate entrances, areas, and facilities.
conditions: When signage provides directional or identification information

subject: Parking Lot Pavement System
rationale: Parking lots generate significant stormwater runoff requiring drainage infrastructure.
applicability: The assertion does not account for cases where the parking lot pavement system is on a rooftop or elevated structure (e.g., rooftop parking deck). In these scenarios, runoff may be handled by the building's roof drainage system rather than a separate stormwater drainage system for the parking lot.

The assertion assumes drainage is required, but does not consider parking lots that are intentionally designed as retention/infiltration basins (e.g., grass pavement or gravel lots where stormwater infiltrates on-site). In such designs, there is no separate 'stormwater drainage system' that conveys water away from the site — infiltration is the primary mechanism.
conditions: Must manage runoff from paved surface
exceptions: Permeable pavement systems may integrate drainage differently

In arid or desert regions with extremely low rainfall (e.g., < 50mm annually), stormwater drainage systems may not be required for parking lot pavement systems as there is effectively no runoff to manage. The existing exception for permeable pavement assumes integration of drainage, but does not cover the scenario where drainage infrastructure is unnecessary altogether.

subject: Canopy / Porte-Cochère
rationale: Canopies and porte-cochères typically support overhead lighting for safety, wayfinding, and architectural effect at building entrances.
applicability: The assertion that a canopy/porte-cochère 'supports lighting fixture' is too broad. In many jurisdictions, porte-cochères used for ambulance or emergency vehicle access (common in Healthcare) have strict height clearance requirements that limit or prohibit hanging or surface-mounted lighting fixtures that could protrude into the clearance envelope. Additionally, in seismic zones, rigidly mounted lighting on canopies must meet additional bracing requirements that may not be feasible with typical canopy structures.
conditions: Canopy structure must accommodate mounting and wiring
Lighting must comply with egress and accessibility codes
exceptions: Exception: Fabric or tensile membrane canopies (often used in hospitality and commercial applications) typically cannot support direct mounting of lighting fixtures because the membrane material lacks structural rigidity and load-bearing capacity. Lighting for such canopies requires separate freestanding poles or attachments to adjacent building structures rather than mounting on the canopy itself.

subject: Outdoor Patio / Terrace
rationale: Outdoor patios need drainage to avoid water accumulation and damage.
applicability: Drainage systems for outdoor patios/terraces may not be required in arid or desert climates where natural percolation is sufficient and ponding is not a concern. The assertion lacks regional/climatic context.
conditions: For proper water runoff
To prevent ponding

subject: Outdoor Patio / Terrace
rationale: Prevents water infiltration into spaces below the patio.
conditions: Above habitable spaces
Rooftop terrace
exceptions: Ground-level patios do not require waterproofing below

subject: Exterior Wall Cladding
rationale: Flashing directs water away from vulnerable areas like windows, doors, and roof-wall intersections.
conditions: At openings, joints, and intersections

subject: Exterior Wall Cladding
rationale: Thermal insulation is typically required behind or within cladding systems to meet energy code.
applicability: The assertion states 'Exterior Wall Cladding requires Insulation' with applicability 'all building types', but this is incorrect for many building types. Uninsulated structures (e.g., unheated sheds, certain agricultural buildings, unconditioned garages, some warehouses, carports, or historic preservation projects) have cladding without insulation. The assertion conflates typical energy-code-compliant construction with universal necessity.
conditions: Often integrated into or behind cladding assembly
exceptions: Exterior insulated finish systems (EIFS) integrate insulation and cladding

subject: Exterior Wall Cladding
rationale: An air barrier is required behind or as part of the cladding system to control air leakage.
conditions: Part of continuous air barrier system
exceptions: Certain cladding types such as rain screen systems or direct-applied finishes may not incorporate a dedicated air barrier layer as part of the cladding assembly itself — the air barrier may be located elsewhere in the wall system. The assertion implies the cladding itself requires an air barrier, which conflates cladding with the overall wall assembly.

subject: Exterior Wall Cladding
rationale: Thermal and moisture movement requires expansion joints to prevent cladding buckling or cracking.
applicability: The assertion is limited to 'commercial buildings; large buildings' but expansion joints depend more on cladding panel dimensions, material thermal movement characteristics, and building geometry than on building type or size classification. A small building with large-format metal panels may still need them; a large building with small shingles may not. The applicability scope is mis-specified.
conditions: For large cladding panels or long runs
exceptions: Small-format cladding like shingles may not need expansion joints

subject: Foundation System
rationale: Foundation systems commonly require concrete for footings, slabs, and piles to transfer loads.
conditions: when foundation type is shallow or deep
exceptions: timber piles may not require concrete
Stone or rubble foundations (e.g., in historic or vernacular construction) do not require concrete; they use stacked stone with mortar. This is not covered by the 'timber piles' exception.

subject: Foundation System
rationale: Proper drainage prevents hydrostatic pressure buildup and water damage to foundation.
conditions: in areas with high water table or precipitation
exceptions: dry climates with well-draining soil

In permafrost regions, foundation systems (e.g., piles with thermosiphons) deliberately avoid drainage systems because draining permafrost causes thaw instability. This contradicts the dependency assertion.

subject: Foundation System
rationale: Foundation walls or footings support load-bearing walls above.
conditions: directly beneath load-bearing walls
exceptions: Point-loaded foundations (e.g., pier and beam systems) where the foundation supports beams/girders rather than directly supporting load-bearing walls; the walls sit on beams spanning between piers.

subject: Foundation System
rationale: Isolated or combined footings support columns.
conditions: where column loads exist

subject: Foundation System
rationale: Foundation walls transfer loads from superstructure to footings and enclose below-grade spaces.
conditions: where basement or crawlspace exists
exceptions: slab-on-grade foundations

subject: Foundation System
rationale: A concrete slab is a common foundation system component.
conditions: when slab foundation is used

subject: Foundation System
rationale: Waterproofing is a component layer applied to foundation systems to prevent moisture intrusion.
conditions: for below-grade foundations
exceptions: Waterproof membrane is not universally required for below-grade foundations in all climates; in arid or desert regions with deep groundwater, damp-proofing rather than full waterproofing is standard for many below-grade walls.

applicability: The assertion applies to kitchens, entertainment centers, and office built-ins, but there are other common contexts (e.g., retail display cases with integrated lighting, library shelving with task lighting, hotel reception millwork with outlets) that are not listed. exceptions: Signage mounted on roofs, parapets, or hung from canopies does not require exterior walls as the structural surface. The condition 'signage must be mounted on a structural surface' is broader than just exterior walls.

subject: Commission Fire Alarm System

applicability: The assertion states Commission Fire Alarm System depends_on Notification Appliance, but in many modern buildings, notification appliances are integrated into the fire alarm control panel itself (e.g., speakers in strobes or combination units). Additionally, some code-compliant systems may use voice evacuation systems where notification appliances are part of a separate mass notification system. This dependency relationship oversimplifies the architecture.
conditions: Must be properly located and audible/visible per code

subject: Commission Fire Alarm System
rationale: Life safety requires that fire alarm activation releases locked doors for egress.
applicability: The assertion states Commission Fire Alarm System connects_to Access Control System, implying a direct connection. However, in many jurisdictions and modern designs, the fire alarm system connects to the fire alarm control panel or building management system, which then interfaces with the access control system. The fire alarm system may have a dry contact or relay output rather than a direct data connection to the access control system. The 'connects_to' relationship is ambiguous and may misrepresent the actual integration topology.
conditions: Alarm must unlock egress doors and release magnetic locks

subject: Bus Shelter
rationale: A bus shelter needs a stable foundation (concrete pad or anchored base) to remain upright and secure against wind and use.
conditions: Load-bearing ground
exceptions: A bus shelter mounted on an existing concrete slab or paved surface (e.g., sidewalk) may not require a separate 'Foundation' element beyond the existing load-bearing ground, as the shelter's base plates can be bolted directly to the slab. subject: Bus Shelter
rationale: Bus shelters depend on bus stop signage or route information to inform passengers of service.
applicability: The assertion 'Bus Shelter depends_on Bus Stop Signage' may not hold in transit systems where the bus shelter itself is the designated stop indicator (e.g., the shelter structure is assigned a stop ID and serves as the identifying marker), eliminating the need for separate signage. exceptions: Shelter integrated with digital display

subject: Bus Stop Bench

A bench inherently implies a frame or supporting structure — requiring a 'bench frame' as a separate component is essentially requiring the bench itself again. conditions: load-bearing support for sitting
exceptions: There are bus stop benches that are monolithic concrete slabs or poured-in-place structures that do not have a separate 'bench frame' — the bench itself is the structural element. Similarly, some benches are made of solid stone or recycled plastic lumber planks attached directly to embedded posts without a distinct frame component.

subject: Bus Stop Foundation
rationale: Bus stop foundations typically require concrete to provide a stable, level base for the shelter structure.
conditions: When using reinforced concrete foundation
exceptions: Small bus stop shelters on well-compacted, load-bearing soil may use gravel or crushed stone bedding instead of a full concrete foundation. This is a common practice for temporary or lightweight transit shelters.

subject: Bus Stop Foundation
rationale: Waterproofing protects the concrete from moisture damage and freeze-thaw deterioration.
conditions: In areas with high water table or moisture
For below-grade portions of foundation
exceptions: Precast concrete bus stop foundations installed on a prepared gravel base with proper drainage may not require an additional waterproof membrane, as the assembly relies on gravel drainage rather than a membrane for moisture management.

The dependency on a formal 'Drainage System' system is not universal; passive drainage solutions are common and sufficient in many jurisdictions.
conditions: outdoor waiting pad areas to prevent water pooling
exceptions: indoor pads with no exposure

subject: Passenger Waiting Pad

conditions: providing access to/from the waiting pad
exceptions: The assertion 'Passenger Waiting Pad connects_to Pedestrian Walkway' may not hold in cases where the waiting pad is directly accessed from a platform (already served by walkways) or from a roadway crossing at grade without an intervening pedestrian walkway. In some transit stations, waiting pads are immediately adjacent to the boarding area with no separate walkway connection needed.

subject: Bus Stop Pole
rationale: Some bus stop poles are designed to mount a solar or electric light to illuminate the stop area.
applicability: The assertion applies only when the pole is designed with an attachment for lighting, but many bus stop poles are not designed for lighting attachment even at stops with lighting requirements, often relying instead on separate lighting columns or nearby streetlights. This significantly limits the scope of the assertion beyond what the 'applicability: Stops with lighting requirements' suggests.
conditions: When pole is designed with attachment for lighting
exceptions: Poles without integrated lighting

subject: Bus Stop Pole

applicability: The assertion implicitly assumes the pole has sufficient structural capacity and electrical infrastructure (power supply, data cabling) to support an RTPI display, which is not universally true even for poles at smart stops. Many poles lack the necessary power feed or structural reinforcement for such displays.
conditions: When electronic display is mounted on pole
exceptions: Poles with static signs only

Poles at smart/connected stops that have an RTPI display mounted on a separate post or on the shelter structure rather than on the pole itself would not satisfy the condition 'When electronic display is mounted on pole', yet the stop could still be considered a smart/connected bus stop. This represents a valid exception not captured.

subject: Windbreak Panel
rationale: A windbreak panel needs a structural frame or support system to be mounted and resist wind loads.
conditions: Must be securely anchored
exceptions: Free-standing temporary windbreaks

subject: Windbreak Panel

exceptions: Freestanding landscape panels

Shelters installed on existing slabs or paved surfaces (e.g., concrete pads, parking lots) may not require a separate Foundation installation step because the ground itself serves as the load-bearing base. The existing exception only mentions 'Temporary shelters may not need permanent foundations' but does not cover this scenario.

subject: Shelter Installation
rationale: The structural frame (steel, timber, or aluminum) forms the skeleton of the shelter.
conditions: Must be pre-fabricated or assembled on-site
exceptions: Some shelter types such as inflatable air shelters, tensioned membrane structures, or yurts use flexible membranes, cables, or compression rings rather than a rigid 'Structural Frame'. These can still be pre-fabricated but do not have a frame in the conventional sense.

subject: Shelter Installation

In these cases, insulation is not a separate installation step that 'supports' thermal insulation but is integral to the structural components themselves.

subject: Signage Installation

applicability: The assertion claims signage installation 'supports' wayfinding system across all building types, but wayfinding systems are substantially more complex (including spatial layout design, cognitive psychology, color-coding systems, braille/tactile elements, digital kiosks, etc.). Signage installation is only one small delivery/implementation aspect. The 'supports' relationship is overly broad and suggests a stronger dependency than exists.

conditions: signage is mounted on exterior walls or roofs

subject: Signage Installation

applicability: The assertion applies to load-bearing walls generally, but many modern load-bearing walls are made of reinforced concrete or masonry where drilling with engineered anchors is standard practice and structurally acceptable. The assertion incorrectly treats all load-bearing walls as equally sensitive to signage installation, whereas the main concern is specific to thin structural walls (e.g., shear walls, load-bearing stud walls) or walls with critical reinforcement that cannot be disturbed.
conditions: signage requires deep drilling or significant penetration
exceptions: engineered mounting solutions that avoid structural compromise

subject: Install food stand cabinetry
rationale: Cooking equipment within cabinetry generates heat, smoke, and grease requiring ventilation for fire safety and air quality.
applicability: The assertion does not specify whether the ventilation system requirement refers to local exhaust (hood/supply) or general mechanical ventilation, nor does it address jurisdiction-specific codes (e.g., IMC, NFPA 96) that may impose different requirements based on cooking appliance type, fuel source, and BTU output.
conditions: if the cabinetry houses cooking equipment such as grills, fryers, or ovens
exceptions: cold food stands or pre-packaged food only

Food stands using induction cooktops or other electric cooking equipment that does not produce combustion gases may not require a ventilation system in the same way as gas-fired grills, fryers, or ovens. The assertion does not distinguish between ventilation needed for grease/odor removal vs. combustion exhaust.

subject: Install countertop and backsplash
rationale: Countertops are typically installed on top of base cabinets, which support their weight.
applicability: The applicability lists 'commercial' but in many commercial kitchens (e.g., restaurants), countertops are often stainless steel and are supported by stainless steel legs or frames, not base cabinets, and the backsplash is frequently an integral part of the countertop or a stainless steel sheet attached to the wall independently.
conditions: countertop is for a kitchen or bathroom vanity
exceptions: freestanding countertops or islands with legs

In some construction sequences, backsplash tile installation can occur before base cabinets are installed, especially when using a full-height backsplash that extends from countertop to upper cabinets, and the backsplash is installed directly on the drywall before base cabinets are placed. This contradicts the dependency claim.

subject: Install hood and exhaust ductwork
rationale: NFPA 96 requires automatic fire suppression systems for commercial cooking exhaust.
applicability: The assertion states that hood and exhaust ductwork installation depends on a fire suppression system, but the existing exception already notes residential hoods do not require fire suppression. However, the assertion does not clarify that this dependency applies only to Type I (grease) hoods required for cooking that produces grease-laden vapors, not Type II (exhaust-only) hoods used for non-grease applications such as dishwashers or heat capture, where fire suppression is typically not required.
conditions: Required for commercial cooking operations
exceptions: Residential hoods generally do not require fire suppression

subject: Sleeping Cubicle
rationale: Enclosed small spaces need mechanical or natural ventilation for occupant health.
conditions: to maintain indoor air quality and prevent CO2 buildup

subject: Sleeping Cubicle
rationale: Sleep quality depends on low noise; acoustic treatment of walls is critical.
conditions: to reduce noise from surrounding environment
exceptions: The assertion says 'Sleeping Cubicle depends_on Acoustic Insulation' to reduce noise from surrounding environment. However, some sleeping cubicle designs intentionally use active noise cancellation or white noise systems instead of (or in addition to) passive acoustic insulation. Also, in very quiet environments (e.g., dedicated quiet zones in libraries), acoustic insulation may not be strictly necessary.

subject: Sleeping Cubicle
rationale: Modern sleeping spaces often need power for phones, alarms, or lamps.
conditions: for charging devices or powering small appliances

subject: Install electrical and data service
rationale: Electrical installation enables lighting fixtures to receive power and be controlled by switches.
conditions: by providing branch circuit wiring and switched connections

subject: Install electrical and data service
rationale: Fire alarm systems require electrical power and signaling wiring, often installed as part of the electrical scope.
conditions: by providing dedicated power and control wiring

subject: Public Dormitory
rationale: High occupancy requires adequate air circulation for health and comfort.
conditions: high occupant density
exceptions: naturally ventilated designs in mild climates

The existing exception already covers naturally ventilated designs in mild climates, but no exception is noted for dormitories that use mechanical ventilation-only strategies (e.g., split systems with no ducted ventilation) in moderate climates where a formal 'ventilation system' might be interpreted as requiring ducted or central ventilation, whereas small through-wall or split-system ventilation may suffice under certain codes.

subject: Public Dormitory
rationale: Life safety systems are mandatory in high-occupancy residential buildings.
applicability: The assertion conditions 'building code compliance' is tautological — all building requirements are for code compliance. The applicability is also overly broad: small dormitories (e.g., under a certain occupancy threshold) may be exempt from full fire detection and alarm system requirements and may only require smoke alarms per code (e.g., IBC exceptions for certain R-2 occupancies below a given occupant load).
conditions: building code compliance

subject: Public Dormitory
rationale: Illumination is necessary for all occupied spaces.
conditions: all habitable spaces
exceptions: Storage rooms, mechanical rooms, and janitorial closets within a public dormitory are habitable spaces? Under most building codes, these are not considered 'habitable spaces' and thus do not require the same lighting fixture standards as sleeping units or living areas. The condition 'all habitable spaces' may be correct, but if the assertion was intended to mean 'all rooms/spaces,' it is overbroad.

subject: Public Dormitory
rationale: Toilets, showers, and sinks require water supply and drainage.

subject: Public Dormitory
rationale: Heating/cooling may be needed depending on climate.
conditions: extreme climate conditions
exceptions: temperate climate with natural ventilation

subject: Public Dormitory
rationale: Laundry facilities are a standard amenity for residents.
conditions: long-term residential stay
exceptions: off-site laundry service

Short-term public dormitories (e.g., hostels catering to tourists staying 1-3 nights, conference dormitories, or emergency shelters) do not require a laundry room even without off-site service, as occupants are not expected to do laundry during such brief stays. The condition 'long-term residential stay' partially addresses this, but the existing exception only covers 'off-site laundry service,' omitting this use-case.

subject: Sleeping Platform
rationale: A sleeping platform typically requires a bed frame or base to elevate the mattress off the ground for ventilation and support.
conditions: when used for sleeping
exceptions: floor sleeping platforms like tatami

Some sleeping platforms (e.g., Murphy bed platforms, wall-bed platforms) are designed as integrated units that include both the platform and the folding bed mechanism, and do not require a separate bed frame.

In some cultures (e.g., traditional Japanese tatami), futons are placed directly on the tatami mat floor without any bed frame, and the tatami itself serves as the sleeping platform without requiring a frame.

subject: Integrated Sleep Pod
rationale: Enclosed sleeping spaces require proper air exchange for occupant safety and comfort
conditions: to maintain fresh air circulation and prevent CO2 buildup
exceptions: A sleep pod may have a self-contained ventilation system with CO2 scrubbers or independent air recirculation and filtration, making a connection to a building-wide ventilation system unnecessary. This is analogous to the existing exception on assertion dc342d68.

subject: Integrated Sleep Pod
rationale: Sleep pods often need tie-ins to building HVAC for thermal comfort
conditions: for conditioned air supply to the pod's interior
exceptions: if pod has independent HVAC unit

subject: Ventilation Grille for Sleep Cubicles
rationale: To prevent dust and particulates from entering the sleep cubicle
applicability: The assertion does not specify the type or class of air filter required (e.g., MERV rating, particulate vs. chemical filtration), which may vary based on local codes, occupancy, and environmental conditions.
conditions: when grille is used for fresh air supply
exceptions: If the grille is used only for exhaust/return air (not fresh air supply), the requirement for an air filter does not apply, as filters are typically needed only on intake/supply paths.

subject: Public Mattress System
rationale: Moisture from occupancy can degrade mattresses in enclosed public environments.
applicability: The assertion does not specify what counts as a 'Ventilation System' — whether active mechanical ventilation (e.g., HVAC, fans) or passive ventilation (e.g., slatted bases, air gaps) is sufficient. This ambiguity could lead to under- or over-application of the rule.
conditions: To prevent moisture buildup and mold growth in mattress storage
exceptions: Open-air/outdoor installations

In buildings with continuously dehumidified environments (e.g., climate-controlled storage with <50% RH maintained by building-wide HVAC), a dedicated ventilation system for the mattress system may be redundant.

subject: Sleeping Area Floor Finish
rationale: Underlayment provides cushioning, sound absorption, and moisture barrier beneath the floor finish.
conditions: If carpet or laminate is used as finish

subject: Sleeping Area Floor Finish
rationale: Sleeping areas require acoustic comfort; floor finish often works with acoustic underlayment or insulation.
applicability: Acoustic insulation is not universally required for all sleeping area floor finishes in multi-family buildings. For example, carpet with a thick pad already provides significant sound attenuation and may meet code without separate acoustic insulation. The assertion should be conditioned on finish type, not just building type.
conditions: In multi-family or multi-story buildings where sound transmission is a concern

subject: Sleeping Area Floor Finish
rationale: A level substrate is required for proper installation and performance of many finishes.
applicability: The assertion states 'If subfloor is uneven' but does not specify what constitutes 'uneven' — different tolerances apply for vinyl vs. tile (e.g., thin-set tile can tolerate some unevenness with build-up, while luxury vinyl tile (LVT) requires very flat surfaces). The single condition lumps all thin finishes together without distinguishing their different flatness requirements.
conditions: If subfloor is uneven prior to installation of thin finishes like vinyl or tile

subject: Emergency Alarm Integration
rationale: Smoke detectors are primary fire detection devices that integrate with the emergency alarm system to provide early warning.
conditions: for automatic fire detection
exceptions: Emergency Alarm Integration does not universally require a Smoke Detector for automatic fire detection. In environments such as clean rooms (e.g., semiconductor fabs), data centers with pre-action suppression systems, or outdoor areas, fire detection may rely on air-sampling (ASD), flame/optical detectors, or linear heat detection instead of spot-type smoke detectors.

subject: Emergency Alarm Integration
rationale: Heat detectors are used in environments where smoke detectors are unsuitable, and they must integrate with the alarm system.
applicability: The assertion lacks consideration of code variations. For example, NFPA 72 allows smoke detectors in kitchens if they are listed for the application and placed at sufficient distance from cooking appliances. The assertion implicitly assumes heat detectors are always required, which may not align with all modern code provisions or local amendments.
conditions: for areas where smoke detectors may cause false alarms
exceptions: Emergency Alarm Integration does not always require a Heat Detector in kitchens, boiler rooms, or garages. In some jurisdictions, rate-of-rise heat detectors, sprinkler flow switches, or even flame detectors may serve as the initiating device. Additionally, small kitchens in residential settings may rely on interconnected smoke alarms with hush features rather than dedicated heat detectors.

subject: Install Privacy Enclosures
rationale: The enclosure system contains a frame that holds everything together.
conditions: load-bearing elements

subject: Commission Sleep Pod Ventilation
rationale: A dedicated ventilation system is required to provide fresh air and remove stale air from sleep pods.
applicability: The assertion assumes that a ventilation system is always present in a sleep pod environment, but in certain jurisdictions or for certain temporary/mobile sleep pods (e.g., airport nap pods, pop-up sleeping cabins), there may be no dedicated mechanical ventilation system at all, only passive or natural ventilation. The assertion does not account for this scenario.
conditions: supply and exhaust must be balanced
airflow rates per pod must meet design specifications
exceptions: Sleep pods used solely for short-term napping (e.g., less than 30 minutes) in some jurisdictions may have relaxed ventilation requirements, and the assertion's requirement for balanced supply/exhaust and per-pod design airflow rates may not apply under such exceptions (e.g., certain building codes exempt short-duration occupancy spaces from full mechanical ventilation requirements).

subject: Day-Night Lighting Control
rationale: The day-night control system often communicates with the BMS for monitoring and scheduling.
applicability: The assertion assumes 'in integrated building designs' covers all relevant integration contexts, but many commercial buildings have integrated design yet still use standalone lighting controllers (e.g., astronomical timeclocks or photocell-based systems) that do not connect to the BMS.
conditions: in integrated building designs
exceptions: Day-night lighting control may connect to a dedicated lighting control panel or standalone timeclock rather than the full BMS, especially in smaller commercial buildings or retrofit scenarios where BMS integration is cost-prohibitive.

subject: Structural System
rationale: A structural system requires a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: Direct load transfer path required
exceptions: Temporary structures (e.g., construction shoring, event staging) have a structural system that does not require a permanent foundation—they may use ground bearing or temporary supports.

subject: Structural System
rationale: Columns are primary vertical load-carrying members in most structural systems.
conditions: Multi-story or framed structures
exceptions: Single-story load-bearing wall structures
Space frame or geodesic dome structures can be multi-story without interior columns, using perimeter supports or a single central mast.

Portal frame or rigid frame buildings (e.g., pre-engineered metal buildings) may use moment-resisting frames where columns and beams are combined into a single rigid frame—not requiring distinct columns.

subject: Structural System
rationale: Beams transfer floor and roof loads to columns or walls.
conditions: Structures with floors or roofs spanning between supports
exceptions: Flat slab or flat plate systems

Two-way flat slab systems (already partially covered by the existing flat plate exception) also include waffle slabs with drop panels that distribute loads without beams—this is a broader class than 'flat slab or flat plate'.

subject: Structural System
rationale: Floor and roof slabs provide horizontal surfaces and distribute loads to beams and columns.
conditions: Multi-story buildings requiring floor separation
exceptions: Single-story structures without floors

subject: Structural System
rationale: The structural system supports cladding, roofing, curtain walls, and other envelope components.
conditions: Enclosure attached to structure
exceptions: In buildings with a curtain wall system that is self-supporting (spanning floor-to-floor independently of the structural frame), the structural system does not structurally support the envelope—the curtain wall is attached but not gravity-supported by the primary structure.

subject: Structural System
rationale: The structural system carries the dead load of interior finishes such as suspended ceilings, partitions, and floor toppings.
conditions: Ceilings, partitions, floor finishes attached to structure

subject: Structural System
rationale: The structural system connects to the foundation system at its base to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: All buildings

subject: Main Building Core
rationale: Main building core typically houses elevator shafts for vertical transportation.
applicability: The assertion applies only where accessibility codes (e.g., ADA, IBC Chapter 11) mandate elevator access. Some multi-story commercial buildings may not trigger elevator requirements if they fall below occupant load thresholds or have no public/common areas on upper floors.
conditions: multi-story buildings
accessibility requirements
exceptions: single-story buildings

Even in multi-story buildings with accessibility requirements, an elevator system is not universally required if the building has fewer than a certain number of stories (e.g., 2-3 stories may only need a lift or ramp per IBC) or if the building is exempt under historic preservation rules or certain jurisdictional exceptions.

subject: Main Building Core
rationale: The core depends on fire-rated walls and doors to maintain compartmentation and protect egress paths.
conditions: fire code compliance

subject: Main Building Core
rationale: Core areas require lighting for safe movement and emergency egress illumination.
conditions: occupancy and egress lighting
exceptions: Emergency egress lighting requirements may be satisfied by battery-pack emergency luminaires or exit signs with integral battery backup, not necessarily a full Lighting System. Additionally, occupancy lighting can be provided by natural daylight harvesting systems or task lighting that does not constitute a dedicated building Lighting System.

subject: Main Building Core
rationale: The core often includes the elevator lobby area on each floor.
conditions: multi-tenant buildings
exceptions: single-residence buildings

In multi-tenant commercial buildings, an Elevator Lobby is not required if the building uses an open elevator bank directly opening into tenant spaces without a segregated lobby, or if the building is fully sprinklered and the elevator hoistway is pressurized per IBC Section 3006 exceptions.

subject: Main Building Core
rationale: The core requires fire alarm devices (smoke detectors, pull stations, horns/strobes) for occupant safety.
conditions: code compliance
life safety

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
applicability: The assertion states 'Annex or Wing requires Foundation' but applies to 'All building types with annexes'. The condition says 'When annex is structurally independent', yet structurally independent annexes typically have their own foundation—this is correct. However, the applicability is too broad: structurally dependent annexes (sharing the main building's foundation) would not require a separate foundation, but the condition restricts to structurally independent ones. This conflates the condition with the applicability scope.
conditions: When annex is structurally independent

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing needs a structural frame (steel, concrete, or timber) to provide stability and load-bearing capacity.
exceptions: An annex or wing that is a lightweight, single-story structure (e.g., a small shed, canopy, or pergola attached to a building) may not require a structural frame. Such structures can use load-bearing walls or other simplified structural systems without a distinct frame.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires a roof to provide weather protection and enclosure.
exceptions: Open-air annexes or wings such as uncovered patios, terraces, or courtyards do not require a roof system. The assertion applies to 'All building types with annexes' without any condition for covered vs. uncovered spaces.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing needs exterior walls to define its enclosure and provide thermal and weather protection.
exceptions: Open-air annexes or wings (e.g., uncovered decks, balconies, or loading docks) may not have exterior walls. The applicability to 'All building types with annexes' is too broad without accounting for semi-enclosed or open annex types.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires heating, ventilation, and air conditioning to maintain comfortable indoor environment.
applicability: All conditioned building types with annexes

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires electrical wiring, lighting, and power distribution for functionality.
exceptions: Unconditioned, unoccupied annexes such as simple storage sheds, open parking structures, or utility enclosures may not require an electrical system. The assertion applies unconditionally to 'All building types with annexes' without exception for uninhabited or unpowered spaces.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires plumbing for water supply and drainage if it includes habitable or wet spaces.
conditions: If the annex contains toilets, kitchens, or wet areas
exceptions: Unoccupied storage wings

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires fire alarms, sprinklers, or fire-rated separations for life safety compliance.
conditions: Depending on local building codes and occupancy type

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing functionally depends on the main building for access, circulation, and often shared services.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing depends on expansion or seismic joints to accommodate differential movement between structures.
conditions: When annex is structurally separated from the main building

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing contains internal circulation spaces connecting the rooms within it.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing physically connects to the main building via link bridges, shared walls, or corridors.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires artificial and/or natural lighting for occupant use and safety.
exceptions: Uninhabited, unconditioned annexes such as simple storage sheds, unenclosed loading areas, or open parking wings may not require a lighting system. The assertion applies to 'All building types with annexes' without consideration of occupancy or use.

subject: Annex or Wing
rationale: An annex or wing requires a floor slab to provide a walking surface and support loads.

subject: Connector / Link Structure
rationale: Connector spaces require lighting for safe passage and wayfinding.
applicability: all building types with interior connectors

The assertion requires lighting for 'connectors used at night' but does not define what constitutes 'night' in this context (e.g., astronomical twilight vs civil twilight vs specific time windows). This ambiguity could lead to inconsistent enforcement across jurisdictions.
conditions: for enclosed or covered connectors
for connectors used at night
exceptions: naturally-lit open connectors during daytime only

subject: Connector / Link Structure
rationale: Building codes typically require fire protection (sprinklers, fire-rated construction) in enclosed link structures.
applicability: The assertion references 'when required by building codes' as a condition, which is circular — it effectively says the connector requires fire protection when codes require it. This does not add substantive domain knowledge; it defers entirely to external codes without specifying what the domain deems necessary.
conditions: when the connector is enclosed and part of a building
when required by building codes
exceptions: open-air connectors exempt from sprinkler requirements

subject: Below-Grade Parking Garage
rationale: Below-grade parking garages require mechanical ventilation to remove exhaust fumes and maintain air quality per building codes (IBC/IMC).
conditions: enclosed space with vehicle occupancy
exceptions: naturally ventilated parking garages

The existing exception mentions 'naturally ventilated parking garages' but for below-grade structures, natural ventilation is extremely limited or impossible due to lack of exterior wall exposure. Below-grade garages typically cannot rely on natural ventilation except at ramp openings or at grade-level portions. This exception may be inappropriate or should be more narrowly scoped (e.g., only applies to partially below-grade garages with significant exterior wall openings).

subject: Below-Grade Parking Garage
rationale: Below-grade structures require waterproofing to prevent groundwater intrusion.
