Additionally, security exits in high-security facilities (e.g., prisons, secured government buildings) may use sally ports or mantraps with interlocking doors where the concept of a single 'Door' requirement is ambiguous.

subject: Thoroughfare Exit
rationale: Fire-rated doors maintain compartmentation at exit points.
conditions: When exit is part of a fire-rated wall or separation
exceptions: Exits not in fire-rated walls

subject: Thoroughfare Exit
rationale: A threshold provides a weather seal and transition between floor finishes at the exit.
applicability: The assertion does not specify the type of threshold. Some exterior exits use a simple pan or saddle threshold, while others use recessed or anti-slip thresholds. The requirement is too generic without specifying minimum performance criteria (height, material, weather sealing).
conditions: At exterior exits
exceptions: Thresholds at exterior exits can be omitted in certain accessibility compliance scenarios (ADA/ICC A117.1) where a flush threshold is required for wheelchair access. Additionally, in flood-prone areas, thresholds may be omitted or designed as part of a flood-proofing system rather than as a raised threshold.

subject: Thoroughfare Exit
rationale: A thoroughfare exit typically contains a door leaf that swings in the direction of egress.
exceptions: Openings without doors

Roll-up doors, overhead sectional doors, and accordion/folding doors used as thoroughfare exits (e.g., loading docks, large commercial openings) do not contain a traditional 'Door Leaf' as typically understood, yet are valid exit door assemblies.

subject: Thoroughfare Exit
rationale: The exit assembly contains a door frame that supports the door leaf and hardware.
exceptions: Some thoroughfare exits use door assemblies that are frameless, such as frameless glass doors (all-glass doors with pivot hinges and no visible frame), which do not contain a traditional door frame.

subject: Thoroughfare Exit
rationale: Building codes require a landing on each side of a door at a thoroughfare exit for safe operation and egress.
conditions: On both sides of the exit door
exceptions: In existing buildings or historic structures, landings on both sides of an exit door may be infeasible due to spatial constraints, and some codes (e.g., IBC Section 1008.1.5, 2021 edition) allow for reduced landing dimensions or a single landing on one side in alterations where it is technically infeasible.

Certain exit types such as revolving doors, and some sliding or automatic doors used as exits, may have landing configurations that differ from standard hinged doors, and the generic 'landing on both sides' requirement may not apply to these specialized door types.

subject: Thoroughfare Floor Finish
rationale: A thoroughfare floor finish requires a stable structural substrate (typically a concrete slab) to be installed upon.
applicability: The assertion states that a bonded thoroughfare floor finish requires a structural slab, but bonded finishes can also be applied over existing sound concrete slabs that are not 'structural' in the load-bearing sense (e.g., topping slabs, existing floor slabs not designed as primary structure). The term 'Structural Slab' is ambiguous and may inappropriately exclude bonded toppings over non-structural slabs or existing slabs.
conditions: For installation as a bonded finish
exceptions: Bonded thin-set floor finishes (e.g., epoxy coatings, thin-set tile) can sometimes be applied directly to a properly prepared concrete slab-on-grade without requiring a distinct structural slab — the slab itself serves as both structural and finish substrate. The assertion does not account for monolithic slab scenarios where the structural slab and finish substrate are one and the same.

subject: Thoroughfare Floor Finish
rationale: To accommodate thermal and moisture movement, expansion joints must be detailed through the floor finish.
applicability: The assertion applies to 'large open plan; corridors over 40 ft length; industrial' but does not specify climate or building system context. In buildings with interior climate control and no thermal or moisture gradient, expansion joints in floor finishes may not be required even in large areas if the finish is dimensionally stable (e.g., sheet vinyl, epoxy terrazzo with proper mix design).
conditions: In large floor areas or where structural expansion joints exist
exceptions: Small rooms without structural joints

subject: Thoroughfare Lighting
rationale: The physical light-emitting components are essential.
conditions: including luminaires, lamp housings, and poles

subject: Thoroughfare Ceiling
rationale: Thoroughfare Ceiling depends on electrical rough-in work for embedded lighting, junction boxes, and wiring before ceiling installation.
applicability: The assertion only holds for lighting and power outlets integrated into the ceiling, but electrical rough-in for switches, junction boxes on walls, or floor-mounted outlets in corridor ceilings has no dependency on the thoroughfare ceiling.
conditions: for lighting and power outlets integrated into ceiling
exceptions: In residential buildings with exposed ceilings (e.g., loft-style apartments, basements without finished ceilings), there is no thoroughfare ceiling to depend on electrical rough-in, yet electrical rough-in still occurs for wall/floor outlets and overhead fixtures via other means.

subject: Thoroughfare Ceiling
rationale: Sprinkler systems and their piping are typically installed above the ceiling, requiring coordination with ceiling layout.
conditions: sprinkler heads must penetrate or integrate with ceiling plane
exceptions: buildings not requiring sprinklers

subject: Thoroughfare Ceiling
rationale: The thoroughfare ceiling provides a mounting surface and structural support for lighting fixtures in corridors and passageways.
conditions: fixtures mounted to or suspended from ceiling structure
exceptions: In buildings with exposed structure or no suspended ceiling (e.g., industrial warehouses, parking garages, some retail), lighting fixtures may be mounted directly to the structural deck or trusses, not to a thoroughfare ceiling, yet the ceiling 'supports' claim would be false.

subject: Thoroughfare Ceiling
rationale: Thoroughfare ceiling plenums often contain acoustic insulation batts to reduce sound transmission.
applicability: The existing exception says 'buildings without acoustic requirements', but many commercial buildings have acoustic requirements that are met via other means (e.g., acoustic ceiling tiles without additional insulation, or sound masking systems), meaning the ceiling does not necessarily contain acoustic insulation even when acoustic requirements exist.
conditions: for sound attenuation between floors or along corridor
exceptions: buildings without acoustic requirements

subject: Thoroughfare Ceiling
rationale: The ceiling system incorporates access panels to allow maintenance of valves, dampers, and junction boxes above.
conditions: for maintenance access to above-ceiling equipment
exceptions: In buildings where all above-ceiling equipment is accessible from the space below (e.g., lay-in ceiling tiles that can be removed without dedicated access panels), access panels and hatches may not be present, yet the assertion states the ceiling contains them.

subject: Thoroughfare Signage
rationale: Signage must be legible in low-light conditions; integrated or external lighting is often required.
conditions: if signage is illuminated or required to be visible at night
exceptions: Thoroughfare signage that is non-illuminated and uses retroreflective materials (e.g., high-intensity prismatic sheeting) does not require a lighting system to meet night visibility requirements, as the signage is visible via vehicle headlights. This is a common practice in roadway signage per MUTCD standards.

subject: Thoroughfare Signage
rationale: Thoroughfare signage supports wayfinding by directing people to destinations and along paths.
applicability: campus, hospital, mall, or large building complexes

Thoroughfare signage may support wayfinding even without being part of a formally coordinated wayfinding strategy. In many contexts, standalone directional signage still contributes to wayfinding. The condition 'signage is part of a coordinated wayfinding strategy' is overly restrictive for the assertion that it 'supports' wayfinding.
conditions: signage is part of a coordinated wayfinding strategy

subject: Thoroughfare Signage
rationale: Thoroughfare signage is typically located at decision points along pedestrian pathways, connecting people to the network.
conditions: signage is placed along pedestrian routes
exceptions: Thoroughfare signage placed along pedestrian routes that is oriented toward vehicular traffic (e.g., street name signs on poles facing the roadway) does not meaningfully connect to pedestrian pathways, as it is not designed or positioned for pedestrian-scale visibility.

subject: Thoroughfare Door
rationale: A thoroughfare door requires a frame to be mounted and to operate correctly.
conditions: for structural support and proper alignment
exceptions: Some thoroughfare doors, such as frameless glass doors (e.g., all-glass storefront doors), use pivots and patch fittings mounted directly to the glass without a separate door frame.

subject: Thoroughfare Door
rationale: Hinges are necessary for the door to swing open and closed.
conditions: for swinging operation
exceptions: sliding or revolving doors use alternatives

subject: Thoroughfare Door
rationale: A threshold seals the bottom gap and provides weather protection and a smooth transition.
conditions: at the bottom of the door opening
exceptions: some interior doors may not have a threshold
Even for exterior doors, thresholds may be omitted when doors are recessed with interior floor finishes extended outward, or in weather-protected covered entries with flush sills.

subject: Thoroughfare Door
rationale: Weatherstripping seals gaps to prevent air and water infiltration, depending on climate exposure.
applicability: The applicability is listed as 'exterior doors' but the condition already limits to 'exterior thoroughfare doors exposed to weather,' which suggests the condition is already more restrictive than the stated applicability—doors in sheltered/exterior but weather-protected locations (e.g., covered walkways) may not need weatherstripping.
conditions: for exterior thoroughfare doors exposed to weather
exceptions: interior doors typically do not need weatherstripping

subject: Thoroughfare Door
rationale: The door supports security by controlling access when lockable or integrated with access control.
conditions: when equipped with locks, access control, or alarms
exceptions: unlocked interior doors

A door with a lock does not necessarily support a building security system—standalone locks (e.g., mechanical deadbolts with no wiring, sensors, or network connectivity) do not integrate with or support a building security system.

subject: Thoroughfare Door
rationale: When automated, the door connects to an operator mechanism for powered opening/closing.
conditions: for ADA accessibility or high-traffic applications
exceptions: manual doors do not connect to operators

subject: Thoroughfare Fire Door
rationale: Any glazing in a fire door must be fire-rated to maintain the fire resistance rating.
applicability: The assertion that a Thoroughfare Fire Door requires Fire-Rated Glazing when vision panels are present does not account for doors located in smoke barriers rather than fire barriers, where vision panel glazing requirements may differ (e.g., wired glass vs. fire-rated glazing per NFPA 80 vs. NFPA 105).
conditions: if door includes vision panels
exceptions: solid doors without glazing

In some jurisdictions, fire doors with vision panels located in stairwell enclosures may be permitted to use 20-minute fire-rated glazing in a 20-minute door assembly, but the applicability of this exception depends on the specific fire-resistance rating of the door assembly, which is not addressed.

subject: Thoroughfare Fire Door
rationale: Intumescent seals expand with heat to seal gaps around the door, preventing smoke and fire spread.
conditions: edges of door or frame

subject: Thoroughfare Fire Door
rationale: Electromagnetic hold-open devices release upon fire alarm signal to allow door closure.
conditions: if door has electromagnetic hold-open device
exceptions: manually self-closing doors

The assertion states that a Thoroughfare Fire Door depends_on Fire Alarm System if it has an electromagnetic hold-open device. However, there is an exception where the building uses a local smoke detector directly wired to the hold-open release mechanism without a centralized fire alarm system, which is permitted under some codes (e.g., NFPA 80 allows local release devices).

subject: Thoroughfare Fire Door
rationale: The threshold completes the door assembly at the bottom and controls the gap under the door.
conditions: required to maintain floor-to-door gap limits
exceptions: doors in paths of egress where thresholds may be tripping hazards

subject: Thoroughfare Smoke Control Damper
rationale: The damper integrates with the building fire alarm system for proper response during fire events.
applicability: all buildings with fire/smoke control systems

The assertion states that a Thoroughfare Smoke Control Damper 'requires' a Fire Alarm System, but in many jurisdictions and building types, smoke control dampers may be actuated by a dedicated Smoke Control Panel (SCP) or Building Management System (BMS) rather than directly by the Fire Alarm System. The Fire Alarm System may provide a supervisory signal but not direct actuation control, especially in buildings where the smoke control system is a separate engineered system.
conditions: for coordination and actuation
exceptions: In simple stairwell pressurization or dedicated smoke control systems governed by IBC or NFPA 92, the damper may be actuated by the smoke control panel directly via hardwired inputs from smoke detectors, not by the Fire Alarm System itself. The Fire Alarm System may simply monitor the smoke control system status without direct control over thoroughfare dampers.

subject: Thoroughfare Smoke Control Damper
rationale: The damper is a key component that regulates smoke flow paths, supporting the overall smoke management strategy.
applicability: The assertion states that a Thoroughfare Smoke Control Damper 'supports' a Smoke control system, but thoroughfare dampers are typically passive components (barriers/doors) that are controlled by the smoke control system, not supportive components that provide active functionality. The phrasing implies the damper is a supporting element of the smoke control system, whereas it is more accurately a controlled device within the system.
conditions: during smoke evacuation or containment modes

subject: Thoroughfare Smoke Control Damper
rationale: The damper's actuator connects to the fire alarm system for coordinated response signals.
applicability: The assertion states that a Thoroughfare Smoke Control Damper 'connects_to' a Fire Alarm System, but in standard smoke control system design (NFPA 92, IBC), smoke control dampers are connected to the Smoke Control Panel or Building Automation System, not directly to the Fire Alarm System. The Fire Alarm System may interface with the smoke control system at a higher level (e.g., via a network interface or dry contacts) rather than having a direct point-to-point connection to each damper.
conditions: via control wiring or wireless interface

subject: Thoroughfare Ventilation Grille
rationale: The grille connects via ductwork to the AHU which conditions and moves the air.
conditions: when part of a mechanical HVAC system
exceptions: A thoroughfare ventilation grille may instead connect to a duct leading to the outside (for natural ventilation or smoke exhaust) with no connection to any AHU, even within a mechanical HVAC system. For example, fire/smoke control grilles in corridors often connect to dedicated smoke exhaust shafts and fans, not to the building's AHU.

subject: Thoroughfare Acoustic Treatment
rationale: Thoroughfare Acoustic Treatment typically requires acoustic panels to absorb and dampen sound along travel paths.
conditions: When used for noise absorption
exceptions: In some cases, acoustic treatment uses sound-diffusing elements (e.g., diffusers) rather than absorptive panels, so the requirement for Acoustic Panel does not hold when diffusion is the goal rather than absorption.

subject: Thoroughfare Acoustic Treatment
rationale: Acoustic treatment often connects to HVAC design to prevent noise transmission via ductwork.
applicability: The condition 'Acoustic duct liners or silencers may be integrated' is vague and does not clarify that only those specific acoustic treatments (duct liners, silencers) connect to HVAC, while the broader category of acoustic treatments does not. This could lead to incorrect modeling of unrelated acoustic elements.
conditions: Acoustic duct liners or silencers may be integrated

subject: Thoroughfare Floor Drain
rationale: A waterproofing membrane integrated with the drain flange is required to prevent water from migrating beneath the floor finish and causing structural damage.
applicability: The assertion applies only at the drain-to-floor interface in wet/exterior areas, but a waterproof membrane may also be required under the entire floor assembly (not just at the drain interface) in many code jurisdictions (e.g., IPC, IBC) for wet rooms, showers, and exterior plazas. The current scope may be too narrow if it implies only the drain penetration needs membrane.
conditions: At drain-to-floor interface
In wet areas or exterior applications
exceptions: In some prefabricated trench drain systems with integral flanges and factory-installed waterproofing gaskets, a separate site-installed waterproof membrane at the drain-to-floor interface may not be required per manufacturer specifications and code approvals.

subject: Thoroughfare Baseboard
rationale: Baseboard is fastened to wall framing (studs) for secure attachment.
applicability: The assertion does not specify what constitutes 'Wall Framing' — e.g., wood studs, metal studs, or any vertical structural member. In commercial construction with metal studs, attachment details differ significantly from residential wood framing, and the assertion is ambiguous about whether metal studs satisfy this requirement.
conditions: for attachment along the wall perimeter
exceptions: In retrofit or renovation scenarios, baseboards may be installed over existing drywall or furring strips without direct access to wall framing studs. The assertion does not account for attachment methods such as adhesive-only mounting, which does not require wall framing.

subject: Thoroughfare Baseboard
rationale: Traditional nailing of baseboard may damage radiant heating elements embedded in the floor.
conditions: if nailed directly into floor with long fasteners that could puncture heating tubes
exceptions: can be installed with adhesive or shorter fasteners

subject: Thoroughfare Expansion Joint
rationale: Thoroughfare expansion joints are installed within structural slabs to accommodate movement.
applicability: The assertion states 'Thoroughfare Expansion Joint requires Structural Slab' with applicability including 'industrial floors', but industrial floors (e.g., warehouse slabs) often do not have a separate structural slab — they are typically slab-on-grade where the wearing surface and structural element are one and the same. A thoroughfare expansion joint in such a slab does not require a separate 'Structural Slab' component.
conditions: when used in bridge or parking structure applications
exceptions: In parking structure applications, some expansion joints span between precast double-tee beams where no continuous structural slab exists at the joint location — the joint is placed between adjacent precast members. In such cases, a thoroughfare expansion joint does not require a monolithic structural slab but rather connection details between precast elements.

subject: Thoroughfare Reception Counter
rationale: The counter serves as the physical host point for visitor check-in.
conditions: Software and hardware (badge printer, sign-in kiosk) placed on or near counter

subject: Thoroughfare Gate or Turnstile
rationale: Gates on egress paths must fail-safe (open) upon fire alarm activation to allow free exit, so they depend on the fire alarm for override signals.
applicability: The assertion that a Thoroughfare Gate or Turnstile depends on a Fire Alarm System where gates serve as egress paths may be overbroad. Many jurisdictions require fire alarm system integration only when the gate serves as a component of a required means of egress serving more than a specific occupant load (e.g., 50+ occupants). Additionally, some gates are fail-safe (power-off unlocked) by mechanical design and do not need electrical fire alarm integration at all — the fire alarm dependency is only for electrically locked gates that require signal release. This nuance is not captured.
conditions: where gates serve as egress paths
exceptions: gates not on egress routes

In some jurisdictions (e.g., certain European countries), a manual break-glass release (without full fire alarm system integration) is permitted as an alternative to fire alarm system dependency for turnstiles on egress paths. The assertion implies a mandatory dependency on the fire alarm system itself, whereas a local override mechanism may suffice under certain codes.

subject: Thoroughfare Gate or Turnstile
rationale: For monitoring, logging, and remote management, the turnstile/gate may depend on a BMS interface.
applicability: The assertion states that Thoroughfare Gate or Turnstile depends_on Building Management System (BMS) in integrated smart building deployments. However, many turnstiles have embedded local controllers that manage access control, occupancy counting, and operational logic independently, communicating with a higher-level system via simple API or protocol without true BMS dependency. The turnstile can continue standalone operation even if the BMS is offline, contradicting a 'depends_on' relationship.
conditions: integrated smart building deployments
exceptions: standalone turnstiles without network integration

subject: Thoroughfare Mat Well
rationale: A Thoroughfare Mat Well is a grated trench or channel designed to collect and drain surface water. It requires a connected drainage system to carry water away.
applicability: The assertion does not specify what type of drainage system is required (e.g., surface drainage, subsurface drainage, French drain, catch basin, etc.). The requirement may vary significantly based on the specific design and configuration of the Thoroughfare Mat Well, making the assertion too generic without further contextual detail about the drainage system type or capacity.
conditions: for water removal
exceptions: The assertion claims a Thoroughfare Mat Well always requires a Drainage System for water removal, but there are exceptions where alternative water management approaches may suffice. For example, in well-drained soil conditions (e.g., sandy soils with high permeability), natural percolation may eliminate the need for an engineered drainage system. Additionally, mat wells designed with permeable surfaces or those in elevated locations with natural runoff may not require a dedicated drainage system.

subject: Entry Door
rationale: An entry door requires a frame to be mounted and to function as a proper closure.
conditions: must be structurally sound
exceptions: frameless glass doors

Pocket doors and barn-style sliding doors that serve as entry doors (e.g., in some commercial or modern residential settings) do not have a traditional door frame but rather a header track or pocket mechanism, yet still function as entry doors.

subject: Entry Door
rationale: Hinges are necessary for the door to swing open and closed.
applicability: all building types with hinged doors
conditions: must support door weight

subject: Entry Door
rationale: Weatherstripping seals gaps to prevent air and water infiltration.
conditions: required for energy efficiency and weather seal
exceptions: interior doors not exposed to exterior

Entry doors in unconditioned spaces such as unheated vestibules, sunrooms, or screen porches that are still exterior-facing may not require weatherstripping since the space beyond is not conditioned and energy efficiency is not a concern.

subject: Entry Door
rationale: A threshold provides a finished bottom seal and transition.
conditions: bottom seal needed
exceptions: doors with drop seals

subject: Entry Door
rationale: Entry doors contribute to building envelope insulation.
conditions: if insulated core and proper seals are present
exceptions: non-insulated metal doors

subject: Entrance Lobby
rationale: Adequate lighting is essential for wayfinding, safety, and aesthetic presentation in an entrance lobby.
exceptions: An entrance lobby in a naturally daylit building or a building with no interior pathways beyond the entrance (e.g., a covered walkway lobby in warm climates) may not require an artificial lighting system if ambient daylight provides sufficient illumination. Also, very small or temporary entrance lobbies (e.g., pop-up retail) may not have a dedicated lighting system separate from general building lighting.

subject: Entrance Lobby
rationale: Lobbies often serve as security checkpoints with access control, cameras, or intercoms.
conditions: controlled access building
exceptions: unstaffed public buildings with open access

subject: Entrance Lobby
rationale: The lobby floor depends on the structural slab for load support.
exceptions: In existing buildings undergoing lobby renovation, the entrance lobby may already be supported by an existing structural floor slab, so the dependency is on the existing element rather than a new one. For mezzanine lobbies or lobbies on elevated structures (e.g., sky lobbies in tall buildings), the supporting slab may not be at grade and the dependency might be on a different structural element.

subject: Entrance Lobby
rationale: Lobbies must have fire alarm notification devices as part of life safety systems.
conditions: building code requirement
exceptions: In very small occupancy buildings (e.g., a tiny house or single-room occupancy where the entrance is directly into the living space) there may be no separate 'entrance lobby' to connect to the fire alarm system, or the building code may not require a fire alarm system at all due to low occupancy load.

subject: Entrance Lobby
rationale: Many entrance lobbies contain a reception or concierge desk for visitor management.
conditions: staffed building
exceptions: unstaffed small lobbies

subject: Entrance Lobby
rationale: The entrance lobby typically connects directly to the elevator bank for vertical circulation.
conditions: multi-story building
exceptions: single-story buildings

subject: Door Hardware Set
rationale: Door hardware sets are physically mounted on doors; without a door there is no substrate for installation.
conditions: Functioning door operation depends on hardware being mounted on the door leaf
exceptions: Sliding door hardware (e.g., bypass door hardware, pocket door hardware) can be mounted to the header or floor track rather than directly on the door leaf, so the condition 'hardware being mounted on the door leaf' is not universally true.

subject: Door Hardware Set
rationale: Door frames provide the structural support for hinges, strike plates, and closers.
conditions: Hardware such as hinges, strikes, and closers require a rigid frame for anchorage
exceptions: Some door hardware sets for sliding or folding doors use floor-mounted or overhead-track-mounted strikes and guides, and do not require a traditional door frame for anchorage.

subject: Door Hardware Set
rationale: Door closers are often included in a complete hardware set for automatic closure.
conditions: Applicable to fire-rated doors, exterior doors, or heavy-traffic interior doors

subject: Door Hardware Set
rationale: Electronic door hardware connects to building access control networks for remote locking/unlocking and monitoring.
applicability: Not all electronic or smart locking hardware connects to a building-wide Access Control System. Many smart locks operate standalone via Bluetooth/WiFi (e.g., residential smart locks) without integration into a centralized access control system.
conditions: Electronic or smart locking hardware is used

subject: Door Hardware Set
rationale: Fire-rated door hardware (e.g., magnetic hold-opens) interfaces with the fire alarm to release doors upon alarm.
applicability: Electromagnetic door holders are used in fire-rated assemblies for hold-open functions, but not all electromagnetic door holders are connected to the building Fire Alarm System — some are triggered by local smoke detectors or are self-contained units without fire alarm integration.
conditions: Electromagnetic door holders are used in fire-rated assemblies

subject: Entrance Canopy
rationale: The canopy structure often supports integrated downlights, pendant lights, or strip lighting for the entrance area.
conditions: When integrated canopy lighting is specified
exceptions: Canopies without integrated lighting

subject: Entrance Canopy
rationale: Canopy roofs can serve as rainwater collection surfaces if properly configured.
applicability: The assertion applies only to 'sustainable/green buildings' but rainwater harvesting from a canopy requires local rainfall data and code compliance for non-potable water systems, which varies by jurisdiction. Additionally, some building codes prohibit rainwater collection from certain roof/canopy materials (e.g., those containing lead flashings or certain treated surfaces). This context is missing.
conditions: When designed with collection gutters and downspouts connected to storage
exceptions: Standard canopies without harvesting integration

subject: Entrance Mat/Grid
rationale: Entrance grids designed to capture water and mud require an underlying drainage system to channel water away.
conditions: When used as a water/dirt collection mat at exterior entrances
exceptions: Interior-only dry mats may not require drainage

Many modern entrance mat/grid systems (e.g., dry-scrape or built-in recessed grid systems with integral drainage channels or self-draining bases) incorporate drainage into the mat assembly itself and do not require a separate building drainage system. The assertion as stated implies a separate drainage system is always needed, which is not accurate.

subject: Entrance Mat/Grid
rationale: For effective removal of water captured by the mat, a floor drain beneath or near the mat is typically needed.
conditions: When mat is used in wet entrance areas

subject: Entrance Mat/Grid
rationale: Entrance mats are a key component of the entry vestibule system, working with doors and weatherstripping to create a clean transition.
conditions: When installed as part of an entryway system

subject: Entrance Mat/Grid
rationale: The entrance mat/grid sits adjacent to or integrates with the door threshold to provide a continuous surface from exterior to interior.
conditions: Always

subject: Entrance Signage
rationale: External or internal lighting may be required for sign legibility in low-light conditions.
applicability: The dependency on a Lighting System may be more accurately scoped to only electrically illuminated entrance signage. The current wording implies all entrance signage in those building types depends on a lighting system, which is an overgeneralization particularly for architecturally integrated signs that rely on natural or reflected light.
conditions: For nighttime visibility or backlit signage
exceptions: Naturally lit or daytime-only signage

subject: Entrance Signage
rationale: Entrance signage helps visitors and occupants identify where to enter a building, supporting overall wayfinding.
applicability: The assertion states Entrance Signage supports Wayfinding System as a primary identifier of the building entry point for all building types. However, in multi-tenant commercial buildings, large campuses, or healthcare facilities, the entrance signage may serve as a secondary or tertiary wayfinding element rather than the primary identifier, as those contexts may rely more on directory signage, numbering systems, or color-coded paths for primary wayfinding.
conditions: As a primary identifier of the building entry point
exceptions: In residential building types (e.g., apartment buildings, condominiums), entrance signage sometimes identifies the building name but is not always part of a formal Wayfinding System, and thus the 'supports' relationship may not universally apply. The assertion claims 'all building types' applicability.

subject: Weather Stripping
rationale: Weather stripping helps maintain the building envelope's air barrier integrity.
conditions: when properly installed and maintained
exceptions: Weather stripping loses its effectiveness if the window or door it is applied to is structurally compromised (warped, rotted, or misaligned), and thus does not support the envelope in such cases regardless of proper installation and maintenance of the stripping itself.

subject: Weather Stripping
rationale: Weather stripping is installed on operable windows to seal the moving parts.
conditions: at the sash-to-frame interface

subject: Weather Stripping
rationale: Weather stripping is installed around door perimeters.
applicability: Weather stripping connects to a door at the door-to-frame and door-to-threshold interfaces only for operable doors. For fixed doors or non-operable door panels (e.g., fixed sidelights), weather stripping may not be present or functional at all interfaces listed.
conditions: at the door-to-frame and door-to-threshold interfaces

subject: Hardware Fitting
rationale: Hardware fittings such as hinges, handles, and locks enable doors to operate and be secured.
conditions: When hinges and handles are installed on doors

subject: Hardware Fitting
rationale: Window hardware fittings support the opening, closing, and locking of window assemblies.
conditions: When hinges, stays, or locks are installed on windows

subject: Intercom/Entry Phone
rationale: An intercom/entry phone often serves as the front-end user interface for an access control system, enabling communication and verification before granting entry.
applicability: The assertion states 'Intercom/Entry Phone supports Access Control System', but the specified conditions (integration with card readers, keypads, or biometric scanners) describe the intercom being used as a component within an access control system, not the intercom itself supporting the system. This is a framing issue — the intercom is an endpoint/interface, not the system that manages access decisions.
conditions: When integrated with card readers, keypads, or biometric scanners
exceptions: Standalone intercom without access control integration

Many modern IP-based intercoms (e.g., 2N, Aiphone, Comelit) have built-in access control capabilities such as onboard relay outputs for door strikes and Wiegand inputs for readers, meaning they can act as standalone access controllers without a separate ACS. The existing exception incorrectly implies that a standalone intercom cannot perform access control, when in fact many can.

subject: Entrance Threshold
rationale: The entrance threshold is typically mounted on or anchored to the door frame or subfloor to provide a transition between flooring surfaces.
conditions: When entrance threshold is part of a door assembly
exceptions: In barrier-free/accessible design (e.g., ADA-compliant entrances), thresholds are often minimized or eliminated altogether to allow wheelchair access, meaning the threshold does not depend on a door frame in the conventional sense — it may be a flush transition strip or a very low-profile threshold that is not structurally tied to a frame.

subject: Entrance Threshold
rationale: The threshold provides a bearing surface for the bottom edge of the door leaf, supporting it when closed and aiding in alignment.
applicability: Hinged doors in all building types
conditions: When door is closed, threshold provides support and sealing surface for bottom of door
exceptions: Sliding doors or overhead doors may not rest directly on a threshold in the same manner

Double-action or swing doors (e.g., in commercial kitchens) often have a gap at the bottom and no threshold contact — the door leaf swings freely and does not use the threshold as a support or sealing surface.

In fire-rated door assemblies, intumescent seals at the bottom edge may provide the sealing surface, and the door leaf is not designed to rest on the threshold for sealing — the threshold gap is maintained for fire-rating compliance.

subject: Paving Surface
rationale: Edge restraints prevent paving units from shifting at edges
conditions: Required for flexible pavers and unit paving to prevent lateral movement
exceptions: Monolithic concrete paving does not require edge restraints

Edge restraint is not required for asphalt paving surfaces (flexible pavement) that are thick enough or have confined edges against curbs or structures; existing exception only covers monolithic concrete but omits this common case.

subject: Paving Surface
rationale: Proper drainage prevents water damage, frost heave, and surface deterioration
conditions: Required to prevent water accumulation on or beneath paving surface
exceptions: Permeable paving designed for water infiltration may substitute

subject: Paving Surface
rationale: Proper subgrade is fundamental to prevent settlement and ensure longevity
applicability: The assertion does not account for paving directly over existing concrete slabs or asphalt overlays where subgrade preparation is neither feasible nor necessary since the existing base serves as the subgrade.
conditions: Soil must be compacted and graded before paving installation
exceptions: Stable undisturbed native soil may require minimal preparation

subject: Wheel Stop
rationale: Wheel stops can act as barriers to protect pedestrian areas from vehicle overhang.
applicability: Wheel stops are only effective if the parking row is perpendicular or angled such that a vehicle would stop before the wheel stop; in parallel parking configurations, wheel stops do not serve the same protective function for adjacent walkways.
conditions: Wheel stops placed at ends of parking rows can prevent vehicle encroachment onto walkways
exceptions: Wheel stops can actually become tripping hazards themselves for pedestrians, especially for individuals with mobility impairments or in low-light conditions, creating a safety problem rather than solely providing protection.

subject: Parking Stall Striping
rationale: Striping and signage together form a cohesive parking guidance system; striping lines lead to and align with signs.
applicability: The applicability states 'all parking facilities', but this connection may not apply to automated or robotic parking garages where there is no visible striping on the driving/stall surfaces and signage follows a different (often digital) system. In such facilities, physical striping does not coordinate with signage in the same way.
conditions: striping layout coordinates with sign placement for stalls and aisles

subject: Parking Lot Lighting
rationale: Fixtures are the primary hardware emitting light.
applicability: The conditions specify 'Weather-resistant, rated for outdoor use,' but different climate zones (e.g., extreme cold, hurricane-prone, desert heat) have additional specific rating requirements such as IP ratings, wind load ratings, or temperature ratings that are not captured. This could lead to specification of fixtures that are not suitable for the actual environment.
conditions: Weather-resistant, rated for outdoor use
exceptions: Parking lot lighting may use light poles or bollards that integrate the light source and fixture into a single assembly, where the 'lighting fixture' as a separately field-installed component does not exist. Examples include integrated LED pole lights where the fixture is not separately identifiable or replaceable.

subject: Entry and Exit Driveways
rationale: At driveway crossings, the driveway connects to or intersects with pedestrian walkways, often requiring marked crossings.
applicability: The assertion states that driveways 'connects_to Pedestrian Walkway' where the driveway crosses a sidewalk, but this conflates 'sidewalk' with 'pedestrian walkway.' A sidewalk is typically a pedestrian walkway, but not all pedestrian walkways are sidewalks (e.g., elevated walkways, paths through plazas or parks may not be crossed by driveways). The condition 'where driveway crosses a sidewalk' is more specific than the asserted connection to 'Pedestrian Walkway' generally.
conditions: where driveway crosses a sidewalk
exceptions: In some jurisdictions, when a driveway crosses a sidewalk there is no direct connection — the driveway simply passes beneath or across the sidewalk grade without any formal junction or walkway connection. Additionally, gated or private driveways that cross a sidewalk may not have a pedestrian walkway connection at all, as the sidewalk may be on public right-of-way while the driveway is private.

subject: Entry and Exit Driveways
rationale: Signage identifying entry/exit points, directional arrows, and speed limits supports safe traffic flow.
conditions: commercial or multi-tenant sites

subject: Parking Lot Landscaping
rationale: Parking lot landscaping requires proper drainage to prevent water damage to plants and pavement.
applicability: The applicability says 'all parking lots' but the assertion is only relevant for parking lots with landscaping (vegetation, permeable surfaces, etc.). A paved parking lot with no landscaping does not require a drainage system specifically for landscaping purposes (it may still need drainage for stormwater, but that is a separate requirement).
conditions: to prevent water pooling
exceptions: In some jurisdictions, stormwater drainage for parking lots is managed via municipal systems or green infrastructure allowances that may not require a dedicated on-site drainage system if runoff is directed to approved municipal storm drains or if permeable paving eliminates the need for a separate drainage system.

subject: Parking Lot Landscaping
rationale: Landscaped areas in parking lots need irrigation to maintain plant health.
conditions: in areas with insufficient rainfall

subject: Parking Barrier or Gate
rationale: Fixed parking barriers and gate posts require a concrete foundation or anchoring system for structural stability.
conditions: for fixed/stationary barriers
exceptions: temporary/movable barriers may not require a permanent foundation

subject: Parking Barrier or Gate
rationale: The barrier physically enforces the access control decisions made by the access management system.
applicability: The assertion assumes the barrier/gate is powered and has a control board capable of interfacing with external access control. Some electromechanical gates require additional controllers or relays to be integrated, meaning the barrier itself does not directly 'support' the system.
conditions: when integrated with ticketing or card readers
exceptions: Some parking barriers and gates (e.g., simple manual lift gates, basic security arms) do not support access control systems even in paid or secured parking facilities.

subject: Pay Station / Ticket Kiosk
rationale: Pay stations often support access control by validating payment and issuing tickets that allow entry or exit through gates.
conditions: integrated entry/exit gates
exceptions: pay-on-foot systems without gates

The assertion claims the kiosk supports Access Control System, but many pay station/kiosk installations operate as standalone units that only issue tickets or process payments without any integration to an access control system (e.g., simple parking meters or transit fare vending machines that do not control gates). This is not just an exception but a common deployment scenario.

subject: Pay Station / Ticket Kiosk
rationale: Users must be able to find the pay station; signage directing them to the kiosk is important for usability.
applicability: large facilities, parking structures, transit hubs
conditions: user needs to locate the kiosk
exceptions: single-entry points with obvious kiosk placement

subject: Pay Station / Ticket Kiosk
rationale: The pay station may connect to a BMS for remote monitoring of status, alarms, cash levels, and operational data.
conditions: integrated facility monitoring
exceptions: standalone unmonitored kiosks

subject: Electric Vehicle Charging Station
rationale: Smart charging stations can connect to BMS for load shedding, energy optimization, and monitoring.
conditions: When configured for load management and energy monitoring
exceptions: Simple standalone chargers may not connect to BMS

Some EV charging stations that are 'OCPP-capable' and configured for load management may connect to a Central Management System (CMS) or Charge Management System (CSMS) via cloud, rather than directly to a local Building Management System (BMS). In such cases, the charger connects to the CMS and the CMS may or may not interface with the BMS. This architectural pattern (cloud-mediated load management) is an exception where the direct 'connects_to BMS' assertion does not hold.

subject: Parking Lot Bicycle Rack
rationale: Parking lot bicycle racks are typically anchored to concrete foundations or asphalt to prevent tipping
conditions: for freestanding racks
when installed on unpaved surfaces
exceptions: There is an exception for racks that are designed to be portable or temporary (e.g., bicycle corrals, movable bike racks used for events), which do not require any concrete foundation regardless of surface type. These racks rely on weight or surface-mounted brackets only.

subject: Asphalt Paving Installation
rationale: Asphalt paving installation requires a properly prepared subgrade (compacted and graded soil base) to provide structural support and prevent settlement.
applicability: In some cases (e.g., permeable asphalt or porous pavement installations), subgrade preparation requirements differ significantly from conventional asphalt — proper drainage and specific base layers may be required that go beyond simple compaction and grading.
conditions: Proper compaction and grading of subgrade required
exceptions: Asphalt overlays (resurfacing) over existing asphalt pavement do not require new subgrade preparation — the existing pavement serves as the base. This is a common exception where subgrade preparation is not performed.

subject: Concrete Curb and Gutter Installation
rationale: Steel reinforcement provides tensile strength to concrete curbs and gutters, preventing cracking.
conditions: when structural reinforcement is specified
for longer curb runs
exceptions: Concrete curb and gutter does not always require rebar. Many residential and light commercial installations use plain concrete (unreinforced) curb and gutter, particularly for shorter runs, low-traffic areas, or when soil conditions are adequate and local codes do not mandate reinforcement. The assertion states rebar is required, but the conditions ('when structural reinforcement is specified; for longer curb runs') actually describe when rebar is used, contradicting the unconditional 'requires' language.

subject: Accessible Parking Space Compliance
rationale: An accessible route connecting the accessible parking to the building entrance is mandatory.
conditions: from parking to building entrance
minimum clear width
firm, stable, slip-resistant surface

subject: Accessible Parking Space Compliance
rationale: Accessible parking space compliance encompasses the individual accessible parking spaces themselves.
conditions: designated for individuals with disabilities

subject: Parking Lot Base and Sub-base
rationale: Geotextile fabric separates subgrade from base material and improves load distribution.
conditions: When subgrade soil is weak or has high moisture content
exceptions: May not be needed on well-draining, stable subgrades

On subgrades with very high plasticity index (e.g., expansive clays), geotextile fabric alone may be insufficient; a geogrid or thicker aggregate separation layer is typically required instead of or in addition to fabric.

subject: Parking Lot Base and Sub-base
rationale: Proper drainage prevents base and sub-base saturation which leads to failure.
applicability: The assertion says 'requires Drainage System' for all parking lot types, but in arid climates with well-draining granular subgrades and permeable base materials, water accumulation is not a concern and a formal drainage system (pipes, drains) may be unnecessary; surface runoff provisions may suffice.
conditions: Must prevent water accumulation in base layers

subject: Parking Lot Base and Sub-base
rationale: Base and sub-base tie into adjacent curb and gutter drainage systems.
conditions: At parking lot perimeter

subject: Cut and Fill
rationale: Topsoil must be stripped and stockpiled before cut/fill operations to preserve fertile soil for later landscaping.
applicability: all projects involving Cut and Fill
conditions: where topsoil is present
exceptions: Cut and Fill does not require topsoil stripping in areas where topsoil was previously removed (e.g., brownfield sites, previously graded lots) or where no topsoil exists (e.g., cut into bedrock). The assertion already conditions on 'where topsoil is present' which partially addresses this, but the statement 'requires Topsoil Stripping' is still too absolute even with that condition — if topsoil is present but the fill material is clean granular fill, stripping may not be necessary if the topsoil is thin or will be incorporated into landscaping.

subject: Cut and Fill
rationale: Proper drainage is critical to prevent erosion of cut slopes and saturation of fill, which could cause instability.
applicability: all projects involving Cut and Fill

The assertion states Cut and Fill 'depends_on Drainage System' for all projects, but for small-scale Cut and Fill operations on well-draining sites with no groundwater concerns, a formal engineered drainage system may not be required — simple surface grading or swales may suffice instead. The dependency on a designed Drainage System is context-dependent on site hydrology, not universal.
conditions: to manage surface and subsurface water during and after earthwork

subject: Cut and Fill
rationale: Cut and Fill creates a stable, level platform on which foundations can be constructed.
conditions: after compaction and achieving design bearing capacity

subject: Cut and Fill
rationale: The graded and compacted earth platform directly supports the building superstructure loads.
conditions: after achieving required subgrade stability

subject: Cut and Fill
rationale: Geotextiles may be placed within fill layers for separation, filtration, or reinforcement.
applicability: projects with poor subgrade or layered fills
conditions: when separating different soil types or for stabilization
exceptions: Cut and Fill does not always 'contain' Geotextile Fabric even when separating different soil types. In many jurisdictions and standard practice, granular filter layers (e.g., graded sand and gravel filters) can be used instead of geotextile fabric for soil separation and stabilization. Geotextile is an option, not a mandatory component.

subject: Subgrade Preparation and Compaction
rationale: Fill must be placed and compacted in thin, uniform lifts to achieve uniform density.
applicability: The assertion states Subgrade Preparation and Compaction requires Lift Thickness Control, but this is only applicable when using materials that can be compacted in lifts (e.g., granular soils, engineered fill). It does not apply to native subgrade preparation where no fill is being placed—only grading and compaction of in-situ soil occurs. The condition 'when placing fill material in layers' partially addresses this, but the phrasing 'Subgrade Preparation and Compaction requires Lift Thickness Control' is overly broad for cases where only in-situ subgrade compaction is performed without fill lifts.
conditions: when placing fill material in layers

subject: Subgrade Preparation and Compaction
rationale: Properly prepared and compacted subgrade provides uniform support for footings and slabs.
applicability: Subgrade Preparation and Compaction supports Foundation System as a load-bearing base, but this does not apply when the foundation system is deep (e.g., piles, caissons) that bypass the subgrade layer entirely to bear on deeper strata. In such cases, the subgrade preparation and compaction at the surface does not structurally support the foundation system.
conditions: as load-bearing base

subject: Subgrade Preparation and Compaction
rationale: Compacted subgrade is the direct base for concrete slabs on grade.
conditions: directly beneath slab

subject: Subgrade Preparation and Compaction
rationale: Geotextiles may be placed within the subgrade for separation, filtration, or reinforcement.
applicability: The assertion states Subgrade Preparation and Compaction contains Geotextile Fabric when subgrade soil is weak or unstable, but geotextile fabric is typically placed on top of the prepared subgrade before the base course, not 'contained within' the subgrade preparation and compaction itself. Additionally, in many cases geotextile is used not just for weak soil but also for separation (preventing base material from mixing with subgrade) even when the subgrade is not particularly weak, and for drainage control. The wording 'contains' is also imprecise—geotextile is a separate layer, not a component contained within the subgrade.
conditions: when subgrade soil is weak or unstable
exceptions: not required on stable native soils

subject: Subgrade Preparation and Compaction
rationale: Proof rolling identifies soft spots or inadequate compaction areas.
conditions: to verify subgrade uniformity before placing base/slab
exceptions: small residential work may omit

subject: Imported Fill Material
rationale: Imported granular fill provides a uniform, stable sub-base for concrete slabs.
conditions: when used as sub-base under slabs
exceptions: If imported fill material contains expansive soils (e.g., high shrink-swell clays), it can cause heave and damage to slab-on-grade, making it unsuitable despite being used as sub-base.

subject: Geotextile and Geogrid
rationale: Anchoring trenches are often needed at edges of geotextile/geogrid installations.
conditions: For edge anchoring and tensioning applications

subject: Geotextile and Geogrid
rationale: Geotextiles can function as drainage filters, connecting to pipe drainage systems.
conditions: When used as drainage geocomposites or filter fabrics

subject: Soil Amendment and Stabilization
rationale: Stabilized soil provides enhanced bearing capacity and reduced settlement for shallow foundations.
conditions: When soil is improved to adequate bearing capacity
exceptions: When foundations are deep-piled to bypass poor soil

The assertion does not hold for organic or highly compressible soils (e.g., peat) where amendment and stabilization techniques (cement/lime mixing, mechanical compaction) are ineffective or provide insufficient improvement. In such cases, deep foundations or soil replacement are required regardless of soil improvement attempts, so amendment does not provide adequate bearing capacity support for the foundation system.

subject: Soil Amendment and Stabilization
rationale: Proper drainage is essential to prevent water accumulation that could compromise stabilized soil performance.
applicability: The assertion claims soil amendment/stabilization 'connects_to' Drainage System, but this is a non-physical/indirect relationship. Soil stabilization is a geotechnical improvement that does not have a physical pipe or flow connection to the drainage system. The relationship is more accurately described as 'interacts_with' or 'influences' rather than a physical 'connects_to' relationship that implies a direct pipe, conduit, or flow path.
conditions: For effective long-term performance of stabilized soils

subject: Backfill and Compaction Around Foundations
rationale: Backfill and compaction occurs around foundation walls; the walls must be in place and structurally ready to receive lateral loads from compacted soil.
applicability: all building types with basements or deep foundations
conditions: prior to backfill
need to be properly cured
exceptions: The assertion states backfill and compaction 'depends_on Foundation Wall' and requires proper curing prior to backfill. However, in cases where foundation walls are waterproofed with rigid insulation boards, drainage boards, or protection board systems (e.g., Delta membranes, rigid XPS insulation), backfilling must often occur after these systems are installed and cured/adhered — not just after the concrete wall cures. The dependency chain omits waterproofing/protection layers.

subject: Backfill and Compaction Around Foundations
rationale: Backfill must be placed in thin, uniform lifts and compacted each layer to prevent differential settlement and achieve uniform density.
conditions: typically 6-12 inch lifts depending on equipment
exceptions: The assertion states backfill and compaction 'requires Lift Thickness Control', but in certain applications such as flowable fill (controlled low-strength material, CLSM) used as backfill, lift thickness control is not applicable because the material self-levels and does not require mechanical compaction in lifts. This is a common alternative backfill method around foundations.

subject: South-Facing Terrace
rationale: The terrace requires a structural floor slab capable of supporting people, furniture, and weather loads.
applicability: The assertion assumes the terrace is at grade or elevated but accessible. In some climates or building codes, a 'South-Facing Terrace' may be classified as a balcony, rooftop deck, or porch, each with different live load requirements (e.g., 1.5 kN/m² vs 4.79 kN/m²). The condition does not account for this variability across jurisdictions.
conditions: must be designed for live load of outdoor occupancy
exceptions: In roof-level or unoccupiable terrace scenarios, the terrace may be designed for snow load or maintenance-only load rather than full outdoor occupancy live load, meaning the structural slab does not always need to be designed for outdoor occupancy live load.

subject: South-Facing Terrace
rationale: Critical to prevent water ingress into the structure below.
conditions: applied beneath terrace flooring
exceptions: In some construction systems (e.g., green roofs, inverted roof membranes, or certain modern adhered systems), the waterproof membrane may be placed above or within insulation layers rather than 'beneath terrace flooring' directly. The condition 'applied beneath terrace flooring' is an overspecification that does not cover all valid waterproofing strategies.

subject: South-Facing Terrace
rationale: Proper drainage prevents ponding, leakage, and structural damage.
conditions: including slope-to-drain and scuppers or drains
exceptions: In terraces with a continuous membrane drainage system (e.g., protected membrane roofs using drainage boards and geotextile layers), traditional scuppers or drains may not be present; instead, drainage occurs through the insulation layer to a concealed drainage mat, without slope-to-drain in the conventional sense. The condition 'including slope-to-drain and scuppers or drains' is not universally required.

subject: South-Facing Balcony
rationale: A waterproof membrane is required on the balcony floor to prevent water ingress into the structure below.
conditions: under balcony floor
exceptions: In warm/dry climates (e.g., arid regions), a south-facing balcony may not require a waterproof membrane if it is designed as a drained, non-sealed deck with appropriate fall and drainage, or if it is a rooftop with alternative waterproofing strategies. The assertion has no climate condition and would be over-applied.

subject: South-Facing Balcony
rationale: A thermal break prevents thermal bridging through the concrete slab, reducing heat loss and condensation risk.
applicability: The assertion only applies to cantilevered concrete slab balconies. Other south-facing balcony constructions (e.g., supported by columns, suspended steel frame, or bolt-on prefabricated units) do not necessarily require a thermal break, even in cold climates, because they do not create a direct thermal bridge through the slab.
conditions: in cold climates
if balcony is cantilevered concrete slab

subject: South-Facing Balcony
rationale: A south-facing balcony provides an outdoor space suitable for seating, dining, or lounging.
conditions: when furnished appropriately

subject: South-Facing Roof Terrace
rationale: A south-facing roof terrace is exposed to rain and snow; waterproofing is essential to prevent leaks into the structure below.
applicability: The assertion specifies 'UV-resistant' as a condition, but on a roof terrace that will have decking, tiles, or planters covering the membrane, UV resistance is not necessary for covered portions — only exposed areas need UV protection. The condition should account for whether the membrane is exposed or covered.
conditions: must be continuous
must be UV-resistant
exceptions: A green roof (vegetated roof terrace) typically requires a root-resistant waterproof membrane, not just a UV-resistant one. Standard UV-resistant membranes may be degraded by root penetration. A separate root barrier is often needed.

subject: South-Facing Roof Terrace
rationale: Standing water on a roof terrace can cause structural loading and leaks; drainage is critical for long-term performance.
conditions: must have proper slope
must include scuppers or drains
exceptions: A South-Facing Roof Terrace in a locale with very low rainfall (e.g., desert climate) may not require a drainage system with scuppers or drains — a simple graded surface to shed minimal rain may suffice. The assertion overgeneralizes to 'all building types' without considering climate exceptions.

subject: South-Facing Roof Terrace
rationale: Thermal insulation is needed to separate the exterior terrace from interior conditioned spaces below.
conditions: must be rigid insulation suitable for roofing
R-value depends on climate zone

subject: South-Facing Roof Terrace
rationale: The terrace provides a usable outdoor space for occupants to sit, relax, or dine.
applicability: The assertion that a South-Facing Roof Terrace 'supports' an Outdoor Seating Area does not specify structural loading requirements. A roof terrace may require additional structural reinforcement to support the live loads of an outdoor seating area (especially for hospitality/commercial use with dense occupancy and furniture), which is a critical dependency not captured.

subject: South-Facing Roof Terrace
rationale: Edge detailing with flashing prevents water intrusion at the roof edge where the terrace meets the parapet.
conditions: must be integrated with parapet
lapped properly to shed water
exceptions: On a South-Facing Roof Terrace with a fully adhered or fluid-applied membrane system that terminates at a curb rather than a parapet, perimeter flashing integrated with a parapet may not be applicable. The assertion assumes a parapet condition which does not apply to all roof terrace edge conditions.

subject: South-Facing Veranda
rationale: Lighting is commonly integrated into the veranda ceiling or walls for nighttime usability.
applicability: In jurisdictions with strict dark-sky ordinances (e.g., Arizona, Chile, Hawaii), outdoor lighting fixtures on verandas may be prohibited, heavily restricted, or require shielding, contradicting the assertion that the veranda 'contains' such fixtures as a default element.
conditions: for evening use and ambiance
exceptions: South-facing verandas in very high latitude regions (e.g., above 60°N) may receive near-constant summer daylight (midnight sun), making outdoor lighting unnecessary for evening use during several months of the year.

subject: South-Facing Glazed Screen
rationale: A glazed screen requires glazing panels as the primary transparent or translucent material to form the screen surface.
applicability: All building types using glazed screens
conditions: Must be thermally efficient
Must be appropriately sized for structural support
exceptions: There are exceptions where a South-Facing Glazed Screen may use spandrel glass, opaque panels, or non-vision glass areas that do not function as glazing panels but still form part of the screen assembly, particularly in curtain wall systems where vision glass and spandrel panels alternate.

subject: South-Facing Railing System
rationale: A handrail is the top gripping element of a railing system.

subject: South-Facing Outdoor Drainage System
rationale: Gutters channel rainwater from the roof edge to downpipes; a south-facing system collects from south-facing roof edges.
applicability: The assertion states that a South-Facing Outdoor Drainage System 'requires' a Gutter System when roof drainage is integrated, but many modern drainage solutions (e.g., French drains, channel drains, or surface grading systems) handle roof runoff without traditional gutters, e.g., via rain chains, permeable paving, or dispersed drainage fields. The 'requires' relationship is too strong; gutters are one option, not a universal requirement.
conditions: When roof drainage is integrated

subject: South-Facing Outdoor Drainage System
rationale: A south-facing drainage system can feed into cisterns or tanks for rainwater collection and reuse.
applicability: The assertion says a South-Facing Outdoor Drainage System 'connects_to' a Rainwater harvesting system when designed for water reuse, but in many jurisdictions (e.g., parts of the US, EU), rainwater harvesting systems must collect from roof gutters/downspouts, not from ground-level drainage systems, due to contamination concerns (pesticides, animal waste, sediments). Ground-level drainage water is often classified as stormwater, not suitable for rainwater harvesting without significant treatment.
conditions: When designed for water reuse

subject: Construction of South-Facing Terrace
rationale: Waterproofing is essential to prevent moisture ingress into the structure below when a south-facing terrace is built above interior spaces.
conditions: If terrace is above habitable space
If terrace is on a roof

subject: Construction of South-Facing Terrace
rationale: Proper drainage (scuppers, drains, sloping) is required to avoid ponding water and structural damage.
conditions: To prevent water accumulation

subject: Construction of South-Facing Terrace
rationale: The terrace structure (if cantilevered or with an overhang) can protect exterior walls from direct rain and sun exposure.
conditions: If terrace provides overhang or shading

subject: Construction of South-Facing Terrace
rationale: A terrace contains expansion joints to accommodate thermal movement and prevent cracking.

subject: Installation of South-Facing Balcony
rationale: Waterproofing prevents water intrusion into the building structure below the balcony.
conditions: Must be applied to balcony deck substrate
exceptions: Covered/glazed balconies with drainage

The existing exception mentions 'Covered/glazed balconies with drainage' but does not account for balconies with integrated waterproof deck coatings (e.g., liquid-applied membranes, sheet membranes) that can serve as the waterproofing layer themselves, potentially removing the need for a separate waterproof membrane installation. This is a missing exception.

subject: Installation of South-Facing Balcony
rationale: Proper drainage (floor drains, scuppers, gutters) prevents standing water and leakage.
conditions: Slope of deck must direct water to drains or scuppers
exceptions: There is no existing exception for balconies with integrated planter or green roof systems where drainage is handled by the planting medium and drainage board rather than conventional drains or scuppers directed by deck slope. Such systems may still provide adequate drainage without meeting the condition as stated.

subject: Installation of South-Facing Balcony
rationale: To prevent thermal bridging, insulation is needed where the balcony slab extends from the interior floor.
conditions: In conditioned buildings, thermal break required at slab edge
exceptions: Unconditioned buildings or mild climates

subject: Installation of South-Facing Balcony
rationale: Lighting fixtures are installed as part of the balcony for safety and usability.
conditions: Typically required for egress and nighttime use

subject: Installation of South-Facing Balcony
rationale: The floor finish (tile, wood, composite decking) is part of the balcony assembly.
conditions: Must be durable, slip-resistant, and weather-resistant

subject: Roof Terrace
rationale: A roof terrace is an exposed horizontal surface; waterproofing is essential to prevent water damage to the structure below.
conditions: to prevent water ingress
exceptions: Green roofs or vegetated roof terraces may use a different waterproofing strategy (e.g., root barrier + drainage composite) that is not a conventional waterproof membrane; some extensive green roof systems rely on the growing medium and drainage layer rather than a dedicated waterproof membrane.

subject: Roof Terrace
rationale: Proper drainage (scuppers, drains, gutters) is needed to prevent ponding water and structural overload.
conditions: to manage rainwater and runoff
exceptions: Small roof terraces using permeable paving or gravel finishes that allow water to drain naturally through the assembly, or terraces designed with a 'blue roof' stormwater detention approach where controlled ponding is intentional, may not require a conventional piped drainage system.

subject: Roof Terrace
rationale: Thermal insulation is typically required between the terrace and the interior below to meet energy codes and comfort.
conditions: for thermal performance and energy efficiency
exceptions: unconditioned spaces below

subject: Roof Terrace
rationale: Path lighting, ambient lighting, and task lighting are typically required for safe evening occupation.
applicability: roof terraces intended for nighttime use

The assertion does not account for jurisdictions where nighttime use is prohibited by zoning or noise ordinances; in such cases, a lighting system may still be required for code-compliant egress and safety even if nighttime 'use' is not intended, or conversely may be minimal. The 'intended for nighttime use' applicability is ambiguous because egress lighting requirements apply regardless of intended use pattern.
conditions: for evening/nighttime usability and safety

subject: Roof Terrace
rationale: The roof terrace connects to adjacent interior spaces (hallways, apartments, lounges) through doorways and circulation paths.
conditions: via doors, stairs, or elevators
exceptions: Roof terraces that are standalone structures (e.g., rooftop decks on separate mechanical penthouses) or terraces on independent freestanding garden structures may not connect to interior spaces at all; the assertion states 'attached to buildings' but some roof terraces are on detached structures that are still part of a building site yet do not connect to interior spaces via doors, stairs, or elevators (e.g., accessed only via external ladder or scaffold).

subject: Loggia
rationale: An open or semi-open loggia must have drainage to avoid ponding.
applicability: The condition 'when floor is exposed to rain' is insufficiently precise. A loggia is by definition a roofed outdoor space, so its floor is inherently rain-exposed unless fully enclosed (in which case it would no longer be a loggia). However, if the loggia is on an upper floor with a waterproofed slab below (e.g., above a habitable room), drainage needs differ from a ground-floor loggia. The assertion should differentiate between loggia positions (ground vs. suspended slab).
conditions: when floor is exposed to rain

subject: Loggia
rationale: Loggias typically include ceiling or wall-mounted lighting for usability at night.
applicability: The condition 'when designed for evening use' is subjective and not a standard design parameter. Evening use does not automatically mandate a lighting fixture — ambient light from adjacent interior rooms or indirect lighting may suffice. A more precise condition would be 'when required by local building code for occupied outdoor spaces' or 'when illumination levels below 50 lux are unacceptable'.
conditions: when designed for evening use

subject: Deck
rationale: Guardrails are required by building codes for safety on elevated decks.
applicability: The assertion applies only to decks under the IRC/IBC framework. Decks regulated under different codes (e.g., NFPA 101 Life Safety Code, local municipal codes, or international codes outside the US) may have different height thresholds (e.g., 36 inches in some Canadian codes or UK Building Regulations Part K). The applicability statement 'building code requirement' is too broad without specifying which code.
conditions: When deck height exceeds 30 inches above adjacent grade
exceptions: The 30-inch threshold for requiring a guardrail is not universal. The International Residential Code (IRC) R312.1 and International Building Code (IBC) 1015.2 specify 30 inches, but some jurisdictions or specific occupancy types may use different thresholds (e.g., 24 inches in certain older codes or state amendments). Additionally, decks below 30 inches may still require a guardrail if they present a fall hazard due to steep slopes, retaining walls, or other site conditions below.

subject: Patio
rationale: Integrated light fixtures (path lights, wall sconces, post lights) are commonly installed within or adjacent to patios.
conditions: for nighttime use
exceptions: day-use-only patios

subject: Patio
rationale: Patios often include pergolas, awnings, umbrellas, or shade sails to provide relief from sun.
applicability: The assertion says 'Patio contains Shade Structure' under conditions of sunny/hot climates and user comfort priority. However, shade structures in desert/tropical climates may need to comply with wind load ratings (e.g., hurricane straps in tropical zones), which is a structural design constraint not captured. The assertion lacks context about climate-specific structural requirements that could affect the type or feasibility of shade structure.
conditions: in sunny/hot climates
user comfort priority
exceptions: patios designed for full sun exposure

subject: Outdoor Seating Area
rationale: Proper drainage prevents water pooling and ensures usability after rain.
conditions: When located on impermeable surfaces
exceptions: If seating area is on permeable/grass surface

The existing exception only mentions permeable/grass surfaces, but there are other exceptions: outdoor seating areas on rooftops with internal building drainage systems that handle runoff through roof drains rather than a dedicated 'drainage system' at the seating level; also seating areas in structures like covered patios where rainfall does not directly reach the surface.

subject: Garden Terrace
rationale: A garden terrace needs proper drainage to prevent water pooling and structural damage.
applicability: all building types with garden terraces

The assertion states Garden Terrace requires Drainage System for rainwater management for all building types, but in some climates (e.g., arid regions with negligible rainfall) or for very small ornamental garden terraces where rainwater can be managed via surface runoff without a dedicated subsurface drainage system, this requirement may not apply.
conditions: for rainwater management

subject: Garden Terrace
rationale: Essential barrier between soil/planting and building structure to prevent water ingress.
applicability: The assertion states Garden Terrace requires Waterproof Membrane as base layer applicable to all building types, but extensive green roofs (with deep soil profiles) on certain structural types may use different waterproofing strategies (e.g., fluid-applied membranes, bentonite panels) rather than a discrete 'membrane' layer, or the membrane requirement may vary by climate zone and substrate depth.
conditions: as base layer

subject: Garden Terrace
rationale: Garden terraces carry substantial dead and live loads (soil, plants, water, people) requiring robust structural support.
conditions: with sufficient load-bearing capacity

subject: Garden Terrace
rationale: Plants on terraces often lack access to natural groundwater and require artificial watering.
conditions: for plant health in dry periods
exceptions: rain-fed climates with drought-tolerant planting

subject: Veranda
rationale: A veranda as a permanent structure requires a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: must support structural loads
exceptions: lightweight prefabricated verandas

subject: Veranda
rationale: Proper drainage is essential to prevent water damage and pooling on the veranda.
conditions: to prevent water accumulation
exceptions: Some verandas, particularly small stoop-type verandas or those with permeable surfaces (e.g., gravel, deck boards with gaps), may not need a dedicated drainage system because water can drain naturally through the ground or gaps. The assertion 'Veranda depends_on Drainage System' is too absolute.

subject: Veranda
rationale: Many verandas include a ceiling finish for aesthetics and insect protection.
conditions: when fully roofed
exceptions: open-beam verandas without ceiling finish

subject: Outdoor Walkway
rationale: Prevents standing water, ice formation, and water damage to the walkway structure.
conditions: when walkway is not permeable
exceptions: permeable pavers may not require separate drainage

subject: Outdoor Walkway
rationale: Safety and accessibility compliance (e.g., IBC/ADA) for elevated or sloped outdoor walkways.
conditions: when walkway is elevated
when slope exceeds 1:20
when required by local building code
exceptions: walkways at grade with gentle slope may not require handrails

The assertion requires handrails when slope exceeds 1:20, but many building codes (e.g., IBC) only require handrails on ramps with slopes exceeding 1:20 and a rise greater than 6 inches. A very short ramp section with slope exceeding 1:20 but negligible rise (e.g., a 1-inch curb ramp) typically does not require handrails. This exception should be added.

The condition 'when walkway is elevated' is vague — a walkway elevated only a few inches (e.g., a single step up) may not require handrails per most codes; handrail requirements typically kick in at specific height thresholds (e.g., 30 inches above adjacent grade per IBC). A condition specifying the elevation threshold is needed.

subject: Outdoor Walkway
rationale: Outdoor walkways often incorporate bollards, wall sconces, or pole lights for safety and wayfinding.
conditions: for nighttime use
when required by code for egress
exceptions: unoccupied walkways not used at night

subject: Outdoor Walkway
rationale: Signage and directional markers are often placed along or within outdoor walkways to guide pedestrians.
