rationale: Access control devices are core components of a comprehensive building security system, enabling authorized entry and restricting unauthorized access.
conditions: when properly installed and configured
exceptions: In locked-down facilities (e.g., psychiatric wards, prisons, high-security government buildings), access control devices may be intentionally isolated from the building security system to prevent a single point of compromise, meaning the assertion does not hold in these contexts.

subject: Install Access Control Devices
rationale: Access control systems must interface with fire alarm systems to unlock doors automatically upon alarm for safe egress.
conditions: for compliance with life safety codes
exceptions: In jurisdictions using modern wireless/interconnected smoke alarms that do not require a central fire alarm panel (e.g., residential buildings under certain codes), access control devices may have no physical or logical connection to a fire alarm system, yet still comply with life safety codes via local smoke detection and magnetic door release.

subject: Install Access Control Devices
rationale: Access control data can be integrated with BMS for centralized monitoring and energy management related to occupancy.
conditions: for integrated building operations
exceptions: standalone security-only systems

In facilities governed by stringent cybersecurity policies (e.g., defense, critical infrastructure), access control devices may be deliberately air-gapped from the BMS network to prevent cross-system cyberattack propagation, even in commercial/institutional settings.

subject: Form & Pour Entry Landing / Stoop
rationale: The stoop/landing often serves as the base or anchorage for handrails and guardrails.
conditions: When steps are present or required by code
exceptions: Not all stoops require handrails/guardrails. If a stoop has fewer than 4 risers (typical code threshold), a handrail may not be required. Additionally, the assertion conflates handrails (for stairs) with guardrails (for open sides of landings/decks), which have different code triggers — a landing under 30 inches above grade may not need a guardrail even if steps are present.

subject: Build Entry Ramp
rationale: Handrails are required by accessibility codes for safety on ramps with significant slope or rise.
applicability: The assertion uses 'requires Handrail' but handrail requirements differ between IBC (commercial) and ADA/ABA Standards. IBC requires handrails on both sides when ramp rise > 6" and slope > 1:20, while ADA Standards only require one handrail. The applicability states 'ADA-compliant ramps' as if it's a single consistent category, but ADA vs IBC have conflicting handrail requirements (one side vs both sides). The assertion does not specify which side handrail requirement applies to which code.
conditions: ramp slope exceeds 1:20
ramp rise exceeds 6 inches
exceptions: private residential ramps in some jurisdictions

In some jurisdictions (e.g., certain Canadian provinces and some US states with amended building codes), handrails are not required on residential entry ramps even when slope exceeds 1:20 and rise exceeds 6 inches, if there is an adjacent wall grab bar. The existing exception only covers 'private residential ramps in some jurisdictions' but does not address this specific grab-bar alternative.

subject: Build Entry Ramp
rationale: Level landings at top, bottom, and intermediate points provide resting areas and turning space for wheelchair users.
conditions: ramp length exceeds maximum run per code (typically 30 ft)
exceptions: very short ramps

subject: Build Entry Stairs
rationale: Entry stairs need a foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: must support stair loads
exceptions: Precast concrete or metal stair systems with integral base supports (e.g., prefabricated stair towers, stairs on steel beams spanning between walls) may not require a separate poured foundation directly beneath them; the load may be transferred through bearing walls or structural frames instead.

subject: Build Entry Stairs
rationale: Treads provide the horizontal stepping surface for stairs.
conditions: for walking surface
exceptions: Monolithic concrete stairs (cast-in-place) or solid stone stair blocks where the tread is formed as an integral part of the stair mass do not require a separately installed 'Stair Tread' component.

subject: Build Entry Stairs
rationale: Risers define the vertical height between treads.
applicability: The existing exception for 'open-riser stair designs' already covers one counterexample, but the assertion also fails for monolithic stairs (cast-in-place concrete) where risers are not separate components but part of the pour.
conditions: for vertical step height
exceptions: open-riser stair designs

subject: Build Entry Stairs
rationale: Handrails provide fall protection and support for users.
conditions: for safety and code compliance
exceptions: very low-rise stairs (e.g. 1-2 steps)

Private stairs within a single dwelling unit (e.g., interior stairs in a single-family home) are not covered by the applicability scope (commercial, public, multi-family residential), but building codes often still require handrails for these stairs beyond 1-2 risers, meaning the assertion incorrectly omits single-family residential from its scope.

subject: Build Entry Stairs
rationale: Stringers are the inclined structural members that carry stair loads.
conditions: to support treads and risers
exceptions: Cast-in-place concrete stairs and some prefabricated steel stair systems may use a monolithic or center-carriage design that does not require traditional stringers (sloping side members) as separate components.
Spiral stairs and certain helical stair designs often use a central column or structural spine rather than traditional stringers to support treads and risers.

subject: Install Vestibule Partition
rationale: Vestibule partitions often house or integrate automatic door opening mechanisms.
applicability: The assertion assumes an automatic door operator is always installed on the vestibule partition, but in accessibility applications (e.g., ADA compliance) the automatic door operator is typically required on the exterior door or interior door, not specifically on the vestibule partition itself. The partition may only house a push plate or sensor, not the operator mechanism.
conditions: When specified for accessibility or high-traffic

subject: Car Parking Space
rationale: Car parking spaces require painted or marked boundaries to define individual spaces and guide vehicle parking.
conditions: standard parking lot operation
exceptions: temporary unpainted lots

In some jurisdictions, parking spaces can be defined via gravel, grass pavers, or other unpaved surfaces that lack painted markings yet still function as legal parking spaces. The existing exception for 'temporary unpainted lots' is too narrow.

subject: Car Parking Space
rationale: Proper drainage prevents water accumulation that can damage vehicles and pavement.
conditions: outdoor or uncovered parking
exceptions: indoor garages with sealed floors and no water ingress

subject: Car Parking Space
rationale: Indoor parking requires mechanical ventilation to remove vehicle exhaust fumes (CO, NOx) and maintain air quality.
conditions: enclosed/indoor parking garage
exceptions: open-air or naturally ventilated parking

subject: Car Parking Space
rationale: Enclosed parking spaces depend on sprinklers or fire suppression for life safety due to vehicle fire risk.
conditions: enclosed parking garage
building code requirements
exceptions: open-deck parking structures exempt by code

Some smaller enclosed parking garages (e.g., residential or very small commercial garages with fewer than a certain vehicle count threshold) may be exempt from fire suppression system requirements under certain building codes (e.g., IBC exceptions for open parking garages or garages under a certain size).

subject: Car Parking Space
rationale: Standard car parking spaces support the provision of adjacent accessible (handicap) spaces as required by code.
applicability: The assertion states Car Parking Space 'supports' Accessible Parking Space, which is semantically ambiguous. A regular parking space does not inherently support or become an accessible space — rather, a subset of parking spaces are designated as accessible. The relationship is more accurately a 'has_accessible_designation' or 'includes' relationship, not a generic 'supports'.
conditions: compliance with accessibility standards

subject: Car Parking Space
rationale: Parking spaces connect to pedestrian walkways to provide safe passage from car to building entrance.
conditions: site design includes pedestrian access
exceptions: very small lots where pedestrians walk in aisle

Some parking facilities (e.g., park-and-ride lots, remote event parking) may connect to shuttle bus stops or transit stations rather than pedestrian walkways. The connection is via a transit intermediary, not directly to a pedestrian walkway.

subject: Car Parking Space
rationale: Each parking space connects directly to the adjacent driving aisle for vehicle access.
applicability: The assertion applies to 'all parking facilities' but does not account for parallel parking spaces on streets, which connect to the travel lane (traffic way), not a dedicated Parking Aisle. The relationship only holds for off-street parking lots with defined aisles.

subject: Parking Guidance System
rationale: The system relies on clearly defined parking spaces to report availability accurately
conditions: physical delineation of individual spaces needed
exceptions: A Parking Guidance System can function without physical space markings if it uses sensor-based detection (e.g., ultrasonic or radar sensors) or camera-based systems that detect vehicle presence and location without relying on painted markings. Many modern parking guidance systems operate in gravel lots, underground garages where markings are faded, or use space-by-space sensor grids.

subject: Parking Guidance System
rationale: The parking guidance system can be integrated into broader building management for data sharing
conditions: if integrated for centralized monitoring
exceptions: A Parking Guidance System can connect to other systems besides the BMS, such as a standalone parking management system, a cloud-based parking platform, or a mobile payment system, without any BMS involvement. The assertion implies BMS is the primary or required integration target, which is not always the case.

subject: Roller Door / Overhead Door
rationale: Motorized roller doors can be integrated with BMS for centralized control and monitoring.
applicability: The assertion specifies 'connects_to Building Management System (BMS)' but does not specify which BMS protocol or interface (e.g., BACnet, Modbus, dry contact). Not all roller/overhead doors in commercial/industrial buildings actually integrate via standard BMS protocols; many use standalone controllers with no BMS integration even in smart buildings, or use proprietary interfaces. The assertion should clarify the subset of doors that support open BMS protocols.
conditions: smart/automated building
exceptions: standalone manually operated doors

Even in smart/automated commercial or industrial buildings, fire-rated roller doors often have dedicated fire alarm system connections rather than BMS integration, or may be required by code to override BMS control during fire events. This is an exception where the door connects to the fire alarm system instead of or in addition to the BMS, and BMS connectivity may be secondary or disabled.

subject: Parking Ventilation System
rationale: Ducts convey exhaust air and supply air throughout the garage.
conditions: For distributing air within the parking structure
exceptions: Jet fan systems may use minimal ductwork

The existing exception already acknowledges jet fan systems use minimal ductwork, but this is actually a fundamental design alternative: many modern parking ventilation systems use impulse/jet fans with no ductwork at all (ductless). The assertion should more clearly indicate that ductwork is not required for jet/impulse fan systems, not merely that they use 'minimal' ductwork.

subject: Parking Ventilation System
rationale: Ventilation systems often interface with fire alarms for smoke management.
applicability: Enclosed parking garages with fire suppression

The dependency on the Fire Alarm System for emergency smoke control mode sequencing may not apply in jurisdictions where the Building Management System (BMS) directly controls smoke mode without requiring signals from a dedicated Fire Alarm System, or where the fire alarm is integrated within the BMS. Additionally, some codes permit standalone carbon monoxide (CO) based fan control without fire alarm integration for smoke purge.
conditions: For emergency smoke control mode sequencing

subject: Parking Ventilation System
rationale: BMS integration enables demand-controlled ventilation based on real-time CO readings.
conditions: For automated control and monitoring of fan operation and CO levels
exceptions: Small garages with standalone controls

In many jurisdictions, code-required CO monitoring and fan control can be provided by a dedicated standalone CO controller/panel rather than a full Building Management System (BMS), even in large facilities. The assertion implies BMS dependency is universal for large/smart facilities, but standalone dedicated controllers are a common alternative.

subject: Pedestrian Walkway in Parking
rationale: ADA compliance requires accessible routes with ramps where walkways meet roadways or curbs.
applicability: The assertion does not specify minimum width requirements for the accessible ramp in the context of a parking facility walkway. In many jurisdictions, the ramp must comply with specific width and slope ratios (e.g., 1:12 max slope, 36-inch minimum width) which are not referenced.
conditions: if walkway crosses curb or grade change
exceptions: not needed if walkway is level with surrounding pavement

subject: Pedestrian Walkway in Parking
rationale: Proper drainage ensures the walkway remains safe and free of standing water or ice.
conditions: to prevent ponding and ice formation on walkway surface
exceptions: This dependency oversimplifies drainage requirements. In many parking garages, the walkway drainage is handled by the garage's overall structural drainage system (floor drains, scuppers, sloped decks) rather than a separate 'Drainage System' dedicated to the walkway. The assertion should clarify that this refers to proper water management on the walkway surface, not necessarily a dedicated drainage system.

subject: Pedestrian Walkway in Parking
rationale: Pedestrian walkways serve as the accessible route connecting accessible parking spaces to building entrances.
conditions: where walkway connects to ADA parking stalls
exceptions: In many parking facilities, an accessible parking space does not always connect to a 'Pedestrian Walkway in Parking' — it may connect directly to a pedestrian access aisle that leads to a curb ramp to the sidewalk. The walkway may be a separate element. The 'supports' relationship is not universally true without clarifying the distinction between walkways and access aisles.

subject: Pedestrian Walkway in Parking
rationale: Accessibility standards require tactile warning strips at transitions to alert visually impaired pedestrians.
conditions: at curb ramps and grade changes for visually impaired users

subject: Car Park Drainage System
rationale: Waterproofing protects the structure from water ingress where drainage is on suspended slabs.
conditions: on suspended slabs
at expansion joints
exceptions: not needed for at-grade car parks on well-draining ground

The assertion states that a Car Park Drainage System 'depends_on' a Waterproof Membrane on suspended slabs and at expansion joints, but the existing exception only covers at-grade car parks on well-draining ground. There are additional exceptions needed: (1) Car parks with fully bonded waterproofing systems that integrate drainage into the membrane layer itself may not require a separate independent drainage system; (2) In some designs, a 'drainage mat' or 'drainage board' serves as the drainage layer directly over the waterproof membrane, blurring the dependency—if the drainage system is defined as the combination of membrane + drainage composite, then the 'depends_on' relationship may be inaccurate; (3) For podium decks with inverted roof membrane protection (where the membrane is placed on top of the drainage layer), the drainage system does not depend on the membrane in the same way—the membrane actually depends on the drainage layer for protection.

subject: Parking Space Marking
rationale: Proper surface preparation is critical for marking adhesion and longevity.
conditions: includes cleaning, crack repair, and drying
exceptions: Temporary parking markings (e.g., for construction zones, events) often use pre-formed tape or removable markings that do not require the same surface preparation steps (cleaning, crack repair, drying) as permanent painted markings.

subject: Parking Space Marking
rationale: Some parking space marking systems incorporate markings for wheel stop placement.
conditions: some markings include wheel stop location indicators
exceptions: not all parking spaces include wheel stops

subject: Parking Space Marking
rationale: Markings visually correspond with parking guidance system sensors and indicators.
applicability: The assertion uses 'connects_to' which implies a physical or data connection, but in many smart parking facilities, the marking itself does not directly connect to the guidance system. Instead, sensors or cameras detect vehicles in marked spaces and feed data to the guidance system independently of the marking. The relationship is better described as the marking being a reference point for the guidance system rather than a direct connection.
conditions: when sensor-based or camera-based guidance is installed
exceptions: not all parking facilities have guidance systems

subject: Plaza
rationale: Plazas must manage rainwater runoff to prevent flooding and water damage.
applicability: The assertion does not specify the jurisdiction. In many municipal codes, only plazas above a certain size threshold (e.g., >500 sq ft) or those with impervious surfaces trigger stormwater drainage requirements. Very small plazas or pocket plazas may be exempt.
conditions: for stormwater management
exceptions: Plazas that are covered (e.g., enclosed atriums, indoor plazas, or plazas under a building overhang) do not receive direct rainfall and therefore do not require a stormwater drainage system.

subject: Sky Garden
rationale: Sky gardens with live plants need irrigation for watering, especially in elevated areas with limited natural water access.
conditions: If containing live plants
exceptions: Sky gardens containing only artificial plants, preserved moss, or decorative non-living vegetation do not require an irrigation system since there is no need for water delivery to living plants.

subject: Sky Garden
rationale: Sky gardens as planted elevated spaces require drainage to manage excess water and prevent structural water damage.

subject: Sky Garden
rationale: Essential to protect building structure below from water ingress from irrigation and rainfall.

subject: Sky Garden
rationale: Sky gardens require lighting for safety, ambiance, and potentially for plant growth support.

subject: Sky Garden
rationale: Sky gardens must be accessible via stairs, elevators, or escalators linking them to main building floors.
exceptions: A sky garden on grade (at ground level) or on a podium that is directly accessible from the ground plane without requiring a vertical circulation core does not need to connect to a vertical circulation core.

subject: Inner Garden
rationale: Plants require regular watering; an irrigation system (drip, sprinkler, or manual) is typically needed.
applicability: The assertion states Inner Garden depends_on Irrigation System, but the existing exception for 'extremely humid climates' is too vague. High humidity alone does not eliminate the need for irrigation — it may reduce frequency but not eliminate dependency. Also, 'self-watering designs' are a counterexample that replaces traditional irrigation but still provides water management, so the dependency is on water delivery, not specifically an 'Irrigation System'.
exceptions: self-watering designs or extremely humid climates

subject: Inner Garden
rationale: Excess water must be drained to prevent water damage to building structure and root rot.
exceptions: The assertion 'Inner Garden depends_on Drainage System' is listed with applicability 'all building types' and has no existing exceptions. However, inner gardens built directly on natural ground (e.g., at-grade gardens in a courtyard) may rely on natural soil percolation rather than a constructed drainage system. This is a missing exception.
Very small, container-based inner gardens (e.g., pots or planters) often do not require a dedicated drainage system — they drain into saucers or trays. The assertion lacks this exception.

subject: Inner Garden
rationale: To protect building structure from moisture intrusion.
conditions: if located above occupied spaces
exceptions: ground-level gardens with direct earth contact

subject: Inner Garden
rationale: Prevents mold, mildew, and maintains air quality for both plants and occupants.
conditions: if enclosed or indoor
exceptions: open-air inner courtyards

subject: Covered Walkway
rationale: A permanent covered walkway needs a structural foundation to bear loads and remain stable.
conditions: covered walkway is permanent structure
exceptions: A temporary or demountable covered walkway (e.g., construction site pedestrian walkway, event tent-like structure) may use surface-mounted or ballasted systems without a permanent foundation. The condition 'covered walkway is permanent structure' attempts to limit this, but temporary covered walkways still exist as a valid exception for the general case.

subject: Covered Walkway
rationale: By definition a covered walkway requires a roof covering to provide overhead shelter.

subject: Covered Walkway
rationale: Vertical structural supports are typically needed to hold up the roof of a covered walkway.
exceptions: cantilevered roof attached to adjacent building

subject: Covered Walkway
rationale: Prevents water accumulation and leaks on the covered walkway.
conditions: roof is sloped or flat

subject: Covered Walkway
rationale: Covered walkways support orientation by providing clear circulation paths.

subject: Covered Walkway
rationale: Required for safety where there is a change in elevation.
conditions: elevated walkway or ramp
exceptions: at-grade walkway without drop-off

A covered walkway with stairs (not a ramp and not elevated in the continuous sense) may require handrails on the stairs but the assertion's condition 'elevated walkway or ramp' misses the stair case. Also, some jurisdictions exempt covered walkways under a certain height (e.g., less than 30 inches elevation) from handrail requirements even if technically elevated.

subject: Arcade
rationale: An arcade is a covered walkway formed by a series of arches supported by columns or piers; structural columns are fundamental to its definition.
applicability: The assertion 'Arcade requires Structural Columns' with condition 'arcade is load-bearing' is contradictory — an arcade is by definition a load-bearing structure (a series of arches supported by columns). The condition implies there are both load-bearing and non-load-bearing arcades, which is architecturally unusual. An arcade that is not load-bearing is typically a 'colonnade' or purely decorative arcade, not a true arcade. The condition may be unnecessary or misstated.
conditions: arcade is load-bearing

subject: Arcade
rationale: Arcades typically contain ambient or task lighting for safe nighttime pedestrian use.
applicability: The assertion has no conditions but 'applicability: all' — this is overly broad. Whether an arcade contains lighting fixtures depends on whether it is interior, exterior, publicly accessible, and whether it has an electrical installation. Many arcades (especially historic or exterior ones) may never have had lighting fixtures installed.
exceptions: An arcade may be unlit (e.g., exterior arcade without artificial lighting, or an arcade in a ruin/conservation state where lighting fixtures are not installed). The assertion 'Arcade contains Lighting Fixture' does not hold in such cases.

subject: Lightwell
rationale: Lightwells typically have windows/glazing on surrounding walls to admit natural light into adjacent spaces.
conditions: to allow daylight transmission

subject: Lightwell
rationale: Lightwells extend to exterior or ground and must prevent water ingress.
applicability: In a lightwell that is open to the exterior (not enclosed), waterproofing at the base and horizontal surfaces may still be required, but the assertion does not distinguish between interior lightwells exposed to rainwater ingress and purely interior lightwells with only incidental moisture. The condition 'at all horizontal surfaces' could be overly broad for interior-only lightwells where only the base needs waterproofing.
conditions: at base of lightwell
at all horizontal surfaces

subject: Lightwell
rationale: Rainwater and debris accumulate at bottom; proper drainage (floor drains, weeping tile) is essential.
conditions: at lightwell base

subject: Lightwell
rationale: Vertical shafts typically require fire-resistance rating per building codes to prevent fire spread.
conditions: when lightwell passes through multiple floors
exceptions: single-story lightwells
open-to-exterior lightwells not requiring fire separation

Existing exceptions already list single-story and open-to-exterior lightwells, but the applicability says 'buildings with >2 stories; commercial buildings' — this conflicts with the exceptions for single-story and open-to-exterior lightwells which could exist in buildings over 2 stories or commercial buildings. The applicability should be refined to avoid contradiction.

subject: Lightwell
rationale: Reflective paints, tiles, or cladding on lightwell walls improve daylight penetration to lower floors.
conditions: to maximize light distribution
exceptions: where light penetration is sufficient without

subject: Courtyard Enclosure Walls
rationale: Courtyard enclosure walls require proper foundations to transfer loads to the ground and ensure stability.
conditions: structural stability needed

subject: Courtyard Enclosure Walls
rationale: Enclosure walls may require a structural frame for lateral stability and load transfer, especially when they are part of the primary structural system.
conditions: if walls are load-bearing or part of the primary structure
exceptions: if walls are non-load-bearing infill panels supported by an independent frame

subject: Courtyard Enclosure Walls
rationale: Waterproofing is essential at the base of enclosure walls and around openings to prevent moisture damage.
applicability: all building types with exposed courtyard walls
conditions: to prevent water ingress at wall base and penetrations

subject: Courtyard Enclosure Walls
rationale: Proper drainage around courtyard walls prevents water accumulation and hydrostatic pressure against the wall.
conditions: to manage surface water runoff near walls

subject: Courtyard Enclosure Walls
rationale: Courtyard enclosure walls often support privacy by creating a visual barrier from the public realm.
applicability: The assertion limits applicability to residential, hospitality, and mixed-use, but privacy screens supported by courtyard enclosure walls are also commonly required in office buildings (e.g., ground-floor courtyards adjacent to public sidewalks), healthcare facilities (patient privacy in healing gardens), and educational buildings (student privacy in outdoor spaces). The scope is too narrow.
conditions: if designed as solid walls or with minimal openings
exceptions: if walls are purely decorative and low-height

subject: Courtyard Floor/Paving
rationale: Courtyard floors must be sloped or drained to prevent standing water damage.
conditions: to prevent water pooling
exceptions: In arid or desert climates (e.g., US Southwest, Middle East) where rainfall is extremely low and water pooling is not a concern, a dedicated drainage system for courtyard paving may not be necessary. The condition 'to prevent water pooling' is context-dependent on climate and local rainfall intensity.

subject: Courtyard Floor/Paving
rationale: Waterproofing prevents moisture infiltration to spaces below.
applicability: The assertion does not address the type of waterproof membrane required. In some jurisdictions, courtyards above habitable space require not just any waterproof membrane but specifically a 'liquid-applied' or 'hot-fluid applied' membrane (not sheet membranes) because sheet membranes can have laps that leak. This is a critical detail that affects compliance with building codes.
conditions: if courtyard is above habitable space
exceptions: ground-level courtyards without underlying spaces

Some modern structural systems use a 'warm roof' or 'inverted roof' assembly where the waterproof membrane is placed below the insulation layer. In such assemblies, the membrane serves the structure below, while the courtyard paving may rest on a drainage layer and insulation without requiring a separate membrane directly beneath the paving. The assertion as stated could be misinterpreted to require a membrane directly under paving in all above-habitable-space cases.

subject: Courtyard Drainage System
rationale: Courtyard drainage systems collect rainwater from surrounding roofs via gutters.
applicability: The assertion states Courtyard Drainage System 'requires' Gutter System for roof drainage collection, but many courtyard drainage designs use scuppers, downspouts connected directly to underground drains, or internal drainage channels that bypass any above-ground gutter system entirely. A gutter system is a common solution, not a requirement.
conditions: For roof drainage collection

subject: Courtyard Drainage System
rationale: Floor drains capture rainwater falling directly into the courtyard and washing water.
applicability: The assertion states Courtyard Drainage System 'requires' Floor Drain for surface water collection, but courtyards can drain via sloped surfaces to perimeter drains, trench drains, channel drains, or permeable paving systems without a traditional floor drain. Floor drains are one option, not a universal requirement for surface water collection in courtyards.
conditions: For surface water collection within courtyard

subject: Courtyard Drainage System
rationale: Proper courtyard drainage prevents water pooling near foundations which can cause structural damage.
conditions: By diverting water away from building perimeter
exceptions: If the Courtyard Drainage System is poorly designed or fails (e.g., clogged drains, undersized pipes, improper slope), it can cause water to pool against the foundation instead of protecting it, or even direct water toward the building perimeter, actively harming the foundation rather than protecting it.

subject: Courtyard Drainage System
rationale: Courtyard drainage can feed into rainwater harvesting tanks.
conditions: When drainage system is designed to collect rather than just dispose of water

subject: Courtyard Drainage System
rationale: Drainage supports proper water management for green roof layers.
applicability: buildings with green roofs or rooftop courtyards
conditions: When courtyard includes green roof or planter areas

subject: Courtyard Planting Beds
rationale: Excess water from irrigation or rain must be drained away to protect plant roots.
conditions: to prevent waterlogging
exceptions: Raised planting beds (e.g., container beds, troughs) with drainage holes and a free-draining growing medium may not require a separate below-grade drainage system. Water simply exits the container. This contradicts 'all courtyard types' applicability.

subject: Courtyard Planting Beds
rationale: Plants in beds often require supplemental watering, especially in dry climates or when covered by overhangs.
applicability: The existing exception mentions 'regions with sufficient natural rainfall', but this is imprecise: even in high-rainfall regions, container planting beds may still need irrigation during dry spells, especially if they have limited soil volume and dry out quickly. The exception conflates regional rainfall with microclimate/container-specific water needs.
conditions: for consistent watering
exceptions: in regions with sufficient natural rainfall

Some arid or semi-arid climate courtyard designs use xeriscaping or native drought-tolerant plants that do not require an irrigation system after establishment. The assertion mandates irrigation for all beds in arid/semi-arid climates, which is not universally true.

subject: Courtyard Planting Beds
rationale: To prevent water damage to the structure below planting beds.
conditions: if courtyard is above grade or over a basement
exceptions: ground-level beds on native soil

Even for above-grade planters, if the planter has an integrated drainage layer (e.g., drainage mat, gravel, and a root barrier) that directs water to a weeping tile or drain pipe, a separate waterproof membrane may not be needed if the structure itself is watertight (e.g., concrete or metal planter). The assertion over-generalizes the need for a waterproof membrane.

subject: Courtyard Lighting
rationale: Courtyard lighting requires lighting fixtures (e.g., wall sconces, pole lights) to emit light.
conditions: mounted on walls or poles
exceptions: Courtyard lighting could also be provided by ground-recessed uplights, bollard lights, string lights hung between structures, or freestanding portable fixtures — none of which are 'mounted on walls or poles' as the condition requires. The condition therefore excludes valid instances of courtyard lighting.

subject: Courtyard Irrigation System
rationale: An irrigation system needs a water source and distribution pipes to deliver water to the courtyard.
conditions: must be connected to main water line or dedicated irrigation water source

subject: Courtyard Irrigation System
rationale: Proper drainage prevents damage to paving, foundations, and overwatering consequences.
applicability: A drainage system is not always a strict requirement; in arid climates, permeable soil, or with drip irrigation systems where water application is precisely controlled, waterlogging and soil erosion may not occur even without a dedicated drainage system. The assertion over-generalizes based on soil and climate conditions.
conditions: to prevent waterlogging and soil erosion

subject: Courtyard Irrigation System
rationale: Backflow preventers are integral components to protect potable water supply.
applicability: While backflow prevention devices are required by code in many jurisdictions, there are exceptions: (1) some low-hazard systems (e.g., drip irrigation with no chemical injection) may only need an atmospheric vacuum breaker rather than a full backflow prevention assembly, (2) jurisdictions with no adopted plumbing code may not require them, and (3) very small residential systems in some areas are exempt. The phrase 'required by code in most jurisdictions' is too sweeping.
conditions: required by code in most jurisdictions

subject: Courtyard Water Feature
rationale: Waterproofing is essential to protect the building structure from water damage.
applicability: all building types with water features

Some water features (e.g., prefabricated self-contained fountain units with integrated basins) come with built-in waterproof liners, making a separate waterproof membrane redundant. The assertion does not account for this exception.
conditions: to prevent leakage into surrounding structure
exceptions: In arid or drought-prone climates, small decorative water features on grade (e.g., a simple birdbath or a self-contained pondless fountain) may not require a waterproof membrane because water infiltration into the ground is minimal and acceptable.

subject: Courtyard Water Feature
rationale: Proper drainage prevents water accumulation and damage.
applicability: all building types with water features

Very small, self-contained courtyard water features (e.g., tabletop fountains, wall-mounted spouts with recirculating reservoirs) do not require a formal drainage system for overflow as they have no permanent connection to a drain and overflow is managed manually.
conditions: for overflow and maintenance
exceptions: In jurisdictions where rainwater harvesting is encouraged, overflow from a water feature may be intentionally directed to landscaping or a rain garden rather than to a formal piped drainage system, making a conventional drainage system unnecessary for that purpose.

subject: Courtyard Seating Elements
rationale: Proper drainage prevents water pooling around seating, which could cause damage or make seating unusable.
applicability: The dependency on Drainage System may not apply in arid or desert climates where rainfall is negligible and courtyards are designed without drainage infrastructure. The condition 'in areas with rainfall' is vague — does trace rainfall qualify? Many regions have rainfall but building codes do not require formal drainage for all courtyard seating elements.
conditions: in areas with rainfall

conditions: Covered arcade function

subject: Arcade colonnade
rationale: Arcade colonnades function primarily as covered pedestrian passageways.
conditions: Adjacent to building or between buildings
exceptions: An arcade colonnade can be freestanding (e.g., in a park or plaza) and does not necessarily require an adjacent pedestrian walkway. Monolithic arcades at building edges are the walkway, not a separate element they 'depend on'.

subject: Arcade colonnade
rationale: The columns of the colonnade directly support the roof or covering above.
conditions: Direct load transfer through columns
exceptions: In some structural systems, columns in an arcade colonnade support beams or arches which in turn support the roof — they do not directly support the roof. The assertion 'direct load transfer through columns' oversimplifies and may be structurally incorrect for arcuated systems.

subject: Arcade colonnade
rationale: A colonnade is defined as a series of columns arranged at regular intervals.
conditions: Regular spacing

subject: Roof Garden Guardrail and Safety Installation
rationale: Proper drainage must be maintained around guardrail installation points to prevent ponding.
conditions: Guardrail base plates or posts must not obstruct drainage flow paths
exceptions: In roof gardens with elevated or pedestal-mounted guardrails (e.g., railings mounted on parapets or raised curbs), the guardrail base plates may be positioned above the drainage layer entirely, meaning they cannot obstruct drainage flow paths because they never intersect them. In such cases, the dependency on a roof drainage system does not apply.

subject: Arcade floor paving
rationale: To prevent water pooling and damage to the paving surface.
conditions: For outdoor arcades
In wet climates
exceptions: Indoor arcades with controlled drainage

subject: Arcade floor paving
rationale: To accommodate thermal expansion and contraction, preventing cracking.
applicability: The assertion applies to 'all arcade floors' but the condition references 'large paving areas' and 'thermal movement risk.' For arcade floors made of materials with very low coefficients of thermal expansion (e.g.,某些 engineered polymer tiles or small-format mosaics), expansion joints may not be necessary even in large areas. The current framing assumes all paving materials behave similarly under thermal stress.
conditions: In large paving areas
With thermal movement risk
exceptions: Very small arcade areas

subject: Arcade floor paving
rationale: Arcade paving often supports display stands, kiosks, or furniture in commercial settings.
conditions: When arcade is used for retail

subject: Arcade floor paving
rationale: Edge restraints like curbs or metal strips prevent paving units from shifting laterally.
conditions: Where paving meets softer ground or different materials
exceptions: Monolithic poured surfaces with integral curbs

The assertion requires edge restraint where paving meets softer ground or different materials. However, there is no exception for cases where the paving abuts a rigid building structure (e.g., a concrete wall, column, or foundation) on one or more sides. In such cases, the building structure itself provides edge restraint, making a separate edge restraint detail redundant or even problematic due to differential movement.

subject: Arcade vaulted ceiling
rationale: The entire vault and its supporting columns/arches depend on adequate foundations to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: All construction

subject: Arcade vaulted ceiling
rationale: Vaulted ceilings often contain recessed or pendant lighting fixtures within the vault structure.
conditions: Integrated design
exceptions: An arcade vaulted ceiling does not inherently 'contain' lighting fixtures. Lighting fixtures are an optional design element that may be mounted on, suspended from, or recessed into a vaulted ceiling, but they are not a constituent part of the ceiling assembly itself. In designs where lighting is provided by other means (e.g., floor lamps, wall sconces, natural light only), the vaulted ceiling has no lighting fixture content.

subject: Arcade vaulted ceiling
rationale: Thermal insulation may be contained within or above the vaulted ceiling assembly.
conditions: Climate-controlled buildings
exceptions: An arcade vaulted ceiling is primarily an architectural/aesthetic ceiling form characterized by arched geometry. In many climate-controlled buildings with vaulted ceilings, insulation is placed in the roof deck or attic space above the vault, not within the vaulted ceiling assembly itself. An 'Insulation Layer' is not an inherent component of an arcade vaulted ceiling - the ceiling finish can exist without integrated insulation.

subject: Arcade keystone
rationale: In most masonry arcades, mortar is placed between voussoirs including the keystone for bedding and load distribution.
conditions: in traditional masonry construction
exceptions: dry-stone arches where friction alone holds the keystone

In modern stone construction with precision-cut stone and steel armatures, keystones can be dry-fit with no mortar. Also, in Roman concrete (opus caementicium) arches, the keystone was often set without traditional mortar.

subject: Arcade keystone
rationale: An arcade keystone sits at the top of an arch that springs from columns; the arch connects the keystone to supporting columns below.
applicability: In arcades with continuous arches (arcade blind or applied arcades), keystones may be decorative masonry inserts that do not bear structural loads connecting to columns.
conditions: in a columnar arcade

subject: Arcade spandrel panel
rationale: If the arcade is enclosed and conditioned, insulation may be required behind or within the panel to meet thermal performance.
applicability: The assertion assumes thermal insulation is universally required for arcade spandrel panels forming part of the building envelope, but the need for insulation depends on local climate zones and energy code requirements (e.g., some climate zones may not mandate insulation for certain assembly types). Additionally, if the arcade is unconditioned or semi-conditioned, the envelope insulation requirement may differ.
conditions: Where the arcade spandrel panel forms part of the building envelope
exceptions: There are exceptions where a spandrel panel forming part of the building envelope does not require thermal insulation, such as when the panel is a structural glazed or curtain wall system where insulation is provided elsewhere in the assembly (e.g., backup wall), or when using insulated glass units (IGUs) with spandrel glass that meet thermal requirements without separate insulation.

subject: Arcade spandrel panel
rationale: Commonly, arcade spandrel panels are constructed from precast concrete, which contains the material itself.
conditions: If the spandrel panel is made of precast concrete material

subject: Arcade entablature
rationale: An arcade entablature is the horizontal structure that rests on the columns (or piers) of an arcade; without columns it cannot function as an entablature.
conditions: supporting the entablature above arcade openings

subject: Arcade entablature
rationale: The entablature is defined by being part of an arcade; it is the horizontal member carried by the arcade's supports.
applicability: The condition 'being part of a colonnaded walkway with arches' is overly narrow. An arcade entablature can exist in any arcade context (e.g., freestanding arcades, wall arcades, blind arcades), not only colonnaded walkways.
conditions: being part of a colonnaded walkway with arches

subject: Arcade drainage channel
rationale: The channel is an intermediate element that feeds into the larger stormwater drainage system.
applicability: The assertion states that arcade drainage channel depends on Stormwater Drainage System, but in many jurisdictions, arcade drainage may discharge to combined sewer systems (sanitary/storm combo), not exclusively a dedicated Stormwater Drainage System. In combined sewer areas, the dependency is on a combined sewer system rather than a separate stormwater system.
conditions: for final disposal of collected rainwater
exceptions: In some buildings, arcade drainage channels may discharge to on-site retention/detention systems (e.g., rain gardens, cisterns, infiltration basins) rather than to a Stormwater Drainage System, particularly in low-impact development or sustainable drainage design approaches.

subject: Arcade column base
rationale: An arcade column base sits on top of a foundation which transfers the column load to the ground.
applicability: The assertion does not differentiate between interior arcade columns (which typically require foundations) and very lightweight/ornamental arcade structures (e.g., small freestanding arcades in gardens) that may be supported on a thickened slab or grade beam without a deep foundation. The statement is overly broad.
conditions: load-bearing capacity must meet structural requirements
exceptions: In some historic or restoration contexts, existing shallow footings or continuous strip footings are used under arcade columns rather than isolated column foundations, so 'Foundation' could be misinterpreted as requiring deep or isolated pad footings.

subject: Arcade installation
rationale: Arcade machines and occupants generate heat requiring climate control.
conditions: Adequate cooling capacity for heat generated by electronics and occupants
Ventilation for indoor air quality
exceptions: Small-scale arcade installations (e.g., a single arcade cabinet in a bar or restaurant) may not require a dedicated HVAC system; the existing building HVAC may suffice. The assertion implies a dedicated HVAC system is required, which would be excessive in such cases.

subject: Arcade installation
rationale: Arcade installations with many electronic devices require fire protection.
applicability: The assertion states arcade installation 'depends_on Fire Suppression System' for all commercial installations, but small-occupancy arcades (e.g., below a certain occupant load threshold per local codes) may only require fire extinguishers and exits rather than a full fire suppression system. The blanket requirement may not hold universally across all local code jurisdictions.
conditions: Compliant with local fire codes for assembly/entertainment occupancies

subject: Arcade installation
rationale: Proper lighting is needed for safe operation and player visibility.
conditions: General ambient lighting for safety
Task lighting near machine areas

subject: Arcade arch voussoirs
rationale: Voussoirs, being wedge-shaped stones or bricks forming an arch, require mortar to be bedded and jointed properly for load transfer and stability.
conditions: for bedding and jointing
exceptions: Reconstructed or temporary centering-supported arches may have dry-laid voussoirs that are later grouted or left unmortared (e.g., some Roman experimental reconstructions). The assertion does not hold for such cases where voussoirs are temporarily placed without mortar.

subject: Arcade masonry construction
rationale: Mortar binds masonry units together and distributes loads in a masonry arcade structure.
conditions: traditional masonry arcade
exceptions: dry-stone construction

subject: Arcade waterproofing application
rationale: Arcade waterproofing application fundamentally requires a waterproofing membrane as the primary barrier against moisture ingress.
applicability: The assertion does not address internal/atrium arcades that are not exposed to exterior moisture. In such contexts, a waterproof membrane may be unnecessary or even detrimental due to vapor trapping.
conditions: must be compatible with arcade substrate

subject: Arcade waterproofing application
rationale: Effective waterproofing depends on adequate drainage to remove water from the waterproofed surface.
conditions: must be properly sloped and sized for expected water volume
exceptions: very small arcades with minimal exposure

The existing exception mentions 'very small arcades with minimal exposure' but does not account for arcades with permeable or decorative paving designed to drain directly into an absorbent sub-base (e.g., permeable pavers, gravel finishes) where a formal drainage system may be omitted in favor of infiltration.

subject: Blind arcade
rationale: A blind arcade is typically a series of arches applied to a wall surface. When structural, it requires a load-bearing wall to support the arches.
applicability: The assertion limits applicability to 'masonry buildings', but even within masonry buildings, a structural blind arcade can be supported by columns, piers, or buttresses rather than a continuous load-bearing wall. Many Romanesque and Gothic blind arcades are supported by engaged columns or pilasters, not full load-bearing walls.
conditions: when blind arcade is structural

subject: Pier arcade
rationale: Piers are supported on piles driven into the ground or seabed for structural stability.
conditions: when extending over water
in soft soil conditions
exceptions: In waterfront/marine environments with very hard or rocky seabed (e.g., granite shoreline), driven piles may not be feasible; instead, spread footings or rock-socketed piers could be used. The requirement 'requires Pile Foundation' is not universally applicable.

subject: Pier arcade
rationale: The deck, roof, and columns depend on a structural frame to transfer loads safely.
conditions: for load transfer from deck to foundations

subject: Pier arcade
rationale: The arcade serves as a covered pedestrian pathway, supporting movement along the pier.
conditions: as primary circulation route

subject: Pier arcade
rationale: Pier arcades incorporate lighting along the walkway for visibility and ambiance.
applicability: Not all pier arcades contain a lighting fixture; a pier arcade could be a minimal structural element (e.g., a simple covered walkway during daytime use only) with no electrical or lighting installation. The assertion assumes electrical infrastructure is always present.
conditions: for nighttime illumination and safety
exceptions: Small or temporary pier arcades (e.g., seasonal market stalls on a pier) may rely on ambient lighting or portable lighting rather than a dedicated installed Lighting Fixture as a contained component.

subject: Pier arcade
rationale: A drainage system is built into the deck to prevent water accumulation.
applicability: A pier arcade without a deck (e.g., an open-frame structure where rainwater passes through directly) does not require a drainage system for rainwater management on a deck surface. The assertion implicitly assumes a solid deck surface is present.
conditions: for rainwater management on deck surface
exceptions: In arid climates with minimal rainfall or where deck surface is designed with permeable materials (e.g., timber slats with gaps), a dedicated Drainage System may not be required for rainwater management.

subject: Arcade cornice
rationale: An arcade cornice is a horizontal projection at the top of an arcade wall; it depends on the wall for structural support.
conditions: arcade cornice is mounted on top of a supporting wall

subject: Arcade cornice
rationale: Some arcade cornices enclose a concealed gutter to manage roof runoff.
conditions: when designed as a box cornice with integrated gutter

subject: Arcade cornice
rationale: In an arcade, the cornice often rests on or is supported by the columns of the arcade.
conditions: in arcade where cornice spans between columns
exceptions: Arcade cornice depends_on Column is listed with condition 'in arcade where cornice spans between columns', but in typical arcade construction the cornice does not directly 'depend on' columns structurally. Cornices spanning between columns are typically supported by the architrave/frieze beam or the wall/arcade arches above the columns, not directly by the columns themselves. The column supports the entablature, and the cornice is the topmost part of the entablature, so there is an indirect dependency chain (cornice -> entablature/architrave -> column), not a direct depends_on relationship.

subject: Arcade cornice
rationale: Flashing is necessary to seal the joint between the roofing and the cornice to prevent leaks.
conditions: at roof-to-cornice junction
exceptions: Arcade cornice depends_on Flashing at roof-to-cornice junction: In some modern or historic constructions with membrane roofing or where the cornice is fully integrated into the roof assembly, flashing may be part of the roof system rather than a separate component upon which the cornice depends. Also, in some details, counter-flashing is installed after the cornice is in place, meaning the dependency order is reversed.

subject: Arcade soffit lining
rationale: The soffit lining supports the final aesthetic ceiling finish of the arcade.
applicability: The assertion applies only when the soffit lining is part of a structural or semi-structural ceiling system. In many arcade designs, the soffit lining is purely decorative (e.g., open louvres, acoustic baffles) and cannot support any additional ceiling finish above it.
conditions: When acting as the visible ceiling surface
exceptions: An arcade soffit lining may serve as a support for ceiling finishes (e.g., plasterboard, panelling) only if it has adequate structural capacity. Lightweight decorative soffit linings (e.g., timber batten, thin metal panels) may not have sufficient strength or fixing capacity to support a ceiling finish safely.

subject: Stairway
rationale: Handrails are required by building codes for stairway safety and support.
conditions: when stairway has more than 3 risers
for public buildings
exceptions: private residential stairs with fewer than 3 risers

subject: Stairway
rationale: Treads are the horizontal stepping surfaces essential for stairway function.

subject: Stairway
rationale: Risers are the vertical components between treads, though some designs omit them.
exceptions: open riser stairs

subject: Stairway
rationale: Landings provide resting points and direction changes, required by code for tall stairs.
conditions: when stairway height exceeds maximum code limits
when stairway changes direction
exceptions: straight stairs within single floor height

subject: Stairway
rationale: Stringers are the structural side supports that carry treads and risers.
exceptions: Some stair designs (e.g., monolithic concrete stairs, metal pan stairs, or stair systems that use stringer-less construction with central spine beams or cantilevered treads) do not require traditional stringers.

subject: Stairway
rationale: Nosing provides the projecting edge of each tread for foot grip and durability.
exceptions: flush or closed riser stairs without overhang

subject: Stairway
rationale: Stairways typically depend on floor slabs for structural support at top and bottom.
applicability: buildings with concrete or steel structures
exceptions: freestanding or cantilevered stairs

subject: Stairway
rationale: Egress stairs require fire-rated walls and doors to protect escape routes.
conditions: for egress stairways
in buildings with more than 2 stories
exceptions: single-family dwellings
open stairs within a dwelling unit

subject: Stairway
rationale: Stairways are fundamental to vertical movement between building levels.
applicability: The existing exception says 'when elevators or ramps are primary circulation' but this should be a condition rather than an exception - stairs in multi-story buildings still support vertical circulation even when elevators exist, they just may not be the primary means. The assertion as stated suggests stairs don't 'support' vertical circulation in those cases, which is incorrect.
exceptions: when elevators or ramps are primary circulation

subject: Stairway
rationale: Guardrails are required by building codes along open sides to prevent falls.
conditions: on open sides of stairway
where drop exceeds 30 inches

subject: Stairway
rationale: A stairway physically contains treads as its stepping surfaces.

subject: Stairway
rationale: Stairways contain risers as the vertical face between treads.
exceptions: open riser stairs

subject: Stairway
rationale: Stringers are integral structural components of a stairway.
exceptions: Similar to the requirement assertion [0d9862d6], some stair designs (cantilevered stairs, spine beam stairs) may not contain stringers as separate components, even though they are generally required for most stair construction.

subject: Stairway
rationale: Landings are part of the stairway assembly between flights.
conditions: when stairway has multiple flights
exceptions: single-flight straight stairs

subject: Stairway
rationale: Stairway landings typically connect to corridor circulation paths.
applicability: The assertion says 'Stairway connects_to Corridor' at each floor level, but this is not universally true. In many building designs, stairs may connect directly to lobbies, common areas, or exit discharge paths without a corridor intervening. Code often allows stairs to open directly into exit passageways or the exterior.
conditions: at each floor level

subject: Exit Passageway
rationale: Handrails provide stability and support for occupants traversing stairs or ramps within the exit passageway.
applicability: all building types with change in elevation
conditions: required if the exit passageway contains stairs or ramps
exceptions: Exit passageways that are purely horizontal (e.g., a level walkway connecting two buildings or a horizontal exit) may not contain stairs or ramps and thus would not require handrails under this assertion, but the assertion implies handrails are an exit passageway requirement. The condition 'required if the exit passageway contains stairs or ramps' is correct, but the assertion title omits this nuance, potentially misleading.

subject: Exit Passageway
rationale: Fire sprinklers can help control fire and reduce the required fire-resistance rating of the exit enclosure.
applicability: The thresholds for requiring sprinklers in exit passageways vary significantly by jurisdiction (IBC, NFPA 101, local amendments). High-rise threshold for sprinkler requirement may be as low as 3 stories or 75 ft in some codes, while the assertion lists 'exceeding certain thresholds' too vaguely. Also, in some low-hazard, small buildings with exit passageways, sprinklers may not be mandated.
conditions: often required for buildings with exit passageways exceeding certain thresholds

subject: Exit Passageway
rationale: The fire alarm system alerts occupants to evacuate via the exit passageway, making it a critical dependency for proper use.
conditions: must initiate upon smoke or fire detection

subject: Exit Passageway
rationale: Exit passageways often connect to building corridors that form part of the exit access.
conditions: when exit access travels through a corridor to reach the exit passageway

subject: Escalator Well
rationale: An escalator well is the structural space/shaft that contains the escalator machinery and moving stairway.
applicability: The assertion that an 'Escalator Well contains Escalator' is circular and tautological. The escalator well is the structural shaft that houses the escalator truss and components, but the escalator itself is more accurately described as being installed within the well, not 'contained' by it as a part-whole relationship. The well contains the truss, motor, steps, and support structure that collectively form the escalator system, not a discrete 'Escalator' entity separate from the well.
conditions: when escalator is installed within the well

subject: Escalator Well
rationale: Building codes typically require escalator wells to be enclosed with fire-rated construction to prevent vertical fire/smoke spread between floors.
conditions: where building code requires fire separation between floors
exceptions: open-plan buildings with atrium exceptions where sprinkler systems are provided

In many jurisdictions (e.g., IBC 2018, Section 3006), escalator wells in buildings equipped throughout with an automatic sprinkler system may use glass enclosures or other alternatives that are not classified as traditional fire-rated enclosures. The existing exception mentions only 'open-plan buildings with atrium exceptions' but not the more common sprinkler-based exception that directly limits the fire-rated enclosure requirement.

subject: Escalator Well
rationale: Sprinklers or other fire suppression may be required within the escalator well opening.
conditions: when required by local building code

subject: Escalator Well
rationale: Escalator motors and equipment generate heat that may need to be ventilated.
conditions: for enclosed escalator wells to prevent heat buildup
exceptions: open escalator wells in naturally ventilated atria

subject: Escalator Well
rationale: Modern escalator wells integrate with BMS for monitoring and emergency control.
conditions: for monitoring escalator operation, fault detection, and fire alarm integration
exceptions: small standalone installations

subject: Escalator Well
rationale: The escalator well contains the mechanical drive system at the top or bottom of the escalator.

subject: Emergency Egress Stair
rationale: Handrails are required on both sides of egress stairs to support occupants during descent, especially in emergency conditions.
applicability: The 30-inch rise threshold for requiring a handrail on emergency egress stairs may vary by jurisdiction. Many building codes (e.g., IBC) require a handrail on stairs having a total rise of more than 30 inches, but some codes or local amendments may use different thresholds (e.g., 4 risers or approximately 28-32 inches). The assertion does not account for code jurisdiction variability.
conditions: stairs with a rise of more than 30 inches (approx 762 mm)
exceptions: Stairs serving a single dwelling unit (e.g., within a private residence) are often exempt from handrail requirements for stairs with a rise of more than 30 inches, as per many residential code provisions, even though the assertion claims applicability to 'all building types'.

subject: Emergency Egress Stair
rationale: Stair pressurization systems maintain a positive pressure in the stairwell to prevent smoke infiltration, ensuring a tenable egress path.
conditions: high-rise buildings (typically > 75 ft / 23 m in height)
exceptions: buildings with an alternative smoke control strategy

subject: Emergency Egress Stair
rationale: Egress stairs contain intermediate landings or platforms between flights to provide resting points and direction changes.
conditions: stairs with more than one flight between floors

subject: Emergency Egress Stair
rationale: Egress stairs often contain or are adjacent to standpipe risers (Class I or III) that provide fire hose connections for firefighting operations within the stairwell.
conditions: buildings exceeding a certain height (typically > 3 stories or 50 ft)
exceptions: buildings with an alternative fire suppression strategy

subject: Egress Path Marking System
rationale: Egress path markings must be visible in low-light or no-light conditions, relying on emergency lighting to illuminate markings.
applicability: The dependency on Emergency Lighting System is likely a regulatory requirement only in certain jurisdictions (e.g., IBC, NFPA 101) and may not apply universally. Some buildings may use self-illuminating (self-luminous) egress path markings that do not require an external emergency lighting system.
conditions: must remain operational during power failure

subject: Egress Path Marking System
rationale: Egress path markings work in conjunction with exit signs to clearly indicate the path of travel to exits.
conditions: required by code for path direction

subject: Egress Path Marking System
rationale: The fire alarm system triggers evacuation, making the path marking system necessary and operational.
conditions: during fire emergency activation
exceptions: Egress Path Marking Systems (especially photoluminescent types designed for continuous illumination without active power) do not always depend on the Fire Alarm System for activation. Many egress path markings are passive and always visible regardless of fire alarm status. The dependency only holds if the system is an active (LED-based) type that requires a signal from the fire alarm to activate.

subject: Egress Path Marking System
rationale: The path markings lead to and connect visually with exit signs at the termination of the egress path.

subject: Guardrail
rationale: Guardrails are physically connected to the building's structural frame or floor system.
applicability: The assertion assumes mechanical fastening is the only valid connection method. In some building types (e.g., concrete structures with embedded anchors, or post-installed adhesive anchors), the connection may not fit a strict definition of 'mechanically fastened' as typically understood (e.g., threaded fasteners, bolts). Epoxy or adhesive anchors are common in retrofit situations.
conditions: guardrail system is mechanically fastened to structural elements

subject: Guardrail
rationale: Guardrails along stairs connect to stair stringers or stair framing.
conditions: when guardrail is installed alongside stairs
exceptions: On stairs with a wall on one side, the guardrail on the wall side may be attached to the wall structure rather than the stair stringer.

subject: Step Nosing
rationale: Step nosing is typically applied to the front edge of stair treads to provide a finished edge and slip resistance.
conditions: when used on stairs

subject: Step Nosing
rationale: Step nosing is installed along the front edge of stair treads, forming a physical and visual connection.
conditions: at the leading edge

subject: Step Nosing
rationale: In many stair designs, the nosing projects over the riser below, connecting the tread to the riser.
conditions: when nosing overhangs the riser
exceptions: flush nosings

The assertion states that Step Nosing connects_to Stair Riser when nosing overhangs the riser, but the existing exception 'flush nosings' already covers the case where there is no overhang and thus no connection to the riser. The condition 'when nosing overhangs the riser' implicitly excludes flush nosings, making the exception redundant or the condition should be refined to be explicit.

subject: Egress Door
rationale: An egress door requires a frame to be mounted securely and to operate properly.
conditions: For proper installation and operation
exceptions: Pocket doors and sliding egress doors may not use a traditional door frame — they use a pocket framing or track system, yet still function as egress doors.

subject: Egress Door
rationale: Hinges are required for the door to pivot open and closed.
conditions: For swinging doors
exceptions: Sliding or automatic doors

subject: Egress Door
rationale: Fire-rated egress doors must be self-closing and self-latching per code.
applicability: The applicability states 'All building types where fire-rated' but the condition says 'For automatic self-closing requirements (fire-rated doors)'. Not all fire-rated doors require self-closing devices — fire-rated doors in rated corridors may require closers, but fire-rated doors in some enclosure assemblies (e.g., elevator lobby doors) may have different requirements depending on local codes and whether the building has sprinklers.
conditions: For automatic self-closing requirements (fire-rated doors)
exceptions: Non-fire-rated doors may not require closers

subject: Egress Door
rationale: The door leaf is the main movable panel of the egress door assembly.
exceptions: Some egress doors, particularly in specialized applications like revolving doors used as egress, may not contain a traditional door leaf in the same sense. Additionally, sliding egress doors or folding egress doors may use panels rather than a conventional door leaf.

subject: Egress Door
rationale: A threshold is typically part of the door assembly to seal the bottom gap.
conditions: At the bottom of the door opening
exceptions: Egress doors in existing building retrofits or certain accessibility routes may use a transition strip or be flush with the floor (zero-threshold) to comply with ADA requirements, meaning no traditional raised threshold is present.

subject: Install Stair Treads and Risers
rationale: Stair treads and risers are mounted onto stair stringers, which form the structural backbone of the staircase.
conditions: must already be installed and structurally sound
exceptions: The assertion states that installing treads and risers requires stair stringers to already be installed and structurally sound. However, some stair systems (e.g., prefabricated staircases with closed stringers, or stairs built with load-bearing walls and notched stringers) may allow tread/riser installation without the stringer being present in the conventional sense, or the stringer may be part of a prefabricated unit. Additionally, there exist stair designs (e.g., floating stairs with hidden stringers) where the stringer is not a distinct prior installation step.

subject: Install Stair Treads and Risers
rationale: Treads are the horizontal walking surface components being installed.

subject: Install Stair Treads and Risers
rationale: Risers are the vertical face components being installed.

rationale: Nosing provides a finished edge and slip resistance on the tread overhang.

The applicability should be further constrained to jurisdictions enforcing specific code requirements.
conditions: typically installed over the front edge of each tread
exceptions: some treads have integral nosing

rationale: Egress signage must remain visible in emergencies when normal power fails.

conditions: Signage must be illuminated during power failure
Battery backup or generator required
exceptions: In some jurisdictions, wayfinding signage for egress in low-occupancy or small buildings may not require any powered illumination (e.g., reflective signs in day-lit corridors). The blanket applicability to 'all building types with egress requirements' is too broad.

subject: Install Wayfinding and Egress Signage
rationale: In some configurations, egress signage may be integrated with fire alarm for emergency mode operation.
applicability: The asserted connection to fire alarm for strobe activation is typically a requirement for audible/visual notification appliances (fire alarm strobes), not for standard egress signage (exit signs). Standard egress signage is not normally connected to the fire alarm system for strobe activation—separate fire alarm strobes serve that purpose.
conditions: Some jurisdictions require emergency signage to interface with alarm for strobe activation

subject: Linear Path Shape
rationale: Linear paths connect to vertical circulation elements to enable floor-to-floor movement.
applicability: The condition 'at path endpoints or intersections' is ambiguous for stairwell connections — stairwells often have multiple entry points on different floors, and the path may intersect the stairwell at a landing rather than at a true endpoint. The assertion does not clarify whether vertical path segments (via stairs) are considered part of the linear path shape.

conditions: nighttime operation or visibility
exceptions: buildings with no nighttime use

The existing exception only covers 'buildings with no nighttime use,' but there are other valid exceptions: (1) buildings with security lighting that meets public safety requirements without a dedicated 'Lighting System' per se, (2) buildings in areas with ambient street lighting already meeting code requirements, and (3) buildings where light trespass/light pollution regulations restrict additional lighting.

subject: Upper Floor Frontage

In buildings with transfer slabs or podium slabs, the upper floor frontage may depend on a structural slab that is not a typical 'floor slab' but a thicker transfer structure. subject: Upper Floor Frontage

subject: Upper Floor Frontage

high humidity interior conditions

subject: Crowd Flow Rate

applicability: The assertion states that 'Crowd Flow Rate requires Wayfinding Signage' under the condition 'in complex or unfamiliar layouts', but this overlooks the fact that crowd flow rate can be estimated or modeled using other methods such as agent-based simulation, video analytics for density measurement, or manual counting, none of which require wayfinding signage to function. Wayfinding signage influences pedestrian route choice and wayfinding behavior but is not a prerequisite for measuring or calculating crowd flow rate.
conditions: in complex or unfamiliar layouts
exceptions: In open layouts (e.g., large exhibition halls, stadium fields, or outdoor festival grounds) that are not complex or unfamiliar, crowd flow rate can be reliably estimated without any wayfinding signage, as movement is primarily determined by ingress/egress capacity and spatial geometry rather than signage guidance.

subject: Standing Density

Building codes (ASHRAE 62.1, IMC) base ventilation on occupancy category and occupant count, not directly on 'standing density'—a space with high standing density (e.g., a concert hall) does need ventilation, but so does a space with low standing density (e.g., an office). subject: Standing Density

applicability: The condition 'different space usage classifications' is vague. International Building Code (IBC) defines occupancy classifications (A, B, E, etc.) and uses occupant load factors (net vs gross) for egress. 'Standing density' and 'seated density' are not distinct usage classifications in modern building codes. The terms are more relevant in transportation planning or event management, not in building code occupancy classification.
conditions: different space usage classifications

subject: Circulation Density

applicability: The assertion is conditioned on 'life safety compliance' but different jurisdictions use different egress calculation methods (e.g., IBC vs NFPA 101 vs local codes), and the relationship between circulation density and egress capacity varies. subject: Circulation Density

subject: Egress Capacity

exceptions: Exit signs are not required along egress paths in rooms or areas that are not part of the means of egress (e.g., mechanical rooms without public access), or in spaces where the exit is obvious and occupancy is low per code exceptions. rationale: The stair seat riser depends on the stair tread for seating and load transfer; the tread is the horizontal component that the riser connects to.
conditions: Stair Seat Riser is installed as part of a stair system

subject: Stair Seat Riser
