exceptions: There exist panic rooms that are designed purely as hardened physical shelters with no electronic communication, sensors, or integration with a building security system. In such cases the room does not 'support' the security system at all—it is merely a passive space. This is an exception to the assertion.

subject: Secret Passage / Hidden Corridor
rationale: Enclosed hidden corridors lack windows and need mechanical or passive ventilation to prevent stuffiness
applicability: The assertion does not account for secret passages that use mechanical ventilation (e.g., hidden fans, ducted HVAC tie-ins) as an alternative to a dedicated 'Ventilation System' as typically defined in building codes. A hidden corridor may rely on concealed mechanical ventilation that meets code but is not a standard registered ventilation system.
conditions: passage longer than 6 meters
no direct exterior openings
exceptions: short passages or those with open ends

A secret passage or hidden corridor that is shorter than 6 meters but has no direct exterior openings and is completely sealed (e.g., a panic room hidden corridor) would still require ventilation for occupant safety, yet the existing exception for 'short passages' would incorrectly exempt it from the ventilation requirement.

subject: Hidden Door Assembly
rationale: A hidden door assembly requires a door frame for structural support and installation.
applicability: The condition 'Must be concealed within wall or cabinetry' is ambiguous — it could mean the assembly itself is hidden, not that the frame requirement changes. This may lead to misinterpretation of when a frame is truly needed.
conditions: Must be concealed within wall or cabinetry
exceptions: Hidden door assemblies in existing openings or structural frame pockets (e.g., sliding pocket doors) may not require a separate door frame; the pocket frame or rough opening serves the same function.

subject: Disguised Wall Panel
rationale: Disguised wall panels, if structural, require attachment to the building's structural framing.
applicability: The condition 'when used as a load-bearing panel' makes the assertion tautological — any load-bearing panel requires structural framing by definition. The assertion conveys no meaningful information beyond rephrasing the condition.
conditions: when used as a load-bearing panel

subject: Disguised Wall Panel
rationale: The panel supports the concealment of a hidden compartment or safe room behind the wall.
applicability: The assertion omits the requirement for the panel to be operable or removable — a disguised wall panel that is fixed in place (e.g., drywall) cannot reasonably support a usable hidden compartment behind it without an access mechanism.
conditions: when panel is used to conceal storage
exceptions: A Hidden Compartment concealed by a Disguised Wall Panel may violate local building codes, fire regulations, or safety inspection requirements in certain jurisdictions (e.g., fire egress paths, mandatory accessibility inspections). The assertion does not account for legal or regulatory exceptions that would prohibit such a configuration.

subject: Concealed Hinge & Hardware Set
rationale: Concealed hinge & hardware sets are mounted onto doors; a door substrate is required for installation and function.
applicability: The assertion states that a Concealed Hinge & Hardware Set 'requires Door', but concealed hinges can also be used on cabinets, furniture (e.g., kitchen cabinets, wardrobes), and other non-door applications. The assertion may be too narrow or the condition should clarify that 'door' includes cabinet doors, or the scope should be broadened to include other hinged panels.
conditions: Must be a compatible door type designed for concealed hinges

subject: Secret Latch / Magnetic Release
rationale: The magnetic release is typically triggered by an access control reader or keypad.
applicability: The 'Secret Latch / Magnetic Release' phrasing conflates two distinct mechanisms: a secret latch (mechanical, hidden release) and an electromagnetic lock (electric release). Their dependencies differ—a magnetic lock requires an access control system AND fire alarm interface (or power interruption relay), while a secret latch may be purely mechanical and have no dependency on an electronic access control system at all. The assertion treats them as identical when they have fundamentally different control dependencies.
conditions: System must be programmed to trigger release upon authorized credential presentation
exceptions: In fire/life safety scenarios, magnetic locks must release upon fire alarm (fail-safe) regardless of credential presentation, per most building/fire codes (e.g., NFPA 101, IBC). The assertion that release depends on the Access Control System alone, conditioned only on 'authorized credential presentation,' is dangerously incomplete—it omits the mandatory life-safety override that supersedes any access control logic.

subject: One-Way Mirror / Observation Window
rationale: Adjustable lighting is needed to maintain the darkness/lightness ratio required for one-way functionality.
applicability: all building types with observation windows

The assertion does not account for modern smart glass technologies (e.g., switchable glass, electrochromic glass) that can achieve one-way observation effects without requiring a lighting differential at all, making the lighting control system requirement irrelevant in those scenarios.
conditions: to maintain proper lighting differential between observation room and viewed room
exceptions: One-way mirror/observation windows can function without a dedicated lighting control system if natural daylight provides sufficient differential, or if fixed lighting with manual switches provides adequate control. The assertion implies an automated lighting control system is required, but in many observation rooms (e.g., simple interview rooms, police lineups), manual dimmers or toggling lights on/off suffices.

subject: Hidden Surveillance System
rationale: Hidden surveillance may connect to access control systems to correlate video with entry/exit events.
applicability: The assertion states that Hidden Surveillance System connects to Access Control System under 'integrated security ecosystems' applicability. However, hidden surveillance systems (e.g., covert cameras, body-worn or hidden recording devices) are often deliberately isolated from access control systems to prevent detection, maintain operational security, and avoid tampering via the access control interface. In sensitive government or corporate settings, covert surveillance feeds are kept on completely separate networks with no physical or logical connection to access control.
conditions: integrated security ecosystems
exceptions: surveillance-only deployments

subject: Acoustic Isolation Construction
rationale: Acoustic sealant is required to seal air gaps that would otherwise compromise sound isolation.
applicability: In fire-rated acoustic assemblies, the required sealant may be a fire-rated (intumescent) acoustic sealant, not a generic acoustic sealant. The assertion does not distinguish between non-rated acoustic sealant and fire-rated acoustic sealant, which are different products with different certifications.
conditions: for all perimeter joints, gaps, and penetrations
exceptions: Pre-manufactured acoustic isolation assemblies (e.g., clip-and-channel systems with pre-formed gaskets at perimeter tracks) often rely on acoustic gaskets or isolation tapes rather than a wet-applied acoustic sealant. In these systems, sealant is only required at small gaps after installation, not as a primary requirement for all perimeter joints.

subject: Concealed Wiring & Conduit System
rationale: Concealed wiring delivers electricity to lighting throughout the building.
applicability: The assertion implicitly assumes that the concealed conduit or wiring system terminates in a box that is adequately sized and rated for the lighting fixture. In some retrofit or older installations, concealed conduit may terminate in boxes too small for modern LED drivers or dimmer modules, or may lack a means of support for the fixture, making the assertion invalid in those contexts.
conditions: when lighting is powered through concealed circuits
exceptions: The assertion does not hold for lighting fixtures installed in wet or damp locations (e.g., exterior wall-mounted lights) where concealed wiring methods must comply with NEC Article 300.6 (protection against corrosion) and fixture listing requirements — standard concealed conduit may not be sufficient without additional corrosion protection.

subject: Secret Floor Trapdoor
rationale: The trapdoor provides access to and physically covers a hidden space below.
applicability: The assertion assumes a secret floor trapdoor necessarily supports a hidden compartment, but a trapdoor could lead to a crawlspace, utility access, or structural void that is not a usable hidden compartment. The term 'Hidden Compartment' implies an intentional storage or concealment space, which is not guaranteed by the presence of a trapdoor alone.

subject: Hidden Staircase
rationale: Sound travel through hidden stairs can reveal their location.
applicability: The dependency on Acoustic Insulation is stated unconditionally for 'if stealth is desired' and 'if staircase passes through quiet zones', but does not account for scenarios where the hidden staircase is constructed with inherently sound-dampening materials (e.g., solid timber, carpeted treads, or floating construction with decoupled structure) that may achieve sufficient acoustic performance without dedicated acoustic insulation. The condition should be more specific about the type of construction, not just the desire for stealth.
conditions: if stealth is desired
if staircase passes through quiet zones
exceptions: not required if noise is not a concern

The existing exception 'not required if noise is not a concern' is ambiguous and possibly contradictory. If stealth is desired, noise IS a concern by definition, so the exception may never apply under the stated conditions. Conversely, if the staircase passes through a quiet zone, noise is inherently a concern regardless of whether 'stealth is desired' explicitly. The exception as written could swallow the rule in many practical scenarios.

subject: Secret Room Wall Construction
rationale: A secret room requires an hidden access point; a hidden door assembly is the primary entry method.
applicability: The assertion states that Secret Room Wall Construction 'requires' Hidden Door Assembly, but there are alternative concealment methods such as removable wall panels, sliding bookcases without a traditional door assembly, or trapdoor/floor-based entries that do not involve a wall-mounted hidden door assembly.
conditions: must be concealed within adjacent wall or joinery
exceptions: A secret room accessed via a ceiling hatch or floor trapdoor does not involve a 'Hidden Door Assembly' in a wall, yet still constitutes a secret room with walls requiring construction. The assertion falsely implies all secret room walls require a hidden door assembly.

subject: Hidden Door Installation
rationale: Hidden doors are installed within wall openings, requiring structural framing to support the door and wall finish.
conditions: Load-bearing walls require reinforcement around opening
exceptions: Hidden doors installed in non-load-bearing walls (e.g., simple partition walls) do not require reinforcement around the opening, yet the condition states 'Load-bearing walls require reinforcement' which implies the assertion only applies to load-bearing walls. This makes the assertion itself ('requires wall framing') universally stated but then conditionally restricted, producing an internal inconsistency.

subject: Acoustic Seal Installation
rationale: Acoustic sealant is the primary material applied to seal gaps and prevent sound leakage.
applicability: all building types requiring sound isolation

Continuous bead application is appropriate for most sound-isolation joints, but for joints wider than typical sealant gap tolerances (e.g., >1/2 inch) or dynamic joints subject to movement, a backer rod with sealant or a different acoustic detailing approach is necessary rather than a simple continuous bead.
conditions: Continuous bead application
exceptions: Pre-formed acoustic gaskets or compression seals (e.g., acoustic tape, gasket assemblies) can be used in lieu of wet-applied acoustic sealant for perimeter joints, especially in demountable partition systems or retrofit applications where sealant curing is impractical.

subject: Acoustic Seal Installation
rationale: Acoustic seal is applied at the junction between walls and floor slabs to prevent flanking.
conditions: At wall-to-floor perimeter joints
exceptions: Acoustic seals at wall-to-floor perimeters are often applied to the floor slab only in new construction; in retrofit or renovation scenarios where the slab is inaccessible (e.g., over existing finished ceilings), acoustic sealant may instead be applied between the wall track and the subfloor or existing slab via a different connection path, or the seal may be made to a continuous air barrier layer rather than directly to the slab.

subject: Concealed Electrical Rough-In
rationale: Electrical rough-in is performed within the structural frame (studs, joists, rafters) before insulation and drywall.
conditions: rough-in occurs after framing is complete
exceptions: In panelized or modular construction, electrical rough-in may be partially or fully completed in the factory before structural framing is erected on-site, so concealed electrical rough-in does not always depend on structural framing occurring first.

subject: Social Hub / Piazza
rationale: Indoor social hubs depend on HVAC for occupant comfort and ventilation.
conditions: for indoor or enclosed social hubs
for thermal comfort in conditioned spaces

subject: Social Hub / Piazza
rationale: The space depends on the building's structural frame for enclosure and safety.
applicability: all building types with social hubs

Social hubs that are open-air plazas (e.g., ground-level outdoor piazzas without a roof or upper floors above them) do not depend on the structural system for overhead roofing or upper floor support. The condition 'to support overhead roofing or upper floors' does not apply to standalone outdoor plazas with no structure above.
conditions: to support overhead roofing or upper floors

subject: Social Hub / Piazza
rationale: Social hubs typically connect to the main circulation routes.
applicability: all building types with social hubs
conditions: as main circulation node

subject: Social Hub / Piazza
rationale: Often the social hub is adjacent to or part of the main entry sequence.
conditions: when functioning as a lobby or atrium

subject: Atrium / Internal Street
rationale: Atria typically have large volumes and significant stack effect, requiring mechanical HVAC for thermal comfort and air quality
conditions: conditioned air supply
ventilation
exceptions: naturally ventilated atria in temperate climates

subject: Atrium / Internal Street
rationale: Atria act as smoke reservoirs; dedicated smoke exhaust/control is mandated by building codes
conditions: fire safety compliance
exceptions: very small atria exempt by local codes

In IBC-based codes, enclosed atria that do not connect more than two adjacent floors might not require a separate smoke control system because they are treated as shaft enclosures rather than open atrium spaces per IBC Table 404. The assertion implies all atria need smoke control, but the definition of 'atrium' per code specifically excludes floor openings connecting only two stories.

subject: Atrium / Internal Street
rationale: Fire separation between atrium and surrounding floors typically requires fire-rated glass
applicability: Fire-rated glazing is required only where the atrium wall provides a fire separation between the atrium and adjacent spaces per IBC 2021 Section 404.6. When the atrium is open to adjacent floors (e.g., open gallery design) without a separating wall, fire-rated glazing is not applicable. The assertion does not distinguish between enclosed atrium walls versus open balcony configurations.
conditions: where atrium separates adjacent occupied spaces
exceptions: sprinklered buildings with alternative compliance

subject: Atrium / Internal Street
rationale: Early detection is critical in large-volume atria for evacuation and smoke control
conditions: life safety compliance

subject: Atrium / Internal Street
rationale: Code often requires sprinkler protection in and around atria
conditions: fire suppression
exceptions: buildings with alternative fire engineering solutions

Small atria (typically under 20,000 sq ft or 3 stories in height depending on code) may not require a sprinkler system as an absolute dependency. Some building codes exempt certain atria sizes from sprinkler requirements if other fire protection measures (e.g., smoke control, rated construction) are provided. The existing exception for 'alternative fire engineering solutions' partially covers this but does not mention size-based exemptions.

subject: Atrium / Internal Street
rationale: Atria serve as orientation landmarks and visual connections between levels
applicability: Wayfinding systems are primarily needed when the atrium contains multiple vertical circulation elements (elevators, escalators, stairs) serving a large or confusing floor plan. A simple, small-volume atrium with clear sightlines to all destinations may not require or 'depend on' a wayfinding system. The assertion overgeneralizes by applying to all atria in public buildings, shopping centers, and hospitals.
conditions: circulation within large volume

subject: Breakout / Lounge Zone
rationale: Acoustic panels, ceiling baffles, and absorptive materials prevent noise disturbance between lounge zones and neighboring workspaces.
conditions: Open plan settings
noise-sensitive adjacent areas
exceptions: In libraries, breakout/lounge zones often intentionally avoid acoustic treatment to maintain study-quiet atmosphere or use only minimal treatment (e.g., soft seating) rather than full acoustic treatment typically required in open-plan offices. In many library contexts, these zones are designed as 'buffer' transition spaces between silent and collaborative zones and may specifically exclude acoustic absorption.

subject: Breakout / Lounge Zone
rationale: Lounge zones depend on HVAC for thermal comfort due to variable occupancy and heat gain from occupants and equipment.
applicability: The assertion states that Breakout/Lounge Zone depends on HVAC System for occupant comfort, but many modern passive house or low-energy breakout/lounge zones rely on radiant cooling/heating with dedicated outdoor air systems (DOAS) rather than full HVAC systems, making the dependency overly broad as these zones can function with significantly simplified mechanical systems.
conditions: Occupant comfort
exceptions: Naturally ventilated buildings with adequate cross-flow

subject: Breakout / Lounge Zone
rationale: Breakout zones often adjoin or are nearby kitchen/pantry areas to support food and beverage access.
conditions: Shared amenity floor
exceptions: Decentralized breakout zones per floor

In modern office designs, breakout/lounge zones are often intentionally separated from kitchen/pantry areas to prevent food odors in soft-furnished lounge zones, reduce pest attraction in carpeted/soft areas, and avoid conflicts between eating/working zones. This is a deliberate design strategy rather than an oversight.

subject: Community / Common Room
rationale: Occupied spaces require thermal comfort and fresh air supply.
applicability: The existing exception already covers naturally ventilated buildings in mild climates, but there are also mechanically ventilated buildings without full HVAC (e.g., buildings with ventilation-only systems and no mechanical cooling) in temperate climates where a common room may still function adequately. The assertion and its current exception do not cover this scenario.
conditions: heating, ventilation, and air conditioning for thermal comfort
exceptions: naturally ventilated buildings in mild climates

subject: Community / Common Room
rationale: Community rooms need power for AV equipment, lighting, and occupant devices.
conditions: accessible wall outlets for devices, AV equipment, and cleaning

subject: Community / Common Room
rationale: Acoustic comfort is important for speech intelligibility and noise control in group settings.
conditions: when used for meetings, presentations, or performances
exceptions: spaces used only for casual socializing

subject: Community / Common Room
rationale: Safety systems are required by code for occupied assembly spaces.
applicability: The assertion states the community room depends on a fire alarm system integrated with the building fire alarm, but in small buildings or some jurisdictions, a fire alarm system may not be required by code at all (e.g., small single-story buildings with low occupancy). In such cases, there is no building fire alarm to integrate with, yet the room can still be compliantly used as a community room.
conditions: integrated with building fire alarm

subject: Community / Common Room
rationale: Community rooms need to connect to building circulation for access.
conditions: primary access from circulation space

subject: Social Stair / Gathering Stair
rationale: Gathering stairs encourage conversation and activity, which can cause noise disturbance to adjacent spaces.
conditions: In open-plan or library/study zones adjacent to the stair
exceptions: In naturally high-noise environments like lobbies/atriums where noise is expected

subject: Social Stair / Gathering Stair
rationale: Like any stair, a social stair includes risers between treads.
applicability: The assertion 'Social Stair / Gathering Stair contains Riser' is listed with applicability 'All' but this is potentially misleading. Many modern gathering stairs are designed as open-tread or bleacher-style seating where traditional risers (vertical components between treads) are omitted for aesthetic or sightline reasons. Thus, not all gathering stairs contain a riser element.

subject: Reception / Welcome Desk
rationale: Reception often manages entry passes and visitor logging.
applicability: office buildings, government buildings, secure facilities

The dependency of Reception/Welcome Desk on Access Control System is stated for managing visitor entry and issuing badges, but in many building types (e.g., small offices, co-working spaces, retail stores), visitor badges and access control systems are not used — reception staff manage visitors manually or with a simple visitor log. The applicability lists 'office buildings, government buildings, secure facilities' which aligns, but the assertion may be over-generalized if interpreted as a universal dependency.
conditions: for managing visitor entry and issuing badges

subject: Reception / Welcome Desk
rationale: Clear signage helps visitors find the reception area.
applicability: Signage/Wayfinding is stated to depend on Reception/Welcome Desk so visitors can locate the desk upon entry. However, in small buildings (e.g., a single-floor office with a visible reception desk right at the entrance), wayfinding signage to locate the reception desk is unnecessary. The assertion holds for larger/complex buildings but is not universally applicable to 'all building types'.
conditions: so visitors can locate the reception desk upon entry

subject: Reception / Welcome Desk
rationale: Comfortable thermal conditions are needed for both staff and waiting visitors.
applicability: The dependency of Reception/Welcome Desk on HVAC System for maintaining comfortable temperature is listed as applicable to 'all building types'. However, in unconditioned buildings (e.g., open-air reception areas, tropical semi-outdoor lobbies, or unconditioned warehouses with a reception desk), there is no HVAC system, or temperature is not mechanically controlled. The assertion should be scoped to buildings with conditioned spaces.
conditions: for maintaining comfortable temperature in the reception zone

subject: Integrated Bench / Window Seat
rationale: The bench integrates with the window opening, requiring a compatible window frame assembly.
applicability: The assertion that an Integrated Bench/Window Seat requires a Window Frame Assembly only holds for framed window systems. In many modern construction contexts (e.g., curtain wall systems, storefront glazing, or structural glazing), there is no traditional 'Window Frame Assembly' — the bench may bear directly on the subfloor or be cantilevered off the wall structure. The condition about sill height alignment is insufficient to capture this.
conditions: Seat must align with window sill height
exceptions: For sliding glass door assemblies or floor-to-ceiling fixed glazing panels, an integrated bench/window seat typically does not require a separate Window Frame Assembly — the seat is installed independently adjacent to the glazing system. The assertion fails in these common scenarios.

subject: Integrated Bench / Window Seat
rationale: The bench surface typically connects directly to the window sill area.
conditions: Seat top is flush with or slightly below sill

subject: Social Zone Floor Finish
rationale: Underlayment provides a smooth surface, moisture barrier, or acoustic insulation for floor finishes.
conditions: depending on finish material type (e.g., tile, wood, vinyl)
exceptions: some glued-down finishes may not need separate underlayment

subject: Social Zone Floor Finish
rationale: Floor finishes like hardwood or LVP can warp or expand if temperature/humidity are uncontrolled.
applicability: The assertion states that Social Zone Floor Finish 'depends_on' HVAC System, but the dependency direction is ambiguous. HVAC does not determine the floor finish material selection; rather, the floor finish may impose constraints on the HVAC (e.g., thermal mass, radiant compatibility). The dependency arrow appears reversed or overstated.
conditions: in climate-controlled social zones to maintain consistent temperature and humidity

subject: Fitted Auditorium Seating / Tiered Benches
rationale: Fitted auditorium seating and tiered benches need a structural floor slab to bear the weight of the seats and occupants.
applicability: Applicability states 'all auditoriums with tiered seating,' but small-scale tiered seating (e.g., lecture halls with demountable tiered platforms) may use adjustable self-supporting platform systems that rest on an existing flat floor slab without requiring a separate dedicated structural floor slab for the seating.
conditions: for load bearing support
exceptions: Tiered benches installed over existing structural fill or compacted earth (e.g., in outdoor amphitheaters or renovation of existing sloped floors) may not require a structural floor slab — the load is transferred directly to ground via the fill/subgrade, not a slab.

subject: Built-in Display / Pin-up Wall
rationale: Built-in displays can serve as information boards or directories that help occupants navigate.
conditions: When used for signage or directories

subject: Built-in Display / Pin-up Wall
rationale: Fabric-wrapped pin-up boards can also serve as acoustic absorbers; some installations may require acoustic backing.
conditions: When located in noise-sensitive areas (e.g., classrooms, open offices)
exceptions: Not needed if the board is non-acoustic and purely visual

The existing exception states 'Not needed if the board is non-acoustic and purely visual' - this is contradictory. A pin-up wall that is purely visual (i.e., used only for display) still requires acoustic insulation if it is located in a noise-sensitive area because the mounting of the board on the wall can affect sound transmission and reverberation regardless of its visual-only function. The exception as written incorrectly implies that non-acoustic boards do not need acoustic insulation, but in noise-sensitive areas even non-acoustic pin-up boards can negatively impact room acoustics (e.g., by creating hard reflective surfaces that increase reverberation time).

subject: Social Zone Lighting System
rationale: BMS integration allows central scheduling and energy optimization
applicability: The dependency on BMS is stated for 'automated control and scheduling', but a Social Zone Lighting System could be integrated with a standalone time clock or astronomical timer that is not part of a full BMS. The assertion implies BMS is the sole means of automated control, which is not universally true.
conditions: if integrated for automated control and scheduling
exceptions: standalone lighting control panel

subject: Social Zone Lighting System
rationale: Sensors enable automatic on/off/dimming based on presence
conditions: for occupancy-based lighting adjustments
exceptions: fixed schedule without sensors

In hospitality (hotel guest rooms) or educational (lecture halls) settings, occupancy-based lighting adjustments may use keycard systems or room booking schedules rather than traditional occupancy sensors. The assertion does not account for these alternative sensing/scheduling methods.

subject: Social Zone Lighting System
rationale: Social zone lighting circuits may tie into emergency lighting for egress
applicability: The connection between Social Zone Lighting and Emergency Lighting is often indirect. Social Zone Lighting may be on normal power while Emergency Lighting is on a separate emergency branch circuit from the emergency generator or battery. They may share a physical enclosure but not necessarily a direct electrical connection. The assertion oversimplifies the relationship.
conditions: life safety code compliance

subject: Social Zone Lighting System
rationale: The lighting system is powered via the building's electrical distribution
conditions: circuit breaker panel connection

subject: Kitchenette / Tea Point
rationale: Ventilation needed to remove steam, odors, and heat from cooking/heating activities.
conditions: Mechanical or natural
exceptions: Kitchenettes/tea points that are exclusively single-serve beverage stations (e.g., a counter with a hot water dispenser and no sink or food preparation) may not require mechanical or natural ventilation under some building codes (e.g., IBC exceptions for 'kitchenettes' under 50 sq ft with no cooking equipment).

subject: Kitchenette / Tea Point
rationale: Fire safety required due to electrical appliances and potential fire risk.
applicability: The assertion does not distinguish between fire alarm/detection systems and automatic fire suppression (sprinkler) systems. A kettle or microwave might trigger smoke detector requirements but would not require a sprinkler suppression system in most code contexts.
conditions: If appliances like microwave or kettle are used
exceptions: Some building codes (e.g., many residential and small commercial) do not require a fire protection system for kitchenettes with small microwave-only setups, as microwaves are considered ancillary appliances not triggering fire suppression requirements. A condensing, grease-producing cooking appliance would be needed.

subject: Kitchenette / Tea Point
rationale: Kitchenette/tea point often connects spatially to break-out or pantry areas.
conditions: In larger floor plans
exceptions: In office/commercial buildings with open-plan layouts, the kitchenette/tea point often serves as a standalone satellite amenity not connected to a break room or pantry, especially in small offices or co-working spaces where no dedicated break room exists.

subject: Install Glazed Social Screens
rationale: Glass panels need a supporting frame (e.g., aluminum or steel) for structural integrity.
applicability: The assertion is stated as applicable to 'all building types', but glazed social screens used in low-rise residential contexts (e.g., attached to a townhouse facade) may fall under different building code provisions where no dedicated structural framing system is separately installed for the screen alone. Applicability should be scoped to commercial and multi-story residential where structural framing is routinely engineered.
exceptions: Glazed social screens may be installed on existing buildings where no new structural framing system is being constructed — e.g., when retrofitting to an existing concrete or masonry wall. In such cases, the screen can be directly anchored to the existing structure without requiring a new structural framing system.

subject: Install Glazed Social Screens
rationale: The screen typically connects at its base to the finished floor or structural slab.
conditions: screen base anchored to floor
exceptions: If the glazed social screen is mounted on a wall bracket or standoff system rather than anchored to the floor structure at its base (e.g., a cantilevered or wall-mounted screen), the screen may connect to the wall structure and not to the floor structure at all. The condition 'screen base anchored to floor' does not cover this case, indicating the assertion as stated is too narrow.

subject: Install Social Zone Flooring
rationale: Leveling compound ensures a smooth, even surface for flooring installation.
conditions: when subfloor is uneven

subject: Install Social Zone Flooring
rationale: Expansion joints accommodate thermal expansion and contraction of flooring materials.
conditions: for large floor areas or where thermal movement is expected
exceptions: Expansion joints are not universally required for all social zone flooring types. For example, resin or poured seamless flooring systems may use control joints instead of dedicated expansion joints, and some glued-down vinyl flooring may not require expansion joints at all if the area is within manufacturer limits.

subject: Install Social Zone Flooring
rationale: The structural slab provides the load-bearing substrate for the flooring system.
applicability: The assertion does not specify what 'complete and cured' means in measurable terms (e.g., minimum compressive strength, moisture content percentage, or curing time in days). Without this, the condition is ambiguous and may be interpreted differently by different trades.
conditions: must be complete and cured

subject: Install Social Zone Flooring
rationale: Underlayment is part of the flooring assembly installed during this activity.
conditions: when specified for acoustic, thermal, or moisture management

subject: Commission Social Zone Lighting
rationale: Commissioning a social zone lighting system first requires the lighting system itself to be installed and present.
conditions: during commissioning process

subject: Commission Social Zone Lighting
rationale: The physical lighting fixtures (luminaires) must be installed to be commissioned.
conditions: installed in social zone areas

subject: Commission Social Zone Lighting
rationale: Social zones often have occupancy or vacancy sensors that need calibration and testing during commissioning.
conditions: where specified in design
exceptions: An occupancy sensor is required for commissioning 'where specified in design', but many social zone lighting designs use time-clock scheduling, astronomical timers, or manual control only. In those cases, there is no occupancy sensor to commission, yet the lighting system still requires commissioning.

subject: Commission Social Zone Lighting
rationale: Commissioning may require verifying BMS integration and communication with lighting controls.
applicability: The assertion describes a dependency on BMS 'if lighting is integrated with BMS', but this does not account for scenarios where the social zone lighting uses a dedicated lighting controller with BACnet/IP or other open protocols that interface with BMS at a supervisory level only. In such cases, commissioning of the lighting system can proceed independently of full BMS commissioning.
conditions: if lighting is integrated with BMS

subject: Commission Social Zone Lighting
rationale: Commissioning includes functional testing of all lighting components and control sequences.
conditions: as a sub-activity of commissioning

subject: Load-Bearing Frame
rationale: A load-bearing frame transfers its loads to the foundation, which distributes them to the ground.
conditions: building must be supported on stable ground

subject: Load-Bearing Frame
rationale: Columns are the primary vertical load-bearing elements in a frame system.
applicability: all building types with vertical frame
conditions: frame is of post-and-beam type

subject: Load-Bearing Frame
rationale: Beams span between columns to carry floor and roof loads.
applicability: all building types with horizontal spans
conditions: frame is of post-and-beam type

subject: Load-Bearing Frame
rationale: Floor slabs rest on beams and transfer live/dead loads to the frame.
conditions: frame supports floors

subject: Load-Bearing Frame
rationale: Lateral bracing (cross-bracing, shear walls, or moment frames) prevents sway and collapse under horizontal loads.
applicability: buildings in seismic or high-wind zones
conditions: lateral stability is required
exceptions: There are exceptions where a Load-Bearing Frame does not require a separate Bracing System — for example, rigid frame (moment-resisting) systems achieve lateral stability through moment connections in the frame itself without a distinct bracing system.

subject: Load-Bearing Frame
rationale: The load-bearing frame carries roof dead loads and live loads such as snow.

subject: Load-Bearing Frame
rationale: The load-bearing frame connects to the foundation at its base to transfer loads.
exceptions: Load-Bearing Frame does not always connect_to Foundation System — in buildings with a continuous load-bearing wall foundation (e.g., strip footing), the load-bearing frame components (columns, posts) may bear directly onto the foundation wall or footing, not connect to a distinct 'Foundation System' entity as an independent system.

subject: Install Social Stair Structure and Seating
rationale: The stair structure must anchor to floor slabs at each level.
applicability: The assertion states that 'Install Social Stair Structure and Seating' depends on 'Structural Floor Slab' at the top and bottom of the stair run. However, social stairs may also be installed on a structural slab that is not a dedicated 'Structural Floor Slab' (e.g., a transfer slab, ground-bearing slab, or composite deck). The dependency may be overly specific to 'Structural Floor Slab' when a more general structural substrate is sufficient.
conditions: at top and bottom of stair run

subject: Lateral Force Resisting System
rationale: A lateral force resisting system must be integrated into the primary structural frame to transfer lateral loads to the foundation.
applicability: All buildings in seismic or high-wind zones

The assertion lists applicability as 'All buildings in seismic or high-wind zones' but the condition restricts to 'When designing for seismic or wind loads.' This is redundant — if applicability already restricts to seismic/high-wind zones, the condition adds nothing. More importantly, in many jurisdictions, LFRS requirements also apply to other lateral loads (e.g., earth pressure, blast), which are not covered.
conditions: When designing for seismic or wind loads

subject: Lateral Force Resisting System
rationale: Lateral forces must be transferred into the ground through an adequate foundation system.

subject: Lateral Force Resisting System
rationale: Shear walls are vertical elements that resist in-plane lateral forces.
conditions: When shear wall system is chosen as LFRS type

subject: Lateral Force Resisting System
rationale: Concentric or eccentric bracing provides lateral stiffness and strength.
conditions: When braced frame system is chosen as LFRS type

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: A structural wall must be supported by a proper foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: load-bearing wall

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: Concrete is a primary material for structural walls.
applicability: The assertion states 'Structural Wall requires Concrete' for cast-in-place structural walls, but cast-in-place structural walls can also use materials other than conventional concrete, such as cast-in-place reinforced masonry (grout-filled block), cast-in-place adobe, or cast-in-place earth (rammed earth). The material requirement is too narrowly specified as 'Concrete' when the broader category would be 'cementitious material' or 'grout' for some cast-in-place systems.
conditions: cast-in-place structural wall

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: Mortar binds masonry units together.
applicability: The assertion states 'Structural Wall requires Mortar' for masonry structural walls, but mortar is only one possible binding material. Dry-stack masonry systems (e.g., with surface bonding, interlocking blocks, or adhesive) do not use traditional mortar. Additionally, some masonry walls use thin-bed adhesive or epoxy mortar which may not fit the generic 'Mortar' classification.
conditions: masonry structural wall

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: Steel may be used as the core material or reinforcement in structural walls.
applicability: The assertion states 'Structural Wall requires Structural Steel' for steel plate walls or composite walls, but composite walls (e.g., steel-concrete composite walls) do not solely require structural steel — they also require concrete (or grout) as a primary material component. The 'requires Structural Steel' relationship is incomplete for composite walls, which have multiple material requirements.
conditions: steel plate wall or composite wall

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: Load-bearing walls support floor slabs above.
conditions: load-bearing structural wall

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: Load-bearing walls support roof trusses, beams, or slabs.
conditions: load-bearing structural wall

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: Structural walls can support beams that frame into them.
conditions: walls with beam bearing

subject: Structural Wall
rationale: Structural walls connect to foundation walls or footings at their base.
conditions: all structural walls

subject: Structural Connection
rationale: Grout fills voids, ensures uniform bearing, and transfers compression forces in many connections.
conditions: For precast concrete connections or column base plates
exceptions: Dry mechanical connections may not require grout

Besides the already noted dry mechanical connections, there are other exceptions: post-tensioned connections, welded connections, and bolted connections with oversized holes using structural fill (not grout) are situations where grout is not required. Also, some proprietary precast connection systems use dry or welded connections without grout.

subject: Structural Connection
rationale: Connections join beams, columns, and braces to create a continuous load path and overall structural stability.
applicability: The assertion that 'Structural Connection supports Structural Frame' in 'all framed structures' is too broad. In many framed structures, connections are part of the frame (not separate supporting elements), and in moment-resisting frames, the connection is integral to the frame's continuity rather than a distinct supporting component. The relationship is more accurately described as 'is part of' or 'transmits forces within' rather than 'supports'.
conditions: In all framed structures

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Structural steelwork must be supported by a foundation system (concrete footings, piles, etc.) that transfers loads to the ground.
conditions: Always

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Concrete is often used in composite slabs, encased steel columns, and foundations for steel structures.
conditions: Composite steel-concrete construction or foundation embedment
exceptions: Purely steel structures on steel foundations

Even in composite steel-concrete construction, the concrete requirement is for the slab/compression component, but the assertion says Structural Steelwork 'requires Concrete' — Steelwork itself does not require concrete for its structural integrity; it is the composite system that requires concrete. The steel members can be erected and stand independently before concrete is poured.

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Structural steel beams and girders support concrete or composite floor slabs.
conditions: When steel beams/framing support floor decks
exceptions: Flat slab concrete structures without steel framing

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Steel trusses, rafters, and purlins support roof coverings and transfer loads.
conditions: Steel-framed roofs
exceptions: Timber or concrete roof structures

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Steel beams are primary components of structural steelwork.
conditions: Always

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Steel columns are primary vertical load-bearing components of structural steelwork.
conditions: Always

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Steel trusses are common elements within structural steelwork for spanning large distances.
conditions: Long-span roofs, bridges, or where large open spaces are needed
exceptions: Small span buildings using simple beams

The assertion says Structural Steelwork 'contains Steel Trusses' with condition 'Long-span roofs, bridges, or where large open spaces are needed' and applicability 'Large-span structures'. However, even in large-span structures, steel trusses may be absent; they could use steel portal frames with tapered rafters, castellated beams, or space frames instead. The presence of trusses is not mandatory for large spans.

subject: Structural Steelwork
rationale: Bracing (cross-bracing, K-bracing, etc.) provides lateral stability against wind and seismic loads.
conditions: Where lateral stability is required
exceptions: Moment-resisting frames used instead of bracing

subject: Structural Timber
rationale: Structural timber is commonly used as beams, rafters, and trusses to support roof structures.
applicability: Structural timber's ability to support a roof structure depends on spanning capability and load rating, not just being used as load-bearing framing. Timber used as rafters, purlins, or truss chords have different load capacities based on species, grade, and span. The assertion lacks specificity about span limits, load classes, and timber grading requirements that should condition the statement.
conditions: when used as load-bearing framing

subject: Structural Timber
rationale: Structural timber wall framing supports both interior and exterior wall cladding materials.
applicability: The assertion covers 'all building types' but in high-wind or seismic zones, structural timber used for wall cladding support must meet specific bracing, hold-down, and deflection requirements that are not referenced. In some such zones, timber framing alone is insufficient and supplemental steel or engineered solutions are required.
conditions: when used as studs or framing members

subject: Structural Timber
rationale: Direct contact between structural timber and concrete can lead to moisture wicking into the timber, promoting rot and decay.
conditions: when in direct contact without moisture barrier
exceptions: when properly separated by vapor barrier or drainage plane

Even with a vapor barrier, timber in contact with concrete can still suffer from moisture damage in below-grade applications (foundation walls, basement slabs) where hydrostatic pressure or capillary wicking occurs through the concrete, overwhelming typical moisture barriers.

subject: Masonry Structure
rationale: Masonry structures need a solid foundation to transfer loads to the ground.
conditions: Must be properly designed to distribute loads

subject: Masonry Structure
rationale: Mortar binds masonry units together and transfers stresses.
applicability: The condition 'For bonded masonry units' already implies mortar is needed, making the assertion somewhat circular. The assertion would benefit from clarifying that mortar is not always cementitious mortar — lime mortar or mud mortar may suffice depending on region and material type, and the assertion doesn't account for historic or earthen masonry traditions.
conditions: For bonded masonry units
exceptions: Dry-stack masonry systems

subject: Masonry Structure
rationale: Masonry walls support roof loads in load-bearing construction.
conditions: When masonry walls act as load-bearing elements
exceptions: Non-load-bearing infill walls

subject: Masonry Structure
rationale: Masonry walls can carry floor loads in traditional construction.
conditions: When masonry walls are load-bearing
exceptions: Steel or concrete frame buildings with masonry infill

In some masonry buildings with timber floor systems, the floor slab (concrete) may not be present at all — timber joists bear on walls. The assertion assumes a concrete floor slab, but many masonry structures historically have timber floors. The condition should clarify this or add an exception for timber/steel deck floors.

subject: Masonry Structure
rationale: Mortar joints are an integral component of masonry construction.
applicability: The assertion uses 'Mortar Joint' as a contained item, but dry-stack systems are listed as an exception, which contradicts 'most masonry structures' applicability. If dry-stack is excluded, the applicability should be 'bonded masonry structures' rather than 'most masonry structures' to avoid confusion.
conditions: For bonded masonry
exceptions: Dry-stack systems

subject: Masonry Structure
rationale: Tie beams connect masonry walls to improve lateral load behavior.
conditions: At wall intersections and floor levels in seismic regions
exceptions: Non-seismic low-rise buildings

subject: Masonry Structure
rationale: Expansion joints accommodate thermal and moisture movement to prevent cracking.
conditions: In long walls or where thermal movement is expected
exceptions: Small structures

Expansion joints are also required in masonry walls due to moisture expansion (clay bricks) or收缩 shrinkage (concrete blocks), not only thermal movement. The assertion only mentions thermal movement. Additionally, control joints (not expansion joints) are typically used for concrete masonry to accommodate shrinkage. The type of joint depends on the masonry unit material.

subject: Precast Concrete Element
rationale: Precast concrete panels often form part of the building envelope, supporting weather resistance
conditions: when used as cladding or wall panels

subject: Precast Concrete Element
rationale: Precast elements often connect to steel or concrete structural frames via brackets or embedded connections
conditions: when used as infill or cladding
exceptions: when precast IS the structural frame

The existing exception only covers the case where precast IS the structural frame. However, there is another exception: in panelized precast systems, precast elements may connect to each other rather than to a separate 'structural frame' (e.g., load-bearing precast wall panels stacked and connected directly), making the connection to 'Structural Frame' via infill/cladding logic inapplicable.

subject: Precast Concrete Element
rationale: Precast columns and walls require proper connection to foundations via grouted sleeves or base plates
conditions: for columns and loadbearing walls

subject: Formwork and Falsework
rationale: Formwork is the mold into which concrete is poured to achieve desired shapes and structural elements.
conditions: when used for concrete construction

subject: Formwork and Falsework
rationale: Formwork and falsework support wet concrete slabs until they reach sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
conditions: during concrete curing

subject: Formwork and Falsework
rationale: Formwork shapes and falsework supports beams during concrete placement and curing.
conditions: during concrete curing
exceptions: Formwork and falsework also supports prestressed or post-tensioned concrete beams where the formwork supports the beam during stressing, but after stressing the beam may be self-supporting while formwork remains for other purposes. Also, in precast construction, beams are cast in a bed (not traditional formwork).

subject: Formwork and Falsework
rationale: Column formwork contains and shapes concrete columns while falsework provides lateral support.
conditions: during concrete curing

subject: Formwork and Falsework
rationale: Wall formwork panels shape and support freshly placed concrete walls until they cure.
conditions: during concrete placement and curing
exceptions: For concrete walls cast using slipforms or jumpforms, the formwork is self-climbing and does not rely on traditional falsework support during placement and curing. The assertion that 'Formwork and Falsework supports Concrete Wall' is misleading for these construction methods.

subject: Formwork and Falsework
rationale: Formwork defines the shape and provides support for foundation concrete until it sets.
conditions: during concrete placement and curing

subject: Reinforcement Installation
rationale: Reinforcement is typically placed within formwork before concrete pouring.
conditions: Formwork must be in place and aligned before rebar placement
exceptions: In some construction sequences, rebar cages can be pre-assembled on the ground and then lifted into place after formwork is partially or fully complete. However, in precast or tilt-up construction, rebar may be placed first and formwork added later. The assertion that reinforcement installation always depends on formwork being already in place has exceptions.

subject: Concrete Placement and Curing
rationale: Steel reinforcement is placed before concrete and provides tensile strength to the composite material.
conditions: where structural reinforcement is needed
exceptions: unreinforced concrete applications like some pavements or mass concrete

subject: Concrete Placement and Curing
rationale: Proper concrete placement relies on a supply of fresh concrete with the correct mix design.
conditions: for most large-scale projects
exceptions: small jobs where on-site mixing is feasible

subject: Concrete Placement and Curing
rationale: Placed and cured concrete forms the load-bearing slabs of structures.
conditions: after curing and gaining sufficient strength
exceptions: none

subject: Concrete Placement and Curing
rationale: Concrete placement and curing creates vertical structural members.
conditions: after placement and curing
exceptions: precast columns placed separately

subject: Concrete Placement and Curing
rationale: Foundation elements (footings, mats, piles) are created through concrete placement and curing.
applicability: The assertion states Concrete Placement and Curing 'supports' Concrete Foundation with applicability 'all'. However, not all concrete foundation types are placed and cured in the same way. For example, deep foundations like drilled shafts (caissons) or driven piles involve concrete placement methods (tremie, auger-cast) and curing conditions that differ significantly from typical shallow foundation placement. The general statement without distinguishing foundation types may be misleading.
conditions: after placement and curing
exceptions: none

subject: Post-Tensioning (if applicable)
rationale: Post-tensioning is applied to concrete structures. The concrete must be strong enough to withstand the compression forces from tensioning.
conditions: Must have sufficient compressive strength before tensioning
Typically required to reach minimum strength of 70-80% of design strength before stressing
exceptions: There is no explicit exception for unbonded post-tensioning systems. In unbonded PT, the tendon is greased and sheathed, and while it still requires concrete to anchor against, the assertion's conditioning phrasing 'requires Concrete' without distinguishing bonded vs unbonded systems could be misleading. In unbonded systems, the concrete does not bond to the tendon; the requirement is for the concrete to provide anchorage and compressive resistance, not bonding.

subject: Post-Tensioning (if applicable)
rationale: Concrete must be properly cured to develop the required compressive strength before post-tensioning forces can be applied.
conditions: Before tensioning can begin
Concrete must reach specified strength

subject: Structural Connection Installation
rationale: Structural connection installation typically requires steel beams or columns as the primary members being connected.
conditions: When using steel frame construction
exceptions: Structural Connection Installation using bolted or welded connections does not require Structural Steel Beams when using concrete-encased embed plates or cast-in-place anchors directly into concrete columns or walls. The assertion fails for connections like beam-to-concrete wall moment connections where embed plates are used instead of steel beams.

subject: Structural Connection Installation
rationale: A concrete foundation provides the base to which structural connections are anchored.
conditions: For base connections
exceptions: Structural Connection Installation does not require a Concrete Foundation for base connections when using pile caps or deep foundations that transfer loads directly to piles without a traditional concrete foundation slab. Also, connections in steel-framed buildings on steel grillage foundations may not involve a concrete foundation at the connection point.

subject: Sustainable Wood
rationale: Sustainable wood can be used as the primary structural material in buildings
applicability: Sustainable Wood for structural framing requires consideration of fire resistance ratings in multi-story buildings. Many building codes require additional fire protection (e.g., fire-rated gypsum board, sprinklers) for wood-framed structures beyond certain heights or occupancies, which may limit the applicability of this assertion in larger commercial or multi-residential projects.
conditions: Engineered for load-bearing capacity
Species appropriate for structural use
exceptions: Non-structural decorative applications

subject: Sustainable Wood
rationale: Wood has natural insulating properties, though less than dedicated insulation materials
conditions: Used in mass timber assemblies
Proper thickness and density
exceptions: Mass timber panels (CLT, NLT, DLT) with sufficient thickness (e.g., 200mm+ CLT panels) can provide some thermal mass and moderate insulation value (around R-1.25 per inch), but this is still far below code-required insulation levels in most climates, meaning additional insulation must be added. The assertion fails to clarify that wood alone rarely meets thermal insulation requirements without supplementary materials.

subject: Natural Stone
rationale: Natural stone units in masonry construction require mortar to bond them together and distribute loads.
conditions: when used in masonry walls or cladding
exceptions: Natural stone veneer used in thin-set adhered systems (e.g., adhered manufactured stone veneer or thin natural stone veneer) does not require mortar — they use adhesive or mechanical fasteners instead. The assertion only holds for full-bed mortar applications in masonry walls or cladding.

subject: Natural Stone
rationale: Stone walls require a proper foundation to evenly distribute weight and prevent settlement.
conditions: for load-bearing stone walls
exceptions: Freestanding stone walls (e.g., dry-stacked garden walls, short retaining walls) may not require a conventional foundation — they can be placed on compacted gravel base or crushed stone. The assertion holds for load-bearing walls in buildings but not for all load-bearing stone walls.

subject: Natural Stone
rationale: Flashing is required at openings and junctions to direct water away and prevent moisture intrusion.
applicability: The assertion assumes through-wall flashing or weep screed is always required for exterior stone cladding. However, some modern rainscreen or ventilated facade systems for stone cladding manage water differently and may not require traditional flashing at every detail — they rely on drainage cavities and compartmentalization instead.
conditions: when used as exterior cladding

subject: Natural Stone
rationale: Natural stone cladding contributes to the building envelope by providing weather resistance and thermal mass.
conditions: when used as exterior cladding

subject: Natural Stone
rationale: Dense stone materials provide excellent sound attenuation properties.
conditions: when used as floor or wall finish

subject: Recycled Glass
rationale: Recycled glass fiber insulation provides thermal resistance similar to virgin fiberglass insulation.
applicability: The assertion implicitly treats 'recycled glass' as a uniform material, but recycled glass used as aggregate in concrete or as cullet in new glass containers does not provide thermal insulation. Only when processed into fiberglass insulation (as stated in conditions) does this hold. The condition is critical but the assertion title omits this, which could mislead users.
conditions: when processed into fiberglass insulation

subject: Green Concrete Mixes
rationale: Green concrete mixes can be designed to achieve necessary compressive strength for structural framing systems.
applicability: The assertion does not specify minimum compressive strength requirements (e.g., f'c) or exposure class conditions (e.g., freeze-thaw, sulfate exposure) which significantly impact structural performance of green concrete mixes in beams, columns, and slabs.
conditions: When used for structural elements like beams, columns, slabs
exceptions: Not suitable for pre-stressed elements without special mix design

subject: Green Concrete Mixes
rationale: Green concrete is commonly used in foundation work, supporting the building's load transfer to the ground.
applicability: The assertion does not account for aggressive soil conditions (e.g., sulfate-rich soils) where green concrete mixes with high SCM content may have different resistance characteristics compared to conventional concrete, requiring specific mix validation.
conditions: When designed with adequate strength and durability

subject: Green Concrete Mixes
rationale: Green concrete can be used for floor slabs, providing durable horizontal surfaces.
applicability: The assertion does not specify minimum curing duration requirements, which are typically longer for green concrete mixes to achieve adequate strength and durability in floor slab applications, especially under variable temperature conditions.
conditions: When properly cured and reinforced
exceptions: Green concrete mixes with high slag or fly ash content can exhibit increased surface finishing difficulties and delayed trowelability, making them unsuitable for floor slabs requiring tight finish schedules or high flatness tolerances.

subject: Recycled Metal Cladding
rationale: Flashing directs water away at vulnerable points such as windows, doors, and base of wall.
applicability: The assertion states that recycled metal cladding 'requires flashing' at openings, corners, and terminations. This may conflate industry requirements for metal cladding generally (which does require flashing) with a property specific to recycled metal cladding. Flashing requirements are standard for all metal cladding systems, not unique to recycled content. Additionally, the assertion does not specify whether continuous flashing, through-wall flashing, or weep flashing is intended, which are distinct details with different applicability.
conditions: at openings, corners, and terminations

subject: Natural Fiber Carpets
rationale: Natural fiber carpeting can be installed on stairs, connecting floor levels.
conditions: on staircases

subject: Low-Carbon Gypsum Board
rationale: Insulation is often placed within wall cavities behind gypsum board to meet thermal and acoustic requirements.
applicability: The assertion states 'Low-Carbon Gypsum Board requires Insulation' but does not specify which type of insulation (thermal, acoustic, or both). The conditions mention 'for acoustic performance' but the requirement is ambiguous—low-carbon gypsum board itself does not inherently require insulation; rather, the wall assembly may require insulation for thermal or acoustic code compliance. The assertion conflates a board product requirement with an assembly requirement.
conditions: When used in exterior walls or for acoustic performance
exceptions: Interior partition applications may not require insulation

subject: Low-Carbon Gypsum Board
rationale: Gypsum board provides a smooth, paintable surface that serves as the final interior wall finish.
conditions: When used as wall cladding

subject: Low-Carbon Gypsum Board
rationale: Gypsum board is a standard material for finished ceilings in dry construction.
applicability: The assertion states Low-Carbon Gypsum Board supports 'Ceiling Finish' with existing exception 'Suspended ceilings may use different materials', but low-carbon gypsum board may have reduced sag resistance compared to standard gypsum board due to formulation differences. This could make it unsuitable for ceiling applications where sag-resistance is critical, especially on larger spans or in humid conditions, representing an additional limitation not captured by the existing exception.
conditions: When installed on ceilings
exceptions: Suspended ceilings may use different materials

subject: Straw Bale Construction
rationale: Straw bales often require a structural frame (timber or steel) to support roof loads, especially in non-load-bearing infill applications.
applicability: The existing exception states self-supporting straw bale structures may use bales as load-bearing without additional framing, but the assertion title 'Straw Bale Construction requires Structural Framing' directly contradicts this exception. The condition 'for load-bearing walls or post-and-beam support' is ambiguous — it could mean that framing is required for load-bearing walls OR post-and-beam support (i.e., both cases require framing), but the exception correctly notes that load-bearing straw bale walls do not require framing. The assertion as stated (including the condition) implies that load-bearing walls need framing, which is false for true load-bearing straw bale systems.
conditions: for load-bearing walls or post-and-beam support
exceptions: self-supporting straw bale structures may use bales as load-bearing without additional framing

subject: Straw Bale Construction
rationale: A raised foundation (e.g., concrete stem wall, rubble trench) is needed to keep straw bales dry and prevent wicking of ground moisture.
conditions: to elevate bales above ground level
exceptions: Some straw bale construction methods use a floating slab or rubble trench foundation that does not elevate bales above ground level; instead, bales sit directly on the foundation surface with only a capillary break. Additionally, in very arid climates, bales have been placed on compacted earth with a damp-proof course, not elevated above ground.

subject: Rammed Earth
rationale: Rammed earth walls can serve as load-bearing elements supporting roof beams, trusses, or slabs.
applicability: Rammed earth can only support a roof structure if the roof loads do not exceed the compressive capacity of the rammed earth, which varies significantly with soil composition (clay/silt/sand ratio) and stabilization method (cement vs. lime vs. unstabilized).
conditions: When designed as load-bearing walls
exceptions: Non-load-bearing infill walls
Rammed earth walls require adequate curing time and moisture content before supporting roof loads; insufficiently cured walls may fail under roof load before reaching design strength.

subject: Rammed Earth
rationale: Rammed earth walls are typically founded on a reinforced concrete strip or raft foundation to provide a level, stable base above grade.
conditions: At wall base
exceptions: Rubberized or stone foundations in traditional construction

Rammed earth walls require a damp-proof course or moisture barrier at the wall-foundation interface; without it, capillary moisture rise from the concrete foundation can degrade the rammed earth, compromising the connection over time.

The connection requires steel starter bars or dowels (vertical reinforcement) embedded in the foundation and into the rammed earth wall in seismic regions; plain contact alone is insufficient in earthquake-prone areas.

subject: Cob Construction
rationale: Thick cob walls provide good sound insulation.
applicability: The assertion states cob construction improves acoustic insulation, but the comparison baseline is unclear. Cob walls may improve insulation compared to lightweight timber frame walls, but they typically provide worse acoustic insulation than modern insulated cavity walls or concrete masonry. The acoustic performance also heavily depends on wall thickness, surface treatment (plaster vs. bare earth), and moisture content. Additionally, cob's acoustic insulation at low frequencies differs significantly from high frequencies, which the blanket claim does not address.
conditions: Due to dense earthen wall construction
exceptions: Cob construction may provide poor acoustic insulation when walls are thin (e.g., less than 300mm), when walls have cracks or gaps from drying shrinkage, or when the wall has not been properly sealed/plastered, as sound can pass through air gaps more readily than through the earthen matrix itself.

subject: Recycled Content Ceiling Tiles
rationale: Ceiling tiles often work in conjunction with acoustic insulation above the ceiling plane to improve sound attenuation.
applicability: In schools, classrooms may require impact-resistant or abuse-resistant ceiling tiles (e.g., in gymnasiums or active learning spaces), and recycled content ceiling tiles may not satisfy these durability requirements even when acoustic performance is specified.
conditions: When acoustic performance is specified
exceptions: Non-acoustic applications

subject: Recycled Content Ceiling Tiles
rationale: Ceiling tiles interface with grid-integrated lighting fixtures in a suspended ceiling system.
conditions: When lights are integrated into ceiling grid
exceptions: Surface-mounted or pendant lighting

When lighting fixtures are heavier than standard (e.g., emergency battery packs, decorative chandeliers, or large LED panels), recycled content ceiling tiles may not have sufficient structural strength to support the additional weight, even if lights are integrated into the ceiling grid.

subject: Bamboo Structural Products
rationale: Bamboo structural products must be integrated with a building's structural framing system to transfer loads effectively.
applicability: The 'depends_on' assertion states bamboo structural products depend on a structural framing system for load-bearing applications, but bamboo structural products (e.g., bamboo beams, columns, trusses) themselves function as part of the structural framing system, not as separate dependent products. This relationship may be better modeled as a composition or subclass relationship rather than a dependency, as bamboo products are themselves structural framing elements rather than something that depends on a separate framing system.
conditions: for load-bearing applications

subject: Bamboo Structural Products
rationale: Bamboo structural products can serve as roof framing members, supporting roof cladding and transferring loads to walls or columns.
conditions: when used as beams, trusses, or purlins
exceptions: Bamboo structural products used as beams, trusses, or purlins do not universally 'support' all roof structures. They are specifically suitable for lightweight roof structures (e.g., thatch, corrugated metal, light tiles) but would be unsuitable for supporting heavy concrete/masonry roof decks or roofs with heavy live loads (e.g., snow loads in cold climates, green roofs) without extensive engineering verification.

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium
rationale: Green roof growing medium requires a drainage layer beneath it to allow excess water to escape and prevent root rot.
conditions: to prevent waterlogging

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium
rationale: The growing medium sits above a waterproofing membrane that protects the roof structure from moisture.
conditions: to protect building structure below

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium
rationale: A root barrier prevents plant roots from penetrating and damaging the waterproofing membrane.
conditions: when woody plants or aggressive root systems are used
exceptions: may not be needed for sedum-only extensive roofs

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium
rationale: The growing medium adds significant dead load (saturated weight) that the roof structure must be designed to support.
conditions: must have adequate load-bearing capacity

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium
rationale: The growing medium needs sufficient moisture to support plant life; supplemental irrigation may be required in certain conditions.
conditions: in dry climates
during drought periods
for intensive green roofs with high water demand plants
exceptions: extensive green roofs with drought-tolerant sedums may not require irrigation after establishment

subject: Hempcrete
rationale: Hempcrete has limited compressive strength and typically requires a timber or steel structural frame to bear loads.
conditions: For load-bearing applications
exceptions: Cast-in-place hempcrete can be load-bearing in low-rise structures

Cast-in-place hempcrete can serve as a load-bearing material in low-rise structures, so the assertion 'requires Structural Frame' does not hold for low-rise cast-in-place applications. The existing exception already acknowledges this but the core assertion remains overly broad.

subject: Hempcrete
rationale: Hempcrete provides excellent thermal insulation with a typical U-value suitable for passive house standards.
conditions: When used at sufficient thickness (typically 250-300mm)

subject: Recycled Bricks
rationale: Recycled bricks, like most bricks, require mortar to be bonded into a stable wall assembly.
applicability: The assertion 'Recycled Bricks requires Mortar' with applicability 'load-bearing walls; facing walls' does not account for mortarless interlocking brick systems (e.g., Megablock, Hydraform) which are specifically designed for load-bearing walls without mortar. The existing dry-stack exception is too narrow—dry-stack is a construction method, while interlocking systems are a product category that inherently eliminates mortar use.
conditions: for bonding bricks together
exceptions: dry-stack brick systems

Recycled bricks used in non-structural decorative applications (e.g., garden edging, interior accent walls, veneers) may not require mortar if other fixing methods (adhesives, mechanical fixings, dry stacking) are employed. The current exception only covers dry-stack brick systems broadly, but a specific exception for non-load-bearing veneer applications where mortar is optional would be appropriate.

subject: Recycled Bricks
rationale: All brick masonry requires a proper foundation to distribute loads.
conditions: for structural support
exceptions: Recycled bricks used in non-structural landscaping applications (e.g., garden paths, raised planter beds, edging) or temporary structures do not necessarily require a poured concrete or engineered foundation; a compacted gravel base or sand bed may suffice. The assertion applies to 'all building types' but should exclude landscape/non-building applications.

subject: Low-Impact Material Installation
rationale: Low-impact material installation is often performed on building envelope components like cladding and insulation.
applicability: The assertion states 'Low-Impact Material Installation connects_to Building Envelope' but the existing exception already acknowledges that interior finish installation does not connect to the building envelope. This suggests the scope is too broad — low-impact materials installed on interior surfaces (e.g., interior gypsum board, acoustic panels) are not envelope-connected even when they are 'low-impact cladding, insulation, or sheathing' by type. The condition should be narrowed to exterior-facing applications only, or the exception should be generalized.
conditions: when installing low-impact cladding, insulation, or sheathing materials
exceptions: interior finish installation does not connect to building envelope

Low-impact materials installed as part of a rainscreen or ventilated facade system may not directly 'connect to' the continuous building envelope (e.g., they are mechanically fastened to a subframe with an air gap). In such cases the material itself does not form part of the air/water/thermal barrier layer and thus may not qualify as connecting to the building envelope in the strict sense.

subject: Material Conditioning & Curing
rationale: Curing compounds are applied to retain moisture in concrete during the curing process.
conditions: for concrete curing when wet curing is impractical

subject: Material Conditioning & Curing
rationale: Insulating blankets help maintain proper temperature during cold-weather curing.
conditions: for thermal curing in cold weather

subject: Material Conditioning & Curing
rationale: Vapor barriers help retain moisture in freshly placed materials during curing.
conditions: for preventing moisture loss during curing
exceptions: Vapor barriers are used to prevent moisture loss from the subgrade or ground, not typically to prevent moisture loss from the curing concrete itself. For preventing moisture loss during concrete curing, curing compounds, wet burlap, or plastic sheeting directly over the concrete are used. A vapor barrier is placed beneath the slab and serves a different purpose (blocking ground moisture vapor from rising into the slab).

subject: Material Conditioning & Curing
rationale: Mortar requires conditioning and curing after application.
conditions: for masonry material conditioning

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium Placement
rationale: Green Roof Growing Medium Placement is an activity that is part of installing a green roof system; it requires the overall green roof system to be designed and ready.
applicability: The assertion states 'Green Roof Growing Medium Placement requires Green Roof System' but a 'Green Roof System' is not a standard discrete layer like root barrier or waterproofing. In some specifications, the growing medium is part of what defines a green roof system, making this a circular dependency. This requirement is ambiguous and could cause confusion about what constitutes the 'Green Roof System' itself.
conditions: prior installation complete

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium Placement
rationale: A root barrier is typically laid down prior to medium to protect the roof membrane from root penetration.
conditions: must be installed before medium placement
exceptions: The assertion claims all green roofs require a root barrier before medium placement, but on intensive green roofs with deep soil (e.g., >12 inches) used for trees or large shrubs, root barriers are sometimes selectively omitted in non-root-zone areas, or are integrated into other layers. Some green roof systems for sedum or moss mats on extensive roofs also use a combined drainage/root barrier mat and do not have a separate root barrier layer installed before medium.

subject: Green Roof Growing Medium Placement
